items.title: [RFC][MP] Multi-replica high availability for the MP coordinator
items.author: pandacooming
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary Run the MP coordinator as **active-standby replicas**. A Kubernetes Lease elects one leader. Only the leader receives traffic (the Service selects a pod label the leader sets on itself) and only the leader runs work with side effects. When the leader fails, a standby takes over by loading state from an object store (cold standby). Split-brain protection has two layers: 1. A leader that cannot renew its lease exits the process. 2. Shared state lives behind a small manifest that every new leader stamps with its epoch, and every write to it is conditional, so a stale leader cannot overwrite state. With HA off, the coordinator behaves exactly as today. Event loss on the HTTP transport during a failover is out of scope; deployments that need complete events should use Kafka. Related: #4025 (Q3 roadmap, Production Deployment), #4226 (coordinator as control plane), #5354 (checkpoint as the Kafka cursor), #5714 (background loop liveness), #5811 (re-register right after a heartbeat 404). ## Motivation The coordinator is the fleet's only control-plane process, and every layer of it assumes there is exactly one. When it crashes or hangs, the data plane keeps working (STORE latency stayed at 5–12 ms in every experiment), but the control plane's view and decisions go wrong, and some of the damage does not heal. ### What happens today I ran failure experiments against real CPU-only MP servers and a coordinator that was killed, stopped, or hung. Results were re-verified on `1ed386c`. The full report is attached below. [Coordinator-Failure-Experiments.pdf](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33697272/Coordinator-Failure-Experiments.pdf) | Scenario | Result | | --- | --- | | kill -9 and restart, HTTP event transport | Events emitted during the outage are lost and never repaired: the directory tracked 2 of 10 L2 objects, unchanged 120 s later | | Same, persistence on | A tenant reached 3.4× its quota with no eviction | | Restart on a node without the old files | Pins and quotas are gone | | SIGSTOP for 40 s, then resume | Every live instance is evicted for missed heartbeats; L1 placements go from 4/4 to 0/4 and never come back | | MP servers re-registering after a restart | One extra heartbeat interval (5 s) of waiting, fixed by #5811 | ### Why more replicas do not work today - **No leader, lease, epoch, or fencing concept** exists anywhere in `lmcache/`. The operator says as much: replicas > 1 "only makes sense behind a shared durable backend" (`operator/api/v1alpha1/lmcachecoordinator_types.go:38-44`), and no such backend exists. - **Persistence is a local file with no concurrency control.** `LocalArtifactStore` is last-writer-wins, uses a fixed `.tmp` name, and has no version or conditional write (`persistence/store.py:90-104`). - **Eviction deletes from shared L2.** The eviction loop sends `DELETE /cache/objects` to a random MP server every 5 s (`controllers/eviction_controller.py:428`). The MP server does not know who is calling. Two coordinators would each evict according to their own view. - **Ingest assumes one consumer per stream.** "A coordinator runs exactly one event source"; with Kafka, two replicas in one consumer group split the partitions between them (`ingest/kafka_event_source.py:66-69`). - **`/healthz` always returns healthy** (`http_apis/health_api.py:14-20`), and the operator uses it for all three probes. ### Why the data plane cares - **P2P peers are torn down after 15–20 s.** The P2P controller polls `GET /instances` every heartbeat interval (5 s). A failed poll counts as a miss for every peer, and a peer is dropped after more than 3 consecutive misses (`multiprocess/modules/p2p_controller.py:53, 499, 621`). A coordinator outage of 15–20 s removes every P2P peer adapter, even though the peers are fine. - **Chunk-size negotiation calls the coordinator synchronously.** With a coordinator URL configured, vLLM–MP chunk-size negotiation does a blocking `PUT /config/chunk-size`; if it fails, negotiation is retried (`multiprocess/server.py:359-364`). - **CacheBlend lookups degrade.** With a coordinator configured, blend lookup asks the coordinator instead of matching locally. A hung coordinator adds up to `blend_timeout` (1 s by default) per lookup before falling back to prefix-only (`multiprocess/modules/blend/lookup.py`). ## Goals 1. **Automatic recovery** from a leader process crash, node loss, or hang, with no human action. 2. **Fast recovery.** After a crash, a new leader serves within about 11 s plus state-load time, and MP servers are re-registered within 5 s after that. A graceful handover (rollout, drain) takes about 3 s plus load time. Both numbers are to be confirmed by measurement. 3. **Durable state survives node loss.** Pins, quotas, the chunk-size binding, and the checkpoint live in shared storage that any replica can read. 4. **At most one leader produces side effects.** The remaining window is stated explicitly below. 5. **No change when HA is off**: same code paths, flags, and dependencies. ## Non-goals - **Active-active.** Exactly one replica works at a time. - **Event loss on the HTTP transport.** Events posted during a failover are lost, as they are on a restart today. Deployments that need complete events use Kafka. Event reliability (resend, rescan) belongs in a separate RFC. - **Hot standby.** Standbys do not consume events; a new leader restores from the checkpoint. Hot standby on Kafka is a follow-up. - **MP-server-side epoch checks.** In the first phase MP servers do not verify which leader a request came from. - **Non-Kubernetes election.** Only a Lease implementation is provided; the interface leaves room for etcd or Redis. - Cross-region deployment, and the C++/Rust coordinator. ## Proposal ### Overview ```mermaid flowchart LR MP["MP servers"] -->|register, heartbeat, events| SVC["Service
selects role=leader"] SVC --> L["coordinator-0
leader"] S["coordinator-1
standby"] L -->|renew| LEASE[("K8s Lease")

items.title: Feature Request: Implement missing ops from backends
items.author: am17an
items.body_excerpt:
### Prerequisites

- [x] I am running the latest code. Mention the version if possible as well.
- [x] I carefully followed the [README.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/README.md).
- [x] I searched using keywords relevant to my issue to make sure that I am creating a new issue that is not already open (or closed).
- [x] I reviewed the [Discussions](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions), and have a new and useful enhancement to share.

### Feature Description

The list of supported operation in ggml per backend is maintained at https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/docs/ops.md

How to contribute to make the list more complete:

1. Pick an operation which is not implemented in a backend (pick ones marked with ❌), pick only one per PR
2. Implement the operation
3. Test your implementation with `test-backend-ops -o <op>`
4. If it passes test for the op, create a PR.
5. Mention performance tests in the PR if they exist (via `test-backend-ops perf -o <op>`)

Notes:
1. The ops suffixed with _BACK are related to training which is WIP and does not require immediate attention
2. Do not link this issue in your PR, which will lead to closing this issue when your PR is merged. Instead, just mention it. Example PRs will be linked below
3. This list can be temporarily out of sync, you can check support by first running `test-backend-ops -o <op>` on master to confirm 
4. Please do not ask to be assigned a particular task, make the PR first if you think it will be useful


### Motivation

items.title: [RFC]: Parallelize long-running Mooncake Store unit tests
items.author: Aionw
items.body_excerpt:
## Status

Draft / implementation in review.

This RFC replaces the oversized prototype PR #2896 with six smaller draft PRs that have an explicit review and merge topology.

## Motivation

Several Mooncake Store unit-test executables contain many semantically unrelated cases and run for a long time as one scheduling unit. Splitting those cases by behavior gives CTest more useful parallel work and makes failures easier to locate, but creating one executable per source file increases compile/link overhead.

The proposal therefore separates two concerns:

1. Keep source files organized by semantic behavior.
2. Use a small CMake helper to combine compatible files into a bounded number of Unity-built test targets.

No hard-coded shard index or test-name routing table is introduced.

## Invariants

- Preserve all 296 source-defined GTest cases.
- Changes to test-only fixture behavior are acceptable when needed for isolation.
- Production behavior must not change.
- Each domain split must remain independently reviewable.
- The final target-balancing change must be isolated in its own commit/PR layer.

## PR topology

```text
                         +--> #2900 DummyClient + offload --------+
                         +--> #2901 SSD + snapshot SSD -----------+
RFC #2898 / main --------+--> #2902 promotion --------------------+--> #2905 Unity/target balance
                         +--> #2903 MasterService core -----------+
                         +--> #2904 snapshot MasterService -------+
```

The five domain PRs are all based directly on the same `main` commit and can be reviewed in parallel. #2905 contains those five commits plus one final CMake-only commit; review that final commit after the domain PRs, then let its diff shrink as #2900–#2904 merge.

## Tracking

| Order | PR | Scope | Source tests | Review dependency |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: | --- |
| 1 | #2900 | DummyClient + offload | 17 | RFC only |
| 2 | #2901 | SSD + snapshot SSD | 26 | RFC only |
| 3 | #2902 | Promotion | 40 | RFC only |
| 4 | #2903 | MasterService core | 144 | RFC only |
| 5 | #2904 | Snapshot MasterService | 69 | RFC only |
| 6 | #2905 | Unity build and target balancing | 296 total | #2900–#2904 |

## CMake design

`add_store_test()` remains the single registration primitive. The final PR adds `add_store_unity_test()`, which delegates to it and enables CMake `UNITY_BUILD` for compatible semantic source groups.

The result is:

- 30 independently registered targets in the five domain PRs, useful for isolated review and validation.
- 21 balanced targets in the final integrated layout.
- Semantic directories and filenames remain intact.
- No numeric shard constants or hard-coded test-case mapping in CMake.

## Validation

Five independent branches:

- All targeted builds passed.
- 30/30 CTest targets passed.
- Source-defined test count: 17 + 26 + 40 + 144 + 69 = 296.
- Four-way group wall times: 32.69s, 43.32s, 36.63s, 85.97s, and 89.85s.

Final integration branch:

- 21/21 targets built on current `main`.
- 21/21 CTest targets passed with `ctest -j4` in 204.53s.
- Isolated prototype measurement: 148.05s target build and 203.81s test time.
- A contended cold build measured 490.52s after four concurrent worktree builds; it is retained as a host-load datapoint and is not used as a regression comparison.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] 296 source-defined tests preserved.
- [x] Semantic source layout replaces the long monoliths.
- [x] Final test wall time is at most 210s at four-way concurrency.
- [x] Isolated changed-target build is at most 160s.
- [x] Combined isolated build + test time is at most 360s.
- [x] Domain PRs can be reviewed in parallel.
- [x] Target balancing is isolated for focused review.

## Rollout

1. Review #2900–#2904 in parallel.
2. Merge accepted domain PRs in any order, resolving only localized CMake registration overlap if needed.
3. Rebase #2905 as those PRs land.
4. Review the final CMake-only target-balancing commit.
5. Mark the drafts ready only after human review of every changed line and successful CI.

## Superseded prototype

#2896 demonstrated the full approach but is too large to review effectively. It is superseded by this RFC and #2900–#2905.

items.title: [RFC]: [Store] Recoverable client liveness states and asynchronous offboarding
items.author: Doube-Suzerain
items.body_excerpt:
### Changes proposed

## Motivation

Mooncake Store currently treats one client heartbeat timeout as a permanent failure. Temporary network jitter, a client pause, or a delayed Master monitor loop can therefore irreversibly unmount recoverable resources and delete their metadata.

We propose adding a recovery window: after the first TTL expires, the Master retains the client's resources but stops routing new requests and work to them; a valid liveness signal makes them serving again. Terminal cleanup starts only if the client remains unavailable for a second TTL.

Resource availability checks are currently distributed across allocation, replica lookup, Copy/Move, task dispatch, drain, offload, and promotion. This proposal also centralizes that decision so the new liveness semantics are applied consistently.

## Changes proposed

- Introduce an **Active → Suspected → Offline** state machine for each client incarnation, with separate active and suspicion TTLs.
- Add a typed `ServingEligibility` seam for all client-owned resource routing, while retaining Suspected resources for possible recovery.
- Separate client liveness from remount readiness and segment lifecycle.
- Express terminal cleanup as a retryable `ClientOffboardingJob`; complete it synchronously first, then move the same job to an asynchronous executor.
- Preserve the existing Ping RPC schema and legacy TTL configuration.
- Rebuild process-local liveness records when restoring Master snapshots; keep NoF on its independent health model.

## Proposed design

### Client liveness

Each client incarnation has a `ClientLivenessRecord`:

```text
Active --active TTL--> Suspected --suspicion TTL--> Offline
   ^                       |
   +---- liveness signal --+
```

- **Active** resources may serve new requests.
- **Suspected** resources are retained but cannot receive new allocations, descriptors, or work. A valid liveness signal recovers the same incarnation.
- **Offline** is terminal for that incarnation and starts offboarding.

The suspicion TTL starts when the Master actually commits `Active -> Suspected`, so a delayed monitor does not shorten the recovery window. Ping and successful segment mounts are liveness signals; ordinary Put/Get traffic and task/offload/promotion heartbeats are not.

Ping remains wire-compatible: a ready Active client receives `OK`; an unknown or Offline client receives `NEED_REMOUNT`; Ping may recover a Suspected client before applying the existing remount-readiness check.

Client liveness, remount readiness (`ok_client_`), and segment lifecycle remain independent. In particular, `ok_client_` will no longer determine whether resources may serve or must be retained.

### `ServingEligibility`

Allocation, metadata reads, task routing, offload, promotion, and drain will use a small typed interface with the following common semantics:

```text
resource can serve
  = resource is intrinsically valid
  && segment lifecycle permits serving
  && owning ClientLivenessRecord is Active

ShouldRetainResources
  = ClientLivenessRecord is Active or Suspected
```

This supplements existing segment checks rather than replacing them. NoF resources continue to use their own probe and lifecycle rules.

While Suspected, the Master blocks new dependencies on the client, including allocations, descriptors, Copy/Move routing, task delivery, offload/promotion work, and drain selection. End, Revoke, failure, and completion callbacks for already-started work remain accepted so refcounts, quota, and task state can converge.

Memory allocator registrations and buffers retain the specific `ClientLivenessRecord` that created them, preventing a later incarnation from reactivating old memory resources.

### Offboarding

Terminal retirement uses one job interface:

```text
PrepareClientOffboarding(record) -> ClientOffboardingJob
CompleteClientOffboarding(job)
```

Prepare commits Offline and immediately isolates the incarnation. Complete performs the expensive work: metadata cleanup, memory segment unmount, LocalDisk/offload/promotion cleanup, quota convergence, and external metadata cleanup. The old record is removed only after all steps succeed; until then it acts as a Mount/ReMount barrier.

The first implementation calls Complete synchronously from the client monitor. A follow-up submits the same job to an asynchronous executor with batching, retry, shutdown draining, and queue observability. This keeps state and cleanup semantics unchanged when execution becomes asynchronous.

### HA restore and compatibility

After snapshot restore, each restored client starts as Active with a fresh active TTL, preserving the current recovery semantics. The Master rebuilds the liveness associations needed by restored resources, while readiness still follows the existing ReMount protocol.

Snapshot creation must not capture partially completed offboarding. The synchronous phase preserves the current exclusion behavior; asynchronous offboarding will add explicit snapshot/offboarding coordination.

New configuration:

```yaml
client_active_ttl_sec: 10
client_suspicion_ttl_sec: 20
```

`client_live_ttl_sec` and `--client_ttl` remain deprecated aliases for the active TTL. If an active/legacy TTL is explicitly configured but suspicion TTL is omitted, suspicion inherits the resolved active TTL. No RPC schema change is required.

LocalDisk and task metadata currently identify ownership by client ID. Initially, complete cleanup plus the Offline remount barrier prevents old resources from overlapping a new incarnation. An explicit incarnation token would provide stricter isolation for artificially reused client IDs, but requires a wire/schema change and is outside the initial scope.

## Development plan

1. Add `ClientLivenessRecord`, dual-TTL configuration, Ping/Mount integration, and the three-state monitor.
2. Introduce `ServingEligibility` across allocation, descriptors, Copy/Move, task/drain, LocalDisk/offload, and promotion.
3. Add synchronous `ClientO

items.title: [RFC]: Add GDS offload for mooncake-store based on existing TENT gds transport
items.author: tong1heng
items.body_excerpt:
### Changes proposed

## Summary

Add opt-in GDS SSD offloading to mooncake store by reusing the existing TENT GDS transport.

The implementation adds:

1. A client-local, fixed-size GDS backing file exposed as a TENT `file://` segment and managed by an aligned extent allocator.
2. A first-class `ReplicaType::GDS` with storage identity, generation, offset, value size, and allocation size in store metadata and wire serialization.
3. Required dual-write behavior for enabled `BatchPut`: memory/NoF writes and GDS writes are submitted in parallel and waited on before finalization.
4. A GDS-only creation fallback when memory replica allocation fails because of capacity or tenant quota.
5. Memory-first `BatchGet` selection, followed by a local matching GDS replica, while retaining existing NoF, local-disk, and disk fallbacks.
6. TENT/Transfer Engine capability checks and GDS buffer-registration tracking needed for sub-slice cuFile requests.

The feature is enabled through environment variables and requires no changes to upstream vLLM, so existing deployments remain unchanged when it is disabled.

## Motivation

Mooncake store currently supports POSIX and `io_uring` file offloading. Its existing data path is as follows:

1. **Write path:** when memory usage in a global segment (CPU memory) reaches the configured eviction watermark, mooncake master selects objects for offloading and places them in the background offload queue. The client then reads the objects from the global segment and writes them to the configured file backend through POSIX or `io_uring`. After the file write completes, the master records the file-backed replica and may release the corresponding memory replica.
2. **Read path:** the client first queries the master for the object's replica metadata and prefers an available memory replica. If the object is no longer present in memory, the client loads it from the file backend through POSIX or `io_uring` and returns the data to the caller.

This data path becomes a bottleneck when host memory is constrained. GPU-to-CPU and CPU-to-SSD bandwidths are not matched: GPU data must first be copied into CPU memory and then written to SSD. **When GPU production outpaces this two-step pipeline, CPU memory and CPU-side file I/O cannot drain the global segment fast enough. Some KV cache is consequently discarded before it can be completely offloaded, preventing more valid KV cache from being offloaded to the SSD even when sufficient SSD capacity remains.**

GPUDirect Storage (GDS) addresses this mismatch by supporting GPU-to-SSD DMA, so the data can bypass the CPU staging path. The GDS transport has already been integrated into TENT, **but the data path between TENT and mooncake store has not yet been connected.** An earlier draft PR (#2731) attempted to add GDS offload at the mooncake store layer by introducing a separate GDS context. This approach would duplicate cuFile resource management and make mooncake store responsible for transport-specific details that already belong to TENT.

Therefore, the central design goal of this change is to preserve the existing separation of mooncake store and TENT while connecting the two components: TENT owns all GDS cuFile operations, transport selection, and buffer registration, while mooncake store owns only object and replica metadata, allocation/lifecycle decisions, and transfer-request submission. Mooncake store should reuse the existing Transfer Engine and TENT GDS transport instead of introducing another GDS/cuFile implementation. This keeps the GDS data path composable with store's replica semantics and avoids a second, divergent GDS context in mooncake store.

## Non-goals

- Replacing the existing `enable_ssd_offload`/`LOCAL_DISK` POSIX or `io_uring` path.
- Providing remote reads from another client's local GDS file. A remote GDS descriptor falls back to the existing memory, NoF, local-disk, or disk paths.
- Recovering a client's GDS index after restart or promising crash/durability semantics for the local file.

## Architecture

```text
RealClient (env opt-in)
  +-- client
      +-- GdsStorageManager
      |    +-- aligned extent allocator
      |    +-- file:// backing segment handle
      |    `-- storage_id + generation + read leases
      +-- TransferSubmitter::submitFile
      |    `-- TransferEngine / TENT GDS / cuFile
      `-- MasterClient RPCs
           `-- MasterService: GDS storage identities and replicas

BatchPut:
  reserve local extent
    +-- BatchPutStart -> MEMORY/NoF PROCESSING replicas
    +-- BatchAddGdsReplicaStart -> GDS PROCESSING replica
    `-- submit both write paths -> wait -> commit + BatchPutEnd

BatchGet:
  local MEMORY -> any MEMORY -> matching local GDS -> NoF/disk fallbacks
```

### Local GDS storage

`GdsStorageManager` creates/truncates and preallocates the configured backing file, opens it once through `openSegment("file://...")`, and allocates raw value extents aligned to 4 KiB. Reservations are move-only and automatically aborted unless committed or explicitly preserved after an uncertain RPC. A reference-counted read lease keeps an extent alive until all GDS read futures finish.

Each client registers a `storage_id` and `storage_generation` with the master. The generation changes when the file is recreated, preventing an old metadata descriptor from addressing the same offset in a new file.

### Store metadata and RPCs

`ReplicaType::GDS` is an independent replica type rather than an alias for `LOCAL_DISK`:

```text
GdsDescriptor {
  owner_client_id
  storage_id
  storage_generation
  value_offset
  value_size
  allocated_size
}
```

The master exposes storage registration/unregistration, `BatchAddGdsReplicaStart`, and `BatchCreateGdsOnlyObjects`. GDS replicas use the existing `PROCESSING` -> `COMPLETE` lifecycle, participate in `BatchPutEnd` / `BatchPutRevoke`, and are removed during stale-client cleanup. MessagePack serialization uses a stable explicit replica type value and validates the six-field G

comments.author: RuixiangMa
comments.body:
@tong1heng Great work! The design  is clean and well-motivated. A few points I'd like to understand better:
1. submitFile splits at 16 MiB and batches at 128 entries, but GdsTransport::submitTransferTasks already does the same splitting (kMaxSliceSize) and batch checking (io_batch_depth_, user-configurable). If a user sets io_batch_depth=32, submitFile still batches 128 — only 32 get accepted per TENT batch. Is this intentional double-protection, and if so, should the batch limit be read from TENT config rather than hardcoded?
2. Main has added some TENT infrastructure since this RFC was written. Transport::tracksLocalBuffer() seems like a natural fit for GDS's cuFileBufRegister (local-only, shouldn't be advertised via desc.transports). Transport::quiesce() could settle cuFile I/O before buffer deregister. And the all-or-nothing submitTransferTasks contract means partial failure needs rollback of pushed params. Would it make sense to reference these in the RFC?
3. Main recently refactored lease (shared_ptr<Lease>, group-shared) and group eviction (GroupDomain, all-or-none). How do GDS-only objects interact — do they get an independent or group-shared lease? Could UnregisterGdsStorage stale cleanup break all-or-none eviction by removing one GDS replica from a group?
4. Preserve creates finalized=false entries that are never auto-cleaned. If finalize RPCs fail repeatedly (network jitter, master restart), the backing file could be exhausted silently. The Roadmap mentions eviction policy as future work — should the gap be acknowledged in the main body with a short-term mitigation (metric, max count, or TTL)?
5. storage_generation algorithm and collision risk aren't specified. The PR uses steady_clock XOR client_id — steady_clock resets on reboot, so if client_id is reused (e.g. vLLM config), a timestamp collision (low but non-zero) could cause stale descriptors to be accepted. Would it be worth specifying the algorithm and confirming generation=0 as an invalid sentinel?

comments.author: tong1heng
comments.body:
Thanks for the thoughtful review! These points identify several implementation gaps and areas where the RFC needs clarification.

1. The two layers serve different purposes: `submitFile` bounds store-level submissions and manages their futures, while `GdsTransport::submitTransferTasks` enforces cuFile limits. However, the hardcoded batch limit of 128 is inconsistent with the configurable `io_batch_depth`. One clarification: an over-capacity submission returns `TooManyRequests`; it does not accept only the first 32 entries. We will expose the effective GDS batch depth through TENT and use it in `submitFile`, counting capacity in terms of entries after splitting. We will also align the splitting limits and add tests for different batch depths and submissions spanning multiple batches.

2. Agreed. We will reference these interfaces in the RFC and adapt the implementation accordingly. GDS will implement `tracksLocalBuffer()` using its local registration registry and stop advertising cuFile registrations through `desc.transports`. We will implement `quiesce()` to stop new submissions and settle outstanding I/O before teardown releases buffers and batch resources. For the all-or-nothing submission contract, we will validate all requests before modifying the sub-batch and restore appended state on failure. We will also verify cuFile’s submission-failure semantics to ensure potentially accepted I/O cannot be treated as a clean rejection and retried through another transport.

3. The PR currently uses the older group-registration path and needs to be adapted to main’s `shared_ptr<Lease>` and `GroupDomain` implementation. GDS-only objects should follow the same semantics as other objects: ungrouped objects have an independent lease, while grouped objects share the group’s lease. The local GDS `ReadLease` separately protects an extent during an in-flight read. `UnregisterGdsStorage` removes matching GDS replicas and deletes an object only when no valid replica remains. We will preserve group bookkeeping through the common metadata-removal path and add mixed MEMORY/GDS group tests. We will also clarify that invalid-storage cleanup is distinct from policy-driven eviction; current main tests permit safe members to be evicted while unsafe members remain, so strict all-or-none wording needs qualification.

4. Yes, we will acknowledge this limitation explicitly in the main body. `Preserve()` retains an allocation because an RPC failure does not establish whether the master applied the operation, but these uncertain entries currently have no reconciliation or automatic reclamation path. The issue also includes entries committed locally before a finalize RPC fails, so tracking only `finalized=false` is insufficient. As a short-term mitigation, we will track uncertain-entry counts, bytes, age, and allocation failures, and introduce a configurable admission limit. A TTL may trigger reconciliation, but it must not directly reclaim an extent without confirming that the master no longer references it and that local I/O has completed.

5. Agreed. `steady_clock` XOR the client ID does not provide a reliable cross-restart uniqueness guarantee when the client ID is reused. We will replace it with a fresh, randomly generated nonzero 64-bit storage-incarnation token whenever the backing file is recreated, preserving the current wire format. The RFC will specify the algorithm and its probabilistic collision properties. `generation=0` is already invalid: initialization avoids it, and `RegisterGdsStorage()` rejects it. We will document this invariant and add tests for zero-generation rejection and stale descriptors after storage recreation with a reused client ID.

items.title: [Store][Offload] SSD reads fail with BUFFER_OVERFLOW when concurrent readers share the default offload staging buffer (1280 MiB); the log gives no hint
items.author: sivabreddy
items.body_excerpt:
Setup: Mooncake 0.3.13.post1. The master runs `--enable_offload=true --offload_on_evict=true`. There are 2 store pods: `mooncake_client --protocol=rdma --global_segment_size=40GB --local_buffer_size=16GB --enable_offload=true`, with `bucket_storage_backend` on local NVMe. The engines use `global_segment_size 0`: vLLM 0.31.0 `MooncakeStoreConnector` (`standalone-store`, `enable_offload`) and SGLang 0.5.20 HiCache, with Llama-3.1-70B TP4. Pod A stores 16 prompts of 28,096 tokens each (≈ 8.6 GB KV per prompt, ≈ 138 GB in total, RAM pool 80 GB). Pod B then reads the 4 oldest prompts, which are now on SSD.

| Store pod setting | Engine | 4 prompts from SSD |
|---|---|---|
| default | vLLM | 0 of 4 gave output (default `kv_load_failure_policy="fail"`). The engine logged 1,804 `SSD read failed ... BUFFER_OVERFLOW` lines. The store pods logged only `Failed to allocate batch objects` |
| `--local_buffer_size=16GB` | vLLM | same result (0 of 4) |
| default offload buffer | SGLang | 8,256 / 16,384 / 28,032 / 0 of 28,096 tokens from storage; SGLang computed the rest |
| `MOONCAKE_OFFLOAD_LOCAL_BUFFER_SIZE_BYTES=17179869184` (16 GiB) | both | 4 of 4 fully from SSD; TTFT 0.92–1.00 s against 2.66–4.93 s compute; 0 `BUFFER_OVERFLOW` |

The SSD owner serves `batch_get_offload_object` from one arena (`FileStorageConfig::local_buffer_size`, default `1280 * kMB`, `storage_backend.h` L213). All concurrent readers share this arena. vLLM limits each TP rank's read batch to 1280 MiB (`DEFAULT_MOONCAKE_DISK_STAGING_BUFFER_BYTES`), so 4 ranks that read at the same time can need 4 × 1280 MiB. `ssd-offload.md` lists the variable as "Client-side staging buffer size". It does not say that the variable must be set on the process that owns the SSD, that all readers share the buffer, or that `--local_buffer_size` does not change it. #3331 already sets 64 GiB, so the need to raise it seems known but is not documented. #2119 (closed without a stated cause) shows the same `Failed to allocate batch objects` / `BUFFER_OVERFLOW` lines on another platform; this may be the same cause.

Suggestions: (1) when `BUFFER_OVERFLOW` occurs, log the requested bytes, the arena size and the variable name; (2) add these points and a troubleshooting entry to `ssd-offload.md`. We can send both as a PR.

comments.author: he-yufeng
comments.body:
Excellent writeup — your reading of the failure is correct. The offload read arena lives in the store pod that owns the SSD (`FileStorage` sizes `client_buffer_allocator_` from `FileStorageConfig::local_buffer_size`, default 1280 MiB), every concurrent reader's staging buffers come out of that one arena, and `--local_buffer_size` on the engine side does not change it. With 4 TP ranks each staging up to 1280 MiB against a 1280 MiB arena, the `BUFFER_OVERFLOW` / `Failed to allocate batch objects` pair is exactly what an exhausted arena produces, and raising `MOONCAKE_OFFLOAD_LOCAL_BUFFER_SIZE_BYTES` on the SSD-owning pod is the right workaround. #2119 shows the same signature, so this is very likely the same cause.

Both of your suggestions are welcome as a PR — please do send it.

1. For the diagnostic: the cheapest honest spot is the failure branch of `FileStorage::LoadBatch` (file_storage.cpp, where it currently logs a bare "Failed to allocate batch objects"). At that point the requested per-batch size is in scope and the allocator can report its capacity, so the log can carry requested bytes, arena size, and a pointer at `MOONCAKE_OFFLOAD_LOCAL_BUFFER_SIZE_BYTES`. One request: keep the arena-capacity read cheap (a cached/config value, not a locking walk of the allocator on the error path).
2. For the docs: adding the ownership rule (the variable is read by the process that owns the SSD, not by the engines) and the concurrency math (concurrent readers × per-rank staging cap vs arena size) to `ssd-offload.md`, plus a troubleshooting entry mapping `BUFFER_OVERFLOW` → arena sizing, would close the gap you hit.

I'll review when it lands.

items.title: Diffusion CUDA JIT: rsqrt host/CRT clash burns tens of seconds before soft-fail (fail fast / skip on sm<80)
items.author: quantz8a
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

On **sm_75** with **pip CUDA 13** (`CUDA_HOME=…/site-packages/nvidia/cu13`), SGLang **diffusion CUDA JIT** kernels fail to compile because host glibc `mathcalls.h` and CUDA CRT disagree on `rsqrt` / `rsqrtf` exception specifications.

Failures are often **soft** (warning + eager fallback), but the **first** Flux denoise step still spends **tens of seconds** attempting nvcc builds that cannot succeed on this toolchain layout.

Affected modules observed (JIT cache under `~/.cache/sglang/jit/sm75/`):

- `sgl_kernel_jit_qknorm_rope_…`
- `sgl_kernel_jit_qknorm_…`
- `sgl_kernel_jit_diffusion_residual_gate_add_…`

Call sites include `sglang.kernels.ops.diffusion.rope.qknorm_rope_jit` → `load_jit(...)`.

## Environment

| Item | Value |
|------|-------|
| GPU | RTX 2080 Ti · CC **7.5** |
| torch | 2.13.0+cu130 |
| nvcc | pip `nvidia-cuda-nvcc` 13.0.x under `…/nvidia/cu13` |
| Host | Ubuntu · `/usr/include/x86_64-linux-gnu/bits/mathcalls.h` |
| Workload | `sglang generate` · FLUX.2-klein-4B · 512² · 4 steps · TE/VAE CPU + DiT layerwise |

## Symptom

```text
Failed to load JIT fused QKNorm+RoPE kernel: Failed to build JIT module …
nvcc … -gencode=arch=compute_75,code=sm_75 … -c cuda.cu

/usr/include/x86_64-linux-gnu/bits/mathcalls.h(…): error: exception specification is incompatible with that of previous function "rsqrt"
  (declared at …/nvidia/cu13/…/include/crt/math_functions.h)
  extern double rsqrt (double __x) noexcept (true);
```

Wall-clock: first denoise step ~**49 s** dominated by failed JIT; subsequent steps ~1–2 s once fallbacks stick for the process.

## Reproduce

```bash
export CUDA_HOME=$VENV/lib/python3.12/site-packages/nvidia/cu13
export PATH=$CUDA_HOME/bin:$PATH

sglang generate \
  --model-path /path/to/FLUX.2-klein-4B \
  --text-encoder-cpu-offload --vae-cpu-offload --dit-layerwise-offload \
  --pin-cpu-memory --performance-mode manual --enable-torch-compile false \
  --height 512 --width 512 --num-inference-steps 4 \
  --prompt "a red apple on a wooden table"
```

Watch for `Failed to load JIT fused QKNorm+RoPE` / `Disabling diffusion residual-gate CUDA fast path` with the `mathcalls.h` / `rsqrt` error.

## Why it matters

1. Diffusion registry already lists many **Triton** backends, yet Flux hot paths still **probe CUDA `load_jit` first** and pay compile latency for guaranteed failure on this common pip-CUDA layout.
2. Soft fallback hides the defect from “does it generate?” checks but destroys **first-request** latency.
3. “Fail fast” here is good UX regardless of whether Turing is a supported production target.

## Expected

1. **Capability / known-bad short-circuit**: if `sm < 80` (or a cheap probe compile fails once), **skip** diffusion CUDA JIT for QKNorm/RoPE/residual-gate and go straight to torch/Triton with one info log; and/or  
2. Fix include order / macros so nvcc from pip cu13 does not pull conflicting host `rsqrt` declarations; and/or  
3. Docs: editable + pip `nvidia/cu13` — expect JIT rsqrt clash; prefer Docker or disable doomed JIT probes.

items.title: [Bug] Large HiCache UCX startup timeout on downstream build; not reproduced on v0.5.20
items.author: ByronHsu
items.body_excerpt:
### Result

**Not reproduced on the latest upstream image (v0.5.20).** A large HiCache pool triggered a UCX startup timeout on our earlier downstream build, but both HiCache and no-HiCache starts passed with the unmodified upstream image.

| Build | HiCache per rank | UCX initialization, all 8 ranks | Server ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Downstream `869abc0605`, NIXL 1.3.0 / UCX 1.21.0 | 234 GB | Six ranks explicitly timed out at 60s; none completed | No |
| Same downstream build, no HiCache | 0 | 3–4s | Yes |
| **Upstream v0.5.20, NIXL 1.4.1 / UCX 1.22.0** | **234 GB** | **~2s** | **234s after launch** |
| Same upstream image, no HiCache | 0 | ~2s | 62s after launch |

Each HiCache/control pair ran on the same eight-H200 node with fresh processes. The upstream pair used a different physical node from the downstream pair, and multiple software components changed: this does **not** identify a fix or prove the cause. Only startup was tested, with no inference requests. Both upstream runs registered all eight KV buffers, passed passive `/ready` checks for 30 seconds, and exited cleanly.

### Reproduction settings

8 H200s, approximately 2014 GiB host RAM; public `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V2-Lite` real weights, revision `604d5664dddd88a0433dbae533b7fe9472482de0`.

Upstream image: `lmsysorg/sglang:latest` resolved to **v0.5.20**, source `94602c9c2b7cbdb8efd5c52802dac6a1c180089e`. Tested amd64 image digest:

```text
lmsysorg/sglang@sha256:b27fce60bc5494c118c4910702812bcfa8cee67abcdd1ff8b0902f21647552f4
```

No source overlay, serving patches, or dependency replacements. Download the model revision above into `$MODEL_DIR`, then run:

```bash
export SGLANG_DISAGGREGATION_ENGINE_INIT_TIMEOUT=60
export SGLANG_NCCL_ALL_GATHER_IN_OVERLAP_SCHEDULER_SYNC_BATCH=1
export SGLANG_FORCE_STREAM_INTERVAL=1
export SGLANG_FORCE_CPU_IMAGE_PREPROCESSING=0

python -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path "$MODEL_DIR" --trust-remote-code \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 30000 \
  --tp-size 8 --dp-size 8 --ep-size 8 --enable-dp-attention \
  --disaggregation-mode prefill --disaggregation-transfer-backend nixl \
  --mem-fraction-static 0.7 --dtype bfloat16 --kv-cache-dtype bf16 \
  --page-size 64 --tokenizer-worker-num 4 \
  --context-length 150000 --max-running-requests 1024 \
  --skip-server-warmup --log-level debug --decode-attention-backend fa3 \
  --enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-size 234 \
  --hicache-write-policy write_through \
  --hicache-mem-layout page_first --hicache-io-backend kernel
```

Remove the five HiCache options for the control. CUDA graphs stay enabled; NIXL is the PD transport, not L3 storage. Actual pool allocation: **234,001,612,800 bytes per rank**, about **1.872 TB total**. Size is per rank and requires sufficient host/cgroup headroom.

### Original failure

The downstream run failed **during UCX backend creation, before KV registration**:

```text
RuntimeError: NIXL create_backend('UCX', {'num_threads': '8'}) did not return within 60s
```

Five seconds before failure: **141.6 GiB host headroom**, **39.2–39.4 GiB free per GPU**, no host OOM-counter increase or CUDA OOM. Host memory pressure and compaction were high. No native stack inside UCX was captured. A later audit found rank 0 in a debugger tracing stop at 21:29:30 UTC, inside the 60-second UCX window, as well as earlier allocation-stage attachments. The retained samples do not establish total pause duration. Other ranks also timed out without a recorded tracing stop, but this run was not free of measurement interference. A telemetry gap further limits the evidence.

The upstream HiCache run kept at least **120 GiB host headroom**, logged no OOM, and completed UCX startup quickly. The underlying reason for the older failure remains unresolved.

<details>
<summary>Upstream runtime</summary>

Python 3.12.3; PyTorch 2.13.0+cu130; NIXL/nixl-cu13 1.4.1; bundled UCX 1.22.0; CUDA 13.0; driver 595.71.05; Linux 6.8.12; FlashInfer 0.6.18; Transformers 5.12.1. THP mode remains `madvise`. The 60-second UCX deadline and eight prefill backend threads were unchanged.

</details>

### Follow-up: the extra host memory is DC receive buffers

On one exclusive node, with the same upstream source/image and **232 GB/rank** HiCache, we compared fresh server processes:

| Native backend | DC interfaces | Receive-buffer chunks | Scheduler anonymous huge pages | UCX startup span |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| NIXL 1.4.1 / UCX 1.22 | 0 | 288 | 12.498 GiB | 2s |
| NIXL 1.3.0 / UCX 1.21 | 288 | 576 | 23.188 GiB | 4s |
| Same 1.3.0 package, only `UCX_TLS=^dc_mlx5` added | 0 | 288 | 12.502 GiB | 3s |

All three initialized all eight ranks, registered KV buffers, and held passive readiness for 30 seconds. No compaction stalls, THP fallbacks, or OOM occurred. No inference or PD transfers were tested. The third case is a diagnostic intervention, **not a verified timeout fix**.

UCX debug logs and per-scheduler memory maps identify the difference: **8 ranks × 9 workers × 4 ports = 288 DC interfaces**, each eagerly allocating a **38 MiB** receive buffer through `rc_recv_desc`. Those extra buffers account for **10.6875 GiB** of huge pages. Excluding only DC on the old package removes them and matches the newer package. Actual loaded UCX versions were verified in server logs.

The old binary includes DC; the new wheel omits it. [NIXL PR 1708](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/nixl/pull/1708) disables DC in the manylinux build. The v1.3.0 source tag also contains that flag despite the tested wheel including DC, so we report observed binary features rather than infer build history from tags.

During the **original failing UCX initialization window**, kernel counters rose by **10,496 compaction attempts, 10,492 failures, 3,407 THP fallbacks, and 3,668 direct-reclaim stalls**. They were flat just before UCX started. The examined SGLang NIXL startup and host-pool files are byte-identical between the downstream and upstream revisions.

This supports a host-memory compact

items.title: Strict tool constraint fails the whole request when one tool schema does not compile
items.author: BorisTyshkevich
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

With `SGLANG_TOOL_STRICT_LEVEL=2` (or `strict: true` on a tool), all tool
schemas go into one structural tag. If xgrammar cannot compile one schema, the
request fails. The other tools are not used. The client cannot recover.

## Evidence

Setup: SGLang 0.5.19-based build, xgrammar 0.2.1, `--tool-call-parser
qwen3_coder`, `SGLANG_TOOL_STRICT_LEVEL=2`.

- Measured: every request from a client with a 177-tool set returned HTTP 400.
  Message: `Failed to compile structural_tag grammar ... Lookahead is not
  supported yet.`
- One tool in that set has 2 distinct `pattern` values with a negative
  lookahead. Level 1 compiles, because it has no schema.
- Repro: one tool with `{"type":"string","pattern":"^(?!\\.)[a-z]+$"}` and
  `tool_choice="auto"` at level 2 returns 400. Expected: 200.

Code path (read): `python/sglang/srt/constrained/xgrammar_backend.py` on
`main` (5385866), `dispatch_structural_tag`, lines 452-454: the
`RuntimeError` becomes `InvalidGrammarObject`, and the request aborts. In v0.5.22
the same code is at lines 414-416.

The root cause is in xgrammar (unsupported regex constructs, see https://github.com/mlc-ai/xgrammar/issues/1001). SGLang can still limit the harm.

## Request

Add a per-tool fallback. Examples:

- On a compile error, find the tool that fails (compile each tool alone),
  and relax only that tool (drop its `pattern`, or use `{}` for its
  parameters). Compile again. Log a warning with the tool name.
- Make the policy a flag (for example fail / relax-tool / drop-tool), with
  fail as the default so current behavior stays.

Measured with a local patch that removes only the uncompilable `pattern`
constraints: the 177-tool set compiles (4 constraints relaxed; the cold compile is about 18 s on CPU with the real
tokenizer, and a cache hit is 0.01 s), 4 of 4 smoke requests return 200, and we saw 0 malformed tool calls
in 320 samples. Relaxing only loosens the schema.

We can open a PR for this.

items.title: qwen3_coder structural tag triggers on the text `<tool_call>\n<function=`; use the `<tool_call>` token (xgrammar token_markers)
items.author: BorisTyshkevich
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

For `qwen3_coder`, xgrammar builds the tag with the text trigger
`<tool_call>\n<function=`. If the model writes other whitespace, or a
different tag, the constraint does not start. SGLang does not use the token
option that xgrammar now has.

## Evidence

- xgrammar `main` (614ab01), `python/xgrammar/builtin_structural_tag.py` lines
  1578-1581: `TOOL_CALL_BEGIN_PREFIX` and `TOOL_CALL_TRIGGER` are both the
  text `<tool_call>\n<function=`. Tag begin is `<tool_call>\n<function=NAME>\n`.
- xgrammar PR #940 (merged) adds `get_model_structural_tag(...,
  token_markers=True)`. It matches `<tool_call>` as a dedicated token for
  `qwen_3_coder`. It is on `main`. It is not in v0.2.8 (0 matches in the v0.2.8
  file).
- SGLang `main` (5385866) `python/sglang/srt/function_call/
  base_format_detector.py` lines 426-432 call `get_model_structural_tag`
  without `token_markers` (and without `any_order`).
- Measured in our offline replay (about 19K recorded turns): level 1 rejected
  412 of 1,160 malformed calls (35.5%), level 2 rejected 1,155 (99.6%). Live
  A/B, 1,840 turns: 166 malformed calls by default, 0 at level 2. Decode
  throughput 317.2 vs 316.8 tok/s. These runs used the text trigger.

## Request

1. Pass `token_markers=True` for detectors whose marker is a single token
   (qwen3_coder), when the installed xgrammar supports it. Keep the text
   trigger as fallback for older xgrammar.
2. Add regression tests: a literal `<tool_call>` in ordinary text and in
   reasoning must not start a constraint (see also #42030).
3. Whitespace after `<tool_call>` is still fixed (`\n`) in the xgrammar tag
   begin. Ask xgrammar to allow any whitespace there (requested in https://github.com/mlc-ai/xgrammar/issues/1002).

Limit: we did not test `token_markers=True` ourselves.

items.title: [Bug] qwen3_coder: one `strict: true` tool under tool_choice="auto" makes a non-strict zero-argument tool get invented arguments
items.author: cmlccie
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [ ] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

Setup: `--tool-call-parser qwen3_coder`, `tool_choice: "auto"`, and two tools:

- `get_schema` takes no arguments (`properties: {}`, `additionalProperties: false`) and has **no** `strict` field.
- `query_database` takes one required string `sql` and sets `"strict": true`.

When the model calls `get_schema`, it gets invented arguments in **4 of 4** runs. We saw `{"sql": ""}`, `{"properties": "{}"}` and `{"parameters": "{}"}`. The model's reasoning says correctly that `get_schema` takes no parameters. It makes the same mistake again on retry.

| Variant (same prompt, n=4 each)                 | `get_schema` arguments                                                                                                                                                                       |
| ----------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `strict: true` on `query_database` only (mixed) | **4/4 invented** (`{"sql": ""}`, `{"properties": "{}"}`, `{"parameters": "{}"}`)                                                                                                             |
| `strict` removed from all tools                 | 4/4 correct `{}`                                                                                                                                                                             |
| `strict: true` on both tools                    | `{}`, but generation never ends (`finish_reason: "length"`, emits whitespace). This is already reported in mlc-ai/xgrammar#802 and vllm-project/vllm#50989, so this issue does not cover it. |

Expected: `strict` applies per tool (as in OpenAI's API). Adding `strict: true` to one tool should not change how a different, non-strict tool is called. `get_schema` should be called with `{}`, as it is when no tool is strict.

**Summary of the cause** (details below). The two failing rows above share one root cause, and the mixed-strict row is a new symptom of it:

1. **SGLang:** if any tool has `strict: true`, `tool_choice="auto"` puts **every** tool under the xgrammar `qwen_3_coder` structural tag, including the non-strict ones.
2. **xgrammar:** the `qwen_3_coder` tag puts a newline on both sides of the parameter zone (`begin` ends in `>\n`, `end` starts with `\n</function>`). Qwen's chat template writes a zero-argument call as `<function=NAME>\n</function>`, with only one newline. **The grammar cannot produce the template's own zero-argument form.**
3. **xgrammar:** a non-strict tool gets a `True` schema, which compiles to an open `xml_object`. So after `<function=get_schema>\n` the grammar allows only whitespace or `<parameter=ANY_NAME>`. The model's own next token, `</function>`, is masked out.

With both tools strict, only whitespace is allowed there, and you get the #802 loop. With the mixed set, `<parameter=` is also allowed, and the model goes that way and invents a parameter. The open fixes for #802 (xgrammar #803 and #837) remove the whitespace loop. They do not make `>\n</function>` reachable, so they do not fix this issue (checked below).


### Reproduction

Server (generic. We ran the `lmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.21-cu130` image):

```bash
python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-FP8 \
  --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder \
  --reasoning-parser qwen3 \
  --port 30000
```

Request (streaming, as measured. In the original run the tool names had a `<server>-` prefix. The names are shortened here):

```bash
curl -sN http://localhost:30000/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "model": "Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-FP8",
  "stream": true,
  "temperature": 0.2,
  "tool_choice": "auto",
  "messages": [
    {"role": "system", "content": "You answer questions about a customer database. Always call get_schema first to learn the tables, then call query_database."},
    {"role": "user", "content": "What are the top customers by dollars spent over the last quarter?"}
  ],
  "tools": [
    {"type": "function", "function": {
      "name": "get_schema",
      "description": "Return the database schema (tables and columns).",
      "parameters": {"properties": {}, "type": "object", "additionalProperties": false}
    }},
    {"type": "function", "function": {
      "name": "query_database",
      "description": "Run a read-only SQL query and return the rows.",
      "parameters": {
        "properties": {"sql": {"type": "string", "description": "A single read-only SQL SELECT statement."}},
        "required": ["sql"], "type": "object", "additionalProperties": false
      },
      "strict": true
    }}
  ]
}'
```

Observed: the first tool call is `get_schema` with arguments such as `{"sql": ""}` or `{"properties": "{}"}`.
Control 1: delete `"strict": true`. The result is `get_schema` with `{}`.
Control 2: add `"strict": true` to `get_schema` as well. The arguments are `{}`, but generation runs to `max_tokens` (xgrammar#802).

**Grammar-level reproduction (no GPU, no model).** This builds the same structural tag SGLang requests and checks which strings it accepts. It needs only `pip install xgrammar==0.2.7`, the version pinned by SGLang 0.5.21 (`python/pyproject.toml`):

```python
import xgrammar as xgr
from xgrammar.testing import _is_grammar_accept_string as acc

def tag(get_schema_strict):
    gs = {"type": "function", "function": {"name": "get_schema

items.title: [Performance]:Skip gaps in sliding-window prefix-cache hit search
items.author: Ifelseer
items.body_excerpt:
### Proposal to improve performance


`SlidingWindowManager.find_longest_cache_hit` currently scans every block from right to left, costing up to `max_num_blocks` `BlockPool.get_cached_block` lookups even when the cache is cold. Sliding-window groups commonly run at a low hit rate, so a 128K-token request with a 4K window performs ~8192 lookups (block_size=16) although a hit only needs `cdiv(sliding_window - 1, block_size) = 256` contiguous blocks. The function already carries a TODO for this. Proposed change: probe every `stride = sliding_window_contiguous_blocks`-th block from the right. Every candidate run of `stride` cached blocks contains exactly one probe, so the lattice cannot skip a hit. On a probe hit, expand to the right (at most `stride - 1` blocks, since the next probe missed), verify only windows containing the probe, and after a miss at `idx` resume at the next aligned edge below `idx - 1`. Alignment retries advance by `alignment_tokens // gcd(alignment_tokens, block_size)` blocks, and the cached-prefix fallback is computed directly. Function-level measurements (`find_longest_cache_hit`, block_size=16, sliding_window=4096, 128K tokens, alignment=16, no EAGLE, single-thread CPU):

| pattern | main lookups | proposed lookups | main time | proposed time |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| cold cache | 8192 | 33 | 4.49 ms | 0.021 ms |
| 1% random cached | 8192 | 33 | 4.61 ms | 0.021 ms |
| tail hit / full cache | 256 | 257 | 0.23 ms | 0.23 ms |
| adversary (cached blocks on the probe lattice) | 8192 | 128 | 4.63 ms | 0.11 ms |

The worst case remains O(max_num_blocks), but the common low-hit-rate case becomes O(max_num_blocks / stride), and the measured adversarial case is still well below the current full scan.



### Report of performance regression

_No response_

### Misc discussion on performance

### Relation to #53276 (not a duplicate)

#53276 targets the same TODO with a different, narrower approach: it checks `block_hashes[i - K + 1]` only when the current block misses and no run is being accumulated, and jumps by K only in that case. Every other path still advances one block at a time, alignment retries remain per-block, the cached-prefix fallback still comes from the full scan, and the PR adds no tests. This proposal is materially different:
- Every probe hit triggers right-expansion and verification bounded to windows containing the probe, so gaps are skipped regardless of which side the miss is on.
- Alignment retries jump by the alignment period, covering hybrid models where `alignment_tokens != block_size`.
- The cached-prefix fallback is computed directly.
- Correctness is backed by an offline exhaustive comparison with the previous implementation (all cached-block patterns up to 13 blocks over a grid of block sizes, windows, alignments, and EAGLE settings: 7,339,584 cases, 0 differences) plus a committed randomized test.

Happy to close this in favor of #53276 if maintainers prefer that direction.

  ### Additional robustness fix

`sliding_window=1` with EAGLE disabled makes `_contiguous_blocks_for_hit` return 0, which would leave the new probe loop's `i -= stride` at the same index. The implementation clamps the stride to 1, reproducing the previous behavior (one cached block is reusable) and terminating; a regression test is included.

  ### Misc discussion on performance

This is a scheduler-side CPU optimization; it does not change hit results, model output, or GPU execution. End-to-end serving numbers have not been collected yet.


### Your current environment (if you think it is necessary)

Python 3.12, torch 2.14.0+cu132, upstream main at ff01a6b14f, CPU unit-test harness. This is a scheduler-side CPU optimization and does not change hit results, model output, or GPU execution.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [Bug]: Mooncake example proxy commits HTTP 200 before decode failures
items.author: jacklin78911-collab
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

- vLLM official main nightly: `ddefe40e16dda6cd3a0ba1b5c83e1ee9f18187fc` (`0.32.1rc1.dev72+gddefe40e1`), including #50984.
- Python 3.12.14, FastAPI 0.136.3, HTTPX 0.28.1.
- GPU confirmation: single-node 1P1D, 2 H20, Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B, Mooncake `1f65cf13c9f886f8db8b88b7733367b18340ebf0`, TENT RDMA.
- The CPU reproduction below needs only FastAPI, HTTPX and pytest, plus the example proxy file.
- The default-branch proxy file independently retrieved on 2026-10-19 UTC has SHA256 `fea24b40fa8ea11d4757c3298271525fdfa16a01b57cc693c00785aa7c28e359`, identical to the file used in these tests. The complete current default-branch GPU build was not separately tested.

### Describe the bug

When D returns an HTTP error, `examples/disaggregated/mooncake_connector/mooncake_connector_proxy.py` can send HTTP 200 to its client and then abort the response body. The upstream status and JSON error are lost. This happens for both completion/chat routes, with either streaming request mode.

`_handle_completions` returns `StreamingResponse` before `stream_service_response` opens D. The latter calls `response.raise_for_status()` inside the response iterator. By then the downstream headers have been sent, and the handler's outer exception block no longer covers iteration.

Affected source at the tested revision:
- [Upstream request and raise inside the iterator](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/ddefe40e16dda6cd3a0ba1b5c83e1ee9f18187fc/examples/disaggregated/mooncake_connector/mooncake_connector_proxy.py#L303).
- [StreamingResponse construction](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/ddefe40e16dda6cd3a0ba1b5c83e1ee9f18187fc/examples/disaggregated/mooncake_connector/mooncake_connector_proxy.py#L346).

### Actual GPU failure evidence

After a successful baseline, a test-only P entry point changed one native transfer call to a single 64-KiB WRITE descriptor with a valid CUDA source and an unregistered null destination. TENT rejected it before posting a work request. The original native engine returned its real failure; the test did not mock a return code or stop either engine. This is an invalid-range failure test, not a physical-link failure claim.

Sanitized excerpts (role prefixes are editorial):

```text
P: batchTransferSync: transfer FAILED ... on retry 0/2
P: batchTransferSync: transfer FAILED ... on retry 1/2
P: batchTransferSync: all 2 retries exhausted ...
P: Sending to <decode-session> failed (ret=-1) ...
D: pulling kv_caches for [<request>] failed: Mooncake transfer engine returned -1
D: Failing 1 request(s) due to KV load failure (failure_policy=fail, 256 tokens affected).
D: "POST /v1/completions HTTP/1.1" 500 Internal Server Error
proxy: "POST /v1/completions HTTP/1.1" 200 OK
proxy: httpx.HTTPStatusError: Server error '500 Internal Server Error' ...
client: http.client.IncompleteRead: IncompleteRead(0 bytes read)
```

The connector correctly terminated the failed request. The separate proxy boundary hid that terminal error.

### CPU reproduction and regression coverage

Save the following as `test_proxy_status.py` in an environment with the dependencies above:

```python
import asyncio
import importlib.util
import json
import os
from pathlib import Path
import sys
import uuid
import httpx
import pytest

@pytest.mark.parametrize('endpoint',['/v1/completions','/v1/chat/completions'])
@pytest.mark.parametrize('stream',[False,True])
def test_backend_error_status_body_and_close(endpoint,stream):
    asyncio.run(scenario(endpoint,stream,500))

@pytest.mark.parametrize('stream',[False,True])
def test_healthy_body_type_and_close(stream):
    asyncio.run(scenario('/v1/completions',stream,200))

async def scenario(endpoint,stream,status):
    name='private_proxy_'+uuid.uuid4().hex
    spec=importlib.util.spec_from_file_location(name,Path(os.environ['PROXY_UNDER_TEST']))
    module=importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec);sys.modules[name]=module;spec.loader.exec_module(module)
    closed=[]
    body=(b'{"error":{"message":"controlled failure","type":"InternalServerError"}}' if status==500
          else b'data: {"choices":[]}\n\ndata: [DONE]\n\n' if stream else b'{"choices":[]}')
    content_type='text/event-stream' if status==200 and stream else 'application/json'
    class Body(httpx.AsyncByteStream):
        async def __aiter__(self):
            yield body[:5];yield body[5:]
        async def aclose(self):closed.append(True)
    async def backend(request):
        assert request.method=='POST' and request.url.path==endpoint
        assert json.loads(request.content)['stream']==stream
        return httpx.Response(status,headers={'content-type':content_type},stream=Body())
    async def prefill(*args,**kwargs):pass
    try:
        async with httpx.AsyncClient(transport=httpx.MockTransport(backend),base_url='http://decode.test') as remote:
            info={'client':remote,'bootstrap_addr':'http://prefill.test:8998','dp_engine_id':{0:'engine'}}
            module.get_next_client=lambda app,role: (info,0) if role=='prefill' else info
            module.send_request_to_service=prefill
            module.app.state.ready=asyncio.Event();module.app.state.ready.set()
            async with httpx.AsyncClient(transport=httpx.ASGITransport(app=module.app,raise_app_exceptions=False),base_url='http://proxy.test') as client:
                response=await client.post(endpoint,json={'model':'test','prompt':'test','stream':stream})
        assert response.status_code==status
        assert response.content==body
        assert response.headers['content-type'].startswith(content_type)
        assert closed==[True]
    finally:sys.modules.pop(name,None)

```

From a vLLM checkout:

```bash
PROXY_UNDER_TEST="$PWD/examples/disaggregated/mooncake_connector/mooncake_connector_proxy.py" \
  python3 -m pytest -q test_proxy_status.py
```

Observed with the unmodified file: **4 failed, 2 passed*

items.title: [Bug][Rust Frontend] Long conversations fail with HTTP 500 (chat template fuel limit)
items.author: ly989264
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

<details>
<summary>Environment</summary>

`collect_env.py` does not cover the Rust binary, so here is the setup instead:

- vLLM `main` at `4e304b4d1` (2026-10-20). `vllm-rs` and `vllm-mock-engine` were built from source with Rust 1.95.0.
- macOS 27.0 on arm64. No GPU is needed: the failure happens in the frontend's chat template rendering, before the engine is involved.
- Model files: GLM-5.3's `config.json`, `tokenizer.json`, `tokenizer_config.json` and `chat_template.jinja`.

</details>

### 🐛 Describe the bug

With the Rust frontend, chat requests fail with HTTP 500 once a conversation reaches about 1,700 messages, even when the prompt is far below the model's context length. With GLM-5.3, a 1,730-message agent conversation (21K tokens, about 2% of the 1M context) is rejected:

```
{"error":{"message":"failed to submit chat request: chat template error: failed to render jinja template: engine ran out of fuel (in chat:64)","type":"server_error","param":null,"code":"server_error"}}
```

transformers, which the Python frontend uses, renders the same conversation in about 0.12 s.

This looks like a side effect of the render budget added in #50300. `DEFAULT_TEMPLATE_FUEL` in `rust/src/chat/src/renderer/hf/template.rs` caps every render at 500K MiniJinja instructions, and the cap also applies to the model's own chat template. Fuel grows with the number of messages rather than their length: GLM-5.3's template uses about 290 instructions per message here. So long agent sessions hit the limit, and once a session crosses it, every later request in that session fails. There is currently no setting to raise the limit.

**Reproduction.** This needs no GPU. Run from the repository root:

```bash
cargo build --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml -p vllm-cmd --bin vllm-rs -p vllm-mock-engine
rust/target/debug/vllm-rs serve /path/to/GLM-5.3 --served-model-name glm --port 8000 \
    --data-parallel-size 1 --data-parallel-size-local 0 --handshake-port 29571 &
rust/target/debug/vllm-mock-engine --handshake-address tcp://127.0.0.1:29571 --engine-count 1 --vocab-size 32000 &

python repro.py 863   # 1728 messages -> 200
python repro.py 864   # 1730 messages -> 500 (engine ran out of fuel)
```

<details>
<summary>repro.py</summary>

```python
import json
import sys
import urllib.error
import urllib.request

turns = int(sys.argv[1])  # tool-call rounds; messages = 2 + 2 * turns
tools = [{"type": "function", "function": {
    "name": "read", "description": "Read a file",
    "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {"path": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["path"]}}}]
messages = [{"role": "system", "content": "You are a coding agent."},
            {"role": "user", "content": "Fix the failing tests."}]
for i in range(turns):
    messages += [
        {"role": "assistant", "content": "", "tool_calls": [{
            "id": f"call_{i}", "type": "function",
            "function": {"name": "read", "arguments": json.dumps({"path": f"src/f{i}.rs"})}}]},
        {"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": f"call_{i}", "content": f"fn f{i}() {{}}"},
    ]

body = {"model": "glm", "messages": messages, "tools": tools, "max_tokens": 1}
req = urllib.request.Request("http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions", json.dumps(body).encode(),
                             {"Content-Type": "application/json"})
try:
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req) as resp:
        print(len(messages), "messages ->", resp.status)
except urllib.error.HTTPError as e:
    print(len(messages), "messages ->", e.code, e.read().decode())
```

</details>

**Expected.** A conversation that fits in the context renders, as it does on the Python frontend. If a hard cap is still needed for safety, an operator should at least be able to raise it for the model's own template.

**Related.**

- The budget from #50300 matters for request-supplied templates (#52025). The Rust frontend cannot yet tell those apart from the model's own template, because it has no `--trust-request-chat-template` gate.
- I opened #62374 as a possible fix. It keeps the 500K default, reads the budget from `VLLM_CHAT_TEMPLATE_FUEL` (`0` disables it), and names that variable in the error. With it and `VLLM_CHAT_TEMPLATE_FUEL=2000000`, the 1,730-message request above returns 200.

**Label**

`good first issue` — filing under [[Onboarding 2026] Good first issues](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/issues/3372).

**Summary**

`lmcache/storage_backend/serde/cachegen_basics.py` still builds five debug log messages with f-strings, so the strings are interpolated even when debug logging is disabled.

**Details**

All five call sites are in `CacheGenGPUEncoderOutput.debug_print_device()`:

```python
logger.debug(f"bytestream device: {self.data_chunks[0].bytestream.device}")
logger.debug(
    f"bytestream_lengths device: "
    f"{self.data_chunks[0].bytestream_lengths.device}"
)
logger.debug(f"cdf device: {self.cdf.device}")
logger.debug(f"max_tensors_key device: {self.max_tensors_key.device}")
logger.debug(f"max_tensors_value device: {self.max_tensors_value.device}")
```

Per @ApostaC's guidance in #3372, `%`-style is preferred so the arguments are formatted only when the record is actually emitted (ruff `G004`).

**Expected Outcome / Goal**

The five calls use `%s` placeholders, and `ruff check --select G004` reports no violations for this file. The rendered log text stays identical — f-string interpolation and `%s` both go through `str()`.

**Additional Context**

- Scope is this one file only, format style only, no behavior change. Whether the (currently uncalled) `debug_print_device` helper should exist at all is a separate question and out of scope here.
- Verification: `ruff check --select G004 <file>` and `pre-commit run --files <file>`.
- Repo-wide there are still 381 `G004` violations (271 under `lmcache/`), so this is one file out of a longer list.

Refs #3372

items.author: imReese

## Checklist

* [x] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
* [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

## Motivation

`PoolName`, `PoolTransfer`, `PoolHitPolicy`, and `PoolTransferResult` are currently defined in `hicache_storage.py`.

These types are no longer really HiCache-specific. They are also used by Unified Cache, `pool_host`, NIXL, HF3FS, and other cache/storage code.

This makes imports like this a bit confusing:

```python
from sglang.srt.mem_cache.hicache_storage import PoolName, PoolTransfer
```

Code that has nothing to do with HiCache still has to depend on a module named `hicache_storage`.

Would it make sense to move these shared types into a neutral module, for example:

```text
mem_cache/pool_transfer.py
```

and let `hicache_storage.py` import/re-export them for compatibility?

This should only be a code organization change, with no behavior change.

Current users include:

* `unified_cache/unified_cache_linker.py`
* `unified_cache/components/full_component.py`
* `pool_host/group.py`
* `storage/nixl/`

items.title: [Bug]: ModelOpt Llama-4 Checkpoints Take 5+ minutes to load
items.author: robertgshaw2-redhat
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

In working on some MoE refactors, I discovered that L4 for ModelOpt takes 5+minutes to load weights even from CPU page cache. 
- https://huggingface.co/nvidia/Llama-4-Scout-17B-16E-Instruct-FP8

The root cause is basically this hack logic to load the state dict that ModelOpt uses
- https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/model_executor/models/llama4.py#L439-L523 [modelopt is the fused case] 

What happens is that the CPU tensor (loaded weight) that we are going to load into the GPU tensor (param) becomes non-contiguous due to this logic. As a result, when we eventually call `_copy()` from CPU->GPU we are calling this on a non-contiguous cpu tensor which takes 3-4s per weight.

To hack around this for local R&D, I simply immediately move the loaded_weight to the GPU. This makes the gather happen on the GPU which accelerates things a lot. This isn't reasonable as an actual solution though

We should investigate where the logic in the weight loader can avoid creating non-contiguous CPU tensors


### Alternatives

_No response_

### Additional context

_No response_

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

comments.body:
@robertgshaw2-redhat tested on H200 with `nvidia/Llama-4-Scout-17B-16E-Instruct-FP8`:

| Approach | Load Time |
|----------|-----------|
| Original (buggy) | 78 sec |
| `.contiguous()` on CPU | 88 sec (slower - adds CPU alloc overhead) |
| **GPU-first** `.to('cuda').transpose()` | **37 sec (2.1x faster)** |

comments.author: robertgshaw2-redhat
comments.body:
> [@robertgshaw2-redhat](https://github.com/robertgshaw2-redhat) tested on H200 with `nvidia/Llama-4-Scout-17B-16E-Instruct-FP8`:
> 
> Approach	Load Time
> Original (buggy)	78 sec
> `.contiguous()` on CPU	88 sec (slower - adds CPU alloc overhead)
> **GPU-first** `.to('cuda').transpose()`	**37 sec (2.1x faster)**
> The GPU-first approach works well. You mentioned it's "not reasonable as an actual solution" - what are the specific concerns? Is it GPU memory during loading, or multi-GPU compatibility?
> 
> Happy to implement a different approach if preferred.

I thought it was a hack because we have:
- the param, which is loaded into gpu memory (empty tensor)
- the loaded_weight, which is coming from disk and is mapped into cpu memory

Right now, we have a simple trustworthy process where we never have a copy of `loaded_weight` in GPU ram. We simply call `._copy()` which copies the loaded wieight into the param. This guarantees that we do not have any straggling gpu memory from weight loading

If we move the loaded weight in to gpu memory, we have to be 100% certain that we put it back. This is kind of a can of worms IMO and I don't think we should do something like this to solve an edge case like a single model with a single quant framework (especially for a model that has limited usage like this)

So my preference would be to figure out if its possible to ensure that the cpu weights remain contiguous rather than moving them to the gpu unless we have a clean way to manage the lifecycle of the weight

comments.author: rohithputha
comments.body:
Hi, 
I have analyzed the possible causes for this issue. 
I have found some to be:
1. I believe there are two types of expert placement strategies: Linear and Round Robin. Linear is better for memory movement between CPU and GPU. I suspected that this problem might have been caused by the use of round-robin placement which causes multiple DMAs. But it turns out that the default is linear and mostly likely linear placement is being used.
2. One more root cause that I learnt might be that .transpose() in torch. PyTorch just Performs metadata remapping for transposing and hence this causes non contagious tensors and hence multiple DMA invokes.

These are some theories. I would like to test some solutions like performing indexing first, transferring to GPU and then performing transpose operations. 

I am new to contributing to vLLM and open source in general. If this approach works for you, I would like this to be assigned to me. Also, one note that I don't have Nvidia gpu to test and benchmark the changes. any leads or help or guidance regarding that would be appreciated.

Hey @rohithputha - thanks for your contribution. I think it will be tough to contribute to this type of feature without a GPU. There are many clouds you can rent them from. Otherwise, I would suggest looking into a different feature.

This does not have anything to do with linear vs round robin. The root cause of the issue is that the model opt checkpoints on disk are in a different "fused" format which require reshaping to get into the runtime format. The indexing associated with this casues the issue. The ideal solution here could be to figure out if its possible to avoid making things non-contiguous. It very well may not be possible and so we might have to hack around it by moving things to the gpu first, whihc as I said above is not ideal

comments.author: jadechip
comments.body:
Ran a few experiments against this issue and wanted to share the results in case they are useful.

- I was able to reproduce the slow post-warmup load: ~`495s` on 2x RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell.
- The trace supports the issue hypothesis: the hot path is CPU -> GPU copies from non-contiguous CPU tensors in the Llama-4/ModelOpt MoE loader.
- Tried two fixes but did **not** help:

1. Make routed expert source tensors contiguous before copy:

```text
measured load: 532.63s
routed_experts.copy: 4080 ms
make_contiguous: 609790 ms
```

This made the copy cheap but made total load time worse -_-

2. Slice the local TP shard first, move only that shard to GPU, transpose on GPU, and skip the later TP narrow:

```text
measured load: 494.73s
routed_experts.copy: 0 measured events
local shard -> device: 465178 ms
```

This removed the `routed_experts.copy` hotspot, but did not improve wall-clock time.

I guess the expensive part is repeatedly consuming these non-contiguous CPU views. The simple fixes above mostly move the cost around. A better fix probably needs to avoid creating those views, or load/reshape the checkpoint tensors in an order closer to the final parameter layout?

comments.author: jadechip
comments.body:
Small follow-up to my earlier benchmark comment.

I tried the “don’t fight the CPU view layout, use an existing GPU safetensors loader” path as well. This is not a real loader-side fix for the non-contiguous tensor issue, but it does seem like the best practical workaround I found so far.

Same model/setup as before:

- `nvidia/Llama-4-Scout-17B-16E-Instruct-FP8`
- TP=2
- 2x RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition
- warm HF cache

| Load path | Load time |
| --- | ---: |
| default safetensors | 495.4s |
| `--load-format fastsafetensors` | 326.6s |
| `--load-format instanttensor` | 301.3s |

So `instanttensor` was ~39% faster than the default path, and `fastsafetensors` was ~34% faster.

Happy to turn this into a small docs PR calling this out for large ModelOpt/Llama-4 FP8 checkpoints? Something like recommending `--load-format instanttensor` or `--load-format fastsafetensors` when startup time is dominated by weight loading.

cc @robertgshaw2-redhat
