comments.author: ishrith-gowda
comments.body:
@guptapiyush16 @LeonxLJX heads up before you start, there are 3 open PRs against this issue already.

| PR | author | approach | file |
|---|---|---|---|
| #46766 | @pratheeknathani | `.contiguous()` before the copy | `models/llama4.py` |
| #50227 | @Dev-with-Mouzan | same, inline at the weight_loader call | `models/llama4.py` |
| #47580 | me | flip the strided side to the destination, no CPU gather | `layers/fused_moe/routed_experts.py` |

#46766 and #50227 are the same fix. `.contiguous()` is a no-op if already contiguous, so the conditional in #46766 and the unconditional call in #50227 do the same thing. #46766 was first, 2026-06-25.

That fix works but it makes the strided CPU gather explicit instead of removing it: `.contiguous()` still walks non-contiguous host memory element by element, then transfers the result densely. Same shape as #32081 (~68s to ~60s above), matches @jadechip's traces showing the cost moving, not disappearing.

#47580 removes the gather. Undoing the transpose recovers the contiguous on-disk slab for free, so the H2D transfer is dense with no CPU-side gather, and the layout change happens as a strided write on the device instead. No loaded weight ever sits in GPU memory, so it doesn't hit @robertgshaw2-redhat's lifecycle concern with GPU-first approaches. TP-narrowed slabs degrade to row-run memcpys instead of elementwise gathers.

Numbers: fp8 62.8ms to 4.0ms (15.8x), bf16 93.4ms to 7.5ms (12.4x) per copy on an A100-80G. End to end on a 24-layer truncation, 18.8s to 12.5s. @eric1932 then ran the full 48-layer model on 1x H200 with source-hash-verified builds and paired runs: 102.58s to 23.63s median, 4.34x, identical output tokens across all six runs. Thanks for that, it's exactly the full-model H200 datapoint this needed.

Two tradeoffs worth naming. It's in `routed_experts.py`, not `llama4.py`, so it covers any fused-MoE checkpoint that arrives transposed, not just Llama-4/ModelOpt. It's also bigger: +145/-3 vs +8/-0 and +5/-1, mostly a test file covering contiguous/transposed/TP-narrowed layouts across fp8/bf16/fp32; the fix itself is about 35 lines. If a maintainer wants the one-liner now and the general fix later, that's a fine call, I'd rather see this issue closed than fight for the merge.

Happy to rebase (it's ~2200 commits behind, still conflict-free) or split out the test file if that helps review.

items.title: [Bug]:  Streaming reasoning content misrouted to `content` when `stop` parameter is set (stop buffer desynchronizes `delta_text` from `delta_token_ids`
items.author: huanghuan3
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment
The output of python collect_env.py ```text Your output of `python collect_env.py` here ```
### 🐛 Describe the bug ## How you would like to use vLLM Using the OpenAI-compatible streaming API with a Qwen3 reasoning model, a `stop` parameter, and `include_stop_str_in_output=false` (the default). When the model's output crosses the `` boundary within a single batch of tokens (e.g. under MTP / speculative decoding / async output), the reasoning tail and `` marker leak into `content` instead of being correctly split between `reasoning_content` and `content`. ## The bug ### Summary When a streaming request carries a non-empty `stop` list and `include_stop_str_in_output=false`, the V1 detokenizer holds back up to `max(len(stop)) - 1` characters of visible text in a **stop buffer** to avoid prematurely emitting a stop string. However, the corresponding `delta_token_ids` are **not** buffered — they reflect all tokens generated in the current round. This creates a desynchronization between two inputs that the reasoning parser receives simultaneously: | Input | Source | Buffered? | |---|---|---| | `delta_text` | `detokenizer.get_next_output_text()` → `output.text` | **Yes** (stop buffer holds tail) | | `delta_token_ids` | `output.token_ids` (raw incremental token IDs) | **No** | The Qwen3 reasoning parser uses `delta_token_ids` to detect `` and `delta_text` to split the string. When the stop buffer delays the `` text but the token IDs already report it, the parser's state machine advances prematurely, and the subsequently released text is routed entirely to `content`. ### Concrete example Suppose the model generates in one batch: ```text 我已经想好了你好 ``` With `stop=["你好"]` and `include_stop_str_in_output=false`, `stop_buffer_length = len("你好") - 1 = 1`. **Round 1** — stop buffer holds back the last character(s): | | Value | |---|---| | `delta_text` (after stop buffer) | `我已经` | | `delta_token_ids` | tokens for `我已经想好了你好` | Parser (`qwen3_reasoning_parser.py:123`): `end_token_id in delta_token_ids` → **True**, but `delta_text.find("")` → **-1** (text not yet visible). Parser returns `None` (line 136). The reasoning text `想好了` is silently dropped. **Round 2** — stop buffer releases the remaining text: | | Value | |---|---| | `delta_text` | `想好了你好` | | `delta_token_ids` | `[]` (no new tokens) | Parser (line 142): `end_token_id in previous_token_ids` → **True** (it was in round 1's tokens). Parser returns `DeltaMessage(content="想好了你好")`. Everything — including `` — goes to `content`. **Result:** ```json { "reasoning_content": "我已经", "content": "想好了你好" } ``` **Expected:** ```json { "reasoning_content": "我已经想好了", "content": "你好" } ``` ### Why MTP / speculative decoding amplifies this MTP and async output make it more likely that a single returned batch spans the `reasoning tail → → content head` boundary. Combined with the stop buffer delaying `delta_text` by one or more rounds, the text window and the token window become misaligned precisely at the `` boundary — the worst possible place for the parser. ## Root cause analysis ### 1. Stop buffer in the detokenizer `vllm/v1/engine/detokenizer.py`: ```python # Line 86-89: stop buffer length if self.stop and not self.include_stop_str_in_output: self.stop_buffer_length = max(len(s) for s in self.stop) - 1 else: self.stop_buffer_length = 0 # Line 148-164: get_next_output_text holds back tail characters def get_next_output_text(self, finished: bool, delta: bool) -> str: buffer_length = 0 if finished else self.stop_buffer_length ... length = len(self.output_text) - buffer_length last_offset = self._last_output_text_offset if last_offset < length: self._last_output_text_offset = length return self.output_text[last_offset:length] return "" ``` When `finished=False` and `stop` is set, the last `stop_buffer_length` characters are withheld from `delta_text`. ### 2. Token IDs are NOT buffered `vllm/entrypoints/openai/chat_completion/serving.py`: ```python # Line 755: delta_text comes from detokenizer (stop-buffered) delta_text = output.text # Line 776-780: current_token_ids from raw output.token_ids (NOT buffered) current_token_ids = previous_token_ids + as_list(output.token_ids) ``` `output.text` has passed through `get_next_output_text()` and is stop-buffered. `output.token_ids` is the raw incremental token IDs for this round — no buffering applied. ### 3. Qwen3 parser uses token IDs for state, text for splitting `vllm/reasoning/qwen3_reasoning_parser.py:95-147`: ```python def extract_reasoning_streaming(self, previous_text, current_text, delta_text, previous_token_ids, current_token_ids, delta_token_ids): ... if self.end_token_id in delta_token_ids: # line 123: token-based detection end_index = delta_text.find(self.end_token) # line 125: text-based split if end_index >= 0: reasoning = delta_text[:end_index] content = delta_text[end_index + len(self.end_token):] ... return DeltaMessage(reasoning=..., content=...) # line 136: end_token_id in IDs but not in text → return None ← BUG return None if not delta_text: return None elif self.end_token_id in previous_token_ids: # line 142: already ended return DeltaMessage(content=delta_text) # ← everything → content else: return DeltaMessage(reasoning=delta_text) ``` The desynchronization scenario: 1. **Round 1**: `end_token_id in delta_token_ids` is True (token is present), but `delta_text.find(end_token)` is -1 (text held by stop buffer). items.title: [Bug] GLM-5.3-Flash on SM120: fa4 attention backend crashes at CUDA-graph capture (hybrid extend reshape) — triton is the only working backend
items.author: Lei-010
items.body_excerpt:
# GLM-5.3-Flash on SM120 (RTX PRO 6000): attention backend matrix — fa4 crashes on hybrid extend, triton is the only working path

## Environment

- 8× NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 (SM120, 96 GB each), driver/CUDA as stock
- SGLang `lmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.20` docker image (built 2026-09-18)
- Model: `zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash` (official FP8 weights, TP8)
- Draft (for spec decoding legs): `incoai/GLM-5.3-Flash-DFlash2` (DFlash2DraftModel, sha256-verified)
- `--trust-remote-code`, `--context-length 131072`, `--mem-fraction-static 0.85`

## Summary

We systematically tested every attention backend that boots for Glm5Next on SM120. **Only `triton` works.** Both `flashinfer`-default (trtllm-gen fmha — already tracked in #40558) and `fa4` crash during engine init / CUDA-graph capture. The fa4 failure is a distinct bug: a shape reshape error in `forward_extend` that also reproduces **without** speculative decoding, i.e. it is not DFlash2-specific.

## Backend matrix (all TP8)

| Config | Result |
|---|---|
| default (trtllm-gen fmha) | ❌ `TllmGenFmhaRunner ... Unsupported architecture` (see #40558) |
| `--attention-backend fa4` + DFLASH | ❌ see below |
| `--attention-backend fa4`, no spec | ❌ same error — **reproduces without spec decoding** |
| `--prefill-attention-backend fa4 --attention-backend triton` + DFLASH | ❌ same error at decode capture |
| `--attention-backend triton` + DFLASH | ✅ healthy, accept len 2.73–3.90 |
| `--attention-backend triton`, no spec | ✅ healthy |

## fa4 failure signature

```python
RuntimeError: shape '[-1, 64, 8, 0]' is invalid for input of size 753975296
```

Stack (abridged):

```
sglang/srt/model_executor/runner/decode_cuda_graph_runner.py, line 464, in __init__ → self.capture()
  ... capture_one_shape → self.backend.capture_one
sglang/srt/layers/radix_attention.py, line 290, in forward
sglang/srt/layers/attention/hybrid_linear_attn_backend.py, line 1327, in forward → 1276, forward_extend
sglang/srt/layers/attention/flashattention_backend.py, line 1704, in forward_extend
RuntimeError: shape '[-1, 64, 8, 0]' is invalid for input of size 753975296
```

Observations:

1. The failing view has a trailing **0** dimension — with Glm5Next's hybrid layout (KDA linear-attention layers interleaved with full-attention layers) the fa4 `forward_extend` path receives a zero-length draft/extend token axis and `reshape` fails instead of short-circuiting.
2. `flash_attention_v4_sm120` (selected automatically when `device_capability[0] == 12`) handles decode `flash_attn_with_kvcache`, but the extend path reshaping assumes a non-empty second batch axis.
3. Repro is deterministic across ≥3 containers; failure occurs at first CUDA-graph capture (bs=48, ~90 s after weights load).

## Reproducer

```bash
docker run --gpus all --network host --ipc host \
  -v /path/GLM-5.3-Flash:/model:ro \
  --entrypoint python3 lmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.20 \
  -m sglang.launch_server --model /model --tp 8 --trust-remote-code \
  --attention-backend fa4 --port 8000 --mem-fraction-static 0.85
# → RuntimeError: shape '[-1, 64, 8, 0]' is invalid ... at decode graph capture
```

## Working config (for anyone blocked on this)

```bash
... --attention-backend triton [--speculative-algorithm DFLASH --speculative-draft-model-path /draft]
```

With `triton`, GLM-5.3-Flash FP8 TP8 serves fine on SM120, and DFLASH spec decoding reaches accept len ~3.3 (block_size 8). Note prefill throughput with triton is low (~140 tok/s on an 8K prompt, single stream), which is why a working fa4/flashinfer path on SM120 matters.

Happy to provide full logs if useful.

items.title: [Feature]  Streamed restore: chunked materialization for oversized storage hits in buffer_only HiCache mode
items.author: R-omk
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Motivation


`--hicache-host-memory-mode buffer_only` (PR #34798 + #36345) turned host RAM
into a pure staging buffer between L3 (disk) and L1 (VRAM), which fixed a
whole class of L2/L1 consistency problems. But it introduced a hard sizing
constraint: **a storage hit larger than the empty host arena is rejected
wholesale** (`_reject_oversized_prefetch` → *"declined: cannot fit in an
empty host arena"*), and the entire prompt is recomputed by prefill even
though every one of its pages exists on disk.

In practice this forces `--hicache-size` to be at least as large as the
longest conversation (host RAM ≈ max context), defeating the point of a
"transit buffer" for long-context agentic workloads:

- Qwen3.8-27B hybrid GDN, 524k context (YaRN), TP=4: `hicache-size 6`
  (~24 GiB of pinned host RAM across ranks) just to guarantee that a 500k
  restore never gets declined.
- Cold prefill of a 300k prompt: **~89 s** at ~3.4k tok/s. The same prompt
  is fully written to L3 via `write_through`, yet it is still re-prefilled
  from scratch whenever it exceeds the arena.

What buffer_only is missing is the ability to **stream an oversized hit
through a small arena in chunks**, the same way a download streams through
a bounded socket buffer — the arena should be a throughput knob, not a
capacity ceiling.



## Proposed approach

Split an oversized hit into arena-sized chunks and pipeline them:

1. **Trim** (`_trim_oversized_prefetch`): instead of rejecting, cut the hit
   to the largest page-aligned prefix that fits an *empty* arena
   (anti-livelock: a busy arena still defers the whole hit) and park the
   remainder in a `pending_stream_tails` registry.
2. **Materialize** (`_materialize_stream_chunk`): an intermediate chunk is
   published straight to the device tree as a **KV-only leaf** (evict →
   `cc.load` H2D → root-relative insert with the stock ownership
   choreography and a fail-stop post-insert check). The mamba state is
   not needed mid-span: the tree keeps FULL-only leaves valid, and the
   joint match excludes them until the endpoint checkpoint lands.
3. **Continue** (`_finish_stream_chunk` at the H2D ack): free the bounce,
   unpin the leaf, settle the chunk's share of the storage-hit accounting,
   and re-issue the parked tail as a fresh prefetch into the hit drain —
   which may trim again for 3+ chunk spans.
4. **Admit**: the *final* chunk rides the normal staged-admission path; by
   then the device tree holds every earlier chunk, `prepare_staged_prefetch`
   plans from the FULL match over the whole span, and the mamba endpoint
   checkpoint arrives with the tail's TRAILING_PAGES fetch.

The main invariants the implementation must preserve: the admission gate
has to hold the request across the whole chunk cycle (it spans scheduler
ticks where `ongoing_prefetch` is empty); each chunk's H2D needs an explicit
`start_loading()` (stock only submits loads during admission, which the
gate withholds) plus a `has_free_load_back_slot()` check; and the Rust
TreeCore currently expects a donated `mamba_value` on every insert
(`rust/sglang-radix-tree/src/components/mamba.rs`), so KV-only leaves today
require `SGLANG_UNIFIED_RADIX_TREE_CORE_BACKEND=python` or a Rust-side
change. The full lifecycle rules (anchor pins, stale-tail rebasing,
accounting) are documented in the patch header linked below.

## Measured results

TP=4 RTX 5090, Qwen3.8-27B NVFP4 hybrid GDN, 298,567-token prompt, L3 on
PCIe Gen5 NVMe RAID0, sglang main `ed8c3139f1` (2026-10-16). `hicache-size`
is per-rank GiB (TP=4): size 6 ≈ 24 GiB total, size 2 ≈ 8 GiB total.

| Metric | Before (size 6, whole-hit-or-decline) | After (size 2, streamed) |
|---|---|---|
| Host staging RAM (TP=4 total) | 24 GiB (arena 647k > max ctx — streaming never triggers) | **8 GiB** (arena 216k) |
| Warm restore from disk (L1 empty) | n/a at size 2 — would decline & re-prefill **~89 s** | **15.5 s** (2 chunks: 215,680 + 82,880; 298,560/298,567 tokens from storage = 99.998%) |
| Repeat hit after restore | 0.4 s (L1) | 0.4 s (L1) |
| Decode / EAGLE over restored ctx | 144 tok/s, accept 0.68 | unchanged |

Server flags for the "After" column (full setup in the Gist):

```bash
--enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-host-memory-mode buffer_only \
--hicache-size 2 --hicache-mem-layout page_first --hicache-io-backend kernel \
--hicache-write-policy write_through --hicache-storage-backend file \
--hicache-storage-prefetch-policy timeout --page-size 64 --tp 4
```

RAM cost drops 3× while keeping the zero-recompute guarantee for any
conversation length; `--hicache-size` becomes a throughput/parallelism knob
instead of a correctness constraint.



### Related resources


- **Working patch (Gist)**: [`streamed-restore.patch` ](https://gist.github.com/R-omk/5ea76d1317147af28393654f58ebd859) 
  against sgl-project/sglang@ed8c3139f1 (main, 2026-10-16), three files
  (`buffer_mode/pipeline.py`, `unified_radix_cache.py`,
  `unified_cache/components/mamba.py`), ~1,100 diff lines.
  Self-contained header documents scope: TP lockstep preserved, SWA models
  excluded (declined as before), PP prefetch excluded (asserted), requires
  the Python TreeCore today.
- The decline being removed: `_reject_oversized_prefetch` in
  `python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/buffer_mode/pipeline.py`.
- Buffer-only mode foundation: #34798, #36345 (Mamba support).
- Adjacent open work the patch builds on: #41453 (in-flight storage prefetch
  retry helper — the tail re-issue reuses the same retry set),
  #44344 (write-backlog throttle — orthogonal, write side).

The patch has been exercised on single-request cold and warm restores,
modified-tail requests, and mid-cycle aborts, with correct decode output
over the restored context

items.title: [Feature]: Recency-based progressive mixed-precision KV cache
items.author: XAEAZii
items.body_excerpt:
## The feature, motivation and pitch

## Summary

I would like to propose a generic recency-based progressive mixed-precision KV cache.

Instead of storing the entire KV cache using one uniform format, vLLM would keep recently created KV blocks in a user-selected higher-precision tier and progressively quantize older completed blocks into lower-precision tiers.

The feature should **not be hardcoded to BF16 as the highest tier**. The ordered precision policy should be configurable. Examples include:

```text
BF16 -> FP8
BF16 -> FP8 -> NVFP4
BF16 -> NVFP4
FP8 -> NVFP4
NVFP4 -> a future lower-precision format
```

Example percentage-based policies:

```text
newest 20%: BF16
next 20%: FP8 E4M3
oldest 60%: NVFP4
```

or, for a cache whose highest selected precision is FP8:

```text
newest 20%: FP8 E4M3
oldest 80%: NVFP4
```

New KV entries and the active partially filled tail block would be written into the **first/highest tier selected by the policy**, which may be BF16, FP8, NVFP4, or another supported format. Once a block is complete and crosses a configured age boundary, it could be asynchronously quantized and moved to the next lower-precision pool.

This proposal is specifically about using different KV-cache formats **within the same attention layer based on block age**. It is different from layer-wise mixed precision, where different transformer layers use different formats.

## Motivation

Long-context KV caches consume a substantial amount of GPU memory. A uniform low-precision KV cache reduces memory usage, but it applies the same precision to recent and old entries.

For long-context and agentic workloads, it may be useful to preserve a recent window in the policy's selected highest precision while compressing older context more aggressively.

The intended abstraction is not a single special-case mode such as BF16 + FP8 + NVFP4. It is a generic ordered list of storage tiers. For example:

- a BF16-based policy can progressively demote blocks into FP8 and NVFP4;
- an FP8-based policy can progressively demote blocks into NVFP4;
- an NVFP4-based policy could use a future lower-precision storage format when one is supported;
- different hardware backends may expose different valid tier combinations.

This should be treated as a hypothesis that needs quality and performance benchmarking rather than an assumption that recent tokens are always more important.

## Example memory calculation

The following example uses a Llama-3.1-70B-style GQA configuration:

- context length: 64,000 tokens
- number of layers: 80
- KV heads: 8
- head dimension: 128
- both K and V are stored
- one fully populated sequence
- values are aggregated across all tensor-parallel ranks

The number of stored scalar values is:

```text
64,000 tokens × 80 layers × 2 (K and V) × 8 KV heads × 128 dimensions
= 10,485,760,000 values
```

The generic calculation for a progressive policy is:

```text
effective bits/value = sum(tier_fraction × tier_effective_bits)

KV-cache size =
    number_of_values × effective_bits_per_value / 8
```

For NVFP4, the estimates below assume packed 4-bit data and one FP8 block scale per 16 values, or approximately 4.5 effective bits per value. FP8 is approximated as 8 bits per value. Small allocator, alignment, block-table, tensor-scale, and kernel-workspace overheads are not included.

### Absolute VRAM comparison

| KV-cache policy | Effective bits/value | Total KV cache | Per GPU with TP=8 | Saving vs uniform BF16 | Capacity vs uniform BF16 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Uniform BF16 | 16.0 | 19.53 GiB | 2.44 GiB | 0.00% | 1.00x |
| Progressive: 20% BF16 + 80% FP8 | 9.6 | 11.72 GiB | 1.46 GiB | 40.00% | 1.67x |
| Uniform FP8 | 8.0 | 9.77 GiB | 1.22 GiB | 50.00% | 2.00x |
| Progressive: 20% BF16 + 20% FP8 + 60% NVFP4 | 7.5 | 9.16 GiB | 1.14 GiB | 53.13% | 2.13x |
| Progressive: 20% BF16 + 80% NVFP4 | 6.8 | 8.30 GiB | 1.04 GiB | 57.50% | 2.35x |
| Progressive: 20% FP8 + 80% NVFP4 | 5.2 | 6.35 GiB | 0.79 GiB | 67.50% | 3.08x |
| Uniform NVFP4 | ~4.5 | 5.49 GiB | 0.69 GiB | 71.88% | 3.56x |

### Correct baseline for each progressive policy

A progressive policy should be compared with a uniform cache using the policy's own highest selected precision.

| Progressive policy | Uniform reference | Progressive KV size | Uniform reference size | Saving vs its own reference | Capacity vs its own reference |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 20% BF16 + 80% FP8 | Uniform BF16 | 11.72 GiB | 19.53 GiB | 40.00% | 1.67x |
| 20% BF16 + 20% FP8 + 60% NVFP4 | Uniform BF16 | 9.16 GiB | 19.53 GiB | 53.13% | 2.13x |
| 20% BF16 + 80% NVFP4 | Uniform BF16 | 8.30 GiB | 19.53 GiB | 57.50% | 2.35x |
| 20% FP8 + 80% NVFP4 | Uniform FP8 | 6.35 GiB | 9.77 GiB | 35.00% | 1.54x |

This distinction is important:

- `BF16 -> FP8 -> NVFP4` is a BF16-based progressive policy and should primarily be compared with uniform BF16.
- `FP8 -> NVFP4` is an FP8-based progressive policy and should primarily be compared with uniform FP8.
- Uniform FP8 is therefore not merely a competing alternative to one BF16-based progressive mode; it can itself be the highest tier of another progressive policy.
- Uniform NVFP4 is the lowest uniform format in this example. The same abstraction should extend below NVFP4 when a supported lower-precision format becomes available.

### Breakdown: BF16 -> FP8 -> NVFP4

Policy:

```text
newest 20%: BF16
next 20%: FP8
oldest 60%: NVFP4
```

| Tier | Tokens | Format | Estimated memory |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Recent/hot | 12,800 | BF16 | 3.91 GiB |
| Intermediate/warm | 12,800 | FP8 | 1.95 GiB |
| Old/cold | 38,400 | NVFP4 | 3.30 GiB |
| **Total** | **64,000** | Mixed | **9.16 GiB** |

Compared with uniform BF16, this policy saves approximately **10.38 GiB**, or **53.13%**, per 64K sequence.

### Breakdown: FP8 -> NVFP4

Policy:

```text
newest 20%: FP8
oldest 80%: NVFP4
```

| Tier | Tokens | Format | Estimated memory |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Recent/hot | 12,800 | FP8 | 1.95 GiB |
| Old/cold | 51,200 | N

items.title: [Bug]: GLM-5.3-Flash (glm5next) — recurring CUDA illegal memory access on 4xB200, surfacing in three unrelated kernels (KDA linear-attention, MHC TileLang, TRT-LLM fused MoE)
items.author: erans
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

- Image: `vllm/vllm-openai:glm53-flash-x86_64-cu130` (`sha256:2e771fa615452282cc331eb418b3ef21636fce355bea0491fca89e6d362ab703`, published 2026-08-26 — the newest `glm53-flash` tag on Docker Hub)
- `vllm.__version__` = `0.1.dev20051+g487ecf187`
- tilelang 0.1.12
- 4x NVIDIA B200 (SM100), TP=4, driver healthy: 0 uncorrected ECC, no pending page retirement, no Xid, `Remapping Failure Occurred: No` on all 4 GPUs
- Model: `zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash` (`Glm5NextForConditionalGeneration`)

Note this model is not upstream yet (#53906 is open), so this is filed against the day-0 image.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

The engine dies with `CUDA error: an illegal memory access was encountered` → `EngineDeadError`, repeatedly, under ordinary production chat traffic. Five crashes over ~6 hours, at 22 min / 10 min / 47 min / 2 h 34 min / 62 min of uptime. Before this the same box ran **15.5 h without a crash**, so it is load/state dependent rather than a startup or config error.

**The distinguishing detail: the fault surfaces in three completely unrelated kernel families, and different TP ranks of the same crash report different kernels.**

| Crash | Time (UTC) | Uptime | Faulting frame |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2026-08-28 22:48:48 | 22 min | `glm5next/nvidia/kda.py:581 _forward` → `flash_linear_attention/ops/kda.py:1576 chunk_kda_with_fused_gate` → `:1488 _fwd` → `ops/index.py:27 prepare_chunk_indices` |
| 2 | 2026-08-28 23:08:46 | 10 min | `glm5next/nvidia/model.py:558 hc_fused_post_pre` → `layers/mhc.py:409 forward_cuda` → `kernels/mhc/tilelang.py:635 mhc_fused_post_pre_tilelang` → `tilelang/jit/kernel.py:202` |
| 3 | 2026-08-29 00:18:55 | 47 min | same as #2 (`mhc_fused_post_pre_tilelang`) |
| 4 | 2026-08-29 02:58:08 | 2 h 34 min | **mixed per rank**: 3 ranks `mhc_fused_post_pre_tilelang` / `mhc_pre_big_fuse_with_norm_tilelang` (TileLang, `CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_ADDRESS`); 1 rank `chunk_kda_with_fused_gate` (`kda.py:581`, Triton) |
| 5 | 2026-08-29 05:04:08 | 62 min (PDL disabled — see below) | **mixed per rank**: TRT-LLM fused MoE `trtllm_fused_moe_dev_kernel.cu:991` on all 4 ranks; `chunk_kda_with_fused_gate` (Triton) also reported |

Because the errors are asynchronous, we read these as *where the fault surfaced*, not where it originated — `prepare_chunk_indices` calls `.tolist()`, which forces the sync that reports crash #1. Two unrelated victims suggests a single upstream corrupter (most likely in the linear-attention/state path) that other kernels then trip over.

### Serve command

```
vllm serve /workspace/models/GLM-5.3-Flash \
  --served-model-name glm-5.3-flash --tensor-parallel-size 4 \
  --max-model-len 524288 --max-num-seqs 1024 --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.94 --enable-prefix-caching \
  --reasoning-parser glm45 --tool-call-parser glm47 --enable-auto-tool-choice \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8001 --enable-prompt-tokens-details
```
`max_num_batched_tokens=16384` (default). No MTP, no LMCache, no `--mamba-cache-mode`.
Traffic is ordinary `/v1/chat/completions` (~95%) plus `/v1/responses` (~5%), 4–23 concurrent.

### What we ruled out

- **Hardware** — 0 ECC/Xid/page-retirement on all 4 GPUs.
- **Disk / JIT cache corruption** — 291 GB free.
- **Host RAM** — 48 of 1996 GB used.
- **A new client or changed workload** — same client IPs before and after the stable period.
- **`--mamba-cache-mode align`** — removed it (it is LMCache-only and LMCache was not running); crashed again at 47 min.
- **TileLang JIT-during-inference.** The JIT monitor does warn (`TileLang JIT compilation during inference: mhc_pre_big_fuse_with_norm_tilelang`) and glm5next has **no mHC warmup module** — `model_executor/warmup/` covers DSv4, Kimi-K3, Qwen and MiniMax but not glm5next, so the DSv4 warmup work (#52941, #51802, #49707, #50178) does not cover this model. **But we correlated compile timestamps against all three crashes and found none nearby** — every compile happens in the first seconds after startup. So missing warmup is a real latency gap here, but it is not this crash.
- **`cu_seqlens` int32→int64 (`878631b60`, "normalize GDN sequence offsets")** — does not apply: that fix is in `fi_chunk_gated_delta_rule` (Qwen GDN + FlashInfer), and the glm5next KDA path is pure FLA Triton and never calls it. PR head's own `glm5next/nvidia/kda.py` has no such cast and `gdn_attn.py` remains int32.

### A failed workaround worth recording

Routing `MHCFusedPostPreOp.forward_cuda` to `self.forward_native(...)` — mirroring what `forward_hip` already does when `HAS_TILELANG_MHC` is false — **produces garbage output**, e.g.

```
', in inin fenslin green tit correct correctver in correctsenswald verververver that-n anglever thatv'
```

and runs ~6x slower. So on CUDA the torch decomposition in `MHCFusedPostPreOp.forward_native` does not appear to be numerically equivalent to `mhc_fused_post_pre_tilelang`. That may be worth a separate look, given `forward_hip` relies on that same fallback for gfx942 (where TileLang MHC is already disabled for "incorrect results").

Also note `MHCFusedPostPreOp.enabled()` returns `True` unconditionally, so `-O.custom_ops=-mhc_fused_post_pre` cannot disable this op — there is no supported way to route around the TileLang kernel on CUDA.

### Code-review observation (mixed batches take the chunk path unpeeled)

`GDNAttentionMetadataBuilder` builds chunk metadata from a *prefill-only, rebased* `cu_seqlens`
and states the invariant explicitly (`gdn_attn.py`):

```python
# In a mixed non-spec batch, decodes are peeled off to the recurrent kernel (decode-first
# front slice), so build chunk metadata from the rebased prefill-only cu_seqlens; otherwise
# use the full non-spec one. _forward_core keys off the same condition, so they agree.
prefill_query_start_loc = non_spec_query_start_loc[num_decodes:] - num_decode_tokens
prefill_state_indices   = non_spec_state_indices_tensor[num_decodes:]
```

`Glm5NextKDA._forward` does **not** peel decodes. It branches `if num_

items.title: [Feature] Add configurable hash-based subdirectories to fs_native
items.author: cage-goat
items.body_excerpt:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

The `fs_native` L2 adapter currently stores all KV cache objects directly
under `base_path`. As the cache grows, this can create a large flat directory
and degrade metadata operations on some filesystems.

Supporting configurable hash-based subdirectories would distribute cache files
across directories and allow users to choose a layout appropriate for their
filesystem and workload.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Add an optional `hash_subdir_levels` setting to the `fs_native` adapter:

- `0` (default): `<base_path>/<filename>`
- `1`: `<base_path>/<hash[0:2]>/<filename>`
- `2`: `<base_path>/<hash[0:2]>/<hash[2:4]>/<filename>`

The default value should remain `0` for backward compatibility. Changing the
value for an existing cache directory would require clearing itscontents.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
A boolean option similar to NIXL dynamic's `shard_dirs` was considered, but it
would only support flat and fixed two-level layout. An explicit level provides
more flexibility while keeping the behavior predictable.

**Additional context**
I plan to submit a PR to implement this feature.

items.title: [RFC] Support VMM Allocations in lmcache-driven
items.author: bluayer
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

Serving processes may outlive their GPU allocations. A long-lived inference engine may release most of its HBM so another colocated workload can use it. When its KV remains reusable, LMCache can retain the logical KV in CPU or storage tiers and later restore it into a replacement GPU allocation. Colocated RL is one use of this pattern. Multi-model serving is another: an inactive engine can return HBM for another model server and later resume.

Engine-driven resolves the active GPU allocation in the inference worker for each transfer. lmcache-driven instead relies on an LMCache server registration of that allocation. That registration must be retired before the physical memory can be safely reclaimed and replaced before transfers resume. LMCache has no common lifecycle contract for this transition today, so choosing a virtual memory management (VMM) allocator can make lmcache-driven unavailable.

This RFC keeps both transfer modes available when an inference engine uses VMM allocations. It defines an engine-independent lifecycle contract that coordinates allocation replacement with LMCache registration retirement and re-registration. `vmm_fd` is the "experimental" registration transport to apply this contract to exportable same-node VMM allocations. `framework_ipc` remains the default, and engine-driven is unchanged.

## Terminology

- **Inference engine:** the vLLM or SGLang serving runtime, including its control components and execution workers. It coordinates scheduling and allocation-lifecycle transitions.
- **Inference worker:** an execution-side process or rank within the inference engine. It runs model execution, creates and holds its local active GPU KV allocation, and hosts the LMCache worker adapter.
- **LMCache server:** the separate LMCache MP process that manages cache storage and server-side transfer work.
- **Engine-driven:** the inference worker performs the GPU-side gather or scatter and exchanges CPU or shared-memory data with the LMCache server.
- **lmcache-driven:** the inference worker submits transfer metadata and synchronization events, while the LMCache server performs the GPU-side transfer against registered device memory.

The transfer-mode names identify where GPU-side KV movement runs. They do not identify allocation ownership. In both modes, each inference worker creates and holds its local active GPU KV allocation, while the inference engine coordinates the allocation lifecycle.

## Motivation

### Preserve transfer choice across GPU-memory handoff

An inference engine may return most of its HBM without exiting. In colocated RL, rollout yields memory to training. In multi-model serving, an inactive engine can yield memory to another model server and later resume. If KV from the same model version remains useful, LMCache can keep it in CPU or storage tiers until a replacement GPU allocation is ready.

Public inference-engine support for these allocation lifecycles is clearest today in colocated RL:

- The [vLLM Q3 2026 RL roadmap](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/48314) models transitions between sleeping and awake, paused and running, old and new weights, and stale and fresh KV. Its [scheduler lifecycle RFC](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/48311) covers drain, sleep, wake, weight update, and releasing only KV between rollout steps.
- [SGLang's RL integration](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/docs/advanced_features/sglang_for_rl.md) exposes tagged release and resume operations for `kv_cache` and `weights`. Releasing `kv_cache` flushes its logical contents, so these operations define the engine-side memory lifecycle but do not preserve reusable KV outside the released allocation.

These interfaces define when the inference engine releases and restores an allocation. They do not define whether logical KV remains valid or where it is stored while the GPU allocation is absent. Engine-driven already works with these lifecycle interfaces because no imported engine allocation survives in the LMCache server. The remaining compatibility gap is lmcache-driven, whose cross-process registration must be retired before the inference worker releases the physical memory.

The lifecycle boundary may support broader reusable-KV policies in the future, but those policies are outside this RFC.

### VMM breaks the current direct-access registration

The current lmcache-driven registration format cannot represent arbitrary VMM allocations held by an inference worker.

VMM separates the virtual address from the lifetime of the physical memory:

```text
allocation lifetime #1: pointer X -> physical allocation A
release:                pointer X -> unmapped
allocation lifetime #2: pointer X -> physical allocation B
```

The pointer can remain `X`, but an IPC registration for allocation A must not be used for allocation B. Supporting only initial VMM import would therefore be unsafe; LMCache must also drain, retire, and replace registrations as part of the inference worker's allocation lifecycle.

### What this proposal changes

The required interface has two ordering points: retire the current registration before allocator mutation, then register the replacement before transfer resumes. It also needs a unique identity for each allocation lifetime so a reused virtual address cannot resolve stale work to new physical memory.

The contract is defined around allocation retirement and replacement. `vmm_fd` applies it to exportable same-node VMM allocations; `framework_ipc` remains the default and engine-driven is unchanged.

## Proposal

The proposal has two parts:

1. An engine-independent lifecycle contract for retiring and replacing an LMCache-visible GPU allocation.
2. `vmm_fd`, an experimental same-node transport for registering POSIX-FD-exportable VMM allocations under this lifecycle contract.

The lifecycle contract is transport-independent. `vmm_fd` uses POSIX FDs on Linux, but a future transport could use CUDA Fabric or another pla

items.title: [L2][fs_native] Failed stores stay visible to lookups — later retrieves serve corrupted KV (gibberish output)
items.author: stefanskiasan
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

With the `fs_native` L2 adapter enabled, `Store task N to adapter 0 failed for
keys: [...]` warnings appear at a low but steady rate — and **every subsequent
retrieve that hits one of those keys returns corrupted KV**. The model answer
degenerates into gibberish, at temperature 0, reproducibly.

The failed store leaves the key visible to lookups. It is only a `WARNING`; no
exception is raised, and the key is not invalidated.

## Environment

- 8× MI355X (gfx950), ROCm 7.2.3, one server per 4-GPU replica
- vLLM with `glm_moe_dsa` (GLM-5.3, full model), TP4, MTP k=4,
  `--kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3`, `--block-size 16`, prefix caching on
- `LMCacheMPConnector`, `lmcache_driven` transfer mode, chunk-size 256
- Server: `--l1-size-gb 150 --separate-object-groups --eviction-policy LRU`
  `--l2-prefetch-policy retain`
  `--l2-adapter '{"type":"fs_native","base_path":"/l2","num_workers":8,"use_odirect":false}'`

## Reproduction

Two replicas, identical except for the L2 adapter:

| | replica A | replica B |
|---|---|---|
| `--l2-adapter fs_native` | yes | **no** |
| failed stores | 44 → 66 during eight requests | **0** in 25 049 stores |
| answers on a cache hit | **gibberish** | correct |

The cleanest probe is `cache_salt`, which changes only the cache key:

```
prompt without salt   (cache hit)   3.4 s   GARBAGE  '0.  district120 is0, the ...'
same prompt, new salt (cache miss)  5.0 s   CORRECT  '73605 The user has provided ...'
same prompt, new salt (cache miss)  5.0 s   CORRECT
prompt without salt   (cache hit)   3.4 s   GARBAGE  '1 district contains1.3,. ...'
```

Note the timing: the corrupted runs are **faster** than the correct ones —
they are served from the cache instead of being computed.

The corruption survives a full vLLM restart (the cache server outlives it) and
survives restarting the cache server itself, because new failures keep
occurring: 22 fresh failures during the eight requests above.

## Not the cause

- Disk: write test 4.9 GB/s into the L2 directory, inodes at 1 %, 459 GB free,
  ext4, no errors in the log and no traceback anywhere.
- vLLM side: with LMCache disabled entirely (prefix caching still on), all
  eight requests are correct.
- Recreating the same server **without** `--l2-adapter` makes the problem
  disappear completely: 0 failed stores, 8/8 correct, needle test 5/5 twice
  (the second run with a warm cache).

## Expected

A store that fails must not leave a lookup-visible key. Either the key is
rolled back on failure, or the retrieve path must validate that all object
groups for a key are actually present before serving it. Silently serving a
partially stored entry turns an I/O warning into a correctness bug that looks
like model failure — it cost us two and a half hours of debugging the model
before we suspected the cache.

Related: #4987 (IPC event churn on ROCm in the same connector).

items.title: [Bug] P2P load timeout can report terminal failure while the transfer is still active
items.author: 0andy
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**

`P2PL2Adapter.query_load_result()` returns a terminal all-zero `Bitmap` as soon as `load_timeout_s` expires, without querying or cancelling the underlying `TransferChannelClient` read ([p2p_l2_adapter.py#L333-L336](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/p2p_l2_adapter.py#L333-L336)). The read may still be in flight at that point, so the adapter reports "finished (failed)" for a load whose transfer has not reached a terminal state.

The existing test `test_load_deadline_expired_yields_failure` asserts exactly this behaviour, so I am raising it as a contract question rather than a regression: is a terminal load result allowed to precede the end of the transfer?

**To Reproduce**

On `dev` @ 8d7d2c47, add this test to `tests/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/test_p2p_l2_adapter.py`:

```python
def test_load_deadline_does_not_report_terminal_while_read_is_in_flight():
    keys = [_key(0)]
    now = [100.0]
    in_flight = TransferChannelReadResult(finished=False)
    with (
        _adapter(load_timeout_s=0.01) as (adapter, _mq, _tc_ctx, tc_client, _n),
        patch.object(p2p_mod.time, "monotonic", side_effect=lambda: now[0]),
    ):
        adapter._remote_addresses[keys[0]] = TransferChannelAddress(offset=100, size=10)
        tc_client.submit_read.return_value = 123
        tc_client.query_read_status.return_value = in_flight
        task_id = adapter.submit_load_task(
            keys, [MagicMock(shm_offset=0, shm_byte_length=10)]
        )
        now[0] = 100.02  # past the 0.01 s load deadline
        assert not in_flight.is_finished()
        assert adapter.query_load_result(task_id) is None
```

```
pytest -v tests/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/test_p2p_l2_adapter.py -k "deadline or not_finished"
```

Result (CPU-only build, transfer channel mocked):

```
>           assert adapter.query_load_result(task_id) is None
E           assert 0 is None
E            +  where 0 = query_load_result(0)

LMCache WARNING: P2P load task 0 timed out; treating as a failure (p2p_l2_adapter.py:335)

test_lookup_deadline_expired_yields_miss PASSED
test_load_not_finished_returns_none PASSED
test_load_deadline_expired_yields_failure PASSED
test_load_deadline_does_not_report_terminal_while_read_is_in_flight FAILED
1 failed, 3 passed
```

(`0` is the repr of a one-key, all-zero `Bitmap`, i.e. a terminal failure.)

This test only demonstrates the current behaviour; its assertion would need adjusting depending on which direction below is preferred.

**Expected behavior**

Either the adapter does not report a terminal load result while its transfer-channel read may still access the destination buffers, or the contract states explicitly that a terminal result does not imply the transfer has quiesced and callers handle that.

**Additional context**

To be clear about what is and is not shown:

*Reproduced (unit test above):* the read is modelled as unfinished, and after the deadline `query_load_result()` returns a terminal failure.

*Derived from reading the code, not reproduced:*
- On that result, `PrefetchController._poll_load_results()` calls `finish_write_and_delete()` for the failed keys and then `submit_unlock()` ([prefetch_controller.py#L1389-L1395](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/storage_controllers/prefetch_controller.py#L1389-L1395)); for P2P, `submit_unlock()` sends `p2p_unlock_objects` to the peer ([#L277-L280](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/p2p_l2_adapter.py#L277-L280)). So both the destination staging buffer and the source-side lock are released.
- The NIXL transfer channel registers the whole L1 buffer once ([nixl_impl.py#L344](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/transfer_channel/impl/nixl_impl.py#L344)). This creates a window in which a late read may write into memory that has since been reassigned to another key.
- After the timeout the adapter no longer queries the read, so the `NixlTransferChannelClient._tasks` entry and its xfer handle are only released on `close()` ([#L178-L181](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/transfer_channel/impl/nixl_impl.py#L178-L181), [#L202-L206](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/transfer_channel/impl/nixl_impl.py#L202-L206)).

*Not reproduced:* actual stale or corrupted KV data end to end. I have not run a two-instance NIXL test for this.

**Possible directions** (not proposing a specific fix yet)

- **A. Stay pending until the transfer is terminal.** After the deadline, keep polling `query_read_status()` and only report once it finishes. Simple ownership model; a hung transfer would hold its buffers and locks indefinitely.
- **B. Add per-task cancellation to `TransferChannelClient`** ([abstract.py#L52-L88](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/transfer_channel/abstract.py#L52-L88) has only `submit_read`, `query_read_status`, `close`), and report terminal only once the cancel is confirmed. For NIXL this would map to `releaseXferReq`, which the BackendGuide says "can return error, meaning it was not successful in aborting the request", so it still needs A as a fallback. The Mooncake wrapper has no cancel today; I have not checked the engine itself.
- **C. Drop the adapter-level load deadline** and rely on the controller-level deadline from #5255, which already keeps late loads' buffers and locks until the load result arrives.

The P2P adapter is the runtime caller of `submit_read()`; the transfer-channel benchmark also calls it directly, so an API change in B would touch both.

**Related**

- #5263 — same ownership family, on the shutdown / TTL paths rat

items.title: Unauthenticated fleet control plane on LMCache MP Coordinator (default 0.0.0.0:9300)
items.author: yyymk
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

The LMCache MP Coordinator — the fleet-level cache control plane — starts by default on 0.0.0.0:9300 with no authentication on any endpoint. A network peer registers fake cache instances, deregisters real ones (removing them from scheduling), rewrites tenant quotas, injects fabricated cache events, and enumerates the fleet's key directory. Runtime-confirmed on lmcache 0.5.5 (latest PyPI release); the companion controller API server (`lmcache.v1.api_server`, default 0.0.0.0:9000) exposes the same unauthenticated /lookup, /clear and /pin surface. Suggested severity: High, CVSS 8.8.

### Details

`lmcache.v1.mp_coordinator.config` hardcodes `host: str = "0.0.0.0", port: int = 9300`. The coordinator's FastAPI app (`lmcache/v1/mp_coordinator/app.py`) mounts routers with no authentication middleware anywhere in the package (a full-source scan for api_key/auth/token primitives returns zero hits):

- `POST /instances` / `PUT /instances/{id}/heartbeat` / `DELETE /instances/{id}` — anyone registers, keeps alive, or removes fleet instances; deletion removes the instance's reported placements from scheduling.
- `PUT /quota/config` and `PUT /quota/{cache_salt}` — fleet and per-tenant quota tampering.
- `POST /cache/pins`, `DELETE /cache/pins`, `POST /events` — pin manipulation and fabricated cache events that feed the coordinator's placement/eviction views.
- `GET /directory/keys` (paged), `POST /directory/lookup`, `POST /directory/blend-lookup` — full key directory with token-id lists and per-instance placements.

The controller API server (`lmcache/v1/api_server/__main__.py`, `--host` default 0.0.0.0, port 9000) adds `POST /lookup` (token-to-placement layout), `POST /clear` and `POST /pin` for any instance_id, likewise with no authentication.

### PoC

Environment: Linux, `pip install lmcache==0.5.5`, `python -m lmcache.v1.mp_coordinator --host 0.0.0.0 --port 9300` (`ss -ltnp` confirms 0.0.0.0:9300). From any peer:

```bash
curl -s http://192.168.105.123:9300/healthz                       # 200
# register a fake instance (schemas read from the installed package's pydantic models)
curl -s -X POST http://192.168.105.123:9300/instances -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @fake_instance.json   # 200/201
curl -s http://192.168.105.123:9300/instances                      # fake instance listed
curl -s -X PUT http://192.168.105.123:9300/instances/attacker-mp-aaa/heartbeat -d @hb.json      # 200
# remove an instance from the fleet
curl -s -X DELETE http://192.168.105.123:9300/instances/attacker-mp-bbb                          # 200
# quota tampering and event injection
curl -s -X PUT http://192.168.105.123:9300/quota/config -d @quota.json                           # 200
curl -s -X PUT http://192.168.105.123:9300/quota/default -d '{"...": 0}'                         # 200
curl -s -X POST http://192.168.105.123:9300/events -d @fake_events.json                          # 200
# fleet key directory
curl -s "http://192.168.105.123:9300/directory/keys?limit=100"                                   # keys+placements
```

Observed on 0.5.5: every call above succeeded without any credential; the fake instance appeared in `GET /instances`, the DELETE removed an instance, quota writes were accepted, `/events` accepted a fabricated batch, and `/directory/keys` returned the directory enumeration surface. The api_server on 0.0.0.0:9000 likewise answered unauthenticated `/lookup` (200 with layout structure) and accepted `/clear` and `/pin` requests. Expected secure behavior: a fleet control plane authenticates callers and authorizes instance/quota mutations.

### Impact

Any network peer that can reach the coordinator port (fixed, documented default 9300, bound on all interfaces) corrupts the fleet's shared cache state: deregistered workers disappear from placement (requests lose their cache or fail over), fake instances redirect placement decisions, quota tampering starves or floods tenants, injected events poison placement and eviction views, and the key directory discloses which prefixes (token id lists) are cached where across the fleet. Confidentiality (directory/placement disclosure), integrity (fleet membership, quotas, events), availability (instance removal, quota starvation). Suggested CVSS:3.1 vector AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:H/A:H (8.8), CWE-306. Affected: lmcache <= 0.5.5 (latest release), deployments running the MP coordinator / controller API server; no patched version yet.

items.author: realAaronWu

Parent: #5780
Dependency: external selector loading child (to be linked).

## Scope

Port only the useful bounded statistics from prior profiling work to current MP events, then provide an external StorePolicy example for DRAM L1 plus local filesystem L2. Keep L1 copies and existing eviction. Reuse canonical ObjectKey; distinguish heuristic reuse score, inter-access distance and true distinct-key reuse distance.

## Experiment

Pin Mooncake FAST25 conversation/toolagent traces and content hashes. Replay historical-only candidate policies against default/LRU/no-offload and a clearly labelled offline upper bound. Freeze capacity, timing/availability and prefix-dependency assumptions. Anonymous hashes are not real tokens: any generated token serving workload must be labelled synthetic.

## Acceptance

- Stats, queues and snapshots remain within declared bounds; no graph or unbounded per-request state is required.
- Actual StoreController submission and fs round-trip demonstrate admission behavior, while L1 copies remain usable.
- Single-GPU data correctness and optional full serving/goodput results are distinguished.
- Write-byte reduction is not sufficient: demonstrate service value at an identified bandwidth/capacity bottleneck without regressing SLOs, or report no demonstrated benefit.
- Default behavior stays unchanged. Model/revision/dtype/layout are fixed and isolated by deployment for this first experiment.

Implementation and performance evidence pending. Algorithm results do not gate the usefulness of the independent external-selector extension.

items.title: [Feature Request] Discuss optional CLOCK-FIFO eviction for MP L1
items.author: WyattJia
items.body_excerpt:
### Is your feature request related to a problem?

I'd like to discuss whether an optional CLOCK-FIFO eviction policy for the MP L1 cache would be useful before preparing a PR.

The goal is to reduce hit-path metadata work under frequent hot-prefix reuse mixed with one-time scans. Recording a reference bit instead of moving an entry on every hit may help, but this is a hypothesis, not a demonstrated end-to-end improvement.

### Describe the solution you'd like

An opt-in FIFO/second-chance eviction policy behind the existing policy interface. The exact queue and aging rules would be documented and agreed on before implementation. Existing LRU/ARC options and defaults would remain unchanged.

Could maintainers advise on:

1. **Acceptance:** Would you consider this addition alongside LRU and ARC, or prefer improvements to the existing policies?
2. **Required comparisons:** Which workloads, metrics, and validation gates would you require? Proposed comparisons against LRU and ARC include:
   - Stable hot prefixes with cold scans, shifting hot sets, all-hot/all-cold cases, and concurrent mixed reads/writes.
   - Effective prefix/token and byte hit rates, hit-path CPU cost, eviction p95/p99 latency, metadata memory, and real-engine TTFT/throughput.
   - Correctness across reservation/admission, pinned or in-flight keys, deletion confirmation, and multiple L1 instances.
3. **Review ownership:** Who would be willing to review the design and a subsequent focused PR?

### Describe alternatives you've considered

Use the existing LRU or ARC policies, or optimize their metadata paths if they address the same bottleneck. CLOCK-FIFO would need to demonstrate a useful trade-off against both; lower hit-path cost alone would not establish an overall improvement.

### Additional context

This issue asks for direction and evaluation criteria, not approval of a completed implementation. It does not propose changes to L2 placement or Mooncake's global eviction.

cc @YaoJiayi @hlin99 @zhengfeihe, listed owners of the eviction policy paths.

items.title: Performance comparison for dense shared prefix + block-diagonal local mask: custom mask in BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper vs MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper
items.author: catnanami
items.body_excerpt: I am trying to evaluate the best way to implement an attention pattern with a dense shared/global prefix plus a local block-diagonal suffix. The mask pattern is shown below: I am considering two implementations: BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper with a custom mask MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper Questions: 1. For this pattern, is cascade attention expected to be faster than paged prefill with a custom mask? 2. Or is this pattern better handled by a custom kernel/backend? My use case is speculative decoding, where all verification tokens share the same prefix KV, but each local block should only attend to its own block.

comments.author: VectorPeak
comments.body:
For the mask in the image - a dense shared prefix on the left plus independent block-diagonal local regions on the right - `MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper` is usually the better fit than `BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper` with one large custom mask.

The reason is that the custom-mask prefill path does not really exploit this structure as well: it still treats the problem like one masked attention problem over the full layout, so the block-diagonal sparsity mostly becomes masking overhead. Cascade attention lets you model this as:

- shared/global prefix KV: attended by all verification tokens
- local suffix KV: split into independent blocks/requests
- final result: merge prefix-attention state with each local block’s attention state

For speculative decoding, this is exactly the kind of case where cascade can help, especially when the shared prefix is large and the local verification blocks are relatively small. Each local block can be represented as a separate batch item sharing the same prefix. If the local part also needs causal masking inside each block, use the normal causal/local mask for that per-block suffix attention.

items.title: Misc. bug: Tokenizer (GPT-4o and Tekken pre-tokenizers): token IDs differ from HF because combining marks are split off their letters (Hindi, Thai)
items.author: tkran2
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

31288c9c6 (2026-10-18), built from source on macOS

### Operating systems

Mac

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

libllama (core library)

### Command line

```shell
./build/bin/llama-tokenize -m ~/Projects/infercheck/data/ollama-gguf/gpt-oss_20b.gguf -p "दी" --log-disable
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

The problem was that for the Hindi text `दी` (U+0926 U+0940), in llama.cpp gpt-oss gives `[2587, 840]` (two tokens), but in Hugging Face it gives `[25589]` (one token). The same problem was found for Mistral NeMo: `[4894, 2063]` versus `[44213]`.

The cause of the problem is that in `src/llama-vocab.cpp`, the rewrite `((?=[\p{L}])([^a-z]))` just checks `\p{L}`, but `\p{M}` is a part of the upstream letter classes. Therefore, a word cannot be continued by a combining mark. Rather, it becomes its own pre-token. This is located in two different places. It was found in the `TEKKEN` case and the `GPT4O`/`MINIMAX_M2` case.

This rewrite was first introduced by PR #8579 in 2024. The author there said that the `M` category is ignored but they could not find a test case that failed. A reviewer said it should be fixed at some point. The दी repro above is this failing case.

This has been fixed before. `GRANITE_EMB_MULTI` (#22716) uses `(?=[\p{L}\p{M}])`. It is the same regex as the other and has applied the fix, but it is just for that specific model.

This affects these `tokenizer.ggml.pre` values: `gpt-4o` (gpt-oss, Muse Spark), `llama4`, `kanana2`, `talkie`, `minimax-m2`, `tekken`.

The impact is that gpt-oss token counts on ordinary sentences differ for certain languages. Hugging Face versus llama.cpp: 15 versus 28 for Hindi, 9 versus 18 for Bengali, 11 versus 17 for Tamil, 8 versus 15 for Telugu, and 12 versus 16 for Thai. The impact is also longer prompts, and there are token sequences which were never seen by the model during its training.

I found this by using differential testing versus Hugging Face using my tool (https://github.com/tkran2/infercheck). For gpt-oss there were 271 disagreements in 7,248 test strings, and with the fix there are none.

I have a two-line fix, which adds `\p{M}` to the lookaheads in each of the two places. All 15 of the already existing `test-tokenizer-0` vocabs continue to pass, and a gpt-oss vocab file run using the standard test strings does not pass on master but does with the fix added. It is caught by the Khmer text in the standard set.

I have a question for the maintainers. Should the test vocab be put in `models/` (around 13 MB) or should it be put in `ggml-org/vocabs`? Should one case be shared by `GPT4O` and `GRANITE_EMB_MULTI` since the regex is the same?

### First Bad Commit

_No response_

<summary>Logs</summary>

```console
$ ./build/bin/llama-tokenize -m gpt-oss_20b.gguf -p "दी" --log-disable

items.title: [Store] Offload completion can attach a stale LOCAL_DISK replica to a republished key
items.author: Aionw
items.body_excerpt:
An offload completion is matched to the key, not to the publication it was queued for. The offload task carries tenant, key and size; the completion carries where it wrote. The master's only link between them is `state.offloading_task`.

`EraseMetadata` clears that marker, but a store worker that has already drained the task keeps writing its SSD copy. If the key is erased and republished before the completion arrives, the completion finds no marker. `handled_existing_object` stays false, and the completion falls through to `AddReplicaForRetainedClient`, which attaches the LOCAL_DISK replica to whatever publication the key holds now. Nothing compares the object's size or content.

A plain `Remove` is enough to trigger it: the lease is already expired after `PutEnd`, and `Remove` does not check for an offload task. (`UpsertStart`, by contrast, refuses while a worker owns the task.)

Possible fixes:
- have the offload task carry a publication identity and the completion echo it back (a wire change), or
- have every erase path refuse, or leave a tombstone, while a worker owns the offload task.

Pre-existing on main. Found by @CAICAIIs in review of #4717.

items.title: [Feature] Unified JIT / Precompilation Cache Directory
items.author: whybeyoung
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [ ] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [ ] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Motivation


## Summary

**Request:** Unify all JIT and precompilation cache paths under a single configurable root so that users and operators can manage cache location, size, and persistence in one place. The current situation is fragmented across multiple env vars and default paths (including `/tmp`), which makes it hard to reason about where compiled artifacts live and to reuse caches across runs or machines.

## Current State (Fragmented)

### 1. Triton JIT cache

| What | Env var / source | Default / behavior |
|------|------------------|--------------------|
| Direct `@triton.jit` (e.g. allocator, MoE kernels) | `TRITON_CACHE_DIR` (Triton runtime) | Triton default: `~/.triton/cache`; often overwritten by Inductor to a path under `/tmp/torchinductor_*` |
| SGLang override | `SGLANG_TRITON_CACHE_DIR` (if implemented) | e.g. `~/.triton/cache` or `~/.cache/triton` |

- Set only in some entry paths (engine, gRPC launcher, scheduler process); custom/PD launchers may not set it.
- When PyTorch Inductor runs first, it can set `TRITON_CACHE_DIR` to its own subdir, so later Triton JIT (including allocator) writes under `/tmp`.

### 2. PyTorch Inductor (torch.compile)

| What | Env var / source | Default / behavior |
|------|------------------|--------------------|
| Inductor cache | `TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR` (PyTorch) | `/tmp/torchinductor_<user>` (or similar) |
| SGLang override | `SGLANG_TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR` (if implemented) | e.g. `~/.cache/sglang/inductor` |

- Default lives in `/tmp`, so cache is often non-persistent and can conflict with other users on shared nodes.

### 3. DeepGEMM JIT cache

| What | Env var / source | Default / behavior |
|------|------------------|--------------------|
| DeepGEMM cache | `SGLANG_DG_CACHE_DIR` / `DG_JIT_CACHE_DIR` | `~/.cache/deep_gemm` |

- Set in `layers/deep_gemm_wrapper/compile_utils.py`; separate from Triton/Inductor.
- 
## Problems

1. **No single root:** Triton, Inductor, SGLang torch_compile, and DeepGEMM each have their own env or default; some write to `/tmp`, others to `~/.cache/...`.

## Proposal

### 1. Introduce a single JIT cache root

- **New env var:** `SGLANG_JIT_CACHE_ROOT` (or `SGLANG_CACHE_ROOT` if we want to align with existing `SGLANG_CACHE_ROOT` in custom_all_reduce_utils).
- **Default:** `~/.cache/sglang` (or `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/sglang` when set).
- **Semantics:** All JIT/precompilation caches that SGLang controls should live under this root in fixed subdirs.

### 2. Standard layout under the root

Suggested subdirs (all under `SGLANG_JIT_CACHE_ROOT`):

| Subdir | Purpose | Maps from |
|--------|---------|-----------|
| `triton/` | Triton JIT (direct `@triton.jit` and, when possible, Triton used by Inductor) | `TRITON_CACHE_DIR` |
| `inductor/` | PyTorch Inductor (torch.compile) | `TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR` |
| `torch_compile/` | SGLang torch.compile cache (hash-based, when using SGLangBackend) | `SGLANG_CACHE_DIR` + `torch_compile_cache` |
| `deep_gemm/` | DeepGEMM JIT | `SGLANG_DG_CACHE_DIR` / `DG_JIT_CACHE_DIR` |

- If we keep backward compatibility, existing env vars (`SGLANG_TRITON_CACHE_DIR`, `SGLANG_TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR`, `SGLANG_CACHE_DIR`, `SGLANG_DG_CACHE_DIR`) could override the default subdir path when set; otherwise they are derived as `{SGLANG_JIT_CACHE_ROOT}/{subdir}`.

CC @Fridge003 @hnyls2002

items.title: RFC: Plugin Extension Points Needed for MetaX GPU Support
items.author: yangxin-mx
items.body_excerpt:
# Proposal: Generalize SGLang Hardware Plugin Interfaces for MetaX GPU Support

> Discussion draft based on a SGLang 0.5.19-derived codebase. The names below are proposed API shapes, not claims that they already exist on the latest `main` branch. If an equivalent upstream seam already exists, we would prefer to use or extend it. This is an umbrella discussion that can be split into smaller PRs.

SGLang already has useful foundations: hardware-platform entry points, `SRTPlatform.init_backend()`, an explicit OOT forward registry for fused ops, and MoE runner/fused-function registration. See the [plugin documentation](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/docs/docs/hardware-platforms/plugin.mdx) and [expert-parallelism documentation](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/docs/docs/advanced_features/expert_parallelism.mdx). When adapting another CUDA-compatible GPU, however, we still encounter framework call sites that select a built-in class, import a vendor implementation, or call a kernel through a module-level symbol before a platform plugin can participate.

Our goal is to make required hardware behavior expressible through platform methods and explicit, typed registries. We do **not** propose replacing module globals or monkey-patching framework functions. A missing optional platform implementation should preserve the current built-in behavior; a selected but unsupported implementation should fail with a clear capability error rather than silently run an incompatible kernel. The plugin owns its vendor kernels and package dependencies. The framework owns common algorithms, selection rules, lifecycle, and validation.

The Python snippets below illustrate **proposed interfaces and call sites, not complete, runnable code already present in the repository**. `ExampleGpuPlatform` and `vendor_ops` stand for any vendor plugin. Exact parameters should be settled against existing types and call paths in the corresponding PRs. Each section shows both where the framework would connect the extension point and how a plugin would use it.

## 1. JIT toolchain and cache identity

### Adaptation problem

In the 0.5.19-derived tree, JIT compilation derives the device compiler, architecture and flags through CUDA/ROCm-oriented paths in `kernels/jit/utils/compile/toolchain.py`. The build path (`ninja.py`) and cache path (`cache.py`) must agree on these values. A plugin cannot safely supply a different device compiler by changing only one path: the cache may reuse a binary built for another SDK or architecture.

### Plugin-oriented proposal

- Add an optional `SRTPlatform.get_jit_toolchain() -> JitToolchainSpec | None`. The immutable spec should include the host/device compilers, toolkit root, target architecture, include/link paths and flags, plus an explicit SDK/ABI cache identity.
- Resolve the spec lazily when compilation starts, and pass the **same resolved spec** to command generation and cache-key generation. `None` keeps the existing built-in toolchain logic.
- Let the vendor plugin package its AOT extensions itself. The common AOT setup need not import or name each vendor SDK.

On the framework side, add the optional method in `srt/platforms/interface.py` and have `kernels/jit/utils/compile/{toolchain,ninja,cache}.py` consume the same spec:

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class JitToolchainSpec:
    host_compiler: str
    device_compiler: str
    toolkit_root: str
    target_arch: str
    device_flags: tuple[str, ...] = ()
    include_dirs: tuple[str, ...] = ()
    link_flags: tuple[str, ...] = ()
    cache_identity: str = ""  # SDK/ABI version

class SRTPlatform(DeviceMixin):
    def get_jit_toolchain(self) -> JitToolchainSpec | None:
        return None

def compile_extension(source, **kwargs):
    spec = resolve_jit_toolchain(get_platform().get_jit_toolchain())
    cache_key = make_cache_key(source, spec=spec, **kwargs)
    return build_with_ninja(source, spec=spec, cache_key=cache_key, **kwargs)
```

The plugin only describes its own SDK; it does not modify global `CUDA_HOME` or framework compiler symbols:

```python
class ExampleGpuPlatform(SRTPlatform):
    def get_jit_toolchain(self) -> JitToolchainSpec:
        return JitToolchainSpec(
            host_compiler="/opt/example/bin/c++",
            device_compiler="/opt/example/bin/device-cc",
            toolkit_root="/opt/example",
            target_arch="example-arch",
            cache_identity="example-sdk-1:abi-1",
        )
```

## 2. Device properties and per-operator Triton tuning

### Adaptation problem

Several launch paths infer hardware behavior from CUDA properties or NVIDIA/AMD architecture names, while `num_stages`, warps, tile sizes and shared-memory limits are selected locally. A plugin may expose a CUDA-compatible device but still need different launch parameters; pretending to be a particular SM is not a sound capability contract.

### Plugin-oriented proposal

- Expose a read-only `DeviceKernelProfile` through the active platform, with architecture identifier, warp size, maximum shared-memory bytes and relevant device capabilities.
- Add an optional `tune_triton_launch(op, shape, dtype, default) -> TritonLaunchConfig`. Each caller first computes its present default, then asks the active platform for a per-operator override and validates it before launch. There should be no global change to Triton's defaults.
- Start with launch sites where hardware differences actually affect correctness or feasibility (MoE, quantization and attention), keeping other paths unchanged.

The framework could define device facts in `srt/platforms/device_mixin.py`/`interface.py` and consume the policy immediately before each Triton launch, keeping hardware facts separate from per-operator tuning:

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class DeviceKernelProfile:
    arch: str
    warp_size: int
    max_shared_memory_bytes: int

@dataclass(frozen=

items.title: [Bug] SGLANG_NGRAM_FORCE_GREEDY_VERIFY does not force greedy NGRAM verification
items.author: SeverinVisionary
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [ ] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [ ] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [ ] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [ ] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

The latest-version box is unchecked because this is source inspection at the recorded main pin, with no installed-runtime comparison.

### Describe the bug

Expected: The [guide](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/6a7abcfc9b603d494cdc58fa54bc793a915b547c/docs/docs/advanced_features/speculative_decoding.mdx#L847) documents that `SGLANG_NGRAM_FORCE_GREEDY_VERIFY=True` selects greedy NGRAM verification.

Actual: In source inspection at the recorded main pin, the flag remains [registered as `EnvBool(False)`](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/6a7abcfc9b603d494cdc58fa54bc793a915b547c/python/sglang/srt/environ.py#L1442), but supplies no input to the verification branch.

NGRAM calls [`eagle_sample`](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/6a7abcfc9b603d494cdc58fa54bc793a915b547c/python/sglang/srt/speculative/ngram_worker.py#L482). Its [greedy predicate](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/6a7abcfc9b603d494cdc58fa54bc793a915b547c/python/sglang/srt/speculative/eagle_utils.py#L705-L717) and [call site](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/6a7abcfc9b603d494cdc58fa54bc793a915b547c/python/sglang/srt/speculative/eagle_utils.py#L815-L820) use sampling, platform, and rejection-sampling conditions, without this flag. The generic [state exporter](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/6a7abcfc9b603d494cdc58fa54bc793a915b547c/python/sglang/srt/environ.py#L1925-L1932) can read its value for reporting, but does not control verification. I have not compared generated outputs.

Could NGRAM read the flag and pass an explicit greedy override, scoped to NGRAM so EAGLE is unchanged? If the option is obsolete, please retire the registry entry and documented references together.

The older implementation in [#13153](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/13153) was merged on 2025-11-12 and read the flag; [#13116](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/13116#issuecomment-4676257473) was superseded by that implementation.

### Reproduction

The raw `git grep` was run in a source-only upstream Git clone. This location-only form searches the tracked tree at the pin and omits match text:

```bash
git grep -n -F 'SGLANG_NGRAM_FORCE_GREEDY_VERIFY' 6a7abcfc9b603d494cdc58fa54bc793a915b547c -- . | cut -d: -f1-3
```

Expected output from the recorded matches:

```text
6a7abcfc9b603d494cdc58fa54bc793a915b547c:docs/docs/advanced_features/speculative_decoding.mdx:847
6a7abcfc9b603d494cdc58fa54bc793a915b547c:docs/docs/advanced_features/speculative_decoding.mdx:1088
6a7abcfc9b603d494cdc58fa54bc793a915b547c:docs/docs/references/environment_variables.mdx:1773
6a7abcfc9b603d494cdc58fa54bc793a915b547c:python/sglang/srt/environ.py:1442
```

These are three documentation references and the registry entry. Together with the call path above, they show registration without a verification consumer.

### Environment

Source inspection of main `6a7abcfc9b603d494cdc58fa54bc793a915b547c`, captured 2026-10-12. The reproducer is the pinned tracked-tree grep and call-path inspection above. No model inference or installed-runtime comparison was performed. `python3 -m sglang.check_env` output is unavailable; I have not run that command.
