items.title: [Bug]: PutEnd silently discards PushOffloadingQueue failures — objects never reach the SSD tier, with no log or metric
items.author: ccgibson
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

With eager offload (`enable_offload=1`, `offload_on_evict=0`), `MasterService::PutEnd` calls `PushOffloadingQueue` and acts **only on success**. There is no `else` branch, no log, no metric, and no retry:

```cpp
// mooncake-store/src/master_service.cpp  (main @ fc04cb1, ~L3283)
auto result = PushOffloadingQueue(object_id, replica);
if (result) {
    if (!task_created) {
        replica.inc_refcnt();
        tenant_state.offloading_tasks.emplace(
            object_id.user_key,
            OffloadingTask{replica.id(), std::chrono::system_clock::now()});
        task_created = true;
    }
}
// failure is discarded here
```

An object whose enqueue fails therefore gets **no offload task**, is never written to the SSD tier, and dies RAM-only at the next memory eviction. Because it never had a disk replica, that eviction removes its last replica and the object leaves the pool entirely — a cache entry silently lost despite the SSD tier having free space.

## Failure modes that can hit this

`PushOffloadingQueue` (`master_service.cpp`, ~L5150) can return:

- `SEGMENT_NOT_FOUND` — segment name not present in the local-disk `client_by_name` map
- `UNABLE_OFFLOADING` — no local disk segment for the resolved client
- `UNABLE_OFFLOADING` — `!enable_offloading` on that segment
- `KEYS_ULTRA_LIMIT` — `offloading_objects.size() >= offloading_queue_limit_`
- `OBJECT_ALREADY_EXISTS` — key already present in `offloading_objects`

None of these are logged inside `PushOffloadingQueue` either, so the failure is invisible end-to-end.

## Why this is inconsistent

The **eviction-path** callers of the same function already count and log these failures, e.g.:

```cpp
LOG(WARNING) << "[EVICT] PushOffloadingQueue failed for "
             << offload_push_failed_forced
             << " object(s); force-evicted without disk offload "
                "(offload_force_evict=true).";
```

Only the `PutEnd` hot-path caller discards them. There is also no offload-related metric anywhere in `master_metric_manager.{h,cpp}`.

## Impact observed

In a production deployment we found roughly **9% of pool exits had no corresponding disk eviction** — i.e. that fraction of objects left the cache without ever reaching SSD — while the SSD tier was well under its eviction watermark and the offload pipeline was healthy (multi-GB/s end-to-end store throughput, no queue backlog, no dropped events). With no log line and no counter anywhere, there was nothing to attribute it to; localising it required reading the source rather than any telemetry.

The measurement that surfaced it, for anyone hitting the same thing: compare cumulative pool exits against cumulative disk evictions. A persistent excess of the former means objects are leaving the cache without a disk replica.

Note this is distinct from #2632 / #2658 (offloading-task orphans causing 600s expiry warnings). That one produces a *visible* `Offloading task expired` warning. This path produces nothing at all.

## Two additional silent-success paths

`PushOffloadingQueue` also returns success (`{}`) while enqueuing nothing:

1. `if (segment_names.empty()) { return {}; }` — early return before the loop
2. a `segment_names` list whose entries are all `nullopt` falls through the loop body

In both cases `PutEnd` sees success and records an `OffloadingTask` + `inc_refcnt()` for work that was never queued, so the task can only be cleared by the TTL expiry path.

## Suggested fix

At minimum, make the failure observable: add an `else` incrementing an offload-enqueue-failure counter and emitting a (sampled, since this is the `PutEnd` hot path) `WARNING` carrying the `ErrorCode`, mirroring what the eviction-path callers already do. That is enough to tell operators which failure mode dominates.

Beyond that, `KEYS_ULTRA_LIMIT` and `OBJECT_ALREADY_EXISTS` arguably warrant retry or dedup handling rather than a dropped object, but making it visible seems like the necessary first step.

Happy to open a PR for the observability part if that is a welcome direction.

Environment: observed on `v0.3.12-pre1`; code path verified unchanged on `main` @ `fc04cb1`.

items.author: waliwali777

### Bug Report

### Describe the bug
We observe silent offload failure against local SSD offload backend. Keys are visible via `/get_all_keys`, but corresponding values return empty when fetched.

We are testing with recent Mooncake commit: https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/commit/67aaf6de74f35c7c5cfd072e8643b0a80eb5999a (2026‑08‑12).
The same workload with June‑end Mooncake code works perfectly without empty‑value issue. This regression appears after we upgraded to newer codebase.

### Master launch command:

```C++
mooncake_master \
--rpc_port=8001 \
--rpc_thread_num=8 \
--metrics_port=8007 \
--default_kv_lease_ttl=5000 \
--allow_evict_soft_pinned_objects=true \

--enable_disk_eviction=true \
--promotion_on_hit=false \
--put_start_discard_timeout_sec=300 \
--put_start_release_timeout_sec=600

```
### Real‑Client Environment Variables & Settings
``` C++
MC_IB_PCI_RELAXED_ORDERING                         = 1
MOONCAKE_LOCAL_BUFFER_SIZE                         = 6442450944
MOONCAKE_OFFLOAD_BUCKET_EVICTION_POLICY            = lru
MOONCAKE_OFFLOAD_BUCKET_KEYS_LIMIT                 = 128
MOONCAKE_OFFLOAD_BUCKET_MAX_TOTAL_SIZE             = 3113851289600
MOONCAKE_OFFLOAD_BUCKET_SIZE_LIMIT_BYTES           = 268435456
MOONCAKE_OFFLOAD_CLIENT_BUFFER_GC_INTERVAL_SECONDS = 2
MOONCAKE_OFFLOAD_FILE_STORAGE_PATH                 = /ssd_file/mooncake_cache/
MOONCAKE_OFFLOAD_HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL_SECONDS        = 1

```
Client launch command:
```C++
mooncake_client \
--master_server_address=<master_ip>:8001 \

--protocol=rdma \
--port=8005 \
--global_segment_size=25GB \
--enable_offload=true \

## To Reproduce

Values offloaded to SSD should return complete original payload when fetched.

comments.author: he-yufeng
comments.body:
I spent some time re-checking this against current main (2b3cefba), since several fixes landed after 2026-08-12 that touch exactly this path.

The "empty value" half is an error-mapping artifact rather than a data state: `get()` in store_py.cpp returns `b""` whenever the C++ read returns nullptr, with no exception, so any failure (SSD read error, no usable replica) surfaces as an empty value. On the "key visible" half, #2877 (merged 08-13, one day after your commit) made `/get_all_keys` filter by readable replica, which narrows that symptom.

On what changed since your build: #3479 fixed the carryover-key bucket NACK storm and its author reproduced with your exact config (330 failures per 100 GiB before, zero after, every value matched on readback). #3601 made WriteBucket datasync before committing bucket metadata (a crash between used to leave a registered bucket with nothing on device). #3620 fixed batch gets landing on a different disk replica than the slices were prepared for. #3726 stopped PushOffloadingQueue from silently dropping enqueues. Any of these could plausibly have produced your symptom.

What is still structurally open on main: a COMPLETE LOCAL_DISK replica whose backing file physically disappeared (manual wipe, RemoveAll broadcast) stays listed and reads return `b""` forever; #3711 self-heals that on the Put path only, by design, and read-only keys never heal. Also `MOONCAKE_STORE_CHECKSUM` still defaults off, so payload corruption is not detected unless you opt in.

To pin your case down definitively, could you re-run the same 100 GiB workload on current main with `MOONCAKE_STORE_CHECKSUM=1` and correlate any empty get with the client log? `SSD read failed for key`, `object_checksum_mismatch`, and `Read size mismatch` each map to a different one of the known causes; empty reads with none of those in the log would mean something new, and that log line would tell us which.

comments.author: he-yufeng
comments.body: The read-side half of this is now covered: #3889 heals a dangling LOCAL_DISK replica when a read fails on it (evict plus honest miss or failover to a surviving replica), which closes the "read-only keys never heal" gap noted above. The broader empty-read surface from #3867's concurrent test shape is a separate matter already handled there.

comments.author: whn09
comments.body:
A likely write-side cause, reproduced on 2x r8idn.96xlarge. `GroupOffloadingKeysByBucket` defers a partial bucket to the ungrouped pool for the next heartbeat. `FileStorage::OffloadObjects` then NACKs every key that is not in this cycle's buckets, including the deferred ones. The master drops their offloading task. Under `offload_on_evict` such an object can then be evicted without an SSD copy, and the next cycle's write is not tracked. With 1 GiB buckets and 8192 x 4 MiB puts, main lost 32-96 tasks in 3 of 5 runs. The count always matched the ungrouped-pool size, and nothing is logged at the default level.

This is #3006, fixed by #3009 or #4739 (both 0/5 on the same repro). Until one of them merges, setting `MOONCAKE_OFFLOAD_FLUSH_PARTIAL_BUCKETS=1` on main avoids it (0/5).

items.title: [Bug] Classic RDMA client (real_client.cpp): crash and silent write failures on peer-membership change
items.author: sivabreddy
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

Two distinct, reproducible problems in the "classic" RDMA client
(`real_client.cpp`), both triggered by a change in who's in the client pool
(a pod joining or leaving, by any method):

1. **A crash.** The client segfaults, taking down the entire host process, not
   just the Mooncake connection.
2. **A silent write failure.** A `Put` can fail with `TRANSFER_FAIL` with no
   error surfaced to the caller — the data is never actually written to the
   shared store, but nothing above the Transfer Engine layer is told this
   happened.

Both are reproducible on the latest PyPI release at time of testing
(`mooncake-transfer-engine==0.3.13.post1`, 2026-08-31). We believe both may
share a root cause with the already-fixed #3595 (a stale/self-referential
peer reference surviving a membership change), but in the older/classic
transport, which does not appear to carry that fix.

## Environment

- **Mooncake version**: `mooncake-transfer-engine` 0.3.13.post1 (PyPI,
  installed via `uv pip install mooncake-transfer-engine`, no source
  modifications)
- **Integration**: vLLM v0.17.1 + LMCache `v0.4.1-gdfc914cba`
  (`LMCacheConnectorV1`), using Mooncake Store as LMCache's remote backend
  (`remote_url: mooncakestore://...`) — not the vLLM-native
  `MooncakeStoreConnector`
- **Deployment**: Kubernetes, 2-3 vLLM pods across 2 physical nodes, Mooncake
  master + metadata server as separate lightweight pods in the same
  namespace
- **Transport**: RDMA (RoCEv2), Mellanox mlx5 devices, `GID index 3`
- **OS / platform**: Linux containers (RHEL/UBI-based vLLM image)

`mooncake-config.yaml` used throughout (templated; `local_hostname` set to
each pod's own IP at container start):
```yaml
chunk_size: 256
remote_url: "mooncakestore://<master-host>:50051/"
remote_serde: "naive"
local_cpu: True
max_local_cpu_size: 100
extra_config:
  local_hostname: "<pod IP, from $POD_IP>"
  metadata_server: "http://<metadata-host>:8080/metadata"
  master_server_address: "<master-host>:50051"
  protocol: "rdma"
  device_name: "mlx5_0,mlx5_1,mlx5_2,mlx5_3,mlx5_6,mlx5_7,mlx5_8,mlx5_9"
  global_segment_size: 17179869184
  local_buffer_size: 8589934592
  transfer_timeout: 1
```
Of the 8 listed devices, only `mlx5_0` has a real network attachment in our
environment; the other 7 fail to open at startup with a clear, non-fatal
warning and are excluded from the data path. This is expected and not itself
the bug — it becomes relevant in one test below.

---

## Issue 1: segfault on peer-membership change

### What we did (1): confirm the mechanism works normally

Deployed 2 vLLM+Mooncake pods (Pod A, Pod B) on separate nodes. Pod A stored a
prefix. Pod B requested the same prefix.

### What we found (1)

A genuine cross-pod RDMA retrieve, confirmed from LMCache's own log line on
Pod B (`Inference Engine computed tokens: 0` — Pod B never computed this
itself — followed by a real `Retrieved N tokens` line). No errors. This is
the expected, working behavior.

### What we did (2): change pool membership, then send a real request

Changed which pods were in the pool, by each of these methods independently:
- Force-deleted one pod (`kubectl delete pod --grace-period=0 --force`) and
  let Kubernetes replace it.
- Gracefully deleted one pod (`kubectl delete pod`, default grace period,
  clean SIGTERM) and let Kubernetes replace it.
- Simply added a brand-new pod to the same pool, with no deletion at all.

After each change, sent a real inference request that would cause a Mooncake
`Get` or `Put` — to **either** the new/replacement pod **or** an existing
pod that was never itself replaced.

### What we found (2)

**Whichever pod's turn it was to perform that next real operation segfaulted
— every time, regardless of which of the three membership-change methods was
used, and regardless of whether it was the new pod or an untouched existing
pod.** This reproduced independently on 4 separate occasions. Exactly one
crash occurred per membership-change event. The affected process self-healed
after one container restart (10-15 seconds) and was stable again until the
next membership change elsewhere in the pool.

Crash log, one example (a replacement pod's first retrieve attempt):
```
(APIServer pid=1) INFO:     Application startup complete.
E1008 17:59:52.045347   870 real_client.cpp:2287] Client is not initialized
E1008 17:59:52.045735   870 real_client.cpp:2287] Client is not initialized
E1008 17:59:52.045954   870 real_client.cpp:2287] Client is not initialized
(EngineCore_DP0 pid=483) LMCache INFO: Reqid: ..., Total tokens 907, Inference Engine computed tokens: 0, LMCache hit tokens: 768, need to load: 768
E1008 17:59:52.051139  1057 real_client.cpp:3154] Client is not initialized
!!!!!!! Segfault encountered !!!!!!!
  File ".../runtime/sys_linux_amd64.s", line 330, in runtime.sigfwd
(APIServer pid=1) ERROR [core_client.py:691] Engine core proc EngineCore_DP0 died unexpectedly, shutting down client.
vllm.v1.engine.exceptions.EngineDeadError: EngineCore encountered an issue.
```

A second example (a replacement pod's own client failing to initialize at
all, before any successful operation) shows the retry-then-crash shape more
fully:
```
W1008 10:00:39.777729   167 real_client.cpp:858] Failed to create client on port 13476, retry 1/20
W1008 10:00:39.987325   167 real_client.cpp:858] Failed to create client on port 14180, retry 2/20
... (18 more retries, a different ephemeral port each time) ...
W1008 10:00:45.268965   167 real_client.cpp:858] Failed to create client on port 12411, retry 20/20
!!!!!!! Segfault encountered !!!!!!!
vllm.v1.engine.exceptions.EngineDeadError: EngineCore encountered an issue.
```

### What we did (3): test a candidate fix (MC_USE_TENT)

Found `MC_USE_TENT` as a string inside the installed `mooncake/engine.so` via
`strings`, hypothesizing it would opt into the newer TENT RDMA transport,
which already has a fix (#3598/#3603) for a structurally similar crash
(#3595: SIGSEGV in `RailMonitor::updateBestMapping()` af

comments.body:
## Follow-up: retested with a corrected RDMA device list and checked TENT directly from source

Posting an update since we found something that changes the picture from the original report above.

### 1. Is TENT available as a way around this? No — confirmed from source, not guessed

We'd read about TENT (the newer failure-handling transport) and wondered if it was reachable from
the published package. Cloned `kvcache-ai/Mooncake` fresh and checked directly:

- `mooncake-common/common.cmake`: `option(USE_TENT "option for building Mooncake TENT" OFF)` —
  **TENT is a CMake build-time flag, default OFF**, not a runtime environment variable.
- This confirms why our earlier `MC_USE_TENT=1` attempt (mentioned in the original report) had no
  effect — there is no such runtime flag in this transport. The published
  `mooncake-transfer-engine` PyPI wheel is a standard build (`USE_TENT` not set), so TENT is not
  present in it regardless of environment variables.

### 2. Our original device-list mismatch, corrected — the crash got worse, not better

The original report used a `device_name` list of 8 devices, of which only 1 (`mlx5_0`) actually
had a routable RoCEv2 identity on our cluster — we wondered if this mismatch itself was a
contributing factor. Re-checked fresh: still true, no change, confirmed via `ibv_devinfo` and a
scan of `/sys/class/infiniband/*/ports/1/gids/*` on both nodes.

Redeployed with `device_name` corrected to `"mlx5_0"` only (the one real device). Result:

**All three client pods failed to establish a working Mooncake RDMA client at startup — 20/20
connection retries exhausted on every pod, 0/3 successful:**

```
W1013 11:51:04.798380  1450 real_client.cpp:858] Failed to create client on port 12628, retry 1/20
...
W1013 11:52:28.016795  1450 real_client.cpp:858] Failed to create client on port 13693, retry 20/20
E1013 11:52:28.116932  1450 real_client.cpp:865] Failed to create client after 20 retries
E1013 11:52:28.118700  1450 real_client.cpp:3379] Client is not initialized
```

**A separate issue found here:** the Mooncake master's own metrics showed `Clients: 0` for the
entire test, even though every pod logged `MooncakeConnector initialized successfully` on the
LMCache side. LMCache's `MooncakestoreConnector` appears to report success regardless of whether
the underlying C++ client actually has a working connection — there's no visible warning anywhere
that the connector is non-functional. (We realize this specific piece may belong on the LMCache
side rather than here, flagging for completeness since it compounds the diagnosis difficulty.)

**The crash itself still reproduced, and more readily than before — not gated behind a
membership-change event anymore, but firing on literally the first real cache operation:**

```
LMCache INFO: Reqid: ..., LMCache hit tokens: 256, need to load: 256
E1013 12:09:16.147480  1949 real_client.cpp:2287] Client is not initialized
E1013 12:09:16.701977  2350 real_client.cpp:3154] Client is not initialized
!!!!!!! Segfault encountered !!!!!!!
```

Confirmed independently on 2 of the 3 pods (identical file/line numbers, identical trigger: a
lookup reporting a partial local hit that needs to load the remainder from the remote tier). One
pod was also force-deleted and replaced to confirm the original membership-change trigger
specifically — same result, crashes immediately on the replacement pod's first real request.
Total: 5 independent crash observations across 3 pods, 100% reproduction rate, 0 successful real
cache operations observed anywhere in this retest.

### 3. What this changes about our read of the original report

- Correcting the device-list mismatch does **not** fix the crash — if anything, it removes the
  one device that was letting any connection succeed at all in our original 8-device config,
  without touching whatever is fragile in `real_client.cpp`'s client-creation/reconnection path.
- We could not re-isolate the silent-write-failure bug from the original repo

comments.author: sivabreddy
comments.body:
**Update after a re-test: the failed writes came from our RDMA configuration; the crash is the null-client path that #4633 fixes.**

On 2026-10-17 we re-tested with the same versions: vLLM 0.17.1, LMCache 0.4.1 (`LMCacheConnectorV1`, `mooncakestore://`), Mooncake 0.3.13.post1 and Llama-3.1-8B TP1. We used the same LMCache YAML and the HTTP metadata server, with 3 pods on 2 nodes. Several RDMA pods on each node share one RoCE device. Differences from the original run: an Ubuntu CUDA image with pip, and LMCache 0.4.1 built from source.

**1. What was wrong on our side**
- **A fixed GID index.** We set `MC_GID_INDEX=3`. A cluster policy also injected `NCCL_IB_GID_INDEX=3`, which Mooncake uses when `MC_GID_INDEX` is not set (`mooncake-transfer-engine/src/config.cpp` L144-145). When pods share one RDMA device, each pod also sees the GID entries of the other pods. So a fixed index points to at most one pod's own GID, or to another pod's GID. Without a fixed index, `findBestGidIndex` ranks GIDs that have a readable sysfs netdev first, and each pod selected its own IPv4 GID (indexes 11–27).
- **RDMA devices without a network in `device_name`.** We listed 8 devices, and only one has a network.

**2. Re-test with automatic GID selection**

| | 8-device list | connected device only |
|---|---|---|
| Requests during and after 3 membership changes (force delete, delete, new pod) | 51 of 51 answered | 51 of 51 answered |
| Segfaults / engine restarts / `Failed to create client` retries | 0 / 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 / 0 |
| `Put ... TRANSFER_FAIL` log lines (4 pods) | 320 (master rate metrics: no completed `PutEnd`) | 0 |
| Cross-pod loads | none | yes (2,560 of 2,560 tokens) |

Store-only test (Python client, 4 clients, 2 per node, 16 keys of 4 MB each, P2PHANDSHAKE, connected device only): with `MC_GID_INDEX=3`, 16 of 16 puts failed on every client and 0 of 64 keys were readable; with automatic selection, 64 of 64 keys were readable.

**3. The crash: #4633 matches our logs**
In our crash logs the process first fails to create the client (`Failed to create client ... retry 20/20`) or logs `Client is not initialized`; in one log the last Mooncake line before the segfault is `real_client.cpp:3154] Client is not initialized` (`batch_get_buffer_internal`, 0.3.13.post1). In 0.3.13.post1, `RealClient::batch_get_buffer` (L3366-3373) passes an always-true success predicate to `execute_timed_operation`, so the observer calls `client_->ObserveTransferOperation(...)` with a null `client_`. The same pattern is in the other 7 batch wrappers (L4024, 4086, 4377, 4656, 5435, 6053, 6097) and is still on `main`. This is exactly what #4633 fixes (thanks @pjdurden). So the chain in our case was: fixed GID index → client creation fails → LMCache keeps calling the batch API (it does not check the `setup()` result) → null `client_` in the metrics observer → segfault. With automatic GID selection the client is created and the crash path is not reached, which is why the re-test had 0 crashes. We did not re-run the crash setup with #4633 applied.

**4. What we suggest**
- Merge #4633 (or an equivalent null check). It turns the crash into per-key errors.
- Docs: `docs/source/design/transfer-engine/index.md` L473 says the default of `MC_GID_INDEX` is 3. In the code the default is -1 = automatic selection (`mooncake-transfer-engine/include/config.h` L46). Proposed text: "`MC_GID_INDEX` (or `NCCL_IB_GID_INDEX` when `MC_GID_INDEX` is not set): GID index per device. Default: automatic selection, which prefers a GID that has a network device. Do not set a fixed index when several containers share one RDMA device: the GID table holds entries for the interfaces of all containers on the node." We can send this as a PR.
- For users: when several pods share one RDMA device, do not set `MC_GID_INDEX` / `NCCL_IB_GID_INDEX`, and list only RDMA devices that have a network in `device_name`.
- The "silent" part (LMCache logs `Stored ...` after a failed Mooncake Put, and continues after a faile

I'm just getting started with Triton.  I can't find any documentation on some very basic concepts.  If you can point me to something I missed I'd be grateful.  If not, perhaps someone could answer these questions?

What types of values can be passed to a kernel?  PyTorch tensors obviously, as well as ints, floats, and bools.  Anything else?

The grid is defined by a lambda that takes a single argument called `meta`.  What is `meta`?

How do I access a single element of a tensor?  Say `a` and `b` are tensors and `i` is an int.  I want to write `c = a[i]*b` to multiply `b` by an element of `a`.  That produces an error.  What's the correct way of doing it?

What is the difference between a `tensor_descriptor` and a `TensorDescriptor`?  What is each used for and how do I use them?

What is the exact significance of annotating an argument with `tl.constexpr`?  Does it mean the kernel will get recompiled every time a new value of that argument is encountered?  What can be done with a constexpr value that can't be done with other ones?

How about `tl.const`?  Is it just for error checking, to avoid accidentally modifying something that shouldn't be modified, or does it have other effects?

Thanks for your help!

items.title: [Bug][MP] Direct copy path (#5308) faults on CUDA when registered host memory is not device-addressable (`cudaDevAttrCanUseHostPointerForRegisteredMem == 0`, e.g. WSL2)
items.author: dmmdea
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug** On a CUDA stack where `cudaDevAttrCanUseHostPointerForRegisteredMem` is 0 (WSL2 here), the MP server's LMCache-driven transfer takes the copy-engine direct path from #5308 (`execute_direct_copy_transfer` → `cudaMemcpyBatchAsync`), and the first store leaves an illegal memory access in the server's CUDA context. It surfaces asynchronously: the first stores log `Stored 1568 tokens in 0.006 seconds`, about 0.4 s later a `~CUDAEvent` warning reports the illegal access, and every later store and retrieve fails in `stage_block_ids` (`lmcache/v1/platform/base/cache_context.py:357`, the non-blocking copy of the block ids). So the traceback does not point at the faulting copy. vLLM's requests then wait on the connector indefinitely, and the engine side logs nothing. The host driver logs a GPU fault on both engine GPUs in the same second. This looks like the case the ROCm branch of `batch_memcpy_supported()` already guards. The batch entries are built from the host virtual address of the pinned L1 pool (`obj.host_ptr + …`, `csrc/cuda/mp_mem_kernels.cu` ~L924-937). The ROCm branch requires `hipDeviceAttributeCanUseHostPointerForRegisteredMem` before it selects the path, because "the copy engine dereferences the host operand directly" (~L776-799, and #5534 for the kernel path). The CUDA branch checks only the runtime and driver versions (L801). Line numbers are at v0.5.6; the CUDA branch is unchanged on `dev`. **Evidence** 1. A plain cudart probe in the same environment (no LMCache) gives, on all three GPUs: `cudaDevAttrUnifiedAddressing = 1`, `cudaDevAttrCanUseHostPointerForRegisteredMem = 0`. After `cudaHostRegister(ptr, 4 MiB, flags)`, `cudaHostGetDevicePointer` returns an address different from the host pointer. That holds for flags `0x02` and `0x03`, whichever device registered the memory and whichever is current. 2. The same seat, run three ways (vLLM 0.32.0 + LMCache 0.5.6, nothing else changed): | LMCache | first store | planted needle cold / warm / after eviction | external hits after eviction | |---|---|---|---| | stock 0.5.6 | illegal memory access | later requests hang | — | | pin flags `0x02` → `0x03` (Portable) in `lazy_memory_allocator.py` | illegal memory access | later requests hang | — | | `_HAS_BATCH_MEMCPY_ASYNC = False` in `object_group_transfer.py` | ok | ok / ok / ok, answer verbatim each time | 23,520 tokens (TTFT 3.0 s vs 24.1 s cold, one run); the same after a full engine + server restart (3.6 s) | LMCache 0.5.4, which predates #5308, ran the same seat (with vLLM 0.28) in production with no illegal-access line in its server log. The seat now runs 0.5.6 in production with the direct path turned off as in the last row. **To reproduce** ``` lmcache server --host 127.0.0.1 --port

--chunk-size 1568 --separate-object-groups --l1-size-gb 8 \ --eviction-policy LRU --supported-transfer-mode auto --l2-adapter '{"type":"fs_native","base_path":"

","num_workers":8}' vllm serve RedHatAI/Qwen3.8-27B-INT4 --tensor-parallel-size 2 --kv-cache-dtype fp8 --mamba-cache-mode align \ --max-model-len 163840 --enable-prefix-caching --max-num-batched-tokens 3135 --max-num-seqs 32 \ --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"LMCacheMPConnector","kv_role":"kv_both","kv_connector_extra_config":{"lmcache.mp.server_urls":"127.0.0.1:

"}}' ``` Then send one prompt longer than a chunk, followed by any other request. A one-time check that should show the same thing without vLLM: `cudaDeviceGetAttribute(&v, cudaDevAttrCanUseHostPointerForRegisteredMem, dev)` returns 0. **Expected behavior** Where registered host memory is not device-addressable, `batch_memcpy_supported()` returns false, or the host operands are translated with `cudaHostGetDevicePointer`, so the server uses the staging path. The staging path works here. **Environment** - LMCache 0.5.6 (PyPI), vLLM 0.32.0, torch 2.13.0+cu130, CUDA runtime 13.0, driver 13.4 - WSL2 (kernel 6.18.33.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2), Ubuntu 24.04.5 - TP=2 engine on an RTX 5070 Ti + an RTX 5060 Ti (sm_120). A third RTX 5060 Ti drives the display, and the server, which has no `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES`, can see it. - `RedHatAI/Qwen3.8-27B-INT4` (hybrid GDN), fp8 KV, LBNHC layout, group edits `mamba-unified-view: 48, subpaged-attention-view: 16` - One local vLLM patch: the KV cache allocation is split into 16 regions so that CUDA IPC export works on WSL2, which is a separate WSL2 limit. The fault happens with and without the patch; without it, the KV pool was smaller. **Suggested fix** Mirror the ROCm gate in the CUDA branch: ```cpp #else if (runtime < 12080 || driver < 12080) return false; int device = 0; int can_use_host_ptr = 0; if (cudaGetDevice(&device) != cudaSuccess) return false; if (cudaDeviceGetAttribute(&can_use_host_ptr, cudaDevAttrCanUseHostPointerForRegisteredMem, device) != cudaSuccess) return false; return can_use_host_ptr != 0; #endif ``` The result is cached in a function-local static, taken from whichever device is current at the first call. Per device would be more exact, although every device here reports 0. A log line naming the path chosen per object group would also have saved a lot of time; #5506 adds one for the direct path. I'll open a PR with this gate and test it on this setup.

items.title: [Bug] Unbounded compiled-grammar cache in BaseGrammarBackend leaks host memory with per-request JSON schemas
items.author: GinDoliee
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist
- [x] 1. I have searched related issues but cannot get the expected help.
- [x] 2. The bug has not been fixed in the latest version (the cache code is unchanged on `main` as of 2026-10-19).
- [x] 3. Environment info and a minimal reproducible script are included below.
- [x] 4. This is a bug report, not a question.
- [x] 5. Written in English.

## Describe the bug

`BaseGrammarBackend.cache` (`python/sglang/srt/constrained/base_grammar_backend.py`) is a plain `dict` with no size limit, and the xgrammar backend creates `GrammarCompiler(tokenizer_info=tokenizer_info)` with xgrammar's default unbounded internal cache. Every request whose `response_format.json_schema` (or regex / EBNF) has not been seen before adds one compiled grammar to both caches, and nothing ever evicts it while the server is up. Only `/flush_cache` clears it, and `/flush_cache` is refused unless the scheduler is completely idle.

When clients send a slightly different schema per request (very common with LLM-agent frameworks that embed per-call enums, defaults, descriptions or examples in the schema), scheduler RSS grows linearly until host RAM and swap are exhausted.

## What we observed (production, 2026-10-13)

- Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-FP8, SGLang 0.5.10.post1, `--tp-size 1 --dp-size 4`, 4× H100 NVL, 128 GB host RAM + 61 GB swap.
- One client sent ~8,000 structured-output requests/day with ~1,250 distinct schemas (same prompt family, per-call enum/const values inside the schema).
- Each DP rank's scheduler process grew from 3.5 GB to 35 GB over 11 days; total 4 ranks ≈ 140 GB (RAM + swap full), server became unresponsive, 25-minute outage until manual restart.
- Memory never returned while idle. Growth happened only while structured-output requests were processed.

Measured cost per *new* schema (vocab 151k, xgrammar 0.1.32): **+250–380 MB RSS per scheduler process**. Re-sending the *same* schema 4× costs ~+6 MB total. A 60 KB schema costs several GB.

## Reproduction

Start any model with default args (xgrammar backend). Then:

```python
import json, requests, uuid
URL = "http://127.0.0.1:30000/v1/chat/completions"
for i in range(20):
    schema = {"type": "object",
              "properties": {f"field_{j}": {"type": "string", "enum": [f"{uuid.uuid4()}" for _ in range(5)]} for j in range(30)},
              "required": [f"field_{j}" for j in range(30)]}
    body = {"model": "default", "max_tokens": 64,
            "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Return an object."}],
            "response_format": {"type": "json_schema", "json_schema": {"name": f"s{i}", "schema": schema}}}
    requests.post(URL, json=body, timeout=120)
```

Watch `VmRSS` of the `sglang::scheduler` process between requests: it grows by hundreds of MB per iteration and does not come back. Sending the same schema 20× does not grow it.

## Expected behavior

The compiled-grammar cache should be bounded (LRU by entry count and/or bytes), and the bound should be configurable. A request that is never repeated should not permanently consume host memory.

## Proposed fix (I can open PRs)

1. Make `BaseGrammarBackend.cache` an LRU (`OrderedDict`, evict oldest on insert) with a configurable max entry count. In-flight requests already hold their own `copy()` of the grammar object, so eviction is safe.
2. Pass `cache_limit_bytes` to xgrammar's `GrammarCompiler` (xgrammar ≥ 0.1.21 supports it) with a sane default (e.g. 1 GiB).
3. Optionally skip caching grammars whose key string exceeds a size threshold (very large schemas are almost never reused and dominate memory).

We have been running (1)+(2)+(3) in production since 2026-10-14: 17.5 h uptime now plateaus at 12–21 GB total across 4 ranks instead of growing without bound, throughput unchanged (333 vs 334 tok/s single stream).

## Environment

- SGLang 0.5.10.post1 (problem code is unchanged on current `main`: `self.cache: Dict[...] = {}`, `GrammarCompiler(tokenizer_info=tokenizer_info)`)
- xgrammar 0.1.32, torch 2.x, CUDA 12.x, 4× NVIDIA H100 NVL, Ubuntu 20.04
- Grammar backend: xgrammar (default)

items.title: sglang:cache_hit_rate gauge drops to 0.0 on prefill reports with zero tokens
items.author: cshintov
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] 1. I have searched related issues but cannot get the expected help.
- [x] 2. The bug has not been fixed in the latest version.
- [x] 3. I have provided environment info and a reproduction.
- [x] 4. This is a bug report, not a question.
- [x] 5. Written in English.

### Describe the bug

`sglang:cache_hit_rate` oscillates between the true value and `0.0` under normal serving load.

In `SchedulerMetricsReporter.report_prefill_stats`, the hit rate is computed as:

```python
total_tokens = effective_input_tokens + effective_hit_tokens
cache_hit_rate = effective_hit_tokens / total_tokens if total_tokens > 0 else 0.0
...
self.stats.cache_hit_rate = cache_hit_rate
```

When `total_tokens == 0` the expression yields `0.0`, and that `0.0` is **assigned to `self.stats.cache_hit_rate`
and published** by the `self.metrics_collector.log_stats(self.stats)` call a few lines later. It is not a
"no data" signal — it is a real, exported zero.

So any Prometheus query over the gauge (`avg_over_time`, `rate`, Grafana panels, alert rules) is dragged
down by samples that carry no information. On a server with a genuine ~96% prefix-cache hit rate the
gauge alternates between ~0.96 and 0.0, which reads as a broken cache.

This is distinct from #12459 / PR #24427, which fixed the **decode** path overwriting the gauge
(the `# cache_hit_rate is prefill-owned (per-report semantics); decode ticks must not reset it`
comment at `report_decode_stats`). The decode path is fine. The remaining leak is the prefill path
publishing a fabricated `0.0` computed from a zero-denominator **prefill report**, not from zero hits.

### Measured evidence

Sampling `sglang:cache_hit_rate` every 4 s on a live server under normal load:

```
12:43:19 gauge=0.9915966386554622
12:43:23 gauge=0.0
12:43:27 gauge=0.0
12:43:32 gauge=0.9333333333333333
12:43:36 gauge=0.0
12:43:40 gauge=0.9583333333333334
12:43:44 gauge=0.9583333333333334
12:43:48 gauge=0.9583333333333334
```

The same server's cumulative counters show the cache is healthy:

```
sglang:prompt_tokens_total  = 44,012,237
sglang:cached_tokens_total  = 36,287,744   -> 82.4% overall hit rate
```

and `usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens` returns 7,424 of 7,625 prompt tokens (97.4%) on a warm
repeat. The gauge is the only place the cache looks broken.

### Reproduction

1. Start a server with `--enable-metrics` and prefix caching (default).
2. Generate load with a mix of short and long prompts, e.g. `bench_serving` or a looping client.
3. `watch -n1 "curl -s localhost:30000/metrics | grep ^sglang:cache_hit_rate"`
4. The value will intermittently drop to `0.0` while the counters continue to show a high hit rate.

### Expected behaviour

A report that carries no cache information should not overwrite the gauge. Either:

- skip the assignment and leave the previous value in place (matching the decode-path fix in #24427), or
- publish `NaN` so Prometheus/`avg_over_time` ignores the sample.

### Environment

- SGLang built from source, `0.0.0.dev0`, upstream `main` @ `f86a04a` (2026-10-19)
- 3× NVIDIA DGX Spark, TP=3, `--enable-metrics`
- Model: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash
- Also observed with `--enable-priority-scheduling`

### Proposed fix

I have a patch ready and will open a PR against `main` that skips the gauge write when
`total_tokens == 0`, keeping the last known-good value, plus a unit test. Happy to adjust if
maintainers prefer the `NaN` variant.

items.title: [Perf] KV sharding overpads all-gather for shared prefixes
items.author: SouthWest7
items.body_excerpt:
Related to #43098 (KV cache sharding communication overhead).

With `--enable-kv-cache-sharding`, `begin_shard_extend` deduplicates shared prefix pages, but sizes each rank's all-gather block as `sum_i ceil(prefix_pages_i / shard_size)`. Unused slots are filled with the reserved trash page and still copied and communicated at every layer.

For eight requests sharing 122,880 prefix tokens, page size 64 and two shard ranks, each rank has 960 useful pages but sends a 7,680-page block. The remaining 6,720 pages are padding.

The block should use a safe bound that accounts for the deduplicated page set. On Qwen3-32B BF16, 2×H100, TP2/CP2 and FA3, tightening this bound reduces the 120K shared-prefix batch's server median latency from 1,020 to 734 ms (8 requests, 128 new input tokens each). Similar gains reproduce at page sizes 4, 16 and 32.

Measured on base `7c99ace127`: real model forward and NCCL gather, with fake P/D transfer and a benchmark-only hook enabling prefix-cache insertion. This is cached-prefix prefill latency, not full P/D or decode performance.

Working on a kernel I got a CompilationError when trying to launch it, and while the CompilationError message points to the "problem" it doesn't specify what the problem is.  I eventually figured out that it doesn't like when you call `load` with `other` set but `mask` set to None.  I don't mind that restriction, but it would be nice if the CompilationError message said something to that effect.  I didn't see any specifics in the error message.  Perhaps it's buried in the traceback, but the trackback gets truncated in Jupyter notebooks because it's so exceedingly long.

Triton version 2.0.0.dev20221202

The kernel:

```
@triton.jit
def _clip_embed_fused(
	A,         # *Pointer* to first input vector (257xN).
	Out,       # *Pointer* to output vector (257xN).
	Position,  # *Pointer* position vector (257xN).
	Weight,    # *Pointer* weight vector (N).
	Bias,      # *Pointer* bias vector (N).
	eps: tl.constexpr,
):
	# position of elements processed by this program
	row = tl.program_id(0)
	Out += row * 1024
	A += row * 1024
	Position += row * 1024

	# loads
	cols = tl.arange(0, 1024)
	mask = cols < 1024
	a = tl.load(A + cols, other=0.).to(tl.float32)
	weight = tl.load(Weight + cols)
	bias = tl.load(Bias + cols)
	position = tl.load(Position + cols, other=0.).to(tl.float32)

	# position embedding
	a += position

	# compute mean
	mean = tl.sum(a, axis=0) / 1024

	# compute variance
	var = tl.sum((a - mean) * (a - mean), axis=0) / 1024
	rstd = 1 / tl.sqrt(var + eps)

	# multiply by weight and add bias
	a_hat = (a - mean) * rstd
	out = a_hat * weight + bias

	# write-back

items.title: [Bug]: cuBLAS NVFP4 GEMM silently rejects M < 128, impacts speech model decode
items.author: 1morello
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment
The output of python collect_env.py ```text ============================== System Info ============================== OS : Ubuntu 24.04.3 LTS (x86_64) GCC version : (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0 Clang version : Could not collect CMake version : Could not collect Libc version : glibc-2.39 ============================== PyTorch Info ============================== PyTorch version : 2.11.0+cu130 Is debug build : False CUDA used to build PyTorch : 13.0 ROCM used to build PyTorch : N/A XPU used to build PyTorch : N/A ============================== Python Environment ============================== Python version : 3.12.3 (main, Jun 19 2026, 12:46:00) [GCC 13.3.0] (64-bit runtime) Python platform : Linux-6.17.0-35-generic-x86_64-with-glibc2.39 ============================== CUDA / GPU Info ============================== Is CUDA available : True ```
### 🐛 Describe the bug `torch._scaled_mm` with float4_e2m1fn_x2 inputs raises `RuntimeError: Invalid scaling configuration` for any M < 128. This is not documented anywhere in CUDA or PyTorch docs. This directly impacts speech model inference: TTS decode (Orpheus-3B) and ASR decode (Whisper) both run at batch=1, meaning M=1 for every decode step. cuBLAS NVFP4 can never be used for decode — it always falls back to Marlin. Repro: ```python import torch M, K, N = 64, 1024, 1024 # M < 128 A = torch.randint(255, (M, K // 2), dtype=torch.uint8, device='cuda').view(torch.float4_e2m1fn_x2) B = torch.randint(255, (N, K // 2), dtype=torch.uint8, device='cuda').view(torch.float4_e2m1fn_x2).T scale_A = torch.randn(M, K // 16, device='cuda').to(torch.float8_e4m3fn) scale_B = torch.randn(N, K // 16, device='cuda').to(torch.float8_e4m3fn) torch._scaled_mm(A, B, scale_A, scale_B, out_dtype=torch.bfloat16) # RuntimeError ``` Works fine at M=128: ```python M = 128 # same code, just M >= 128 # runs successfully, returns correct result ``` Also found that M must be padded to a multiple of 128 (e.g. M=200 fails, M=256 works). Discovered during FP4 inference benchmarking on RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (SM 12.0). Verified on vLLM 0.22.1 with PyTorch 2.11+cu130, CUDA 13.0. This is probably a cuBLAS constraint rather than a vLLM bug, but it would help to either document it or provide a Triton fallback kernel for small M on SM120. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [RFC]: ReplaySSM: cache SSM inputs instead of state for faster standard and speculative decode (Mamba2 + GDN)
items.author: askliar
items.body_excerpt:
### Motivation.

> This RFC also serves as the tracking hub for ReplaySSM across vLLM, FlashInfer, and TensorRT-LLM. Status tables are kept live as work lands; PRs are linked rather than duplicated. It supersedes [RFC #47572](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/47572)

[ReplaySSM](https://dao-lab.ai/blog/2026/replayssm/) ([vllm#47576](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/47576)) is a memory-bandwidth optimization for the decode kernels of state space model (SSM) and linear-attention layers. It was developed concurrently and independently by @Johnny-Liou at Dao AI Lab and @hnover-nv at NVIDIA. A concurrent cross-framework implementation is in [TensorRT-LLM (#14203)](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/pull/14203), developed by @hnover-nv.
 
SSM decode is memory-bound: today each step reads and writes back the full recurrent state. ReplaySSM instead keeps a single checkpoint state and caches recent SSM inputs in a ring buffer. It reconstructs the state only when needed, computing the output directly from the checkpoint plus cached inputs on every other step, and writes the full state back only once every `L` steps.
 
This helps two cases:
 
1. **Standard decode.** Writing the state back once every `L` steps instead of every step roughly halves the dominant memory traffic in the bandwidth-bound SSM kernel.
2. **Speculative decode.** The SSM state update is irreversible, so today's implementation keeps a separate recurrent state per draft token (~`(1 + num_spec)×` the state). Caching inputs instead makes rollback a ring-buffer pointer move — `O(1)` instead of `O(T)` — and enables verifying a draft window in one shot rather than by serial recurrence, improving both latency and maximum concurrency.
Gains are largest at high serving batch sizes, where the kernel is fully memory-bound, and for hybrid models at short-to-medium output lengths, where the SSM layers dominate latency.

### Proposed Change.

The full implementation lands first as a single large draft PR ([vllm#47576](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/47576)) containing everything below, for end-to-end review and alignment; it is then split into smaller, self-contained PRs for merging.
 
### Scope
 
- Mamba2 and Gated DeltaNet (GDN) SSM layers.
- Standard and speculative decode.
- Stochastic rounding (SR) and prefix caching supported from the initial PRs.
- New Triton kernels plus vLLM integration (mixer dispatch, attention-metadata cursors, state-shape sizing). The conv path reuses vLLM's existing `causal_conv1d_update` unchanged.
- Integration of CUDA kernels from FlashInfer for a selected set of architectures.
### Config flags (all default off)
 
- `--use-replayssm` — Mamba2/GDN standard cached decode.
- `--use-replayssm-spec` — speculative cached decode (requires speculative decoding and `--mamba-cache-mode none`).
- `--replayssm-buffer-len` — history buffer length (default 16).
### Integration
 
The feature is opt-in through config flags that default to off; when off, the decode path is byte-for-byte the baseline. ReplaySSM caches are added as extra tensors on the existing paged mamba state, reusing vLLM's paged-block allocation and block-table indexing (continuous batching, per-request allocation/eviction, prefix caching). Only small per-block cursors live in the metadata builder.
 
Speculative decode uses two device-routed launches (verify and flush), with the flush decision and rollback computed on-device, so the launch sequence is fixed and one captured CUDA graph per batch size covers the path. Only state-building inputs are cached; the output read vector (Mamba2 `C`, GDN `q`) is taken from current activations. The ring buffer is sized `B + T` and flushes when `history + T > B` (`B` = buffer length, `T = num_spec_tokens + 1`).
 
### Two kernel tracks
 
By design there are checkpointing kernels in both Triton and CUDA:
 
- **Triton (vLLM)** — broad coverage across a wider class of SSM types.
- **CUDA (FlashInfer)** — tuned and specialized for Mamba2 / GDN ([flashinfer#3975](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/3975), [flashinfer#3324](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/3324/)).
The kernel↔runtime contract (accepted-token count, CUDA-graph compatibility, cache shapes/dtypes) is fixed so any conforming kernel can be dropped in. The approach is orthogonal to precision, so kernels port across FP16/BF16/FP8/INT8 as needed.
 
---
 
## Roadmap & status
 
Legend: ✅ done · 🔄 in progress · ⏳ planned · 🅿️ backlog
 
**Short-term**
 
| Item | Framework | Status |
|------|-----------|--------|
| Mamba2 standard decode (first PR, incl. SR + prefix caching) ([vllm#48018](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48018)) | vLLM | 🔄 |
| GDN standard decode | vLLM | 🔄 |
| Finalize kernel↔runtime contract (GDN) | all | 🔄 |
| Speculative (cached) decode — Mamba2/GDN | vLLM | 🔄 |
 
**Mid-term**
 
| Item | Framework | Status |
|------|-----------|--------|
| Quantized SSM-state format | vLLM | ⏳ |
| FlashInfer CUDA kernel + integration ([flashinfer#3975](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/3975), [flashinfer#3324](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/3324/)) | FlashInfer | 🔄 |
| Additional precisions | vLLM | ⏳ |
| More SSM types: Mamba3, KDA, GDP | — | ⏳ |
 
**Longer-term**
 
- Quantization + SR: FP16, FP8 block-scale, INT8 block-scale.
- More SSM types and Hopper / DGX Spark support.
- Full treatment of both checkpointing (STP) and replay (MTP) modes.
---
 
## Performance (reference numbers)
 
### Standard decode
 
Whole-model per-step speedup (baseline / ReplaySSM), FP32 state, buffer length 16:
 
| Model (SSM, HW) | bs 1 | bs 32 | bs 128 | bs 512 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Nemotron-Nano-4B (Mamba2, H100) | 0.99 | 1.17 | 1.40 | 1.55 |
| Qwen3.5-4B (GDN, H100) | 0.99 | 1.08 | 1.21 | 1.31 |
| Nemotron-Super-120B (Mamba2, B300) | 0.98 | 1.10 | 1.27 | 1.67 |
| Qwen3.5-122B (GDN, B300) | 0.98 | 1.07 | 1.14 | 1.20 |

items.title: [Bug]: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash cannot serve on SM120/SM121 (GB10) at e77daef89 — SWA cache block 32 vs SM120 decode page 64; ratio-1 indexer block_kv=128 vs DeepGEMM sm120 (64 only)
items.author: legwork-sh
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

- vLLM `0.1.1.dev5+ge77daef89` — the per-commit aarch64 wheel of `e77daef89e18e08321ae7b8b24827eedd5fe8673` ("[Model] Support DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (#56214)") installed `--no-deps` over `vllm/vllm-openai:nightly-e7edf17cea217e52701f913cd8491fcacf2d9490` (arm64; CUDA 13.0, torch `2.13.0+cu130`, flashinfer `0.6.18.post1` + `flashinfer-jit-cache 0.6.18.post1+cu130`, DeepGEMM vendored at `vllm.third_party.deep_gemm`, the `nv_dev@8b1392b` pin).
- Host: NVIDIA DGX Spark (GB10, `torch.cuda.get_device_capability() == (12, 1)`, unified memory), driver 580.173.02, Ubuntu 24.04, kernel `6.17.0-1032-nvidia`, Docker 29.2.1 + nvidia-container-toolkit 1.20.0 (`--gpus all`).

### 🐛 Describe the bug

`DeepseekV41ForCausalLM` takes the SM12x route on capability 12.x (`vllm/models/deepseek_v4_1/nvidia/model.py`: `major == 12` → `DeepseekV4FlashInferSM120Attention`), but two host-side geometry choices make the model fail during `flashinfer_sparse_mla_warmup` before serving anything. Both are deterministic and independent of the weights — reproduced with `--load-format dummy` and a layer-trimmed `config.json` of `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash` (heads / head_dim / index_topk / sliding_window untouched).

**1. Sliding-window cache block 32 vs the SM120 sparse-MLA decode dispatch (page 64).**
`vllm/models/deepseek_v4_1/attention.py` constructs `DeepseekV4SWACache(..., block_size=32)` (hardcoded; `deepseek_v4` uses the default 64). On SWA-only layers (`compress_ratio == 0`) `nvidia/flashinfer_sparse.py` hands that cache to the SM120 sparse kernel as the KV cache (`compressed_kv_cache = swa_k_cache`, `compressed_block_size = swa_metadata.block_size`), and FlashInfer's `mla/_sparse_mla_sm120.py` only has DSV4 decode kernels for `page_block_size == 64` (`_DECODE_DSV4_PAGE_BLOCK_SIZE = 64`; `_decode_dsv4_dispatchable`):

```
File ".../vllm/model_executor/warmup/flashinfer_sparse_mla_warmup.py", line 201, in ...
ValueError: SM120 sparse-MLA has no decode kernel for this shape: num_tokens=2, num_heads=64, topk=128, d_qk=512, page_block_size=32, model_type=1, extra_topk=0. Supported decode shapes are enumerated in _DECODE_DSV4_DISPATCH and _DECODE_DSV3_2_DISPATCH.
```

A one-line in-container change `block_size=32 → 64` at that constructor makes the SWA warmup pass (the (64,128) decode entry then dispatches).

**2. Ratio-1 layers hand the DeepGEMM SM120 paged-MQA-logits indexer `block_kv=128`; it accepts only 64.**
`vllm/v1/attention/backends/mla/indexer.py` (`DeepseekV41IndexerBackend.get_supported_kernel_block_sizes`) returns 64 on Hopper and **128 otherwise**; `num_states = block_size // compress_ratio` (`kv_cache_interface.py`) is what the indexer passes as `block_size` into `get_paged_mqa_logits_metadata`. Ratio-2 layers → 64 (fine), ratio-1 layers → 128, and the `kernel_block_size` split only applies to `compress_ratio > 1`. With the SWA fix above in place:

```
File ".../vllm/model_executor/warmup/flashinfer_sparse_mla_warmup.py", line 204, in ...
File ".../vllm/v1/attention/backends/mla/indexer.py", line 1287, in ... get_paged_mqa_logits_metadata
RuntimeError: Assertion error (deepgemm-src/csrc/apis/attention.hpp:262): block_kv == 32 or block_kv == 64
```

The vendored DeepGEMM `_C` additionally guards `(arch_major == 12 and ((is_fp4 and (32|64)) or (not is_fp4 and block_kv == 64)))` — on arch 12 the non-fp4 paged kernel takes only 64. The real model has 20 ratio-1 layers out of 40 (`compress_ratios` = 2×0, 18×2, 20×1), so this is not a corner case. Same class as #53635 (V4's `num_states` vs `block_kv`), reached from V4.1's 128-token indexer block.

**What does work** (with fix 1 applied and a ratio-2-only trimmed topology `[0,0,2,2,2,2]`): the server comes up in ~96 s; FlashInfer SM120 sparse-MLA prefill + decode (the prebuilt `sm_120` cubins from `flashinfer-jit-cache` run on sm_121 without `cudaErrorIllegalInstruction`), DeepGEMM `sm120_fp8_paged_mqa_logits<…, 64, …>`, and `DEEPGEMM_MXFP4` MoE all JIT and serve completions (2k / 3.5k-token prompts, 4 concurrent 1k prompts) with finite logprobs and zero tracebacks. Note: the `deepseek_v4/nvidia/ops/o_proj.py` FP8 einsum was not reached — `wo_a` is dequantized to BF16 at load by `EmulationMxfp8LinearKernel` (chosen for the bmm-shaped MXFP8 weight on SM120), so o_proj took the `torch.bmm` branch.

### Reproduction

```bash
# model dir: config.json + tokenizer files from deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, then edit config.json → text_config:
#   num_hidden_layers 6, compress_ratios [0,0,2,2,1,1], kv_source_layer_ids [2,4], index_source_layer_ids [2,4],
#   candidate_topk_blocks 0, candidate_source_layer_id -1, engram_layer_ids [], engram_num_embeddings [],
#   num_nextn_predict_layers 0, dspark_target_layer_ids [], n_routed_experts 64; vision_config.num_hidden_layers 0
docker run --rm --gpus all --ipc=host --network host -v $PWD/model:/smoke/model \
  -e VLLM_LOGGING_LEVEL=DEBUG vllm/vllm-openai:nightly-e7edf17cea217e52701f913cd8491fcacf2d9490 \
  # (with the e77daef89 wheel pip-installed --no-deps on top)
  /smoke/model --served-model-name dsv41-smoke --load-format dummy --dtype bfloat16 \
  --max-model-len 4096 --max-num-seqs 4 --max-num-batched-tokens 4096 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.25 --enforce-eager --kv-cache-dtype fp8_ds_mla --trust-remote-code
```

Failure 1 appears as shipped; failure 2 appears once `DeepseekV4SWACache(block_size=64)` is applied. Both are in warmup, before `/health` goes 200.

### Expected behavior / suggestion

On arch 12 the V4.1 SWA cache should use the 64-token pages the SM120 dispatch has (as V4 does), and the indexer's kernel block should be 64 on arch 12 as on Hopper (or DeepGEMM's sm120 paged kernel should accept 128) — the two choices interact through `compressed_block_size = block_size // compress_ratio` (ratio-2 wants a 128 block to land on 64), so the fix likely belongs in the `kernel_block_size` remapping for ratio 1 rather than a global block change. Happy to re-run the smoke on GB10 against

items.title: [Bug]: Cross-request context contamination via shared-prefix KV reuse in PD disaggregation with automatic prefix caching — clean with `--no-enable-prefix-caching`
items.author: Siquan-Li
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

With automatic prefix caching enabled (the default) in a NIXL prefill/decode disaggregated deployment serving DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, responses intermittently contain **content from other requests** — cross-request context contamination ("crosstalk"). We have a scriptable reproducer on `/v1/chat/completions` (details below): with a long **identical shared prefix** across requests, 46/48 *sequential* requests returned another request's canary code; at concurrency 128 it was 122/128. Disabling prefix caching on the prefill node **and** all decode nodes (`--no-enable-prefix-caching`) eliminated the contamination.

## Deployment topology (at reproduction time)

```
Clients (multi-turn agent sessions; every request starts with the same large system prompt)
        |
        v
vllm-router 0.1.15  --policy round_robin --kv-connector nixl   (port 30000)
        |
   +----+------------------+
   v                       v
Prefill node              2x Decode nodes
1x node, 8x H100, TP=8    1x node each, 8x H100, TP=8
kv_producer  :8001        kv_consumer  :8002
        \____ NIXL KV transfer ____/
```

(Since 2026-10-12 we run 2P1D; all reproduction data below was collected on the 1P2D topology above.)

## Environment

- vLLM 0.31.0, built from main @ `db9527a46` (2026-10-02), local build tagged `+cu129`; torch 2.13.0+cu129, transformers 5.17.0, nixl 1.4.1
- Driver 550.54.15, nodes of 8× H100 80GB (sm90)
- Model: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (1M context), `FLASHMLA_SPARSE_DSV41` attention backend, block size 64
- Speculative decoding: `{"method":"dspark","num_speculative_tokens":5,"draft_sample_method":"probabilistic","rejection_sample_method":"block","enable_adaptive_verification":true}`
- `--max-num-batched-tokens 4096 --max-num-seqs 32 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92`
- Note: PR #57662 (fix for #57661) was **not merged** at the time of writing, so this build cannot contain it.

## Symptom

Every request shares a long common prefix — in the wild this was Claude Code on the Anthropic-compatible `/v1/messages` endpoint, whose fixed large system prompt is identical across all sessions. With automatic prefix caching on, users in **different, unrelated sessions** intermittently received responses containing content from *another* session (the model "remembered" details, file names, or instructions belonging to someone else's conversation). Affected requests completed with HTTP 200; no errors or warnings in server logs.

## Reproducer (scriptable, `/v1/chat/completions`)

Design: N requests, each consisting of a **long identical shared prefix** plus a per-request distinct tail that embeds a unique canary code. After all responses complete, each output is scanned for canary codes belonging to *other* requests ("foreign" hits).

Results with automatic prefix caching **enabled** (default):

| Scenario | Requests | Outputs containing a foreign canary code |
|---|---|---|
| Sequential (C=1) | 48 | **46/48** |
| Concurrent (C=128) | 128 | **122/128** |

Key observations:

- Concurrency is **not** required — sequential single-stream requests contaminate at ~96%. Sharing a long identical prefix is the trigger.
- Canaries that varied the prefix, or shared only long *suffixes*, did **not** reproduce; earlier negative canary results were a design gap, not evidence against the bug.
- With `--no-enable-prefix-caching` on P **and** both D nodes: 0 foreign hits, and the Claude Code symptom disappeared entirely (verified by the same users plus a 16-way concurrent keepalive, ~3,000 rounds over 17 h).

The canary script is available on request.

## What we have *not* isolated

- We disabled prefix caching on all three nodes at once, so we cannot attribute the reuse to the prefill-side cache, the decode-side cache, or the P↔D KV-transfer interplay (e.g. a consumer trusting producer block IDs for freed/reused blocks, or refcount/eviction asymmetry between P and D).
- No root-cause analysis on the vLLM side yet; happy to invest in narrowing this down with maintainer guidance.

## Hypothesis (unverified)

Under PD disaggregation, prefix-cache blocks belonging to a completed request are re-served to a later request that hashes to the same shared prefix, but the physical KV content behind those blocks has been freed/reassigned — so the later request decodes against another request's KV. The serial (C=1) repro suggests the race is between request completion/reuse bookkeeping rather than simultaneous scheduling.

## Why this is not #57661

#57661 (and fix PR #57662 — still unmerged) describes NIXL transfer regions deduplicated by `base_addr` alone, truncating the compressor `state_cache` transfer for hybrid-attention layers, producing **garbled/empty output**. Our failure mode is different:

1. Symptom: our outputs are coherent but contain **another request's content**; we never observed garbling or empty content/reasoning fields.
2. Toggle sensitivity: our contamination disappears completely with `--no-enable-prefix-caching`; the region-geometry bug in #57661 is independent of the prefix-caching toggle.
3. Mechanism: truncated/misaligned compressor state cannot inject well-formed content from a different request.

We plan to validate our repro against #57662's branch as well, to rule out any interaction; both issues affect the same model + NIXL PD combination with silent HTTP-200 failures.

## Related issues

- #57661 — NIXL P/D silent output corruption (hybrid-attention region dedup), fix PR #57662 (unmerged at writing)
- #56009 — request/response cross-talk symptom, no root cause identified
- #52627 — silent output corruption in 1P1D NIXL PD, different connector combination
- #47930 — DSpark draft acceptance collapse with automatic prefix caching (another prefix-caching × disaggregation interaction)

## Offer

We keep a H100 1P2D/2P1D testbed with this exact model and can: share the canary script, run targeted repro attempts on candidate patches (including #57662), or provide `collect_env.py` output on request.

items.title: What is the first practical limit of persistent KV across Agent steps?
items.author: RyanX0198
items.body_excerpt:
Hi maintainers — I’m Rui from Psync.labs. Recent sampling and decode-interface work led me to a question about long-running local Agent workloads.

Persistent KV could reduce repeated prefill, but only if cache identity, layout, eviction and framework boundaries stay correct as models, adapters and stages change. Which condition is most likely to invalidate the idea in practice: layout incompatibility, model or tokenizer changes, fragmentation, eviction quality loss, scheduler interference, or missing cross-framework contracts?

One counterexample or minimum test would be especially useful. @yzh119

— Rui, Psync.labs

comments.author: eprogressing
comments.body:
For an agent that changes adapters or rewrites its prompt between steps, I would check **cache identity/correctness before fragmentation or scheduling**. That is a conditional priority, not a measured ranking of workloads.

A concrete counterexample is switching from adapter A to adapter B while retaining A's KV. If B changes the value projection (or earlier hidden states), identical token IDs and identical tensor shapes do not make those cached values valid for B. Similarly, editing earlier tool results breaks reuse past the unchanged token prefix in an ordinary causal transformer. Rendering the same conversation differently can also change that prefix.

I would start with this small integration test:

1. Under A, prefill a short token prefix P, then process suffix S using the cached prefix. Compare the next-token logits with a fresh A forward pass on P+S, within an appropriate numerical tolerance.
2. Use a distinct, nonzero B adapter that affects `v_proj`. Repeat with a fresh B prefill as the reference. Your cache manager should reject A's cache; forcibly reusing it is the negative control, which can expose a discrepancy.
3. Edit one early token in P and verify that cache lookup stops at the unchanged prefix. Check logits, rather than just generated text: argmax can hide a difference.

This is consistent with [vLLM's prefix-cache design](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/design/prefix_caching/), which keys blocks using the parent hash, block tokens and extra hashes such as LoRA IDs. Adapter IDs also need versioning/invalidation if their weights can change in place.

After that, check the storage contract separately: [FlashInfer's KV layout documentation](https://docs.flashinfer.ai/tutorials/kv_layout.html) specifies NHD/HND layouts and page metadata. Matching semantics alone does not make a buffer portable between frameworks.

Prepared with Codex assistance from the linked documentation. The integration test above was initially a proposal; the execution update below now supplies an actual mechanism test. Is your agent retaining one model/adapter with append-only history, or switching adapters and rewriting history?


---
**GPU experiment update (2026-10-11):** I ran the actual Transformers/PEFT forward path on an A100-SXM4-40GB, plus CPU controls: Torch 2.14.1+cu130, Transformers 5.19.0, PEFT 0.21.2. This is a random three-layer Llama (hidden 64, four attention heads/two KV heads), with rank-four v_proj LoRA; it does not exercise FlashInfer's attention kernel or a production agent cache manager.

Across seeds 0/1/2, CPU/CUDA and float32/float64, all 72 comparison expectations held. Correct same-adapter reuse, an adapter-name change with exactly zero update, and reuse limited to the two tokens preceding a prefix edit agreed with fresh forwarding (maximum absolute logit error <=1.49e-7; predeclared tolerances float32 1e-5 / float64 1e-10). Forcibly reusing A's KV with nonzero B produced max-absolute differences 0.2205–0.2727; retaining the old full prefix after the edit produced 0.1082–0.2622. Each stale-cache case changed argmax in only 4/12 trials, so comparing all logits matters. Each path used a newly created cache with asserted sequence lengths.

This supports the specific correctness counterexample, not a universal ranking against fragmentation/scheduling. It does not measure answer quality, throughput, cross-framework layout compatibility, or automatic rejection by a cache manager. [Reproduction scripts, full inputs/logits, versions and results](https://gist.github.com/eprogressing/84db3e068aabbe449f8629a3f362a6e5). Prepared with Codex assistance; these runs were actually executed.

items.title: Misc. bug: LoRA loader accepts a MoE expert-count mismatch, causing an OOB write in CPU MUL_MAT_ID
items.author: paeyz
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

Product: ggml-org/llama.cpp / llama-server
Tested source commit: 65091386227039bfb81ee3426537656e3b4a3f83
Reported build number: 10427 (650913862)
Build: CMake Release (NDEBUG), CPU backend, ASan disabled
Compiler: GCC 13.3.0
Platform: Ubuntu 24.04.3 LTS x86-64 under WSL2

Source-level status was also checked against master at
b23701f77d47dad9de834d59ebfcbe25c9e8b46f on 2026-09-19. The missing
LoRA ne[2] validation and the Release-elided standard C assert described
below were still present. The dynamic reproduction was performed on the
pinned tested commit above, not on current master.

### Operating systems

Linux

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

libllama (core library), llama-server

### Command line

```shell
git clone https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp
cd llama.cpp
git checkout 65091386227039bfb81ee3426537656e3b4a3f83
cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DGGML_CUDA=OFF
cmake --build build --target llama-server -j

# From the extracted attachment directory:
./prepare_assets.sh
./run_poc.sh control /absolute/path/to/llama.cpp/build/bin/llama-server
./run_poc.sh malicious /absolute/path/to/llama.cpp/build/bin/llama-server
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

### Summary

For a Mixture-of-Experts base model, the LoRA loader accepts an adapter whose expert dimension (`ne[2]`) is smaller than the corresponding base-model tensor's expert dimension. The loader checks the first two matrix dimensions and the A/B rank relationship, but not the expert dimension.

`build_lora_mm_id()` reuses the base model's router-selected expert IDs for the base tensor and for both LoRA A and B `ggml_mul_mat_id()` operations. On CPU, `n_as` is derived from the current LoRA tensor's `ne[2]`, while the direct range check on the selected expert ID is a standard C `assert()` that is removed in Release builds with `NDEBUG`.

The attached adapter changes one LoRA A tensor from four experts to one. It is accepted by the loader. With `--parallel 2`, two concurrent completion requests then trigger an 8-byte out-of-bounds write and terminate `llama-server` with SIGSEGV during `llama_decode`.

**Expected behavior:** reject the adapter during loading with a tensor-shape error.

**Actual behavior:** the adapter is accepted; inference reaches an out-of-bounds write in CPU `MUL_MAT_ID` and the server terminates.

### Root cause

#### 1. The LoRA loader does not validate the expert dimension

In [`src/llama-adapter.cpp`](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/65091386227039bfb81ee3426537656e3b4a3f83/src/llama-adapter.cpp#L355-L368), the non-embedding path validates:

```cpp
if (model_tensor->ne[0] != w.a->ne[0] || model_tensor->ne[1] != w.b->ne[1]) {
    throw std::runtime_error(...);
}
if (w.a->ne[1] != w.b->ne[0]) {
    throw std::runtime_error(...);
}
```

There is no comparison between `model_tensor->ne[2]` and the expert dimensions of `w.a` and `w.b`.

The crafted adapter changes:

```text
blk.0.ffn_gate_exps.weight.lora_a.ne[2]: 4 -> 1
```

and is still accepted.

#### 2. Base-derived expert IDs are reused for the undersized LoRA tensor

[`build_lora_mm_id()`](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/65091386227039bfb81ee3426537656e3b4a3f83/src/llama-graph.cpp#L1518-L1554) passes the same `ids` tensor to the base operation and both LoRA operations:

```cpp
ggml_tensor * ab_cur = ggml_mul_mat_id(
        ctx0, lw->b,
        ggml_mul_mat_id(ctx0, lw->a, cur, ids),
        ids
        );
```

An expert ID in `0..3` is valid for the four-expert base model, but IDs `1..3` are invalid for the crafted LoRA tensor with `ne[2] == 1`.

On CPU, [`ggml_compute_forward_mul_mat_id()`](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/65091386227039bfb81ee3426537656e3b4a3f83/ggml/src/ggml-cpu/ggml-cpu.c#L1564-L1635) derives `n_as` from that tensor and guards the ID only with:

```c
const int n_as = ne02;

assert(i02 >= 0 && i02 < n_as);

MMID_MATRIX_ROW(i02, matrix_row_counts[i02]) =
    (struct mmid_row_mapping) {id, iid1};
matrix_row_counts[i02] += 1;
```

With `NDEBUG`, the assertion is absent. The instrumented run confirms an out-of-range expert ID and a write far beyond the graph work allocation:

```text
n_as=1
i02=2
count_read=4294967296
work-data size=1,311,744 bytes
target_off=34,359,744,456 bytes
```

The following write faults inside `ggml_compute_forward_mul_mat_id()`.

### Reproduction

The attached archive, [llama-cpp-lora-moe-oob-write.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/32414017/llama-cpp-lora-moe-oob-write.zip), contains the crafted adapter, deterministic construction script, pinned asset/hash verification, trigger scripts, and Release/GDB and ASan evidence.

Build the pinned commit and run the commands in the Command line field above. The helper starts the server on `127.0.0.1` with:

```text
--parallel 2 -c 256 -b 64 -ub 64 --no-webui
```

The trigger sends two concurrent requests with `n_predict: 1`.

**Control adapter:** both requests return HTTP 200 and the server remains alive.

**Crafted adapter:** both connections terminate without complete HTTP responses, and `llama-server` exits with SIGSEGV during `llama_decode`.

### Scope and confirmed impact

The operator must first load the crafted third-party adapter with `--lora`; this is not an unauthenticated adapter-upload issue. Once loaded, two ordinary concurrent completion requests are sufficient to trigger the crash.

The confirmed impact is process-wide denial of service. I did not verify information disclosure, controlled corruption, or code execution. I confirmed the out-of-bounds write on the CPU backend. Validating the expert dimension in the loader would reject the malformed adapter earlier.

### Suggested fix

1. Validate `ne[2]` for LoRA tensors used by `ggml_mul_mat_id()`. For the current MoE `ffn_*_exps` layout, both A and B should match `model_tensor->ne[2]`.
2. Replace the `assert()` with an always-on bounds check.
3. Add regression tests for undersized A/

items.title: [RFC]: COO-format sparse weight transfer and reshard for RL
items.author: zxpdemonio
items.body_excerpt:
# [RFC] COO-format sparse weight transfer and reshard for RL

## Status

- **Status:** Draft
- **Modules:** Mooncake Store, Mooncake Reshard, Mooncake RL
- **Type:** New feature / Performance improvement

## Changes proposed

During RL training, MoE weight updates should be transferred as sparse deltas instead of
complete dense weights. The training side computes `delta = W_current - W_snapshot`, applies
a threshold, and encodes the result as a COO sparse tensor. One update is committed as one
global COO source object using a Mooncake structured object with named buffers for `indices`,
`values`, and a compact tile index.

The inference topology may use EP and TP differently from the training topology. Mooncake
must therefore materialize the source object into target-local COO objects according to target
logical boxes. The Store read path invokes a `mooncake.reshard.sparse` planner, reads only the
COO entry ranges intersecting each target box, performs boundary filtering and global-to-local
coordinate rebasing, and publishes target-local structured objects. The inference side only
applies the result with `scatter_add`.

The RL adapter does not call a public `reshard` API. The public entry points remain
Store-oriented operations such as `put_sparse_object()` and `read_sparse_objects()`; placement
routing, COO range planning, duplicate-read suppression, caching, and target object
materialization are Mooncake responsibilities.

## Motivation

### RL produces sparse weight deltas

RL training and inference usually run in separate resource pools. A training job periodically
publishes model updates to inference. Sending the complete model weight for every update makes
the communication volume proportional to the model size and can turn the update into the
dominant synchronization point.

For MoE weights, an update often changes only a fraction of the elements. The natural wire
representation is therefore:

```text
delta = W_current - W_snapshot
nonzero(delta) -> COO(indices, values)
```

The COO is the content of the source update object, not a temporary format that every target
has to rediscover. `indices` stores coordinates in the complete tensor coordinate space and
`values` stores the corresponding delta values. Both arrays use the same entry order so that
the Store can read them with aligned axis-0 ranges.

### Training and inference layouts differ

The source-side rule is defined per logical weight object. For an EP expert, one source EP owner
computes the complete expert delta. For a non-EP/shared weight, one source owner produces one
complete delta, even when the weight is visible on multiple training ranks. The inference side
may use a different EP/TP topology, so Mooncake routes and slices that one source object at the
target:

| Scenario | Source semantics | Target semantics |
| --- | --- | --- |
| EP expert | One source EP owner computes one complete expert delta | Route only to the corresponding target EP; split by TP inside that EP |
| non-EP/shared weight | One complete delta is produced | All target EP replicas reuse the same source object and take their TP boxes |
| EP-only | One complete expert or shared-weight object | The target logical box is the complete tensor; no TP split |

This rules out two tempting implementations. The source cannot create one COO object per
target replica, and each target cannot download the complete source object and filter it
locally. The required abstraction is one complete source object followed by target-side
sparse-aware reshard.

### Current bottlenecks

Treating `indices` and `values` as ordinary Python objects introduces object-level
serialization and deserialization. It also encourages separate Store keys for metadata,
indices, and values. More importantly, a non-EP source object can be downloaded repeatedly by
each EP×TP target even though all replicas need overlapping ranges. A centralized storage
endpoint then becomes a bandwidth bottleneck.

This RFC is driven by three measurable requirements:

1. **Reduce serialization overhead.** Use a named-buffer structured object. A copy inside the
   structured-object implementation is acceptable for the first version; zero-copy is not a
   protocol prerequisite.
2. **Avoid redundant transfer.** A non-EP update has one source object. On one node, the same
   `(source_ref, generation, range)` is physically read once and then fanned out to local
   targets.
3. **Preserve transport efficiency.** The planner reads only the compact tile index and
   requests the `indices`/`values` ranges covered by a target box. It must not materialize the
   complete COO payload for every target.

## Goals

1. Represent one sparse update with a generic COO structured-object contract that is not tied
   to EP, TP, or a particular RL framework.
2. Support EP expert, non-EP/shared weight, and EP-only target layouts.
3. Put sparse-aware logical planning in `mooncake-reshard`; let the Store executor perform
   reads, filtering, rebasing, and target-object publication.
4. Keep the RL training/inference adapter thin: it computes the delta, encodes global COO,
   and supplies descriptors and generations.
5. Preserve de-duplication as source and target counts grow: no repeated source computation or
   PUT, and no repeated physical GET of the same range on one node.

## Non-goals

1. Changing the continuous-byte-region semantics of the existing dense model-weight reshard
   planner.
2. Requiring zero-copy in the first implementation. The structured-object copy path is an
   accepted baseline.
3. Inferring layer, expert, TP dimension, or other model semantics inside Mooncake. Framework
   adapters must provide these facts in descriptors and placement policies.
4. Defining the quantization algorithm for mismatched source/target dtypes such as BF16 and
   FP8. That is a separate protocol decision.
5. Making a full source COO GET the normal fallback. Unsupported N-D indexes or explicit dense
   fallback must be visible in metrics.

This issue tracks how the `MasterService` half of RFC #3670 lands in `main`. #4370 carries the whole migration as one PR (+7.3k/−6.6k), which is too large to review, so the work is split into 17 PRs. Each PR builds, passes the tests and is correct on its own, and the order below is the order they can merge in. The code for the whole series is already written. Each PR is cut from the finished end state, so reviewing it means reviewing that slice of a design that is already complete, not code still in progress. Review comments are welcome on any PR in the series, and on this issue for the overall plan. Anyone whose review suggestion is adopted is added as a co-author of the PR that takes it. ## Status Last updated 2026-10-20.
