items.title: Feature Request: Graceful reasoning budget termination. Avoid mid-sentence cutoff.
items.author: CleStil
items.body_excerpt:
### Prerequisites

- [x] I am running the latest code. Mention the version if possible as well.
- [x] I carefully followed the [README.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/README.md).
- [x] I searched using keywords relevant to my issue to make sure that I am creating a new issue that is not already open (or closed).
- [x] I reviewed the [Discussions](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions), and have a new and useful enhancement to share.

### Feature Description

PR #20297 (merged ~2025-03-11) added `--reasoning-budget-message`, which injects
a string at the hard token cutoff to signal the model to wrap up. The injection
still happens at exactly token N with zero warning. The model gets no time to
finish its current thought before the `</think>` boundary.

Graceful termination before the cutoff is expected to improve reasoning
performance. See Motivation and Possible Implementation for details.


### Motivation

Raw truncation of the thinking trace measurably reduces answer quality compared
to graceful termination. Muennighoff et al. (s1: Simple test-time scaling,
arXiv:2501.19393) showed that appending an end-of-thinking delimiter with
"Final Answer:" before the hard cut outperforms naïve truncation. This was
confirmed by follow-up work (arXiv:2505.05315), which states directly that
"the S1 approach performs better than directly truncating the full reasoning
trajectory, underscoring the importance of preserving the solution segment."

The current --reasoning-budget-message implementation injects a wrap-up message
at exactly token N, leaving the model zero tokens to actually act on it. This is
functionally equivalent to truncation with a cosmetic suffix — the model cannot
produce a meaningful conclusion within 0 remaining tokens.

### Possible Implementation

Three approaches in increasing complexity:

Option A — message offset
Inject the budget message at `budget - offset` instead of `budget`, giving the
model `offset` tokens to act on the wrap-up signal. The s1 paper
(https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.19393) shows this outperforms raw truncation.
Change in the COUNTING state of reasoning-budget.cpp:

    if (ctx->remaining <= ctx->warn_offset)  // was: <= 0

Files: reasoning-budget.cpp, reasoning-budget.h, common.h, arg.cpp,
sampling.cpp. Default 0 preserves current behavior.

Option B — separate budgeting
Split total budget into thinking (t) and conclusion (s) phases, t + s = budget.
Force `</think>` at token t, leave s tokens for a conclusion before the answer.
Follow-up work on s1 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.05315) shows this outperforms
the basic offset approach. Would add a second parameter, e.g.
--reasoning-budget-conclusion M.

Option C — logit biasing toward `</think>`
Ramp up the logit weight of `</think>` as the budget runs low, then force it at
the hard limit. No dependency on an injected phrase, model-agnostic. NVIDIA NIM
uses this approach with a 10% extension window for sentence completion. More
invasive (sampler changes) but cleanest long-term.

Options A and B build on the existing message injection architecture. Option C
is a parallel approach that could coexist with either.

Happy to test on ROCm/gfx1100 (Qwen3.5-27B) and contribute a draft of Option A
or B if there is interest.

items.title: [Bug]: [Store] BatchGet returns TRANSFER_FAIL at the 60 s wait while RDMA READs are still in flight; caller reuses the destination GPU buffers and gets corrupted KV
items.author: ThisFat
items.body_excerpt:
### Bug Report

## Environment

| | |
|---|---|
| Mooncake | `mooncake-transfer-engine` 0.3.13.post1 (PyPI wheel). Log line `transfer_task.cpp:891` matches tag `v0.3.13.post1` (commit `719735896c86`), i.e. the non-event-driven polling branch of `wait_for_completion()` |
| vLLM | 0.30.0, built-in `MooncakeStoreConnector`; `{"kv_connector":"MooncakeStoreConnector","kv_role":"kv_both","kv_load_failure_policy":"recompute","kv_connector_extra_config":{"lookup_async":true}}` |
| Model / serving | GLM-5.3-Flash (hybrid; `kv cache group sizes [640, 4, 640, 640, 640, 640]`), TP=8, `--max-model-len 262144`, `--enable-prefix-caching`, `--enable-chunked-prefill`, `--max-num-batched-tokens 8192`, `--prefix-match-unit 128` |
| Nodes | 3 nodes (A, B, C), each 8× NVIDIA H20-3e, 2× Xeon Platinum 8558P, 2 TiB RAM |
| OS / drivers | Ubuntu 22.04.5, kernel 5.15.0-187-generic, NVIDIA driver 610.43.02 with `nvidia_peermem` loaded, MLNX_OFED 24.10-5.1.6.1 |
| Python stack | Python 3.12.13, torch 2.13.0+cu130 |
| Network | RoCE v2, one ConnectX NIC per node for Mooncake (`mlx5_0`, 400 Gb/s NDR), netdev MTU 9000 / active MTU 4096, GID index 3 |
| Mooncake topology | `mooncake_master` on A: `--default_kv_lease_ttl=60s --eviction_high_watermark_ratio=0.85 --eviction_ratio=0.02`. One `mooncake_client` Store per node: `--protocol=rdma --device_names=mlx5_0 --global_segment_size=1099511627776 --local_buffer_size=8589934592 --metadata_server=P2PHANDSHAKE`. vLLM on each node uses the store as a client. Pool ~84% used, eviction continuously active |
| Env vars | No `MC_*` set (defaults: `MC_SLICE_TIMEOUT=-1`, `MC_RETRY_CNT=9`) |

### Description

`TransferEngineOperationState::wait_for_completion()` gives up after a hard-coded 60 s, sets `TRANSFER_FAIL` and returns, without cancelling or draining the batch. `Client::BatchGet` then returns to the caller. vLLM's `MooncakeStoreConnector` treats the failure as "these blocks are invalid": the scheduler reschedules the request and the GPU KV blocks are freed and reallocated (to other requests, or to the same request for recompute). The RDMA READs of the timed-out batch that are still queued or in flight keep the old local destination addresses. When they complete later, they write stale KV into GPU blocks that now hold other data.

This is the read-side counterpart of #4491 (timed-out put overwrites the next object).

**Expected:** after `BatchGet` returns an error for a key, Mooncake no longer writes into that key's destination buffer, or the API tells the caller the buffer is not yet safe to reuse.

**Actual:** `TRANSFER_FAIL` is returned while transfers targeting the buffer may still complete. The batch's `freeBatchID()` fails silently, and nothing in the logs shows that transfers were left behind.

### Observed behavior

1. After node C's Store joined the pool (2 → 3 TiB), all three vLLM processes started logging bursts of:

   ```
   E.... transfer_task.cpp:891] Failed to complete transfers after 60000 milliseconds for batch ...
   E.... client_service.cpp:...] Transfer failed for key: <key> with error: -800
   W.... client_service.cpp:...] lease_expired_before_data_transfer_completed key=<key>
   E.... real_client.cpp:...] BatchGet failed for key '<key>': LEASE_EXPIRED   (or TRANSFER_FAIL)
   WARNING [worker.py:1471] Failed to get N Mooncake keys from sub-batch (...)
   WARNING [scheduler.py:3240] Recovered from KV load failure: 1 request(s) rescheduled (N tokens affected).
   ```

   Over ~3.3 days: node A 8,825 timed-out batches, node B 5,849, node C 35,166. Nodes A and B had **zero** of these in the preceding 3 days with a 1- and then 2-Store pool (including ~18 h of A↔B cross-node reads). Load does not explain it: a day peaking at ~1.2 TB/h of `load_get` had none; a later day peaking at ~0.33 TB/h still had >1,000 timed-out batches per hour on node A.

2. No RDMA-level errors in the same logs: no `Process failed for slice`, no `Cannot redispatch slice`, no `BatchID cannot be freed`. `LEASE_EXPIRED` outnumbers `TRANSFER_FAIL` about 3:1, so many of these transfers did finish, just after 60 s.

3. Output corruption correlates with the timeouts. Over two days we matched every `Recovered from KV load failure` event (tokens > 0) to gateway requests on the same node (arrived before the event, first token after it, prompt ≥ affected tokens). An output counts as broken if it is garbled from the first token or runs away (hits `max_tokens` or ends in endless repetition):

   | Group (prompt ≥ 40k tokens) | Requests | Broken outputs |
   |---|---|---|
   | Rescheduled after a KV load failure | 169 | 6 (3.55%), garbled **from the first token** |
   | Same node, prefill overlapping the 60 s before a timeout, not rescheduled | 588 | 5 (0.85%), normal start, runaway later |
   | Same nodes, other times | 46,365 | 79 (0.17%) |
   | Nodes without Mooncake | 89,196 | 56 (0.06%) |

Example: one request (49,713-token prompt, clean conversation history) waited 81.7 s for its first token. About 60 s after it arrived, the log on that node shows `Failed to get 65 Mooncake keys` → `rescheduled (49152 tokens affected)`, and the response was garbage from the first token.

4. Mitigation in progress: we stopped node C's Store (back to 2 Stores). The timeout and reschedule counters on A and B have not increased since.

items.title: [Feature] kv-shard: Pass Q instead of KV for short prefills with long cached prefixes
items.author: Shunkangz
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Motivation

## Background

With `--enable-kv-cache-sharding`, each CP rank stores \(1/N\) of every cached prefix. Today, extend batches are zigzag-split across all ranks, and every request’s prefix KV is all-gathered to every rank one layer ahead.

For agentic and multi-turn workloads, a short prefill often extends a long cached prefix, so prefix KV dominates communication. DCP avoids this for decode by passing Q instead of KV, but directly applying it to prefill would replicate new-token computation across ranks.

## Overall Design

Use **per-request placement**: each request has one home CP rank that computes all its new tokens. Choose the communication policy per request based on \(P/T\):

- Pass-KV for short prefixes: the home fetches only its requests’ prefix stripes via all-to-all.
- Pass-Q for long prefixes: all-gather Q, attend over each rank’s local prefix stripes, and return partial outputs and LSE to the home for merging with its causal new-token attention.

Overlap both pass-Q collectives with the home’s local attention and use copy-engine transfers for large messages. In the 8× B200 per-layer harness, exposed communication is 0.1–1.2% of layer time at 128K–256K prefixes; choosing pass-Q when \(P/T > 128\) is within 1.9% of the best measured split on average.

## PR Stack

The following PRs will be released soon.

### 1/5 — Enable FA4 for GQA KV Sharding and Fix Sharded KV Writes

- Enable FA4 for GQA KV sharding on Blackwell.
- Fix a silent wrong-logits bug where fused RoPE + KV writes bypass the sharded pool on short extends, affecting both FA3 and FA4.
- Validation: sharded and unsharded outputs are bit-exact at CP4.

### 2/5 — Add Symmetric-Memory Transports for Pass-Q Attention

- Add `PassQCommunicator` with variable-size Q all-gather, partial O + LSE all-to-all, and LSE merging.
- Support Triton SM-push and copy-engine transports using Torch symmetric memory.
- Add multi-GPU tests.

### 3/5 — Add Per-Request CP Placement for Prefill

- Assign whole requests to CP ranks when the batch can be balanced, using one FA call per rank.
- Fetch only each rank’s own requests’ prefix stripes via all-to-all instead of all-gathering every prefix.
- Validation: sharded and unsharded outputs are bit-exact at CP4 with B=4.
- Reduce latency versus zigzag placement by 8 ms unsharded and 5 ms sharded at 32K/64K.

### 4/5 — Pass Q Instead of KV for Long-Prefix Requests

- Add `--kv-shard-pass-q-ratio` for per-request P/T policy selection.
- Add pass-Q-aware placement, including B < N, and pool stripe tables.
- Implement Q all-gather, local prefix-stripe attention, partial O + LSE all-to-all, and merging.
- Start with a serial schedule.

### 5/5 — Overlap Pass-Q Communication with Local Attention

- Run communication on a side stream.
- Split the home rank’s local attention across both collectives to **overlap** communication and computation.
- Select the transport by message size.
- Run end-to-end A/B validation at CP8.

### Related resources

_No response_

items.title: Use atomic_cas inside a loop
items.author: giorgio-arena
items.body_excerpt:
Hi, I'm experimenting with a simple kernel that reduces a rank-3 tensor on its last dimension. The kernel uses atomics to sum across one tensor row (I know it's not efficient, this is just a simple reproducer). I'm using two versions of the atomics, the first using atomic_add, and the second using the lock-like mechanism with atomic_cas and atomic_xchg.

```
@triton.jit
def _sum_kernel(X, Locks, O, width: tl.constexpr, use_atomic_add: tl.constexpr):
  in_off = tl.program_id(0) * width
  out_off = tl.program_id(0)

  for w in range(0, width):
    x = tl.load(X + in_off + w)
    if use_atomic_add:
      tl.atomic_add(O + out_off, x)
    else:
      while tl.atomic_cas(Locks + out_off, 0, 1) == 1:
        pass
      tl.store(O + out_off, tl.load(O + out_off) + x)
      tl.atomic_xchg(Locks + out_off, 0)


def _sum_fn(a, use_atomic_add):
  b, h, w = a.shape
  locks = torch.zeros([b, h], dtype=torch.int32, device='cuda')
  out = torch.zeros([b, h], dtype=a.dtype, device='cuda')
  _sum_kernel[(b * h,)](a, locks, out, width=w, use_atomic_add=use_atomic_add)
  return out

if __name__ == "__main__":
  x = torch.empty((8, 64, 128), dtype=torch.float32, device="cuda").normal_()
  ref = torch.sum(x, axis=-1)
  rtol = 1e-03

  print(torch.allclose(ref, _sum_fn(x, True), rtol=rtol))
  print(torch.allclose(ref, _sum_fn(x, False), rtol=rtol))
```

Unfortunately for the second version I get
```

  File "/usr/local/home/giorgio/triton/python/triton/compiler.py", line 741, in visit_For
    assert for_op_region.size() == 1, "We use SCF, so the loop body should only have one block"
AssertionError: We use SCF, so the loop body should only have one block
```

Any help would be appreciated, thanks.

items.title: [RFC][Plugin] Add MLIR Dialect Whitelist for Preserving TypeIDs and Generic Plugin Module Extension
items.author: hongziqi
items.body_excerpt:
## Abstract

The upstream Triton plugin system only supports table-driven registration of Passes, Dialects, and OpInfo. **It cannot let a plugin inject a custom IR Builder subclass.** At the same time, `libtriton.so` built with `--as-needed` drops TypeIDs of dialects such as Linalg and Tensor.
Triton-Ascend ships as the out-of-tree plugin `libtriton_ascend.so` and shares one MLIRContext / PassManager with the host. In that setup, Pass execution breaks and IR construction fails.

This proposal has two parts:

1. Bump the plugin ABI to v3. Add a host-side module extension callback, `HostExtendCallback`, and a top-level Python API, `ir.extend_module_with`. Build nanobind as its own shared library.
2. Add a dialect whitelist so the listed dialect TypeIDs stay in `libtriton.so` at link time.

After the change, an out-of-tree plugin can attach a custom IR Builder, extend the Python IR with a submodule, and reuse the host MLIR context and Pass pipeline.

## 1. Background

Triton-Ascend uses the **out-of-tree plugin** `libtriton_ascend.so`. It shares the upstream Triton MLIRContext and PassManager, reuses the existing Dialects, Passes, and OpInfo, and does not fork the main repository.

Two gaps show up when this is wired up: a custom IR Builder cannot be injected, and MLIR dialect TypeIDs are missing between the host and the plugin.

### 1.1 GAP-P2: Missing Linalg/Tensor TypeIDs

Upstream `libtriton.so` is built with `--as-needed` by default. If a symbol in a static library is not referenced directly by a host translation unit, the linker drops that archive member. TypeIDs for Linalg, Tensor, and the Complex and Bufferization dialects that Ascend lowering depends on are stripped. When the plugin and the host share one MLIRContext, the required MLIR symbols are missing and Pass execution fails.

### 1.2 GAP-P1: The current plugin mechanism cannot support a custom IR Builder subclass

What the existing plugin extension APIs can and cannot do:

| API | Capability | Typical use | Limit for Ascend |
| :-- | :-- | :-- | :-- |
| `passes.plugin.extend_with` | Register Passes and expose `add_*` callbacks | Add an MLIR Pass | Sufficient for Passes |
| `ir.extend_dialects_with` | Register a new Dialect | Add a standalone dialect | Sufficient for Dialect registration |
| `ir.builder.extend_with` (OpInfo table) | Attach op factories on the upstream `ir.builder`. C++ ABI is `void (*)(TritonOpBuilder&, vector<Value>&)`. Host Python wraps it as `create_*(list[Value]) → Value` | Add a simple Op whose arguments are a fixed list of Values | **Not sufficient** |

`ir.builder.extend_with` only supports flat op factory functions. **It does not support a Builder subclass, kwargs, or affine expressions.**
Ascend's `AscendNPUIROpBuilder` subclasses `TritonOpBuilder`, and the IR construction lives in `ascend_ir.cc`. The OpInfo table can only append `create_*` factories. **It cannot replace the Builder type, and it cannot add a Python IR submodule.**

The missing piece is a **host IR module extension hook (HostExtend)** so a plugin can initialize its own IR module inside the host process.

## 2. Design

Each gap maps to an upstream change and a plugin-side hookup:

| Gap | Upstream change | Ascend plugin hookup |
| :-- | :-- | :-- |
| **Linalg / Tensor TypeIDs are not visible** | Add a dialect TypeID whitelist, `python/src/plugin_ext_dialects.whitelist`. CMake reads it and generates `plugin_ext_dialects.gen.cc`, which takes a strong reference with `TypeID::get`. On GNU ld, `--whole-archive` pulls the corresponding dialect static libraries into `libtriton.so`. The initial list is Linalg, Tensor, Complex, and Bufferization. | The plugin reuses the whitelisted dialect TypeIDs exported by the host. TypeIDs of plugin-defined dialects stay inside the plugin `.so`. |
| **`ir.builder` factories are not expressive enough** | Add `HostExtensionArgs` and `HostExtendCallback`. Append an `extend` field at the end of `PluginInfo`, read only when `apiVersion >= 3`. Add the top-level Python API `ir.extend_module_with`. When `TRITON_EXT_ENABLED=1`, build nanobind as a separate `libnanobind.so`. | The plugin sets `PluginInfo.extend = ascendExtendHost`. The callback registers a nanobind submodule and exposes `ir._ascend` and `AscendNPUIROpBuilder`. The plugin is built with `NB_SHARED` and links the host `libnanobind.so`. |

Benefits:

- **IR**: An out-of-tree plugin can inject a Builder subclass, with kwargs, affine expressions, and custom op wrappers, instead of being limited to the fixed OpInfo signature `create_*(list[Value])`.
- **ABI**: The v3 `extend` field is appended at the end of `PluginInfo`. The host reads it only when `apiVersion >= 3`, so existing v2 plugins still load. The `OpInfo` layout is unchanged.
- **whitelisted MLIR symbols**: Each whitelisted dialect TypeID exists once in the host `.so`. Type identity is consistent inside one MLIRContext.
- **Python bindings**: The host and the plugin share `libnanobind.so`. IR objects can cross the `.so` boundary, and Python can use the plugin submodule `ir._ascend` directly.

## 3. Implementation

### 3.1 Support MLIR whitelist: Keeping Linalg/Tensor and related symbols

The whitelist `python/src/plugin_ext_dialects.whitelist` names the MLIR dialects whose TypeIDs must be exported. Each line has three columns: CMake target, header, and C++ type.

```text
# format: cmake_target|include_header|TypeExpr
MLIRLinalgDialect|mlir/Dialect/Linalg/IR/Linalg.h|mlir::linalg::LinalgDialect
MLIRTensorDialect|mlir/Dialect/Tensor/IR/Tensor.h|mlir::tensor::TensorDialect
MLIRComplexDialect|mlir/Dialect/Complex/IR/Complex.h|mlir::complex::ComplexDialect
MLIRBufferizationDialect|mlir/Dialect/Bufferization/IR/Bufferization.h|mlir::bufferization::BufferizationDialect
```

`CMakeLists.txt` reads the whitelist and does two things:

1. Collect the CMake targets into `TRITON_PLUGIN_EXT_DIALECT_LIBS` and, on GNU ld, link them into `libtriton.so` with `--whole-archive`.
2. Generate `plugin_ext_dialects.gen.cc`

items.title: Qwen 3.5 MTP fails to load compact draft vocabularies (missing d2t mapping support)
items.author: Shreesh-Sree
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

When using Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) speculative decoding with draft models or sidecars that utilize a trimmed/compact vocabulary (such as FastMTP with a `d2t` draft-to-target mapping tensor), `llama_model_qwen35` and `llama_model_qwen35moe` fail during model loading or graph evaluation.

### Root Cause
1. **Dimension Mismatch in Loader:** The draft LM head (`output.weight` or `layer.nextn.shared_head_head`) has dimensions `[n_embd, n_draft_vocab]` (e.g. 32,768 tokens). In `src/models/qwen35.cpp` and `src/models/qwen35moe.cpp`, `load_arch_tensors` unconditionally expected `n_vocab` (152,064 tokens), triggering a loader assertion failure or crash.
2. **Incorrect Fallback:** When `output == NULL`, it unconditionally fell back to duplicating `LLM_TENSOR_TOKEN_EMBD` with full `n_vocab`, clobbering the compact draft head.
3. **Missing Logits Scatter:** Unlike `dflash.cpp` and `eagle3.cpp`, `qwen35.cpp` and `qwen35moe.cpp` did not scatter draft candidate logits onto the full `-inf` target canvas using `ggml_set_rows`.

### We Have Solved This Ourselves

We diagnosed the issue, implemented the complete fix for both `qwen35` and `qwen35moe`, and verified it with physical hardware testing on dual NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Ada/Blackwell GPUs (achieving 102.2 – 113.9 tok/s, ~2.3x speedup).

We have opened a clean, 1-commit pull request with the complete fix:
👉 **Pull Request:** https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/29143

### Authors & Attribution
- **Sreesanth R** ([@Shreesh-Sree](https://github.com/Shreesh-Sree))
- **Allen Joseph** ([@unknownhackerworld](https://github.com/unknownhackerworld))

items.title: jinja: gpt-oss template 500s ('Function is not a bool value') on array tool params without items
items.author: rapuckett
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

With the gpt-oss chat template, every chat request that defines a tool with an `array` parameter *without* an `items` key fails with HTTP 500: `Function is not a bool value`.

### Cause

`models/templates/openai-gpt-oss-120b.jinja` (line 12, also embedded in the gpt-oss GGUFs) does:

```jinja
{%- if param_spec['items'] -%}
```

When `param_spec` has no `items` key, the subscript falls back to the attribute lookup and returns the mapping's built-in `items` method. The jinja engine in `common/jinja/` then raises from `value::as_bool()` (`common/jinja/value.h`, "is not a bool value") when that callable is used in a boolean context.

Python Jinja2 treats a callable as truthy, so the same template renders there. Either the engine should treat callables as truthy, matching Jinja2, or the template should test for the key (`{%- if 'items' in param_spec -%}`). Probably both.

### Repro

- llama.cpp b11395 (CUDA build), `ggml-org/gpt-oss-20b-GGUF` (MXFP4).
- Send `POST /v1/chat/completions` with one tool whose parameters include `{"type": "array"}` with no `items`. This is common in tool schemas generated by agent frameworks.
- Result: a 500 with "Function is not a bool value". Adding `items`, or patching the template line to `'items' in param_spec` and passing it with `--chat-template-file`, fixes it.

Ollama's own gpt-oss renderer doesn't hit this.

items.title: [RFC] An Extensible Collective Framework for Mooncake PG
items.author: caozhanhao
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

This RFC proposes an extensible GPU collective framework for Mooncake PG. The framework separates PG-level backend dispatch from group-wide algorithm selection, rank-local planning, GPU execution, and device data movement, while preserving the existing PG APIs and elastic semantics.

This proposal builds on #2716 by turning its device-collective direction into a concrete framework for GPU collectives. The framework is introduced incrementally alongside the legacy implementation, and the new collective path remains opt-in during the rollout.

## Motivation

The legacy GPU collective path couples collective protocols with host workers, transfer submission, synchronization, and failure handling. Adding several algorithms per operation and tuning them for different message sizes and topologies would otherwise duplicate these concerns and make cross-rank consistency harder to maintain.

The new framework gives GPU collective algorithms a narrower responsibility: implement a protocol against a rank-local plan and a device transfer interface. Membership, capability negotiation, backend dispatch, algorithm selection, resource ownership, and recovery remain framework responsibilities.

## Goals

- Define reusable planning and execution boundaries for GPU collective operations.
- Define algorithm selection within the new path so every rank receives the same policy and runs a consistent collective protocol.
- Decouple device collective algorithms from route-specific transfer details.
- Allow membership or algorithm changes to reuse a CUDA Graph capture.
- Migrate incrementally with explicit opt-in while the legacy path remains the default.

## Non-Goals

- Replacing all legacy collectives during the initial rollout.
- Switching to another route after a transfer failure in the initial implementation.

## Architecture

```
                                      +-------------------+
                                      | torch.distributed |
                                      +---------+---------+
                                                |
                                                v
+===================================================================================================+
| Mooncake PG                                                                                       |
|                                                                                                   |
|                                  +-------------------------+                                      |
|                                  | Mooncake Communicator   |                                      |
|                                  +------------+------------+                                      |
|                                               |                                                   |
|              +--------------------------------+-----------------------+                           |
|              |                                |                       |                           |
|              v                                v                       v                           |
|   +-------------------+        +---------------------------------------------------+              |
|   | Legacy Collective |        | New Collective Runtime                            |              |
|   | Runtime           |        |                                                   |              |
|   +---------+---------+        | +----------------+          +--------------+      |              |
|             |                  | | Device Runtime |          | CPU Runtime  |------+-------+      |
|             |                  | +--------+-------+          +--------------+      |       |      |
|             |                  +----------|----------------------------------------+       |      |
|             |                             |                                                |      |
|             |                             v                                                |      |
|             |        +-----------------------------------------------------------+         |      |
|             |        | Device Transfer Service                                   |         |      |
|             |        |                                                           |         |      |
|             |        | +-----------+ +------------+ +-----------+ +------------+ |         |      |
|             |        | | P2P Route | | RDMA Route | | GIN Route | | Host Proxy | |         |      |
|             |        | +-----+-----+ +-----+------+ +-----+-----+ +------+-----+ |         |      |
|             |        +-------|-------------|--------------|--------------|-------+         |      |
|             |                |             |              |              |                 |      |
+=============|================|=============|==============|==============|=================|======+
              |                +-------------+--------------+              |                 |
              |                              |                             |                 |
              |                              v                             v                 |
              |                 +--------------------------+   +------------------------+    |
              |                 | Transfer Engine (Device) |   | Transfer Engine (Host) |<---+
              |                 +--------------------------+   +------------------------+
              |                                                            ^
              |                                                            |
              +------------------------------------------------------------+
```

The public collective APIs remain unchanged. The Coordinator owns authoritative membership and publishes group-wide decisions. `MooncakeCommunicator` dispatches operations to the selected legacy or new backend

items.title: [AOTAutogradCache] Stale compile after editing a torch.library.triton_op: the cache key covers only the kernels a scan of the op's source finds
items.author: edmundshieh
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

I ran into this while tuning the Triton kernels of a `triton_op` (the GeGLU MLP of the pi0.5 robot policy) with torch.compile on a Jetson AGX Thor. After I changed a kernel's launch config, the next run still executed the old kernels, so a timing I took for the new config actually came from the previous one. Turning off the AOTAutograd cache with `TORCHINDUCTOR_AUTOGRAD_CACHE=0` fixed it. I'd expect any edit to a `triton_op`'s code to miss the cache, as editing a kernel the op launches directly already does. The analysis below was prepared with an AI assistant (Claude Code); the reproducer was run on my machine and reviewed by me. I don't have a fix ready and would like a maintainer's view on the options at the end of the analysis.

#### AI-generated analysis (Claude Code)

> A `torch.library.triton_op` is traced into the compiled graph: AOTAutograd replaces the op with the `triton_kernel_wrapper_*` calls its body makes, so the compiled code bakes in the body and its kernels. The AOTAutograd cache (`torch/_functorch/_aot_autograd/autograd_cache.py`) keys the Dynamo graph, where the op is a call to `torch.ops.<namespace>.<name>`. `check_node_safe` accepts any `OpOverload`, and the op's implementation enters the key only through `triton_kernel_source_codes`: the sources of the kernels that `torch._library.triton.get_inner_triton_kernels` finds when it scans the op's source at registration. Edits outside what the scan finds leave the key unchanged, and a warm cache returns the compile from before the edit:
>
> - the op's own code, e.g. a scalar or launch parameter it passes to a kernel, its grid, or the torch ops it calls;
> - kernels the scan does not reach, e.g. one launched through a helper that receives `wrap_triton` as an argument, or through a call on a module attribute such as `kernels.launch(...)`. When all of an op's launches go through such helpers, the key includes no kernel source at all.
>
> On a hit, AOTAutograd loads the compiled code that its entry bundles or references by FX graph cache key, so Inductor's FX graph cache, whose key covers the traced kernels, never sees the edited op. A `torch.library.custom_op` is not affected, since its implementation runs at run time instead of being traced into the graph.
>
> The reproducer compiles a `triton_op` in two fresh processes that share a cache directory, and edits the op's source between them, for three kinds of edit. After the first two, the second process gets an AOTAutograd cache hit and returns the result from before the edit. Editing a kernel that the op launches itself changes the key, and the second process recompiles. With `TORCHINDUCTOR_AUTOGRAD_CACHE=0`, which keeps Inductor's FX graph cache, all three return the edited result. The runs below used torch 2.15.0.dev20261005 and Triton 3.9.0 on a Jetson AGX Thor; main has the same key computation and source scan.
>
> Possible fixes: also hash the source of the op and of the functions the scan already walks, or bypass the AOTAutograd cache for graphs that call a `triton_op`.

Reproducer:

```python
import os
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile

OP = """
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl
from torch.library import triton_op, wrap_triton


@triton.jit
def scale_kernel(x_ptr, out_ptr, scale, n, BLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    offsets = tl.program_id(0) * BLOCK + tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
    mask = offsets < n
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + offsets, mask=mask)
    tl.store(out_ptr + offsets, x * scale * KERNEL_FACTOR, mask=mask)


def launch(x, out, scale, wrap):
    wrap(scale_kernel)[(triton.cdiv(x.numel(), 1024),)](x, out, scale, x.numel(), BLOCK=1024)


@triton_op("repro::scale", mutates_args={})
def scale(x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    out = torch.empty_like(x)
    LAUNCH
    return out
"""
DIRECT = "wrap_triton(scale_kernel)[(triton.cdiv(x.numel(), 1024),)](x, out, BODY_SCALE, x.numel(), BLOCK=1024)"
HELPER = "launch(x, out, BODY_SCALE, wrap_triton)"

RUN = """
import torch
import repro_op
from torch._dynamo.utils import counters

y = torch.compile(lambda x: torch.ops.repro.scale(x))(torch.ones(8, device="cuda"))
print(y[0].item(), counters["aot_autograd"]["autograd_cache_hit"])
"""

# (description, launch, (body scale, kernel factor) before and after the edit)
CASES = [
    ("edit the scalar the op passes to its kernel", DIRECT, [("2.0", "1.0"), ("3.0", "1.0")]),
    ("edit the kernel, launched through a helper", HELPER, [("1.0", "2.0"), ("1.0", "3.0")]),
    ("edit the kernel, launched by the op itself", DIRECT, [("1.0", "2.0"), ("1.0", "3.0")]),
]

for description, launch, versions in CASES:
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
        env = dict(
            os.environ,
            PYTHONPATH=tmp,
            PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE="1",
            TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR=os.path.join(tmp, "inductor"),
        )
        results = []
        for body_scale, kernel_factor in versions:
            source = OP.replace("LAUNCH", launch).replace("BODY_SCALE", body_scale)
            with open(os.path.join(tmp, "repro_op.py"), "w") as f:
                f.write(source.replace("KERNEL_FACTOR", kernel_factor))
            out = subprocess.run(
                [sys.executable, "-c", RUN], env=env, capture_output=True, text=True, check=True
            ).stdout.split()
            expected = float(body_scale) * float(kernel_factor)
            results.append(f"expected {expected}, got {float(out[0])} (AOTAutograd cache hits: {out[1]})")
        print(f"{description}:\n  before: {results[0]}\n  after:  {results[1]}")
```

Output:

```
edit the scalar the op passes to its kernel:
  before: expected 2.0, got 2.0 (AOTAutograd cache hits: 0)
  after:  expected 3.0, got 2.0 (AOTAutograd cache hits: 1)
edit the kernel, launched through a helper:
  before: expected 2.0, got 2.0 (AOTAutograd cache hits: 0)
  after:  expected 3.0, got 2.0 (AOTAutograd cache hits: 1)
edit the kernel, launched by the op itself:
  before: expected 2.0,

items.title: torch.i0 / torch.special.i1 (and modified_bessel_i0/i1) overflow to inf for 709.78 < x < 713.98 where the value is finite: exp(x) overflows before I(x)/sqrt(2πx) does
items.author: bahumanyarg11
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`torch.i0` (alias `torch.special.i0`) and `torch.special.i1` return `inf` in float64 for 709.78 < x < 713.98 although the true values are finite there. The kernels evaluate `exp(x) * P(x) / sqrt(x)` (Cephes form), and `exp(x)` overflows at x = 709.782712893384 while `I0(x) ≈ exp(x) / sqrt(2πx)` only exceeds the float64 maximum at x = 713.986908544 (I1 at 713.987609819). `torch.special.modified_bessel_i0` and `modified_bessel_i1` use the same expression (`std::exp(std::abs(x)) * (...) / std::sqrt(std::abs(x))`).

```python
import torch, mpmath
mpmath.mp.dps = 30
for x in [709.0, 709.78, 709.79, 710.0, 712.0, 713.9]:
    t = torch.tensor(x, dtype=torch.float64)
    print(x, torch.i0(t).item(), torch.special.i1(t).item(),
          float(mpmath.besseli(0, x)), float(mpmath.besseli(1, x)))
```

Reference values (mpmath at 30 digits):

| x | I0(x) | I1(x) |
|---|---|---|
| 709.0 | 1.231547707e+306 | 1.23067889e+306 |
| 709.78 | 2.685110051e+306 | 2.683217875e+306 |
| 709.79 | 2.712076744e+306 | 2.710165591e+306 |
| 710.0 | 3.345334559e+306 | 3.342977859e+306 |
| 712.0 | 2.468411058e+307 | 2.466677014e+307 |
| 713.9 | 1.648155187e+308 | 1.64700045e+308 |

Measured on PyTorch 2.14.1 (CPU wheel, macOS 26.3 arm64, Python 3.13) with 500 log-uniform float64 samples per function: `torch.i0` returned `inf` at x = 709.9612985980363 (true 3.2184264790061533e+306), 710.262767233197 (4.3498826205797261e+306), 711.5883292023453 (1.6359000292660463e+307) and 712.9146849235525 (6.15717102267673e+307); `torch.special.i1` at 709.8372510823607 (2.8412030462785448e+306), 710.7266864427472 (6.9104687946512046e+306) and 710.9297125470182 (8.4648383914887804e+306). Everywhere else both functions are within 3.4 ULP of the reference. The same holds in float32, where `exp` overflows at x = 88.72 while I0 stays finite to about x = 91.9.

Where the expression lives: `calc_i0` / `calc_i1` in `aten/src/ATen/native/Math.h` (the `x > 8` branch, `std::exp(x) * chbevl(...) / std::sqrt(x)`), `modified_bessel_i0_forward` / `modified_bessel_i1_forward` in the same file, and the copies in `aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/Math.cuh` and `c10/metal/special_math.h`.

### Expected behavior

Finite values up to the true overflow point, e.g. `torch.i0(torch.tensor(712.0, dtype=torch.float64))` = 2.4e+307. A fix that keeps the other branches untouched is to split the exponential on the large-x branch: `(exp(x/2) * chbevl(...) / sqrt(x)) * exp(x/2)`, or equivalently `i0e(x) * exp(x/2) * exp(x/2)`. SciPy's and JAX's `i0` have the same Cephes-derived overflow, so this is not a regression against them, but the values are representable and `scipy.special.i0e(x) * exp(x)` style workarounds are what users resort to.

### Versions

PyTorch 2.14.1 (CPU wheel), Python 3.13.7, macOS 26.3.1 arm64. Reference: mpmath 1.3.0.

Found with [specaudit](https://github.com/bahumanyarg11/specaudit), an accuracy audit of special functions against mpmath references.

items.title: [docs] Slurm: fix multi-node example, add single-node and offline batch examples
items.author: holtwood
items.body_excerpt:
## Motivation

Contributes to #3244.

The existing multi-node example expands `$SLURM_NODEID` in the batch shell, before `srun` creates its per-task environments. Both launches can therefore receive the same node rank. The existing readiness loop also checks only whether a TCP port is open.

This PR covers basic multi-node serving, single-node serving, and offline batch inference. #29991 has a separate scope around PD disaggregation and Apptainer.

## Changes

- Evaluate `$SLURM_PROCID` inside each `srun` task and use Slurm `%n` patterns for per-node logs.
- Use configurable HTTP and distributed-init ports, a bounded `/health` check, and early process-exit detection.
- Add a single-node serving job with cleanup and an SSH forwarding hint.
- Add an offline job that writes a real Python file with a `__main__` guard, as required by the Engine multiprocessing setup.
- Document the log-directory prerequisite and cluster-specific scheduler, network, port, and model-cache settings.

## Validation

- `bash -n` on all three batch scripts.
- `mint validate`.
- `mint broken-links`.
- Parsed and mock-executed the offline Python example, including Engine context cleanup.
- Checked task-side rank expansion with `SLURM_PROCID=0` and `SLURM_PROCID=1`.
- Cross-checked the Engine `spawn` setup, context-manager support, `/health` behavior, and referenced server arguments against the PR base revision.

I did not run these examples end to end on a Slurm GPU cluster. The `#SBATCH` resource values, partition name, network interfaces, and port availability remain site-specific.

items.title: Why does num_warps affect numerical precision?
items.author: yaozhenghangma
items.body_excerpt:
I'm testing a Flash Attention kernel, and I've placed the test code at the end. In short, when performing an attention operation using q, k, and v matrices with `num_batchs = 8`, `seq_len = 128`, `num_heads = 128`, and `head_dim = 128`, I observed that setting `num_warps = 4` and `num_warps = 8` produce different output results. The maximum difference between the output matrices is `0.00048828125`, and this difference remains consistent across repeated runs. Moreover, when keeping all other parameters the same and setting `seq_len` to 32 or smaller, the discrepancy disappears. 

I'm using an Nvidia T4 GPU, with CUDA version 12.4 and Triton version 3.1.0.

```python
import math
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def flash_attention_kernel(
    q_ptr, k_ptr, v_ptr, o_ptr,
    start_loc, seq_len,
    q_stride_batch_seq, q_stride_head, q_stride_dim,
    k_stride_batch_seq, k_stride_head, k_stride_dim,
    v_stride_batch_seq, v_stride_head, v_stride_dim,
    o_stride_batch_seq, o_stride_head, o_stride_dim,
    num_head,
    kv_group_size,
    d_scale,
    BLOCK_SIZE_M: tl.constexpr,
    BLOCK_SIZE_N: tl.constexpr,
    BLOCK_SIZE_D: tl.constexpr
):
    # q k v: [batchs*seq, heads, dim]
    q_block_id = tl.program_id(0) # m id
    batch_and_head_id = tl.program_id(1)
    batch_id = batch_and_head_id // num_head
    head_id = batch_and_head_id % num_head
    kv_head_id = head_id // kv_group_size

    batch_start = tl.load(start_loc + batch_id)
    batch_seq_len = tl.load(seq_len + batch_id)

    m_ranges = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE_M)
    n_ranges = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE_N)
    m_start = q_block_id * BLOCK_SIZE_M
    m_offsets = m_ranges + m_start
    embed_offsets = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE_D)

    q_offsets = (
        (batch_start + m_offsets[:,None]) * q_stride_batch_seq
        + head_id * q_stride_head
        + embed_offsets[None,:] * q_stride_dim
    )

    k_offsets = (
        (batch_start + n_ranges[:,None]) * k_stride_batch_seq
        + kv_head_id * k_stride_head
        + embed_offsets[None,:] * k_stride_dim
    )

    v_offsets = (
        (batch_start + n_ranges[:,None]) * v_stride_batch_seq
        + kv_head_id * v_stride_head
        + embed_offsets[None,:] * v_stride_dim
    )

    o_offsets = (
        (batch_start + m_offsets[:,None]) * o_stride_batch_seq
        + head_id * o_stride_head
        + embed_offsets[None,:] * o_stride_dim
    )

    q_mask = m_offsets[:,None]  < batch_seq_len
    q = tl.load(q_ptr + q_offsets, mask=q_mask, other=0.0)

    acc = tl.zeros((BLOCK_SIZE_M, BLOCK_SIZE_D), dtype=tl.float32)
    m_i = tl.zeros((BLOCK_SIZE_M,), dtype=tl.float32) - float("inf")
    l_i = tl.zeros((BLOCK_SIZE_M,), dtype=tl.float32)

    m_mask = tl.where(m_start < batch_seq_len, 1, 0) # loop for m > seq_len is ignored
    n_size = tl.minimum(m_start + BLOCK_SIZE_M, batch_seq_len) # inter block casual mask

    for n_idx in range(0, n_size * m_mask, BLOCK_SIZE_N):
        k_mask = n_idx + n_ranges[:,None] < n_size
        k = tl.load(k_ptr + k_offsets + n_idx * k_stride_batch_seq, mask=k_mask, other=0.0)
        v = tl.load(v_ptr + v_offsets + n_idx * v_stride_batch_seq, mask=k_mask, other=0.0)

        qk = tl.zeros((BLOCK_SIZE_M, BLOCK_SIZE_N), dtype=tl.float32)
        qk += tl.dot(q, tl.trans(k))

        # intra block casual mask
        q_off = m_offsets
        k_off = n_idx + n_ranges
        mask = q_off[:,None] >= k_off[None,:]
        qk = tl.where(mask, qk * d_scale, -float("inf"))

        pad_mask = n_idx + n_ranges < n_size
        qk = tl.where(pad_mask[None,:], qk, -float("inf"))

        m_j = tl.max(qk, axis=1)
        m_new = tl.maximum(m_i, m_j)
        alpha = tl.exp2(m_i - m_new)

        P_j = tl.exp2(qk - m_new[:,None])
        l_j = tl.sum(P_j, axis=1)
        l_i = l_i * alpha + l_j

        o_scale = alpha
        acc = acc * o_scale[:, None]
        P_j = P_j.to(v_ptr.dtype.element_ty)
        acc += tl.dot(P_j, v)

        m_i = m_new

    acc = acc / l_i[:, None]

    tl.store(o_ptr + o_offsets, acc, mask=q_mask)


def flash_attention(q: torch.Tensor, k, v, start_loc, seq_len, num_warps):
    _, num_head, d_size = q.shape
    _, num_kv_head, _ = k.shape
    kv_group_size = num_head // num_kv_head
    num_batch = seq_len.shape[0]
    max_seq_len = int(torch.max(seq_len).item())
    d_scale = 1.0 / math.sqrt(d_size) * 1.4426950408889634

    grid = lambda meta: (
        triton.cdiv(max_seq_len, meta["BLOCK_SIZE_M"]),
        num_batch * num_head,
        1
    )
    num_stages = 1

    o = torch.empty_like(q, dtype=q.dtype, device=q.device)
    flash_attention_kernel[grid](
        q, k, v, o,
        start_loc, seq_len,
        *q.stride(), *k.stride(), *v.stride(), *o.stride(),
        num_head=num_head,
        kv_group_size=kv_group_size,
        d_scale=d_scale,
        BLOCK_SIZE_M=64,
        BLOCK_SIZE_N=64,
        BLOCK_SIZE_D=d_size,
        num_warps=num_warps,
        num_stages=num_stages,
    )

    return o


class TestFlashAttention:
    def test_flash_attention(self):
        num_batchs = 8
        seq_len = 32
        num_heads = 128
        head_dim = 128
        dtype = torch.float16
        device = 'cuda'
        tensor_shape = (num_batchs, num_heads, seq_len, head_dim)

        q = torch.rand(tensor_shape, dtype=dtype, device=device)
        k = torch.rand(tensor_shape, dtype=dtype, device=device)
        v = torch.rand(tensor_shape, dtype=dtype, device=device)

        qt = q.permute(0,2,1,3).contiguous().view(-1, num_heads, head_dim)
        kt = k.permute(0,2,1,3).contiguous().view(-1, num_heads, head_dim)
        vt = v.permute(0,2,1,3).contiguous().view(-1, num_heads, head_dim)
        start_loc = torch.arange(0, num_batchs*seq_len, seq_len, device=device)
        seq_len_list = torch.full((num_batchs,), seq_len, device=d

items.title: Constexprs that compare equal but differ in type or sign (1 and 1.0, 0.0 and -0.0) reuse each other's binary
items.author: shuyilinn
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

When a kernel is launched with a constexpr that compares equal to the value of an earlier launch but has a different type or sign (`1` and `1.0`, or `0.0` and `-0.0`), the second launch reuses the binary compiled for the first one. The result depends on which value was launched first.

```python
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def kernel(X, out, C: tl.constexpr):
    tl.store(out, tl.load(X) * C)


x = torch.tensor([2**30 + 1], dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda")
for order in [(1, 1.0), (1.0, 1)]:
    kernel.device_caches.clear()
    results = []
    for c in order:
        out = torch.zeros(1, dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda")
        kernel[(1, )](x, out, c)
        results.append(out.item())
    print(order, results)
```

```
(1, 1.0) [1073741825, 1073741825]
(1.0, 1) [1073741824, 1073741824]
```

Expected: `x * 1` is `1073741825` and `x * 1.0` (computed in fp32) is `1073741824`, regardless of launch order. In the same way, launching with `C=0.0` and then `C=-0.0` stores `0.0` for the second launch.

The on-disk cache is not affected: the string key built from the specialization differs (`1` vs `1.0`, `0.0` vs `-0.0`). The problem is the in-memory lookup in `compute_cache_key` (`python/triton/runtime/jit.py`):

```python
key = (tuple(specialization), str(options))
cache_key = kernel_key_cache.get(key, None)
```

The specialization contains `("constexpr", value)`, and tuple equality treats `1 == 1.0 == True` and `0.0 == -0.0` (with equal hashes) as the same key, so the string key of the first launch is returned. This cache was added in #7768.

### Environment details

Triton: main @ 41846bc965
GPU: NVIDIA RTX 4090 (sm_89), driver 570 / CUDA 12.8

items.title: CPU: copy of a transposed 2-D tensor is single-threaded and slow
items.author: icodywu
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Existing tensor transpose is slow, furthermore, permutes which moves the innermost dimension are also slow. 
I have a faster implementation I'd like to contribute. It boosts speed by 2.5-18X.

```
import time, torch

def gbps(f, nbytes, reps=5):
    f()
    best = float("inf")
    for _ in range(reps):
        t0 = time.perf_counter(); f(); best = min(best, time.perf_counter() - t0)
    return 2 * nbytes / best / 1e9  # bytes read + written

print(torch.__version__)
cases = [("2-D x.t()", torch.randn(16384, 16384), (1, 0)),
         ("batched x.transpose(1, 2)", torch.randn(64, 1024, 2048), (0, 2, 1)),
         ("NHWC -> NCHW", torch.randn(64, 56, 56, 256), (0, 3, 1, 2))]
for name, x, p in cases:
    out = torch.empty(x.permute(p).shape)
    row = []
    for t in (1, 8, 32):
        torch.set_num_threads(t)
        row.append("%d threads %5.1f GB/s" % (t, gbps(lambda: out.copy_(x.permute(p)), x.numel() * 4)))
    print("%-26s" % name, " | ".join(row))

```

items.title: [inductor] Compile worker pool can lose a job when it re-forks right after a quiesce
items.author: yyming009
items.body_excerpt:
（Update: the proposed fix below has a flaw; see the correction in the comments.） ### 🐛 Describe the bug We found the issue that Multi-node training in miles hangs at step 1 because an Inductor compilation task on one rank never returns ([radixark/miles#4046](https://github.com/radixark/miles/issues/4046)). The compiler process pool shuts down after 60 seconds of inactivity and forks new workers for the next compilation; if that fork happens during the tens-of-milliseconds window when the old pool is shutting down, a new worker inherits a locked lock and hangs forever. I’ve run the reproduction script below myself, and the patch is ready—I’ll open a PR once the issue is marked actionable. The analysis in the collapsed section below was prepared by an AI assistant and reviewed by me. **Minimal repro** (CPU only, standard library; it mirrors `SubprocMain._start_pool` and `SubprocMain._quiesce`): ```python # CPython 3.12, Linux or macOS: prints "job lost" after 10 s. # With old.shutdown(wait=True) in place of the lock.acquire() line, it prints "ok". import concurrent.futures as cf, multiprocessing as mp, multiprocessing.util as mpu, os, sys ctx = mp.get_context("fork") old = cf.ProcessPoolExecutor(2, mp_context=ctx) old.submit(int).result() mpu.Finalize(None, old.shutdown, exitpriority=sys.maxsize) # SubprocMain._start_pool old.shutdown(wait=False) # SubprocMain._quiesce lock = old._shutdown_lock; lock.acquire() # the manager thread, mid-join old = None new = cf.ProcessPoolExecutor(2, mp_context=ctx) # the next SubprocMain._start_pool try: print("ok", new.submit(os.getpid).result(timeout=10), flush=True) except cf.TimeoutError: print("job lost: workers stuck in concurrent/futures/process.py weakref_cb", flush=True) for p in mp.active_children(): # the stuck workers never exit on their own p.kill() os._exit(0) ```
AI-assisted analysis (drafted with an AI coding assistant from our logs, stack dumps and experiments; reviewed by me) ### Mechanism - With `quiesce_async_compile_pool` on (the default), the compile sidecar calls `pool.shutdown(wait=False)` after `quiesce_async_compile_time` (60 s) without results. The next WAKEUP or JOB forks a new pool (`SubprocMain._start_pool` → `_warm_process_pool`). - CPython 3.12 holds the old executor's `_shutdown_lock` in `_ExecutorManagerThread.join_executor_internals()` while it joins the old workers, a window of tens of milliseconds. Every worker of a pool forked in that window inherits the lock in the held state. - `_start_pool` registers `multiprocessing.util.Finalize(None, self.pool.shutdown, exitpriority=sys.maxsize)`, and the quiesce never cancels it, so the old executor stays reachable. When it is collected inside the new worker (in multiprocessing's `_after_fork()` or in a later GC), its weakref callback runs `with shutdown_lock: thread_wakeup.wakeup()` and blocks forever. - The job that worker took never returns, so `AsyncCompile.wait` waits forever. - We believe this is also why `test_quiesce_repeatedly` is flaky and disabled on Linux (#176968). We have not checked CPython versions other than 3.12. ### Impact - Multi-node training (radixark/miles#4046), 32 ranks with a 32-worker pool each: about 1 in 8 runs hung in the first training step. The rank whose compile job was lost never issued its next collective, and its peers blocked in NCCL until the watchdog aborted the job an hour later. - With `quiesce_async_compile_time` lowered to 2 s, 6 attempts per arm on the same inputs: | arm | hung | |---|---| | default (quiesce on) | 4 of 6 | | `TORCHINDUCTOR_QUIESCE_ASYNC_COMPILE_POOL=0` | 0 of 6 | | join the old pool before forking | 0 of 6 | - Every hang traced to a fork 0–52 ms after a quiesce, with the old lock still held. py-spy showed the stuck worker in `concurrent/futures/process.py:312 weakref_cb`, during an import inside `_worker_compile_triton`. ### Proposed fix - On quiesce, keep the old pool and its finalizer. Before `_start_pool` forks a new pool, join the old one with `shutdown(wait=True)` and cancel its finalizer. The quiesce itself stays non-blocking, and `_shutdown_pool(terminate_workers=True)` also terminates an old pool that has not been joined yet. - The patch changes `torch/_inductor/compile_worker/subproc_pool.py` (+33/−5) and adds a regression test to `test/inductor/test_compile_worker.py` that fails on main and passes with the patch. - Alternatives: join at quiesce time (simpler, but it blocks the sidecar's message loop until the old workers exit), or use `forkserver`/`spawn` for re-created pools (cf. #148651, #108586). ### Workarounds `TORCHINDUCTOR_QUIESCE_ASYNC_COMPILE_POOL=0`, or `TORCHINDUCTOR_COMPILE_THREADS=1`.
### Error logs _No response_ ### Versions ``` # Original hang (multi-node training): Linux x86_64, torch 2.11.0+cu130, CPython 3.12.3 # The CPU repro above, run on: Collecting environment information... PyTorch version: 2.11.0 Is debug build: False CUDA used to build PyTorch: None ROCM used to build PyTorch: N/A OS: macOS 26.7.1 (arm64) GCC version: Could not collect Clang version: 21.0.0 (clang-2100.3.34.2) CMake version: Could not collect Libc version: N/A Python version: 3.12.7 (main, Nov 15 2024, 17:32:29) [Clang 16.0.0 (clang-1600.0.26.4)] (64-bit runtime) Python platform: macOS-26.7.1-arm64-arm-64bit Is CUDA available: False CUDA runtime version: No CUDA CUDA_MODULE_LOADING set to: N/A GPU models and configuration: No CUDA Nvidia driver version: No CUDA cuDNN version: No CUDA Is XPU available: False HIP runtime version: N/A MIOpen runtime version: N/A Is XNNPACK available: True Caching allocator config: N/A CPU: Apple M2 Pro Versions of relevant libraries: [pip3] Could not collect [conda] numpy 1.26.4 py312h7f4fdc5_0 [conda] numpy-base 1.26.4 py312he047099_0 [conda] numpydoc

items.title: Docs: MP mode needs GPU memory headroom (first request OOM at --gpu-memory-utilization 0.90 with GLM-5.3, TP8)
items.author: sivabreddy
items.body_excerpt:
With vLLM 0.31.0 + `LMCacheMPConnector` (LMCache v0.5.6, Mooncake Store L2), GLM-5.3 (NVFP4 checkpoint), TP8 on 80 GB H100, `--kv-cache-dtype fp8 --block-size 64 --max-model-len 65536 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.90`, the first request failed on all 8 GPUs:

- `CUDACachingAllocator`: "trying to allocate 2147483648 bytes (free: 1439236096)", that is 2.00 GiB requested with 1.34 GiB free.
- It surfaced as `RuntimeError: torch_call_dispatcher("aten::new_empty" ...)` in FlashMLA `sparse_decode_fwd`, not as a clear out-of-memory error.

With `--gpu-memory-utilization 0.85` it worked (vLLM then reported 6.5 GiB of KV cache memory instead of 10.46 GiB). The same model and flags with vLLM's built-in `MooncakeStoreConnector` (no LMCache) worked at 0.90.

We think the `lmcache server` process uses GPU memory (CUDA contexts / streams on each GPU) after vLLM has sized its KV cache, but we did not measure it.

The GLM-5.3 recipe (`docs/source/recipes/glm5_3.rst`) uses the vLLM default (0.9). A note there and in the MP docs (for example: "leave headroom for the LMCache server process; lower `--gpu-memory-utilization` if the first request fails with a CUDA out-of-memory error") would save time. If you know how much memory the server process needs per GPU, that number would help even more.

items.title: trtllm-gen 2-CTA FP4 MoE GEMM cubins fault on B300 under per-thread scheduling skew at UTCBAR.2CTA.MULTICAST (0.6.18.post1, 0.7.0.post1, 0.7.1rc5)
items.author: henrylhtsang
items.body_excerpt:
## Before submitting

- [x] I have searched existing issues and did not find a solution or an existing report.

## Environment

```text
GPU: NVIDIA B300 SXM6 AC (SM103, 148 SMs) | Driver 580.159.03 | CUDA 13.0
torch 2.11.0+cu130, python 3.11, Ubuntu 22.04
flashinfer-python / flashinfer-cubin (release wheels): 0.6.18.post1, 0.7.0.post1, 0.7.1rc5
Method: NVBit-based SASS delay injection - per-thread delays inserted before selected
SASS instructions in the running kernel.
```

## Bug description

On B300, the 2-CTA-cluster (`c2x1x1`) trtllm-gen FP4 block-scale routed-MoE GEMM cubins intermittently die with a sticky CUDA error when the cluster-barrier arrivals of one CTA of a 2-CTA pair are delayed relative to their peer by ~1 ms. Without perturbation the kernels are stable: hundreds of clean runs, bitwise-deterministic output, including under heavy external contention - explicitly: 400-iteration output-check runs under SM-saturation and L2-thrash sidecars and a 1,159,193-iteration 20-minute async soak with SM+HBM sidecars, all clean on 0.7.1rc5. Every trial that does not crash produces bitwise-correct output, so no wrong-result behavior is implied.

**What we perturb.** Only SASS sites matching `UTCBAR` in kernels matching `bmm_`. These cubins implement their 2-CTA-pair synchronization with `UTCBAR.2CTA.MULTICAST` instructions, by which each CTA of the pair arrives on the shared cluster mbarrier, alongside `UTCQMMA.2CTA` (paired MMA) and `UTMALDG.3D.MULTICAST.2CTA` (paired TMA loads). Injection evidence on the faulting cubin (28 sites matched, all enabled):

```text
kernel=bmm_MxE4m3_MxE2m1MxE4m3_Fp32_Ab32_Bb32_Cb32_t128x192x256u2_s3_et128x32_m256x192x32_c2x1x1_..._sm100f
  pc=0x50c0  sass='UTCBAR.2CTA.MULTICAST [UR14], URZ, UR19 ;'  delay=1000000
  pc=0x50e0  sass='UTCBAR.2CTA.MULTICAST [UR15], URZ, UR19 ;'  delay=1000000
  pc=0x53b0  sass='UTCBAR.2CTA.MULTICAST [UR14], URZ, UR20 ;'  delay=1000000
  pc=0x53d0  sass='UTCBAR.2CTA.MULTICAST [UR15], URZ, UR20 ;'  delay=1000000
  pc=0x6c90  sass='UTCBAR.2CTA.MULTICAST [UR35], URZ, UR51 ;'  delay=1000000
  ... (28 sites total)
kernel=bmm_Bfloat16_MxE2m1MxE4m3_Fp32_Ab32_Bb32_t128x192x256u2_s3_et128x64_m256x192x32_c2x1x1_..._sm100f
  sass='UTCBAR.2CTA.MULTICAST [UR18], [UR22], UR24 ;'  delay=1000000
```

Delay modes tested: per-thread random (main trigger) and fixed-uniform; magnitudes 100 us (always passes) and 1 ms (crashes); enable probability 1.0. Per-thread random delay at these sites is what skews one CTA's arrivals against its paired peer's.

**What the failure looks like.** The faulted launch raises a sticky CUDA error that surfaces at the next CUDA API call, and the process aborts shortly after the first injected launch, typically within 10-60 s. On the current builds I observe it through the injector's post-launch error check (assertion below); on the September-era build it surfaced directly as CUDA error 719 ("unspecified launch failure") at the sync point. Either way this is not a hang: the grid does not spin; the kernel faults. The GPU itself stays healthy (0 ECC errors, no retired pages, fresh CUDA contexts on the same card work normally afterwards). On an earlier cubin build (0.6.18rc-era, September 2026) the same signature was attributed via node DCGM to Xid 13 (Graphics Engine Exception, an SM-level hardware exception), and a separate experiment showed the cubin's own ptxas-injected tcgen05 breakpoint self-checks did NOT execute before that fault - i.e., the hardware raises the exception, not a software guardrail. That evidence is from a different cubin build and is cited only as corroboration.

Evidence boundary: the sticky error is first observed by the instrumentation hook after the faulted launch, and I cannot exclude an instrumentation interaction at the cluster-barrier instructions. The reason this still looks like a cubin robustness gap: the fault is repeatable across three released versions, tactic-specific (a second 2-CTA tactic at a different geometry passes 9/9 at the same magnitudes), dose-dependent (100 us passes, 1 ms faults), and site-specific (delays at LDTM sites in the same kernels pass).

Affected cubins observed faulting (versions per path listed below):

- `bmm_Bfloat16_MxE2m1MxE4m3_Fp32_Ab32_Bb32_t128x192x256u2_s3_..._c2x1x1_..._sm100f` (MXFP8-activation path)
- `bmm_MxE4m3_MxE2m1MxE4m3_Fp32_Ab32_Bb32_Cb32_t128x192x256u2_s3_..._c2x1x1_..._sm100f`
- `bmm_E2m1_E2m1E2m1_Fp32_Ab16_Bb16_Cb16_t128x192x256u2_s3_et128x64_m256x192x64_c2x1x1_..._sm100f` (NVFP4-activation path - the GLM-5-class production configuration)

Both activation paths fault: MXFP8-activation (MXFP4 weights) crashed 2/3 arms on 0.6.18.post1, 3/3 on 0.7.0.post1, 2/5 on 0.7.1rc5; NVFP4-activation (NVFP4 weights) crashed 1/1 on 0.6.18.post1 and 3/3 on 0.7.1rc5 (not tested on 0.7.0.post1). Async launches, batch 2048. These are per-arm counts from the runs listed, not an estimated rate. Paired enable_pdl on/off arms at 1 ms both crash, so the programmatic dependent-launch setting does not gate the failure.

Expected: stable execution of the 2-CTA cluster tactic under supported scheduling conditions. Whether SASS delay injection preserves those conditions is an open question I cannot fully answer; I am reporting because the fault is repeatable, tactic-specific, and dose-dependent, which looks more like a robustness gap in the cubin than an instrumentation artifact.

## Minimal reproduction

The workload below is self-contained (torch + flashinfer only). Running it plain must print `CLEAN` repeatedly. The failure appears when the same script runs under SASS delay injection targeting `UTCBAR` sites in `bmm_` kernels with ~1 ms per-thread random delays (any NVBit-based injector that can insert per-thread delays before selected SASS instructions works; we used one built for sm_103a).

```python

"""trtllm-gen 2-CTA FP4 MoE GEMM skew repro. Oracle: bitwise determinism + finiteness."""
import sys, torch
from flashinfer.fused_moe import

### Bug description

## Setup
- flashinfer 399b6c1d (#6346 merge point), source tree on PYTHONPATH, NCCL 2.30.7 found via `NCCL_HOME`, CUDA 13.3, torch 2.13.
- 8x sm_120 GPUs (72 GB, 110 SMs, CC 12.0), one host, two PCIe Gen5 switches with 4 GPUs each, no NVLink; EP8 over an NCCL process group, GIN available (RDMA NICs behind each switch).
- Geometry: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash routed experts E=384, H=5120, I=2304, top-k 6, `swiglu_limit=10`, `max_tokens_per_rank=2048`, noshared variant.

## What happens
`validate_init` passes (EP8 <= `REGISTER_BUDGET_VERIFIED_MAX_RANKS`, so nothing is compiled there), but the first `warmup()` / forward raises in `_build_workspace`:
- `transport_table="all_gin"` -> `RuntimeError: sm120_mxfp4_mxfp8_bf16_cake: m128_nocopier uses local memory`
- any table with LSA cells (`all_lsa`, `lsa_where_reachable`, explicit tuple) -> `... m64_copier uses local memory`

`cuobjdump --dump-resource-usage` on the JIT cubins: the refused instances report STACK 16 B (one 8-byte slot above `LOCAL_BYTES_LIMIT = 8`), LOCAL 0, REG 168/166.

| instance | REG | STACK | LOCAL |
|---|---|---|---|
| m128_copier (MOE_LSA_COPIERS 1 / 3 / 7) | 168 | 8 | 0 |
| m64_copier | 166 | 16 | 0 |
| m128_nocopier | 168 | 16 | 0 |
| m64_nocopier | 166 | 8 | 0 |

So at this geometry the device build spills one register and the backend refuses to load the workspace for every transport table, i.e. the kernel cannot be used for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on sm_120 as shipped.

## What I expected
The README's qualified "DeepSeek-V4-Flash" point is E256/H4096/I2048; the released DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash routed geometry is E384/H5120/I2304 (48 experts per rank at EP8). I expected either a spill-free build for it or `validate_init` rejecting it up front.

With `LOCAL_BYTES_LIMIT` raised to 16 for measurement (host constant only, device code and cubins unchanged) every table runs and is correct: output matches the pure-torch kernel-boundary oracle of `tests/moe_ep/test_moe_ep_sm120_w4a8_cake_mega.py` (rel L2 1.6e-4 .. 3.2e-4 over 512 rows/rank, three routings incl. one 2.5x hot rank), `protocol_error` stays 0, CUDA-graph replay is bit-identical to eager.

Ask: cover this geometry in the register-budget grid (or ship a build that does not spill at it), or document the local-memory limit as advisory. The layer-time comparison against the unfused PCIe path and the feature asks that follow from it are filed separately as #6757; this issue is only the spill and the refused workspace.

### Minimal reproduction

```python
# torchrun --standalone --nproc_per_node=8 repro.py
# 8x sm_120 GPUs on one PCIe host; NCCL 2.30.7 found via NCCL_HOME (nccl.h, nccl_device.h, libnccl.so.2)
import os
import torch
import torch.distributed as dist
from flashinfer.moe_ep.backends.mega.kernel.sm120.mxfp4_mxfp8_bf16_cake.cake_synthetic import (
    Geometry, make_layer, random_inputs, random_weights)

local = int(os.environ["LOCAL_RANK"])
torch.cuda.set_device(local)
dist.init_process_group("nccl", device_id=torch.cuda.current_device())
rank, world = dist.get_rank(), dist.get_world_size()

# DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash routed experts (not the E256/H4096/I2048 "v4flash" point of the test matrix)
g = Geometry(hidden=5120, intermediate=2304, experts=384, top_k=6)
table = os.environ.get("TABLE", "all_gin")  # all_gin -> m128_nocopier spills; all_lsa / any LSA table -> m64_copier spills
layer = make_layer(rank, world, random_weights(rank, world, g, shared=False), g,
                   max_tokens_per_rank=2048, shared=False, transport_table=table, swiglu_limit=10)
layer.warmup(random_inputs(2048, g, seed=rank))
# RuntimeError: sm120_mxfp4_mxfp8_bf16_cake: m128_nocopier uses local memory   (cake_backend._build_workspace)

items.title: [Bug] MNNVL one-shot fused allreduce+RMSNorm zeroes fp16 tokens with |x| > 256 (fp16 square overflow)
items.author: Raphael-Jin
items.body_excerpt:
### Before submitting

- [x] I have searched existing issues and did not find a solution or an existing report.

### Environment

```text
- GPU: NVIDIA GB200 (SM 10.0a), 2 nodes × 4 GPUs, MNNVL/NVLink
- CUDA 12.9, driver as shipped with the cluster image
- flashinfer-python 0.6.13 (+ flashinfer-cubin / flashinfer-jit-cache 0.6.13); the affected line is unchanged on `main` (87422668, 2026-10-13)
- torch 2.11.0+cu129, vLLM 0.25.1
- Python 3.12, Linux aarch64
```

### Bug description

`include/flashinfer/comm/trtllm_mnnvl_allreduce.cuh`, one-shot fused all-reduce + RMSNorm
kernel (lines 1009–1010 on `main`, 914–915 in v0.6.13):

```cpp
// FIXME: Use float square if accuracy issue
threadSum += toFloat<T>(packedAccum.elements[i] * packedAccum.elements[i]);
```

The product is evaluated in the input dtype. With `T = half`, any activation with
|x| > 255.94 (sqrt of the fp16 max 65504) overflows to `inf`, the sum of squares is `inf`,
`rsqrtf(inf) = 0`, and the whole token's normalized output is all zeros. The two-shot kernel
in the same file (`float const value = toFloat<T>(...); threadSum += value * value;`) and the
`trtllm` all-reduce fusion backend convert to fp32 first and are correct. bf16 is unaffected
because its range matches fp32.

Real-world impact: vLLM 0.25.1 enables `fuse_allreduce_rms` at TP > 1, the FlashInfer
all-reduce backend resolves to MNNVL, and FlashInfer selects one-shot for decode-sized
batches (≤ 1 MiB). Qwen3.5-27B in fp16 exceeds 256 at the final RMSNorm on ~9.5% of decode
tokens, so every fp16 TP=2 generation degenerates into `!!!!…` (all-zero logits → token id 0)
and an RL training run scored 0 reward. TP=1 (no fusion), bf16, and
`VLLM_FLASHINFER_ALLREDUCE_BACKEND=trtllm` are all fine.


### Minimal reproduction

```python
Two GPUs, ~10 s: `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1 python kernel_repro.py` (attached). It calls
`flashinfer.comm.allreduce_fusion(pattern=kARResidualRMSNorm, weight_bias=1.0, hidden=5120)`
the way vLLM does, sets one element of the summed activation to `peak`, and compares against
an fp32 reference. Result on GB200 with v0.6.13:

| backend | dtype | strategy | tokens | peak 200 / 250 | peak 260 / 300 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| mnnvl | fp16 | auto → one-shot | 1, 40 | OK | **all-zero rows** |
| mnnvl | fp16 | two-shot (auto or forced) | 1, 256 | OK | OK |
| mnnvl | bf16 | all of the above | 1, 40, 256 | OK | OK |
| trtllm | fp16, bf16 | one-shot | 1, 256 | OK | OK |

Patching the header so the one-shot kernel squares in fp32 (same as the two-shot kernel)
makes every row match the reference, and restores the vLLM/Qwen3.5-27B fp16 TP=2 run
(validation accuracy 0.0 → 0.698, same as bf16).
```

### Error messages / logs

```text
No error is raised; the kernel silently returns zeros. In vLLM the symptom is generated text
consisting only of `!` (token id 0).
```

### Additional context

- The existing tests in `tests/comm/test_trtllm_mnnvl_allreduce.py` use `randn` inputs
  (|x| < 5) so they cannot reach the overflow; a regression test with large-magnitude rows is
  included in the fix PR.
- Related but different: vLLM #48324 (`!!!!` from a bf16/fp32 norm-weight dtype mismatch,
  already fixed), FlashInfer #5995 (PDL ordering in a different norm kernel).

[kernel_repro.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33694127/kernel_repro.py)

items.title: [Question] How to force certain computations to occur in float16?
items.author: vedantroy
items.body_excerpt:
I have the following kernel:
```python3
@triton.jit
def unmasked_blend_kernel(
    img1_ptr, img2_ptr, ratio: float, total_items: int, BLOCK_SIZE: tl.constexpr
):
    block_idx = tl.program_id(0)
    offset = block_idx * BLOCK_SIZE
    item_element_idxs = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)
    img1_item_ptrs = img1_ptr + offset + item_element_idxs
    img2_item_ptrs = img2_ptr + offset + item_element_idxs

    if offset + BLOCK_SIZE > total_items:
        mask = item_element_idxs < total_items % BLOCK_SIZE
        img1 = tl.load(img1_item_ptrs, mask=mask, other=0)
        img2 = tl.load(img2_item_ptrs, mask=mask, other=0)
        out = ratio * img1 + (1.0 - ratio) * img2
        tl.store(img1_item_ptrs, out, mask=mask)
    else:
        img1 = tl.load(img1_item_ptrs)
        img2 = tl.load(img2_item_ptrs)
        out = ratio * img1 + (1.0 - ratio) * img2
        tl.store(img1_item_ptrs, out)
```

Given that this kernel is blending 2 uint8  tensors, I figured it would make sense to do the computation ` out = ratio * img1 + (1.0 - ratio) * img2`  since I don't need high precision.

However, I can't figure out how to force the Triton compiler to do the computations in FP16.
I tried doing:

```python3
        img1 = tl.load(img1_item_ptrs, mask=mask, other=0).to(tl.float16)
        img2 = tl.load(img2_item_ptrs, mask=mask, other=0).to(tl.float16)
```
but from looking at the generated PTX, it just seems like the float16s are just converted to float32s before the multiplication 
occurs.

Is there a way I can force the Triton  compiler  to make the multiplications float16? (Or is this impossible for a good reason;  i.e maybe this is not what I actually want)?

items.title: [WS] getPartitionOutputs assertion in NVWSHoistTmemStore with warp_specialize=True on a pointer-load persistent matmul
items.author: builtin-pb
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

**Summary.** Compiling for Blackwell (`cuda:100` or `cuda:103`) stops with an internal assertion in `getPartitionOutputs`, during `NVWSHoistTmemStore`, when the outer tile loop uses `tl.range(..., warp_specialize=True)`, the inner K loop uses plain pointer loads and `tl.dot`, and C is written with a plain `tl.store`. We are not asking for this loop to be specialized, only for no assertion. Adding to HoistTmemStore's loop collection the `hasPartition(loop)` check that `NVWSInsertAref` uses may be sufficient; see Suggested fix.

#### Reproduce

The script is compile-only and needs no GPU; the kernel is never launched (it assumes full tiles and 16-byte-aligned, contiguous fp16 A and B and fp32 C).

```python
"""Compile-only reproducer (no GPU needed).

Requesting automatic warp specialization on a persistent tile loop whose body is
an ordinary pointer-load matmul makes Triton hit an internal assertion:
    getPartitionOutputs: Assertion `op->hasAttr(kPartitionOutputsAttrName)' failed.

    python ws_assert_min.py              # warp_specialize=True: assertion
    python ws_assert_min.py --ws 0       # same kernel without it: compiles

--inner 0 drops the inner K loop (one tl.dot per tile); --dot 0 replaces tl.dot
with row/column sums; --cdesc 1 stores C through a TMA tensor descriptor
(as Triton's own persistent warp-specialization test does); --arch picks the target (100 = B200, 103 = B300, 90 = H100);
--warps and --stages set num_warps (default 4) and num_stages (default 3).
"""
import argparse
import inspect

import triton
import triton.language as tl
from triton.backends.compiler import GPUTarget
from triton.compiler import ASTSource


@triton.jit
def ws_min(A, B, C, num_tiles, k_iters,
           BM: tl.constexpr, BN: tl.constexpr, BK: tl.constexpr,
           WS: tl.constexpr, INNER: tl.constexpr, DOT: tl.constexpr, CDESC: tl.constexpr):
    rm = tl.arange(0, BM)
    rn = tl.arange(0, BN)
    rk = tl.arange(0, BK)
    K = k_iters * BK
    if CDESC:
        c_desc = tl.make_tensor_descriptor(C, shape=[num_tiles * BM, BN], strides=[BN, 1], block_shape=[BM, BN])
    for tile in tl.range(tl.program_id(0), num_tiles, tl.num_programs(0), warp_specialize=WS):
        rows = tile * BM + rm
        acc = tl.zeros((BM, BN), tl.float32)
        if INNER:
            for k in range(k_iters):
                a = tl.load(A + rows[:, None] * K + (k * BK + rk)[None, :])
                b = tl.load(B + (k * BK + rk)[:, None] * BN + rn[None, :])
                if DOT:
                    acc = tl.dot(a, b, acc)
                else:
                    acc += tl.sum(a.to(tl.float32), 1)[:, None] + tl.sum(b.to(tl.float32), 0)[None, :]
        else:
            a = tl.load(A + rows[:, None] * K + rk[None, :])
            b = tl.load(B + rk[:, None] * BN + rn[None, :])
            if DOT:
                acc = tl.dot(a, b, acc)
            else:
                acc += tl.sum(a.to(tl.float32), 1)[:, None] + tl.sum(b.to(tl.float32), 0)[None, :]
        if CDESC:
            c_desc.store([tile * BM, 0], acc)
        else:
            tl.store(C + rows[:, None] * BN + rn[None, :], acc)


def main():
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    p.add_argument("--ws", type=int, default=1)
    p.add_argument("--inner", type=int, default=1)
    p.add_argument("--dot", type=int, default=1)
    p.add_argument("--cdesc", type=int, default=0)
    p.add_argument("--arch", type=int, default=100)
    p.add_argument("--warps", type=int, default=4)
    p.add_argument("--stages", type=int, default=3)
    args = p.parse_args()

    constants = dict(BM=128, BN=64, BK=64, WS=bool(args.ws), INNER=bool(args.inner), DOT=bool(args.dot), CDESC=bool(args.cdesc))
    runtime = dict(A="*fp16", B="*fp16", C="*fp32", num_tiles="i32", k_iters="i32")
    names = list(ws_min.arg_names)
    signature = {n: runtime.get(n, "constexpr") for n in names}
    attrs = {(names.index(n),): [["tt.divisibility", 16]] for n in ("A", "B", "C")}
    key = "constexprs" if "constexprs" in inspect.signature(ASTSource).parameters else "constants"
    src = ASTSource(ws_min, signature=signature, attrs=attrs, **{key: constants})
    print(f"triton {triton.__version__}, target cuda:{args.arch}, warps {args.warps}, stages {args.stages}, {constants}", flush=True)
    compiled = triton.compile(src, target=GPUTarget("cuda", args.arch, 32),
                              options=dict(num_warps=args.warps, num_stages=args.stages))
    ttgir = compiled.asm["ttgir"]
    print("COMPILED; ttg.warp_specialize ops in TTGIR:", ttgir.count("ttg.warp_specialize("), flush=True)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

`python ws_assert_min.py` stops with:

```
Partitioning.cpp:24: ... mlir::triton::gpu::getPartitionOutputs(mlir::Operation*): Assertion `op->hasAttr(kPartitionOutputsAttrName)' failed.
... Pipeline failed while executing [`TritonGPUAutomaticWarpSpecialization` on 'builtin.module' operation, `NVWSHoistTmemStore` on 'builtin.module' operation]
RuntimeError: PassManager::run failed
```

This reproduces on Triton 3.8.0 (PyPI wheel; there the assertion is at `Partition.cpp:354`) and on main (`0d4e0a0c`). The controls:

| Command (`--arch 100` or `--arch 103`) | 3.8.0 and main |
|---|---|
| `python ws_assert_min.py` (also with `--stages 1` or `--warps 8`) | assertion |
| `--ws 0` | compiles |
| `--cdesc 1` (C stored through a tensor descriptor) | compiles and emits one `ttg.warp_specialize` |
| `--inner 0` or `--dot 0` | compiles, without specialization |

We ask only for no assertion: `warp_specialize` is documented as an attempt, and loops it cannot partition are otherwise left alone, as with the controls above. Triton's own `test_warp_specialize_tma_matmul_persistent` has the same structure with pointer loads for A and B and expects `ttg.warp_specialize`; it differs only in storing C through a descriptor.

#### Cause

From reading the source at `0d4e0a0c` (we did not trace the passes):
- Partition scheduling writes `ttg.partition` and `ttg.partit
