items.title: Should LMCacheMPConnector honor kv_transfer_config.kv_role — or is MP mode intentionally always-kv_both?
items.author: kezboard233
items.body_excerpt:
## Context

We run a production-shaped POC on 8×V100 (two vLLM TP4 instances of Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 sharing one LMCache MP server with a CPU L1 tier) and filed #5143 with a runtime-verified repro: an engine launched with `kv_role="kv_consumer"` still stores every request's KV into the shared L1 — a single 32K-token cold request produced `168 × "Stored 784"` lines (= full prefix × 4 TP ranks), and the only engine that received any request in that window was the `kv_consumer` one.

We later found #4665 (closed by its author without maintainer response) reporting the same mechanism from the CacheBlend angle: the single-process connector honors `kv_role` / `skip_save`, the MP connector honors neither. As of today's `dev`, `lmcache_mp_connector.py` still contains no occurrence of `kv_role` / `kv_consumer` / `kv_producer` / `force_skip_save`.

## The design question

Before we contribute a patch, we want to check intent: **is MP mode intentionally "every connected engine writes"?** Two readings:

1. **Contract gap** — vLLM makes `kv_role` mandatory, documents it as "Whether this vLLM instance produces, consumes KV cache, or both", and exposes `is_kv_producer` / `is_kv_consumer` for connectors to branch on; LMCache's own single-process adapter honors it (`force_skip_save` in `vllm_v1_adapter.py`). Under this reading we'd gladly contribute a small PR that skips store-metadata generation when `is_kv_consumer` (mirroring the single-process gate), so warm-then-read-only fleets and PD-style topologies become possible on the MP path.

2. **Intentional always-kv_both** — the MP tier is a shared scratch space where every connected engine contributes. Under this reading we'd instead ask for the intent to be documented, plus ideally a one-line warning at connector init when `kv_role != "kv_both"`, so users aren't misled (we only noticed via instrumented counter evidence ourselves).

Happy to do either — a steer from maintainers decides which.

(Impact context: no correctness issue — stored content is identical — but a consumer-role engine burns D2H bandwidth and shared-L1 capacity; a 32K prefix on our model is ≈8.6 GB across 4 ranks.)

items.title: [Performance]: CuTe DSL MLA split-KV plan kernel takes ~75 us per decode step at small batch
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### Proposal to improve performance

The CuTe DSL MLA decode computes a per-request split-KV plan once per step (`launch_mla_split_kv_plan` in `attention/backends/fmha/cute_dsl_mla.py`, launched by the first MLA layer of the step). `_mla_split_kv_plan_kernel` is a single program with `BLOCK = 1024` lanes that loops over the 32 candidate piece counts, each iteration doing two block-wide reductions over 1024 lanes, whatever the batch size. On Rubin single GPU (200-SM engineering sample) that launch takes about 75 us for a batch of 16 or fewer requests, and the decode step waits for it: for Kimi K3 decode at small batch it is about 0.07 ms per step.

Proposal: for batches up to 512 requests, evaluate all candidate piece counts at once as a (candidates x requests) tile with the request block sized to the batch (`next_power_of_2(num_requests)`, at least 16), pick the cheapest candidate (ties to fewer pieces, as now), and keep the loop kernel for larger batches. The plan is unchanged. Measured on the same GPU: 2.3 us for 16 or fewer requests, 7.9 us for 64.

Separately, the loop kernel always evaluates 32 candidates while the host mirror `plan_mla_split_kv` stops at `max_split`, so for `max_split < 32` the two can disagree (101 of 200 random batches with `max_split` in {1, 4, 8, 16}). No caller passes `max_split` today, so this is latent; the PR restricts the kernel's candidates to `max_split` as well. PR to follow.

items.title: [Performance]: MLA DSpark drafter runs each layer's q and kv paths serially on one stream
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### Proposal to improve performance

In `MLADSparkForCausalLM.dflash_forward` (MLA DSpark drafter block decode), every drafter layer runs its q path (`q_a_proj` -> `q_a_layernorm` -> `q_b_proj` -> RoPE -> k absorption) and its kv path (`kv_a_proj_with_mqa` -> RMSNorm/RoPE -> block write into the context pool) one after another on one stream. The two paths are independent until attention, and at decode sizes each is a chain of small GEMMs and elementwise kernels that leaves most of the GPU idle. On top of that, the kv path writes its RMSNorm/RoPE output to a staging buffer that is then scattered into the pool.

Proposal: an opt-in switch that runs the kv path on an aux stream concurrently with the q path, joined before attention. On the CuTe DSL block-decode variant, the RMSNorm/RoPE kernel also stores the block latents straight into the pool, at the block fixup's pages / offsets. Same kernels and same arithmetic, so it is bit-exact.

Measured on Rubin, TP8 across 2 nodes (MNNVL), Kimi K3 with an MLA DSpark drafter, CUDA graphs, single request, decode step time, on top of #20548: -0.053 / -0.038 / -0.025 / -0.037 / -0.023 / -0.018 ms at 2K / 32K / 64K / 96K / 128K / 393K context (cross-job comparison). Accepted tokens per step unchanged. On a later stack, turning it off cost about +0.06 ms per step.

PR to follow (draft, stacked on the #20548 PR).

items.title: [Performance]: DFlash prefill context store blocks on a D2H read at every chunk, idling the GPU between chunks
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### Proposal to improve performance

With a DFlash drafter bound to the draft KV cache manager, `DFlashWorker._store_prefill_context` (`tensorrt_llm/_torch/speculative/dflash.py`) reads the context rows' draft page counts with `(self._ctx_block_counts[:num_contexts] * page_size).tolist()` at the end of every context forward. `_ctx_block_counts` is filled on the GPU earlier in the same forward, so this `.tolist()` waits for the whole forward's GPU work. The executor's host work between chunks (resource update, scheduling, input preparation) then cannot overlap the next chunk, and with chunked prefill the GPU idles at every chunk boundary.

Measured on Rubin, TP8 across 2 nodes (MNNVL), Kimi K3 with a DFlash-style drafter, 128K prompt with chunked prefill: about 11 ms of GPU idle at every chunk boundary, and the `.tolist()` itself blocks for up to about 190 ms (the rest of the forward).

Proposal: the page counts are a function of `draft_kv_cache_block_offsets`, which `attn_metadata.prepare()` fills before the forward is enqueued. Compute them in `DFlashSpecMetadata.prepare()` with the same formula on the same tensor, copy them non-blocking into pinned memory behind an event, and let `_store_prefill_context` use that snapshot (waiting only on the event, which completes when the forward starts). Fall back to the current read whenever the snapshot does not match the forward (different tensor, row count, manager or pool). Opt-in first via `TLLM_DFLASH_PREFILL_CTX_SNAPSHOT=1`. With it, 128K TTFT dropped by about 0.36 s in the setup above. PR to follow.

items.title: [Performance]: Kimi KDA verify runs the qkvg and [f_a | b] projections as two GEMMs on two streams
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### Proposal to improve performance

In the Kimi KDA mixer's MTP verify (`KimiKDALinearAttention._project_verify_inputs`, `tensorrt_llm/_torch/modules/kimi_kda/kimi_kda_mixer.py`), the BF16 full-rank-gate path runs two GEMMs on the same input: the fused `[q | k | v | g]` projection (`_qkvg_proj_weight`) and the fused `[f_a | b]` gate projection (`_bfa_proj_weight`, padded to 8 rows), forked onto two streams for up to 128 rows. At decode sizes (M = 8 x batch rows) both GEMMs are tiny, so two launches plus the stream fork / join cost more than one GEMM with 144 more output rows.

Measured on Rubin single GPU, Kimi K3 KDA layer shapes per rank, own weights per layer, CUDA graph, µs per layer for the verify projection GEMMs, batch 1 / 2 / 3 / 4 / 6 / 8 / 12 / 16 (M = 8 x batch):

| | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 6 | 8 | 12 | 16 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| qkvg and [f_a \| b] (two GEMMs) | 15.6 | 15.7 | 17.7 | 15.2 | 19.7 | 17.0 | 18.2 | 18.5 |
| one stacked GEMM | 12.9 | 13.2 | 15.8 | 13.5 | 13.0 | 13.1 | 14.1 | 13.7 |

Proposal: in `finalize_decode_weights`, stack the two fused weights into one `[q | k | v | g | f_a | b | pad]` buffer and repoint `_qkvg_proj_weight`, `_bfa_proj_weight` and the per-projection weights to row views of it (no extra memory; prefill and decode GEMMs unchanged). The verify projection then runs one GEMM and takes qkvg and `[f_a | b]` as column views of its output; the verify kernel already reads the sections as strided views. Opt-in first via `TLLM_KDA_FUSE_VERIFY_PROJECTION=1`. PR to follow.

Related: #20174 routes `_project_gate_inputs` through the low-M dispatcher. The two compose (the stacked GEMM can go through the dispatcher too: 10.3–11.5 µs per layer at batch 1–4 in the same setup).

items.title: [Performance]: CuTe DSL MLA decode split-KV reduction is load-latency bound at small batch
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### Proposal to improve performance

The split-KV reduction of the CuTe DSL MLA decode kernels (`reduction_kernel` in `cute_dsl_kernels/blackwell/attention/mla/mla_decode_fp16.py` and `mla_decode_fp8.py`) accumulates the per-split partials one split at a time: each iteration issues a global load of `gAccO[i, ...]` and immediately consumes it, so with tens of splits the loop is load-latency bound. The runner also always launches it with one D band per row (`reducer_d_tiles = 1`), so at small batch (few rows) only a handful of CTAs run it.

Measured on Rubin single GPU (200-SM engineering sample), CUDA graph, Kimi K3 shapes (target FP8 KV, 12 heads, q = 8; drafter BF16, 8 heads, q = 7; batch 1, page 32), reduction time per call with the production split plan, current → prefetching loop with 4 D bands per row:

| KV (splits) | 2K (16) | 32K (64) | 128K (94) | 393K (100) | 1M (100) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FP8 reduction µs | 5.10 → 4.00 | 10.79 → 4.95 | 14.63 → 6.43 | 15.73 → 6.91 | 8.47 → 2.88 |
| BF16 reduction µs | 4.83 → 3.73 | 10.73 → 4.98 | 14.95 → 5.95 | 15.45 → 6.77 | 15.30 → 6.66 |

Proposal: an optional prefetch in the reduction loop (load a group of 32 splits' partials into registers with a clamped split index, then accumulate them in split order with a mask, so every output element sees the same multiply-adds in the same order and the result is bitwise unchanged), and have the runner use 4 D bands per row while that grid fits a few SM waves. Opt-in first via `TLLM_CUTE_DSL_MLA_REDUCTION_PREFETCH=1`. End to end on Rubin, TP8 across 2 nodes (MNNVL), Kimi K3 with MTP decode, the decode step period dropped by 0.05 ms at 2K and 0.15–0.22 ms at 32K–393K context, with accepted tokens per step unchanged. PR to follow.
score_reasons: 匹配 KV 与存储、Kernel 与正确性

items.title: [Bug]: DeepSeek-V4.1 CSA2: intermittent illegal address in the dynamic-token-sparse MLA generation kernel, which loads -1 index padding past the sparse length
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

- GPU: Vera Rubin, compute capability 10.7
- TensorRT-LLM main (CSA2 sparse backend code is byte-identical to main as of 2026-10-19), PyTorch backend
- Model: `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash`, CSA2 sparse attention, FP8 KV

### Who can help?

@NVIDIA/trt-llm-torch-attention-devs

### Information

- [ ] The official example scripts
- [x] My own modified scripts

### Reproduction

With the CSA2 sparse backend, decode intermittently fails with `cudaErrorIllegalAddress` (an illegal memory access). The error usually surfaces asynchronously in an unrelated later op (indexer, MoE launch, a cuBLAS GEMM). On the full model (TP4/EP4, CUDA graphs) about 40% of freshly started servers hit it within the first ~20 requests.

On a reduced-layer model (layers 0, 20, 21, 24 of the checkpoint; TP1, eager, block reuse off) it is deterministic: it fails on the first decode step of the first real request, 6/6 runs, also with `CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1`. With launch blocking the error is returned by the launch itself (`AttentionOp::mlaGeneration` -> `launchFmhaKernel`):

- kernel: `fmhaSm107aKernel_QkvE4m3OBfloat16H512HVPerCta128PagedKvDenseDynamicTokenSparseP1MultiCtasKvGmemSepVarSeqQ64Kv128StaticKeepsAbForGen`
- CSA layer, generation, `num_tokens=1`, sparse top-k 640, grid (3,4,1), max KV length 640
- `sparse_attn_kv_lens` (the prepared lengths) = 78; `prepared_indices[:, :78]` are all valid and in range, `prepared_indices[:, 78:640]` are the `-1` padding written by the CSA2 staging step.

The same kernel passes in warmup (prepared length 2), and the non-multi-CTA variant used by the SWA layer just before passes.

### Expected behavior

Index slots past the per-token sparse length are ignored by the kernel (no loads issued for them), so the `-1` padding is never dereferenced.

### Actual behavior

The kernel issues KV loads for slots beyond the sparse length. The `-1` entries turn into addresses before the paged pool; whether that faults depends on what happens to be mapped there, which is why it is intermittent on the full model.

Evidence, same reduced model and prompts:

| variant | requests | illegal address |
|---|---|---|
| unchanged | first request of 6 runs | 6/6 |
| padding `-1` replaced by `0` before the FMHA call | 12 (async) + 12 (launch blocking) | 0 |
| same, plus 150 stress batches | 168 | 0 |

compute-sanitizer memcheck does not report it (TMA loads are not checked by default, and the allocation layout changes under the tool, so the fault disappears).

### Additional notes

Workaround in `tensorrt_llm/_torch/attention/backends/sparse/csa2/backend.py`, `sparse_attn_predict`, before returning:

```python
metadata.prepared_indices[: metadata.num_tokens].clamp_(min=0)
```

This assumes the kernel masks the scores of slots past the sparse length, so pointing the padding at a valid row is numerically a no-op. We are verifying that bit-exactly at the op level and will report back here.

Suggested proper fix, kernel side: predicate (or clamp) the index and page loads for slots `>= ptrSparseMlaTopKLens[token]`, not only mask their scores. Alternatively, document that the padding must be a valid index and have CSA2 pad with a valid row while still masking by length.

Unrelated and benign, for completeness: `deep_gemm::sm100_sparse_mqa_logits` reads up to 16 B past the end of `sf_kv` by design ("Tail reads rely on PyTorch allocator padding"); it only shows up with `PYTORCH_NO_CUDA_MEMORY_CACHING=1`.

items.title: [Perf]: DeepSeek-V4.1 Engram n-gram hash falls back to ~150 eager torch kernels per step with multiple tokens per request (speculative decoding)
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

- GPU: Vera Rubin, compute capability 10.7, single node, TP4/EP4
- TensorRT-LLM main (`tensorrt_llm/_torch/modules/engram/engram.py` unchanged on main since #19727), PyTorch backend, CUDA graphs
- Model: `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash` with speculative decoding (several tokens per request per step)

### Who can help?

@NVIDIA/trt-llm-torch-models-devs

### Information

- [ ] The official example scripts
- [x] My own modified scripts

### Reproduction

Serve DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with speculative decoding enabled and CUDA graphs on, run a single-request decode and profile it with nsys (`--cuda-graph-trace=node`).

### Expected behavior

The Engram n-gram hash computation for generation steps runs as a few fused launches, like the single-token decode fast path (`_compute_decode_hashes` -> `_decode_hash_kernel`).

### Actual behavior

`_compute_decode_hashes` returns `None` as soon as any request has more than one token in the forward:

```python
lengths = tuple(seq_lens_host[: len(request_ids)].tolist())
if any(length != 1 for length in lengths):
    return None
```

So every speculative generation step (draft tokens + verify, 6 tokens per request in our setup) falls back to the general torch path in `compute_hashes`. That path runs eagerly from the pre-replay hook (`refresh_captured_hashes`), outside the CUDA graph, and launches about 150 small kernels per step (`remainder` x48, `mul` x18, `bitwise_xor` x12, `bitwise_or` x8, stacks/copies), each a few µs but host-launch bound at ~7-8 µs apart.

Measured at batch 1, 32K context: the decode step period is 11.5 ms and the GPU is idle for 2.2 ms of it; about 1.4 ms of that idle time is this eager hash path. Without speculative decoding (1 token per request) the fast path is taken and the hash cost is negligible.

### Additional notes

The existing pieces almost cover the multi-token case. A prototype that keeps the current host-side bookkeeping, writes the forward's tokens into the history with one small Triton kernel and then calls the existing `_decode_hash_kernel` in `READ_CURRENT_HISTORY` mode per layer reduces the work to 3 launches + 1 H2D copy per step. It is bitwise identical to the torch path in our tests (hashes, history buffer, row mapping and cached outputs) for: seeded context chunks, 4 requests x 6 tokens padded to 32 with rollback to the accepted length, int32 inputs, out-of-range token ids, a context + generation mix, freed-and-reused rows. Duplicate request ids and token masks still take the torch path.

We are measuring the end-to-end gain and are happy to send this as a PR if the approach looks right.

items.title: [Bug]: fill_template.py fails with ValueError when a substitution value contains a colon
items.author: ShryukGrandhi
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

- CPU architecture: arm64 (also reproducible on x86_64; the script is pure Python)
- TensorRT-LLM branch: main (commit c6350002f)
- Python 3.12
- No GPU needed to reproduce

### Who can help?

_No response_

### Information

- [x] The official example scripts

### Reproduction

`triton_backend/tools/fill_template.py` says substitutions support escaping, but a value that contains a colon (escaped or not) crashes the script:

```bash
printf 'url: "${url}"\n' > config.pbtxt
python3 triton_backend/tools/fill_template.py config.pbtxt 'url:http\://localhost\:8000'
```

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "triton_backend/tools/fill_template.py", line 70, in <module>
    main(**vars(args))
  File "triton_backend/tools/fill_template.py", line 43, in main
    key, value = split(sub, ":")
ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 2)
```

`main()` first runs `split(substitutions, ",")`, which already removes every backslash, and then runs `split(sub, ":")` on the result. By the time the second split runs, `\:` has turned into a plain `:`. So the value gets split again. The same double unescaping means a literal backslash in a value has to be written as four backslashes.

### Expected behavior

`url:http\://localhost\:8000` should produce `url: "http://localhost:8000"`. Only the first colon should separate the key from the value, so values such as URLs, `host:port` or Windows paths can be passed.

### actual behavior

The script exits with `ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 2)` and the template is left unfilled.

### additional notes

Splitting each `key:value` pair on its first colon only (`sub.split(":", 1)`) fixes it.

items.title: [Inductor] _dump_launch_params races under pytest-xdist
items.author: kevint324
items.body_excerpt:
## Describe the bug

`test/inductor/test_triton_kernels.py` can fail intermittently when it is run with pytest-xdist. The `_dump_launch_params` helper derives one shared path from `sys.argv[0]`. In the CI invocation below, every worker sees `sys.argv[0] == "-c"`, so all workers use the same `-c.launch_params` file.

The helper checks `os.path.exists()` and then calls `os.remove()`. Another worker can remove the file between those two operations, causing a `FileNotFoundError` before the test body starts. The same race can occur in the cleanup in `finally`.

The failure is in the upstream test helper and does not depend on the computation performed by the test. The failure is intermittent because it depends on worker scheduling.

The relevant test was:

```text
KernelTests::test_triton_kernel_2d_autotune_grad_False_dynamic_True_backend_inductor_grid_type_2_tdlp_1
```

The current helper on PyTorch `main` still uses the shared path:

```python
launch_params_file = f"{os.path.abspath(sys.argv[0])}.launch_params"
if value == "1" and os.path.exists(launch_params_file):
    os.remove(launch_params_file)
```

## Error logs

The failing command was:

```bash
coverage run -m pytest -p no:faulthandler \
  pytorch/test/inductor/test_triton_kernels.py \
  -v -n 8 --timeout=720 --disable-warnings
```

Observed traceback:

```text
File ".../test/inductor/test_triton_kernels.py", line 1336, in test_triton_kernel_2d_autotune
    with _dump_launch_params(tdlp):
File "/usr/lib/python3.12/contextlib.py", line 137, in __enter__
    return next(self.gen)
File ".../test/inductor/test_triton_kernels.py", line 73, in _dump_launch_params
    os.remove(launch_params_file)
FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: '.../test/inductor/-c.launch_params'
```

The module result was:

```text
1 failed, 333 passed, 103 skipped
```

## Versions

- PyTorch source revision: `6f49d1f0287c449c186339782878346ad34847bd`
- PyTorch `main` checked on 2026-10-15: `64f6a5984749fc382465a3713ddd180bd60484e1`
- Python: 3.12.3
- pytest: 7.4.3
- pytest-xdist: 3.8.0
- Triton: 3.4.0

The source-level race can occur whenever multiple workers share the same launch-params path, while whether it manifests depends on worker scheduling.

## Proposed fix

Use a launch-params path unique to each xdist worker/process, and make the producer and cleanup code use that same path. Merely ignoring `FileNotFoundError` would hide the exception but would still allow workers to delete one another's files.

A possible implementation is to add the xdist worker name only when pytest-xdist is active, preserving the existing filename for serial runs:

```python
def _launch_params_file():
    path = os.path.abspath(sys.argv[0])
    worker = os.environ.get("PYTEST_XDIST_WORKER")
    if worker:
        path = f"{path}.{worker}"
    return f"{path}.launch_params"
```

The launch-params writer and `_dump_launch_params` cleanup should both use this helper.

items.title: [MPS][Inductor] `expm1` and `log1p` compile to `exp(x)-1` and `log(1+x)`, losing precision for small x
items.author: jzluo
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

This is the compiled counterpart of #198708.  On MPS, Inductor lowers `torch.expm1` to `exp(x) - 1` and `torch.log1p` to `log(1 + x)`, which loses precision for small `x`. #198771 addressed eager `expm1`. 
`F.softplus` decomposes to `log1p(exp(x))`, so it's also affected. Eager softplus was addressed in #197000. 

Repro (printing largest relative error against fp64 CPU reference):
```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

x = torch.tensor([1e-4, 1e-3], device="mps")
ops = {"expm1": torch.expm1, "log1p": torch.log1p, "softplus": lambda t: F.softplus(t.log())}
for name, op in ops.items():
    ref = op(x.cpu().double())
    for mode, fn in (("eager", op), ("compiled", torch.compile(op))):
        print(name, mode, f"{((fn(x).cpu().double() - ref) / ref).abs().max().item():.2e}")
```

On 2.14.0:
```
expm1 eager 1.16e-04
expm1 compiled 1.16e-04
log1p eager 1.24e-08
log1p compiled 1.66e-04
softplus eager 1.66e-04
softplus compiled 1.66e-04
```

On 2.16.0.dev20261018:
```
expm1 eager 4.65e-08
expm1 compiled 1.16e-04
log1p eager 1.24e-08
log1p compiled 1.66e-04
softplus eager 1.04e-07
softplus compiled 1.66e-04
```

Opus 5.5's suggested fix:

> `MetalOverrides` in `torch/_inductor/codegen/mps.py` defines neither op, so the generic versions in `codegen/common.py` are used instead. Lowering them the way the eager kernels compute them fixes it:
> - `log1p`: call `c10::metal::log1p`.
> - `expm1`: use the same piecewise expression as `expm1_functor`, `|x| < 0.1 ? c10::metal::expm1f(x) : exp(x) - 1`.
>

items.title: [Bug] `_could_dynamic_scale_rblock` gates on a hardcoded device-name allowlist (`type in ["cuda","hip"]`), so any other device type can never use occupancy-driven `R0_BLOCK` scaling
items.author: li-lizhe
items.body_excerpt:
**Affected file:** `torch/_inductor/runtime/triton_heuristics.py` (`_could_dynamic_scale_rblock`)
**Type:** device-specific hardcoding in a backend-agnostic decision path

## 1. Background

While running the combo-kernel test suite from PR [#192734](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/192734)
on a non-CUDA accelerator, `test_combo_kernel_dynamic_scale_rblock` fails deterministically.

We initially approached this as "the backend does not expose the three occupancy fields"
(`major` / `regs_per_multiprocessor` / `warp_size` on `DeviceProperties`). **After fixing those on the
backend side, the test still failed** — because the actual gate is a *device-name allowlist* upstream:

```python
# torch/_inductor/runtime/triton_heuristics.py  _could_dynamic_scale_rblock
... and device_prop.type in ["cuda", "hip"] ...
```

Any device whose `type` is not `cuda`/`hip` is rejected outright, **regardless of whether it can supply
equivalent occupancy information**. This is the same class of issue as the hardware-decoupling
refactoring work: a decision that should be capability-based is instead based on a device name.

## 2. Environment

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Hardware | Ascend 910B2 (single card, chip 7) |
| torch | `2.15.0.dev20260917+cpu` |
| torch_npu | `2.15.0.dev20260917+gitec69335` |
| Backend | Inductor + triton-ascend (`TORCHINDUCTOR_NPU_BACKEND=triton_experimental`) |
| Test file | `test/inductor/test_combo_kernels.py` as refactored by PR [#192734](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/192734) |
| Date found | 2026-10-15 |

## 3. Reproduction

```bash
export TORCHINDUCTOR_NPU_BACKEND=triton_experimental
python -m pytest -q test/inductor/test_combo_kernels_pr192734.py \
  -k "dynamic_scale_rblock_npu"
```

Minimal reproduction (no test file needed, plain `torch.compile`):

```python
import torch, torch_npu

def fn(a, b, c, d):
    r1 = (a * torch.sigmoid(a) + b).sum(dim=1)
    r2 = (c * torch.sigmoid(c) + d).sum(dim=1)
    return r1, r2

inps = [torch.randn(8192, 2560, device="npu:0") for _ in range(4)]
with torch._inductor.config.patch({"combo_kernel_per_subkernel_blocks": True}):
    torch.compile(fn)(*inps)

from torch._inductor.runtime.triton_heuristics import CachingAutotuner
# Observe: the reduction autotuner carrying combo_grid_meta has _could_rblock_scale == False
```

## 4. Error output

```text
AssertionError: False is not true : _could_rblock_scale should be True for a combo reduction
```

Compilation succeeds; the failure is at the assertion. Measured device properties on this backend:

```text
DeviceProperties(type='npu', index=0, multi_processor_count=48, cc='Ascend910B2',
                 major=None, regs_per_multiprocessor=None, warp_size=None)
```

A direct single-variable probe of the gate confirms the blocker is the name check, not the missing
fields. Calling `_could_dynamic_scale_rblock` with the *same* otherwise-valid inputs and changing only
`device_prop.type`:

```text
device_prop.type = 'npu',  major=8, regs_per_multiprocessor=65536, warp_size=64   ->  False
device_prop.type = 'cuda', major=8, regs_per_multiprocessor=65536, warp_size=64   ->  True
```

(and with the backend's real values, all three fields `None`: `False`)

Everything else is held constant, so the name check alone flips the result. Since this condition
short-circuits before the field checks, a backend that fills in a valid occupancy model is still
permanently excluded.

## 5. Analysis

`_could_dynamic_scale_rblock` is the master switch for occupancy-driven `R0_BLOCK` scaling. It ANDs a
number of conditions, one of which is:

```python
device_prop.type in ["cuda", "hip"]
```

Because this condition short-circuits early, a backend can supply a perfectly usable occupancy model
and still be permanently excluded from the optimization. The decision is keyed on **device name**
rather than **capability**.

**Suggested directions (either):**

1. Replace the name allowlist with a **capability check** — e.g. participate when
   `major` / `regs_per_multiprocessor` / `warp_size` are all non-`None` and the backend exposes a
   usable occupancy model;
2. Or, if widening it now is undesirable, let the backend **declare** whether it supports this
   optimization (a capability flag / an explicit field on `DeviceProperties`) instead of being
   filtered by name.

## What we verified / what we did not

- **Verified** on Ascend 910B2 with the versions above: the test fails deterministically with the
  exact message quoted; the measured `DeviceProperties` values are as quoted; and forcing the three
  occupancy fields non-`None` does **not** flip the gate (i.e. the defect is upstream, not only on the
  backend side).
- **Not verified**: whether other non-`cuda`/`hip` device types (XPU, MPS, …) are affected the same
  way — we only tested one backend. We also do **not** propose a ready-to-merge patch: the exact shape
  of the capability check is a design decision for maintainers.

## Open questions

1. Would maintainers prefer "gate on capability" or "add a backend-declarable flag"?
2. If widened, who defines the *semantics* of the occupancy model? Device types differ in what
   `regs_per_multiprocessor` / `warp_size` mean — is a backend self-report sufficient?

comments.author: ramon725
comments.body:
**Root cause found: this is a firewall partial-connectivity trap, not an overloaded machine**

We hit the identical failure on a 10-node bare-metal cluster (Ubuntu 26.04, Ray 2.59.0) behind a restrictive host firewall (ufw), and confirmed it with a controlled experiment. Posting here in case it helps others hitting the same thing.

**Mechanism**

- Worker→GCS registration goes to the head's fixed port (6379). A fixed-port firewall whitelist allows it, so `ray start` reports success and the node briefly appears in `ray status`.
- GCS then health-checks the worker by calling its **node manager gRPC port, which is random by default** (`--node-manager-port`, documented as "Default: Random value", registered in the GCS node table).
- The whitelist blocks that reverse direction. After 5 failed probes, GCS marks the node dead and raylet exits with exactly the fatal in this issue (`node_manager.cc:959` on 2.20.0 / `node_manager.cc:969` on 2.59.0). The logs posted earlier in this thread show the signature precisely: `IsAlive = 1` → `IsAlive = 0` after ~31 seconds, then the fatal:

  ```
  Exiting because this node manager has mistakenly been marked as dead by the GCS:
  GCS failed to check the health of this node for 5 times.
  ```

- Note that the suffix "This is likely because the machine or raylet has become overloaded" is misleading in this scenario. Our machines were idle; only the health-check packets were dropped. That message sent us chasing CPU and memory ghosts for days.

**Controlled experiment**

One worker ran behind ufw with a fixed-port whitelist:

1. Deleting the whitelist rules on a **running** cluster does *not* kill nodes, because existing ESTABLISHED flows keep working (conntrack). This is why the failure is easy to miss on long-lived clusters.
2. Deleting the rules **and restarting the worker** (forcing re-registration) reproduces the death loop deterministically: join → alive ~30s (5 probes) → marked dead → raylet exits → restart → dies again. Cycle ~35s, 13/13 rounds; worker `raylet.err` matches this issue verbatim.
3. Restoring `ufw allow from <cluster-subnet>` and the node re-joins and stays stable (recovered in ~54s via our watchdog, no manual intervention).

**Workaround**

- Allow all traffic from the cluster subnet (what we did), or
- Pin the random ports in firewall environments: `--node-manager-port`, `--object-manager-port`, `--runtime-env-agent-port`, `--dashboard-agent-grpc-port`, `--metrics-export-port`, plus `--worker-port-list`.

**Why the `RAY_health_check_*` workarounds appear to help (but don't fix)**

Several comments above found that setting `RAY_health_check_initial_delay_ms` / `RAY_health_check_period_ms` to very large values stops the crash. That actually fits this root cause rather than contradicting it. Those settings postpone the probes indefinitely, i.e. they disable failure detection instead of restoring connectivity. That also explains why a later commenter still sees workers crashing within seconds on a plain LAN: a host-level firewall between LAN peers produces exactly this signature, so "same LAN" does not imply the reverse direction is open.

Tuning the threshold would only postpone the death; the probes still cannot reach a blocked port.

**Minimal repro**

```bash
# head (192.168.2.11)
sudo ufw default deny incoming && sudo ufw allow ssh
sudo ufw allow 6379/tcp 8265/tcp 10001/tcp    # fixed ports only
ray start --head --port=6379

# worker
sudo ufw default deny incoming && sudo ufw allow ssh
ray start --address=192.168.2.11:6379         # joins OK...
# observe: node disappears from `ray status` after ~30s
# worker raylet.err: "marked as dead by the GCS ... for 5 times"

# fix
sudo ufw allow from 192.168.2.0/24            # allow subnet (or pin the random ports)
# restart worker -> joins and stays alive
```

**Docs suggestion**

The docs already state "Ray requires bi-directional communication among its nodes" and that `--node-manager-port` defaults to a random value, but the on-p

items.title: [Serve] Calls to a Serve Deployment's .remote(), hang after some amount of time / requests.
items.author: JadenFiotto-Kaufman
items.body_excerpt:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

After some amount of time and some amount of calls to .remote(), my deployment no longer receives requests. When this happens it corresponds with logs In the Deployment that is calling .remote() like:

"WARNING 2024-09-24 09:51:14,270 serve 20 pow_2_scheduler.py:536 - Failed to get queue length from Replica(id=‘was0z9gr’, deployment=‘ModelDeployment’, app=‘Model:nnsight-models-languagemodel-languagemodel-repo-id-eleutherai-gpt-j-6b’) within 1.0s. If this happens repeatedly it’s likely caused by high network latency in the cluster. You can configure the deadline using the RAY_SERVE_QUEUE_LENGTH_RESPONSE_DEADLINE_S environment variable.”

Here is my setup. I have three services in my architecture.
1.) My own FastApi server.
2.) A Request pre-processing Ray Deployment.
3.) A Compute Ray Deployment.

The FastApi server is my own custom ingress endpoint, not using Ray’s ingress functionality. It connects to an existing Ray cluster via ray.init() on initialization. When the async request endpoint is hit, it uses serve.get_app_handle("RequestApplication").remote(request) to send the request to the Request Deployment.

The Request deployment is on the Ray head node and based on the request received, sends the request to the correct compute deployment like serve.get_app_handle(<compute app name>).remote(request). This happens in the deployment’s async __call__ method.

The Compute deployment is on a different ray node on a different machine than the FastApi server and Ray head node. The Compute deployment receives the request also on its async __call__ method, executes the compute heavy request, and handles sending the data back to the FastApi server.

Things to note:

Neither the FastApi server nor the Request Deployment wait for the response from .remote(request) as the Compute deployment handles the result separate from Ray.
The request is a pydantic object which contains a large object as one of its attributes. In the FastApi server, it calls ray.put on that attribute, which then the Compute deployment calls ray.get
In the logs for for the Request deployment, I consistently see “LongPollClient polling timed out. Retrying.” Not sure if this is a problem.
In the FastApi server I sometimes see: “WARNING 2024-09-24 09:51:14,270 serve 20 pow_2_scheduler.py:536 - Failed to get queue length from Replica(id=‘was0z9gr’, deployment=‘ModelDeployment’, app=‘Model:nnsight-models-languagemodel-languagemodel-repo-id-eleutherai-gpt-j-6b’) within 1.0s. If this happens repeatedly it’s likely caused by high network latency in the cluster. You can configure the deadline using the RAY_SERVE_QUEUE_LENGTH_RESPONSE_DEADLINE_S environment variable.”
This is often followed by: “concurrent.futures._base.InvalidStateError: CANCELLED: <Future at 0x7f118c190910 state=cancelled>”
Is there anything I need to do as I’m not waiting for the results of requests to .remote()? Should I be “closing” the DeploymentHandles in some way after I’ve sent data via their .remote() method?

Sorry for the long post. Please let me know if theres any logs or information I can provide.

### Versions / Dependencies

Ray: '2.36.0'
Python: '3.10.15'
OS: 'Ubuntu 20.04.6 LTS (Focal Fossa)'

### Reproduction script

Not something I can reproduce in one script. Here is a link to our software, specifically the Ray Deployment that calls .remote() and hangs: https://github.com/ndif-team/ndif/blob/dev/ray/deployments/request.py

### Issue Severity

High: It blocks me from completing my task.

comments.author: JoshKarpel
comments.body:
I think we might be seeing the same issue as well. Some additional data points for debugging, though we also don't know what the actual cause is, and maybe these are specific to our setup... ok, enough caveats!

- We see this in high-traffic clusters only - so that indicates that it's something about load that triggers it.
- It starts *abruptly*. Request latencies do not get longer before the problem manifests, then requests suddenly start hanging.
- Restarting the intermediate "router" application replica is sufficient to get rid of the issue. Other "router" replicas are not affected, even when sending requests to the same "processor" deployment. Therefore it seems likely that the problem is in the `DeploymentHandle` on the client side, and that something can ephemerally put it into a broken state.

On the bright side (?!?!) this was reported before our changes to the `LongPollClient` in https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/48807, so it's probably not related to https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/52793 or https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/53613 (both of which we're running patched fixes for anyway).

items.title: Support otlp_traces_endpoint for trtllm
items.author: Jeffwan
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 Feature Description and Motivation

v1.2.0 and above.

```
  # disagg_config.yaml (proxy)
  otlp_config:
    otlp_traces_endpoint: "http://jaeger:4317"
```

the disagg proxy itself does NOT create spans.
```
Client (traceparent) → Proxy (no span) → CTX Worker (llm_request span) -> → GEN Worker (llm_request span)
```

The two worker spans share the same traceparent from the client, so they appear as siblings under the same trace in Jaeger/Zipkin, but there's no parent span from the proxy showing the orchestration (ctx→gen sequencing, routing decisions, etc.).


some limitations
- No proxy-level spans — routing decisions, ctx/gen orchestration timing not traced
- Worker spans are created at request completion, not request start — they're retroactive spans with corrected timestamps
- No automatic span propagation between proxy→worker HTTP calls — the OpenAIHttpClient doesn't inject traceparent headers into forwarded requests (it passes through the original client's headers if present)
- return_perf_metrics: true is required on workers for spans to have meaningful timing data

### Use Case

items.title: [RFC]: Support Encode/Prefill/Decode (EPD) Disaggregation in AIBrix Gateway
items.author: varungup90
items.body_excerpt: ### Summary This RFC proposes adding Encode/Prefill/Decode (EPD) disaggregation support to AIBrix Gateway. Today, AIBrix supports Prefill/Decode (PD) disaggregation. With growing multimodal workloads, the encoding stage can also become a significant and independently scalable part of inference. EPD disaggregation separates inference into three stages: * Encode (E): Process multimodal inputs such as image, video, or audio and generate intermediate representations. * Prefill (P): Process prompt tokens and encoder outputs and generate KV cache. * Decode (D): Perform autoregressive token generation. The Gateway should become aware of these worker roles and route requests to the appropriate Encode, Prefill, and Decode worker pools. ### Motivation Encode, Prefill, and Decode have different compute and memory characteristics. Running all stages on the same workers can lead to resource contention and makes it difficult to scale each stage independently. EPD disaggregation enables: * Independent scaling of Encode, Prefill, and Decode workers. * Better resource utilization for multimodal workloads. * Different hardware or parallelism configurations for each stage. * Isolation of expensive multimodal encoding from Prefill/Decode workloads. * Reuse of the existing AIBrix PD routing architecture for multimodal serving. vLLM has started supporting disaggregated encoder architectures, including EPD-style deployments: * https://docs.vllm.ai/projects/ascend/en/latest/user_guide/feature_guide/epd_disaggregation.html * https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/features/disagg_encoder/ ### Proposed Change Extend AIBrix Gateway’s existing PD disaggregation support to understand an additional Encode worker role. Conceptually: For multimodal requests, the Gateway should: 1. Identify compatible Encode, Prefill, and Decode workers. 2. Select workers using the existing AIBrix load-balancing framework. 3. Pass the required routing/transfer metadata to the inference engine. 4. Allow the inference engine and its connectors to handle encoder-output and KV-cache transfers. For text-only requests, the Encode stage can be bypassed and existing PD routing can continue to be used. The implementation should reuse the existing PD routing infrastructure as much as possible rather than introducing a separate routing architecture. Initial Scope * Add encode as a supported worker role alongside prefill and decode. * Discover and maintain Encode/Prefill/Decode worker pools. * Extend PD routing to select a compatible E/P/D execution path. * Support multimodal requests requiring an Encode stage. * Keep encoder-output and KV-cache transfer outside of the Gateway. * Add basic stage-level routing metrics and failure handling. Future work can explore encoder-cache-aware routing, heterogeneous hardware selection, and independent autoscaling of E/P/D worker pools. Open Questions * Should Encode workers be shared across multiple Prefill/Decode pools? * What metadata should the Gateway provide to coordinate encoder-output transfer? * Should worker selection happen in E → P → D order, or should Decode/Prefill capacity drive the selection first? * How much of the existing PD router can be generalized into an EPD stage-aware router? ### Alternatives Considered _No response_ ### Area Not sure

### Summary

This RFC proposes implementing deadline- and capacity-aware admission control to replace naive Gateway-side queuing. By evaluating queue depth, expected wait times, and remaining client deadlines, the system can fail-fast (return HTTP 429) rather than queueing. This prevents wasted GPU capacity on requests that will inevitably time out and ensures the autoscaler accurately observes true system load.

### Motivation

Queuing can absorb short traffic bursts, but in production, we found that it can also hide demand from the autoscaler and amplify overload when traffic continues to increase. 

We experimented with Gateway-side queuing for a workload serving approximately 1,500+ QPS. During periods of high load, queuing reduced the amount of traffic reaching the inference replicas. As a result, the autoscaler did not always observe enough load to scale out as aggressively as needed. If incoming QPS continued to increase, the queue could then grow rapidly—crossing 100k+ queued requests in a short time—with requests waiting hundreds of milliseconds or even seconds before reaching a replica.

Long queues introduce another critical problem: the remaining client deadline matters more than simply finding capacity. For example, with a 30-second client timeout, a request that spends 10 seconds waiting in the queue has only 20 seconds left to complete inference. If the request is unlikely to finish within that remaining budget, dequeuing and executing it wastes expensive GPU capacity, as the client will likely cancel before receiving the result.

### Proposed Change

We propose building a **deadline- and capacity-aware admission control system**. Instead of simply deciding whether to queue or reject a request based on static limits, the system will consider:
*   Current queue depth and expected wait time
*   Estimated execution time for the request
*   Remaining client deadline
*   Expected near-term capacity

The revised flow would be:
`Request → Can it start and finish within its deadline? → Admit / Queue / 429`

By returning a 429 early, we allow the client to retry efficiently rather than accepting work that is unlikely to complete. This forces the system to answer the broader question dynamically: when should we absorb a temporary burst, when should queuing trigger additional capacity, and when should we fail fast?

### Alternatives Considered

*   **Unbounded or Static Queuing (Status Quo):** Continuing to queue requests indefinitely or based on a high static threshold. This hides true demand from the autoscaler and leads to severe GPU waste when executing requests that have already exceeded client timeouts.
*   **Strict concurrency limits without queuing:** Rejecting all requests immediately once replica inflight limits are hit. While this prevents GPU waste, it fails to absorb minor, transient traffic bursts that could be easily handled without scaling.

### Area

Gateway

items.title: [Gluon] async_load accepts a pointer whose element type differs from the shared memory buffer
items.author: shuyilinn
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

Gluon's `async_copy.async_load` (and `async_copy_global_to_local` in general) does not check that the pointer element type matches the shared memory element type. Copying from an fp32 pointer into an fp16 buffer compiles and copies raw bytes, and the reverse faults with a misaligned address. `smem.store` rejects the same mismatch at compile time.

```python
import torch
from triton.experimental import gluon
from triton.experimental.gluon import language as gl
from triton.experimental.gluon.language.nvidia.ampere import async_copy


@gluon.jit
def kernel(inp, out, SMEM_DTYPE: gl.constexpr, N: gl.constexpr):
    L: gl.constexpr = gl.BlockedLayout([4], [32], [4], [0])
    offs = gl.arange(0, N, L)
    smem = gl.allocate_shared_memory(SMEM_DTYPE, [N], gl.SwizzledSharedLayout(1, 1, 1, [0]))
    async_copy.async_load(smem, inp + offs)
    async_copy.commit_group()
    async_copy.wait_group(0)
    gl.store(out + offs, smem.load(L))


N = 512
inp = torch.arange(N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32) + 0.5
out = torch.zeros(N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
kernel[(1, )](inp, out, gl.float16, N)  # fp32 pointer -> fp16 smem: compiles, wrong values
print(out[:8].tolist())

inp = torch.arange(N, device="cuda").to(torch.float16)
out = torch.zeros(N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)
kernel[(1, )](inp, out, gl.float32, N)  # fp16 pointer -> fp32 smem
torch.cuda.synchronize()                # RuntimeError: CUDA error: misaligned address
```

```
[0.0, 1.75, 0.0, 1.9375, 0.0, 2.28125, 0.0, 2.34375]
RuntimeError: CUDA error: misaligned address
```

The first kernel should print `[0.5, 1.5, 2.5, ...]`; instead each 8-byte copy moves the raw bytes of two fp32 values into four fp16 slots.

Expected: a compile-time error for both, like `smem.store` gives for a value whose dtype does not match the buffer.

The frontend (`python/triton/experimental/gluon/language/nvidia/ampere/async_copy.py`, and the AMD `cdna4`/`cdna5` versions) only checks the shapes, and `AsyncCopyGlobalToLocalOp::verify` only checks that the destination is mutable. The lowering sizes each copy by the shared memory element type, so a mismatch reads with the wrong stride.

### Environment details

Triton: main @ 41846bc965
GPU: NVIDIA RTX 4090 (sm_89), driver 570 / CUDA 12.8

comments.author: he-yufeng
comments.body:
Opened #12341, picking up where the closed #12250 left off (same verifier + frontend-check shape, extended to both AMD copy directions).

The builtins now reject the mismatch at the frontend on every NVIDIA and AMD async-copy path, and AsyncCopyGlobalToLocalOp verifies it for non-Gluon producers. The regression test is red without the frontend check and green with it on this machine (no GPU here, so the byte-level runtime repro stays as documented in the issue).

items.title: [Bug]: Kimi K3 / MLA unit tests on SM107: two KDA files skip SM107, a cute_dsl_mla routing case contradicts the perf table, and an indexed-pool decode test compares two code paths bit-exactly
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

- TensorRT-LLM main @ e88d19ca3b, PyTorch backend
- GPU with compute capability 10.7 (SM107). Item 2 is a host-side routing test (it monkeypatches the SM version) and fails independently of the GPU.

### Who can help?

Related: #19960 (adds the `test_cute_dsl_mla` case below and extends Kimi K3 to SM107), #18599 (the `(96, 1)` entry in the FP8 perf table), #18938 (the KDA decode kernel and dispatch).

### Reproduction

Three test-only problems seen when running the Kimi K3 / MLA unit tests on SM107. They are grouped here to keep the noise down. None of them is a product bug as far as I can tell. Each item lists the fix I verified.

**1. Two KDA test files skip everything on SM107**

`tests/unittest/_torch/modules/kimi_kda/test_kda_cache_soundness.py:57` and `test_kda_prefill_state_parity.py:40` gate on

```python
torch.cuda.get_device_capability(0) in {(10, 0), (10, 3)}
```

with reason "Kimi K3 is supported only on Blackwell (SM100/SM103)". The runtime predicate `is_kda_optimized_supported()` (`_torch/modules/kimi_kda/_kda_kernels.py:66`) accepts `(100, 103, 107)`, and the neighbouring files (`test_kda_decode_op.py`, `test_kda_prefill_op.py`) already gate on it. So on SM107 these two files report 6 and 15 skips and cover nothing.

Fix: gate on `is_kda_optimized_supported()` like the other files. With `(10, 7)` added, `test_kda_cache_soundness.py` gives 5 passed and 1 skipped on SM107; the remaining skip is its own runtime condition, "could not obtain a recycled cu_seqlens tensor ID". `test_kda_prefill_state_parity.py` gives 15 passed.

Related stale comment: the `_has_supported_gpu()` comments in `test_kda_decode_op.py:33` and `test_kda_prefill_op.py:38` still say the predicate "accepts SM100/SM103 only; SM107 takes the FLA fallback".

**2. `test_cute_dsl_mla.py::test_mla_generation_routes_wide_head_fp8_verify_away_from_trtllm_gen[103-96-1-True-False-cute_dsl_mla]` fails independently of the GPU**

```
pytest tests/unittest/_torch/attention/test_cute_dsl_mla.py -k routes_wide_head
E       AssertionError: assert 'trtllm_gen' == 'cute_dsl_mla'
```

The case `(103, 96, 1, True, False, "cute_dsl_mla")` ("Single-token H=96 is unchanged (measured perf-table entry)") goes through the FP8 perf gate. `_PERF_MIN_BATCH_FP8[(96, 1)] = 8` (`attention/backends/fmha/cute_dsl_mla.py:419`), but `_select_mla_generation_fmha` always builds a decode batch of `batch_size = 4` (`test_cute_dsl_mla.py:148`). So the gate rejects CuTe DSL MLA and the selection falls through to the TRTLLM-Gen stub. The code behaves as the table says; the expectation is wrong for batch 4.

Fix: either expect `"trtllm_gen"` for that case (verified: the parametrization then gives 10/10 passed), or add a `batch_size` parameter to the helper and assert `"cute_dsl_mla"` at batch 8, which would test the table entry the comment refers to.

**3. `test_kda_decode_op.py::test_optimized_decode_updates_indexed_recurrent_state_pool_in_place` (all 3 ids) fails on SM107**

```
torch.testing.assert_close(indexed_output, local_output, rtol=0, atol=0)
E       Mismatched elements: 2154 / 21504 (10.0%)
E       Greatest absolute difference: 0.00048828125
```

The test compares two different code paths bit-exactly:

- The "local" reference calls `_run_production_decode(...)` without `ssm_state_indices`. `KimiKDALinearAttention.forward_decode` then routes to `forward_decode_fallback` (`ssm_state_indices is None`), which runs separate q/k/v/g projections.
- The indexed call passes `ssm_state_indices` and takes the optimized path with the fused `qkvg` projection.

On SM107 the two GEMM shapes round differently, by one bf16 ulp on 10% of the elements. That difference then also shows up in the fp32 recurrent state. Each path is deterministic: two local runs are bit-identical. Running the same core output through `_project_output` twice is bit-identical too.

Fix: compute the local reference on the same path with dense indices, so that the test checks only the pool addressing:

```python
dense_indices = torch.arange(batch_size, dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda")
local_output, local_cache = _run_production_decode(
    optimized,
    hidden_states,
    copy.deepcopy(initial_cache),
    slot_indices=dense_indices.long(),
    ssm_state_indices=dense_indices,
)
```

With this, the indexed output and the indexed recurrent state are bit-identical to the reference for `many-dense-pool`, `many-strided-pool` and `compact-dense-pool`. The test then gives 3 passed on SM107. I have not checked whether the two paths happen to agree bit-exactly on SM100/SM103.

### Expected behavior

These tests run and pass on SM107 (items 1 and 3), and item 2 passes on any GPU.

### Actual behavior

On SM107, item 1 skips everything and item 3 fails as shown above. Item 2 fails independently of the GPU.

### Additional notes

All three fixes are test-only. I can put them in one PR.

items.title: [Bug]: DeepSeek-V4.1 vision tower fails on SM107: cuDNN SDPA "No valid execution plans built" during KV-cache profiling
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

- GPU: Vera Rubin, compute capability 10.7
- TensorRT-LLM main (`tensorrt_llm/_torch/models/deepseek_v41_vision.py` unchanged up to 0372799d15), PyTorch backend
- torch 2.14.0+cu132 with its bundled cuDNN 9.24.0, NVRTC 13.4.92
- Model: `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash` (`DeepseekV41ForConditionalGeneration`, vision encoder enabled), TP4/EP4

### Who can help?

_No response_

### Information

- [ ] The official example scripts
- [x] My own modified scripts

### Reproduction

`trtllm-serve` on the model above, with the multimodal encoder enabled, dies on every rank while estimating KV-cache capacity, in the dummy image encode:

```
_util.py configure_kv_cache_capacity -> _encode_dummy_inputs
modeling_deepseekv41_multimodal.py encode_multimodal_inputs
deepseek_v41_vision.py -> F.scaled_dot_product_attention
RuntimeError: cuDNN Frontend error: [cudnn_frontend] Error: No valid execution plans built.
```

Standalone (1 GPU, compute capability 10.7, torch 2.14 + cuDNN 9.24), the same shape the vision attention uses for the 8192-patch profiling dummy:

```python
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F
x = torch.randn(8192, 3 * 1024, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
q, k, v = (t.reshape(8192, 16, 64).transpose(0, 1).unsqueeze(0) for t in x.chunk(3, -1))
F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v)  # RuntimeError: ... No valid execution plans built.
```

### Expected behavior

The server starts and image requests are served, as on SM100/SM103.

### actual behavior

Startup fails as above. Only `disable_mm_encoder: true` gets the server up (text only).

### additional notes

Root cause:
- PyTorch 2.14 (CUDA >= 13 builds) prefers the cuDNN SDPA backend on every SM 10.x device, including 10.7, and does not fall back to another backend when cuDNN plan building fails.
- cuDNN 9.24 offers only runtime-compiled engines (eng8/eng10) for SM 10.7 SDPA forward, and all of them fail NVRTC compilation (`CUDNN_STATUS_INTERNAL_ERROR_COMPILATION_FAILED`). This holds for every shape that dispatches to cuDNN (head_dim 32/64/128, BF16/FP16, contiguous or strided), with NVRTC 13.2 or 13.4. cuDNN 9.25.1.1, 9.26.1.1 and 9.27.0.42 provide an engine (eng18) that builds on SM 10.7.
- A try/except fallback in the model is not safe: after a failed build PyTorch caches a null graph for that shape and the next call on the same shape segfaults. Reported upstream as pytorch/pytorch#201420.
- The vision tower's unit tests are CPU-only, and the V4.1 GPU tests (added with #19727) are text-only and do not run on SM 10.7, so CI does not cover this path.

Vision tower forward on one Vera Rubin GPU (full 32-layer tower + aligner, real weights, BF16; 1022x1022 image = 5329 patches / 8192-patch profiling dummy):

| SDPA backend | 5329 patches | 8192 patches |
|---|---|---|
| cuDNN 9.24 (as shipped) | fails | fails |
| FLASH | 30.8 ms | 53.0 ms |
| EFFICIENT | 44.6 ms | 86.3 ms |
| MATH | 260 ms | 567 ms |
| cuDNN 9.27 | 22.8 ms | 35.5 ms |

Against an FP32 reference (the checkpoint's `inference/vision.py`), every BF16 backend has a relative L2 error of 3.5–3.8% at the aligner output (MATH in BF16: 3.7%), so the choice of backend is within BF16 noise.

Proposed fix: on SM 10.7 with cuDNN < 9.25, exclude only the cuDNN backend around the vision SDPA call; leave every other configuration unchanged, since cuDNN is the fastest backend where it works. PR to follow.

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and checked the documentation and examples for answers to frequently asked questions.

items.title: [BUG] CuTe DSL >= 4.6: FlashAttention-4 SM100 backward with block-sparse masks spills registers, up to 1.8x slower than 4.5.3 (same kernel source)
items.author: janhuenermann
items.body_excerpt:
### Which component has the problem?

CuTe DSL

### Bug Report

**Describe the bug**

With the same kernel source, CuTe DSL 4.6.0.dev0 and later generate PTX for the FlashAttention-4 SM100 backward kernel (`flash_attn.cute.flash_bwd_sm100.FlashAttentionBackwardSm100`) that spills registers. The spills appear when the kernel is specialized for block-sparse attention with a `mask_mod`. That is the path `torch.nn.attention.flex_attention(..., kernel_options={"BACKEND": "FLASH"})` takes. With CuTe DSL 4.5.3, the same source compiles to PTX with no spills, or almost none. The kernel is at the 128-register cap (512 threads per CTA), so the extra pressure becomes local-memory traffic. On B200 the backward kernel is 22% slower with a sliding-window mask and 82% slower with a document mask. The dense, causal, GQA and native `window_size` specializations of the same kernel are not affected.

This looks like the backward counterpart of #3701 (forward kernel, 4.7/4.8 vs 4.5.1), and it narrows down where the regression landed. 4.5.3 is fine. 4.6.0.dev0 already regresses, and it is the first release whose PTX header says `Based on NVVM 23.0.0` (4.5.3: `NVVM 20.0.0`).

**Backward kernel GPU time**, ms (B200, bf16, head dim 128, 16 heads; median of 50; main backward kernel only, from the torch profiler; a repeat run agrees within 1% for the block-sparse rows and within 5% for the others)

| attention | 4.5.3 | 4.6.0.dev0 | 4.8.0 ¹ |
|---|---|---|---|
| full, batch 2 × 8192 | 2.039 | 2.010 (−1%) | 2.084 |
| causal, 2 × 8192 | 1.121 | 1.140 (+2%) | 1.177 |
| GQA causal (32 q / 4 kv heads), 2 × 8192 | 2.287 | 2.266 (−1%) | 2.366 |
| native sliding window 1024 (`window_size`), 2 × 16384 | 0.714 | 0.713 (0%) | 0.756 |
| **block-sparse `mask_mod`: sliding window 1024**, 2 × 16384 | 0.858 | **1.045 (+22%)** | **1.027 (+20%)** |
| **block-sparse `mask_mod`: document mask** (causal within random-length documents), 1 × 32768 | 1.279 | **2.329 (+82%)** | **2.209 (+73%)** |

The 4.5.3 and 4.6.0.dev0 columns run the same FA4 source (b20, see "Same source" below).
¹ The 4.8.0 column runs FA4 4.0.0b32, the latest release at the time of testing (b33 has a byte-identical backward kernel). FA4 changed between b20 and b32, so this column shows that the regression persists; it is not a clean A/B.

**The same PTX files assembled by one ptxas** (CUDA 13.0, V13.0.88, `ptxas -arch=sm_100a -O3 -v`)

| backward specialization | PTX from | spill stores / loads | SASS instr. | IMAD | STL / LDL |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| causal | 4.5.3 (CUDA 12.9 / NVVM 20.0.0) | 0 / 0 B | 3496 | 242 | 0 / 0 |
| causal | 4.6.0.dev0 (CUDA 13.3 / NVVM 23.0.0) | 0 / 0 B | 3360 | 216 | 0 / 0 |
| sliding window `mask_mod` | 4.5.3 | 0 / 0 B | 3800 | 294 | 0 / 0 |
| sliding window `mask_mod` | 4.6.0.dev0 | 124 / 228 B | 4528 | 703 | 31 / 57 |
| sliding window `mask_mod` | 4.8.0 (CUDA 13.4 / NVVM 23.0.0) ¹ | 260 / 264 B | 4192 | 318 | 65 / 55 |
| document `mask_mod` | 4.5.3 | 28 / 16 B | 4512 | 653 | 7 / 4 |
| document `mask_mod` | 4.6.0.dev0 | 204 / 204 B | 5952 | 1049 | 51 / 42 |
| document `mask_mod` | 4.8.0 ¹ | 184 / 184 B | 5456 | 968 | 46 / 37 |

All of these are at 128 registers (`.reqntid 512`), with warp-specialized budgets (`setmaxnreg.inc` 136/152, `setmaxnreg.dec` 88/24). The PTX files have no `.local` declarations, so ptxas introduces the spills from register pressure in the NVVM 23 PTX. The SASS that 4.8.0 ships through its own ptxas has 50 STL / 42 LDL for the document mask and 35 / 26 for the sliding window (causal: 2 / 2).

**Likely pressure region.** `CUTE_DSL_COMPILER_OPT="remarks{ptx}" CUTE_DSL_LINEINFO=1` on 4.8.0 marks `flash_attn/cute/block_sparse_utils.py:1564` in `get_block_sparse_iteration_info_bwd`. That line loads the block-sparse count and index tensors: `curr_q_cnt = q_cnt[batch_idx, head_idx, n_block]` and `q_idx[batch_idx, head_idx, n_block, None]`. #3701 found the same kind of small metadata-tensor load for the forward kernel (`cu_seqlens` in the varlen scheduler). Here the IMAD count rises together with the spills (document mask: 653 → 1049). We suspect the address arithmetic of these indexed loads, but have not verified it.

**Steps/Code to reproduce bug**

The attached `nvvm23-sm100-bwd-repro.zip` has the scripts, the nine PTX files and our raw results. Its README has more detail.

*1. No GPU needed.* Assemble the attached PTX pair:

```
ptxas -arch=sm_100a -O3 -v ptx/bwd.document_mask.fa4-b20.cutlass-dsl-4.5.3.nvvm20.ptx -o /dev/null
    16 bytes stack frame, 28 bytes spill stores, 16 bytes spill loads
ptxas -arch=sm_100a -O3 -v ptx/bwd.document_mask.fa4-b20.cutlass-dsl-4.6.0.dev0.nvvm23.ptx -o /dev/null
    152 bytes stack frame, 204 bytes spill stores, 204 bytes spill loads
```

*2. On a B200: time the backward* with the script below (FA4 through `flex_attention`, about 50 lines), once per environment:

```
python3.12 -m venv nvvm20 && . nvvm20/bin/activate
pip install torch==2.14.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu130
pip install torch==2.14.0 numpy flash-attn-4==4.0.0b19 nvidia-cutlass-dsl==4.5.3 quack-kernels==0.5.0 apache-tvm-ffi==0.1.11
python minimal_repro.py

python3.12 -m venv nvvm23 && . nvvm23/bin/activate
pip install torch==2.14.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu130
pip install torch==2.14.0 numpy flash-attn-4==4.0.0b20 nvidia-cutlass-dsl==4.6.0.dev0 quack-kernels==0.5.3 apache-tvm-ffi==0.1.12
python minimal_repro.py

items.title: Experimental tracking: Qwen 3.5 gated attention block on Rubin (cuDNN Frontend FROST kernels), the proof of concept before Qwen 3.8 Flash-Next
items.author: RomanAnders90
items.body_excerpt:
Owner: @RomanAnders90

This tracks the experimental `flashinfer.qwen_3_5_block` API (PR #6573), with its backend in `flashinfer/experimental/qwen_3_5_block/`: the Qwen 3.5 full-attention sub-layer as one call, from the post-layernorm hidden states to the attention output, over the serving stack's own paged KV cache. One plan runs the QKV + gate projection, QK-RMSNorm with partial RoPE, the paged-KV write-through, GQA attention at head dim 256 with split-KV, the sigmoid output gate and the out projection. Three serving forms, each its own compiled plan: dense prefill, extend (chunked prefill, prefix-cache hit, speculative verify) and decode (`q_len = 1 + drafts`). The kernels are CuTe DSL kernels vendored from cuDNN Frontend (the FROST kernels), with the import roots rewritten and a small set of declared patches; the deployed process imports neither the `cudnn` package nor the cuDNN library. The intended consumer is vLLM's Qwen 3.5 attention layer through FlashInfer.

It fits the experimental path as a model-specific fused block on one part: bf16 and SM107 (Rubin, cc 10.7) only, deliberately overfit to one model family; the kernels are still moving on the cuDNN Frontend side (the vendored pin follows cuDNN Frontend `develop` and is re-vendored as that side lands improvements); the SDPA launch binder is served in Python rather than by the native extension; and the API should settle once the vLLM integration is in use. It is explicit-only, with no `backend="auto"` routing and no AOT packaging.

Execution contract: compute capability 10.7, bf16 activations and weights, head_dim 256, `rope_dim` a positive multiple of 64 below head_dim (64 default), GQA with the model's head counts, a paged KV cache addressed by `slot_mapping` for the write-through and by block tables for the reads, `page_size` a positive multiple of 16 (16 / 32 / 64 / 128 validated), int32 index tensors whose form is checked host-side before any launch so a first `run` can be captured into a CUDA graph. Every other device, DSL version, dtype or geometry is a typed `NotImplementedError`; `qwen_3_5_block_support()` is the init-time dispatch predicate.

Roadmap: Qwen 3.5 is the proof of concept. The next step is Qwen 3.8 Flash-Next, whose attention layers add Qwen Sparse Attention (QSA) with an indexer on top of this block: decode first, then prefill. Those kernels land in cuDNN Frontend first and are then vendored here, either as an extension of this API or as a sibling experimental API under this issue, decided with the maintainers when the 3.8 PR opens.

Graduation target: the first release on or after **2026-11-04**, subject to maintainer review. Before graduation:

- Run the GPU tests through the experimental CI lane on an SM107 runner once one is available (today the CPU tests run everywhere and the GPU tests skip in CI; they are validated on the intended hardware before each push).
- Land the vLLM integration of the Qwen 3.5 attention layer and confirm the API needs no change for it.
- Pin the vendored cuDNN Frontend sources to a released version instead of a `develop` commit, and keep the one-command re-vendor path.
- Decide whether the Python SDPA launch binder stays or the native binder is adopted.
- Settle the stable name and module, and the relation to the Qwen 3.8 Flash-Next work.
- Remove the backend instead if vLLM does not adopt it.

This issue tracks qualification and API integration of the Qwen 3.5 block; the Qwen 3.8 Flash-Next kernels get their own PR(s).

items.title: [Bug] trtllm-gen DSV4 sparse-MLA batch decode: multi-query-per-request spans are not numerically equal to single-query decode (SM120, fp8 KV)
items.author: xzwgit
items.body_excerpt:
## Environment

- Hardware: 8x RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition 96G (SM120), single node, TP8
- vLLM 0.32.0 release and 0.32.1rc1.dev24 nightly (both reproduce), torch 2.13/2.14, FlashInfer python 0.7.1rc5 + jit-cache rc5 (cubin package at the shipped 0.7.0.post1)
- Model: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (1017 update; identical config/tokenizer to launch V4.1-Flash), `FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE_DSV41` attention backend, fp8 KV + fp8 indexer, block size 64
- The multi-query spans come from DSpark speculative decoding: each decode step submits `k+1` query rows per request (anchor + k draft positions) through `flashinfer_trtllm_batch_decode_sparse_mla_dsv4` with per-request `query_start_loc` spans.

## Symptom

With speculation on, greedy generation is **not token-identical** to the same server without speculation:

- the **first token always matches**;
- occasional later tokens diverge (e.g. after `The capital of France is` -> ` Paris`, the next token is `.` with spec vs `.\n` without; both sides stay fully coherent — this is a distribution shift, not corruption);
- the returned logprobs show the shift is present at **every verify row including the anchor row** (row 0, whose query is a re-forward of the last context token and whose KV view is pure context): e.g. `Paris` at **-0.41858813** with spec vs ~0 (argmax certainty) without.

The fingerprint: the anchor-row logit bias is **exactly identical at k=1 (2 rows/request) and k=3 (4 rows/request)** — -0.41858813 to 8 decimal places. A constant, k-independent shift points at the multi-row batch path itself, not at cross-row visibility or batch-derived scaling (which would vary with row count).

## What we verified on the vLLM side (all correct)

Instrumented the vLLM call path; for the verify steps:

- per-row SWA lens are causal and correct: `[6, 7, 8, 9]` for a 6-token context + 3 draft rows;
- indexer top-k bounds use the same per-row derivation (`seq_len - block + local_idx + 1`) and are correct;
- verify positions are the expected `[ctx-1, ctx, ctx+1, ctx+2]` anchor layout;
- row-0 sparse index sets (SWA window slots + compressed top-k) are structurally normal.

Also ruled out: CUDA graph dispatch (a separate vLLM-side graph dispatch bug producing actual garbage was found and fixed in vllm-project/vllm#62535; the residual here is identical with `--enforce-eager` and with cudagraph-NONE), k=1..7, EP on/off, torch 2.13/2.14. Full isolation matrix in vllm-project/vllm#62417 (this residual is the "remaining subtler issue" section of our follow-up comment there).

## Question

Is exact equivalence between a `q_len > 1` span and `q_len == 1` calls a supported guarantee of `flashinfer_trtllm_batch_decode_sparse_mla_dsv4` on SM120, or is multi-query best-effort? If it is supposed to be exact, we can reproduce trivially (the box is idle and scripted); if not, vLLM likely needs to either split verify rows into per-row calls (perf cost) or switch the verify pass to a different path.

## Repro sketch

```
# same prompt, same checkpoint, greedy:
spec off (q_len=1 per request)  -> tokens [' Paris', '.\n', EOS], logprob('Paris') ~ 0
spec on  (k+1 rows per request) -> tokens [' Paris', '.',   EOS], logprob('Paris') = -0.41858813
```

Happy to run any experiment or dump any tensor (call args, indices, logits) the maintainers need — the machine is dedicated to this for now.

items.title: autotune: a failed `trtllm_utils` JIT build is retried for every tactic and reported only as "unsupported tactic"
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

With flashinfer-python 0.6.18, 0.7.1, 0.7.2 and current main (5209e883), if the JIT module `trtllm_utils` (used by the
autotuner's `delay_kernel` before timing each tactic) cannot be built, `AutoTuner.choose_one` silently fails **every** tactic of
**every** profile:

- `get_trtllm_utils_module()` is wrapped in `functools.cache`, which does not cache exceptions, and `JitSpec.build()` runs
  ninja again on every call, so the build is started again for each tactic (~0.08 s per attempt in the single-process repro
  below, ~0.6 s per attempt with 4 ranks building concurrently in our server);
- `choose_one` catches the error per tactic and logs it at DEBUG level ("Skipping tactic ... due to failure while profiling:
  Ninja build failed"); the only INFO lines are "Skipped 32 unsupported tactic(s) for mxfp8_gemm" and, since 0.7, a single
  "Building JIT module trtllm_utils; this can take several minutes on first use." (`info_once`, so it reads as if one
  build were in progress);
- nothing reaches `profiling_cache`, so `autotune(cache=...)` writes no file and the op silently runs its fallback tactic.

In our deployment (one 4-GPU server, `mm_mxfp8` tuned through `autotune(True)` during warmup) this cost about 20 minutes of
startup per server (21 profiles x 32 tactics, repeated in several warmup passes) without producing any tuning result, and it took
debug logging to see that the cause was a build failure and not unsupported kernels.

On SM107 a JIT build of `trtllm_utils` happens even with `flashinfer-jit-cache-sm107a` installed: `aot.py` on main registers
`gen_trtllm_utils_module()` only for SM90 / SM100 / SM103 (#6795, open, adds SM107).

## Environment

- flashinfer-python main 5209e883 (built from source, `0.7.2+g5209e883`) with flashinfer-cubin from the same commit; also 0.7.2,
  0.7.1 and 0.6.18 (pip wheels). JIT only, no `flashinfer-jit-cache`.
- PyTorch 2.14.0+cu132, CUDA 13.x, nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.8.0.dev0, aarch64
- GPU: compute capability 10.7 (the issue does not depend on the GPU)
- Trigger in our case: `CUDA_HOME` pointed at a conda-style environment whose `include/` has no CUDA headers (they live under
  `targets/<arch>/include`). nvcc still finds its headers, so the CUDA sources of the GEMM module build fine; only the host
  C++ files of `trtllm_utils` (compiled with `-isystem $CUDA_HOME/include`) fail with `fatal error: cuda_fp16.h: No such file
  or directory`. That misconfiguration is ours; the point of this issue is how the autotuner reacts to it.

## Reproduction

`repro.py` (below) creates a copy of `$CUDA_HOME` without headers in `include/`, uses a fresh `FLASHINFER_WORKSPACE_BASE`,
and tunes `mm_mxfp8(backend="cutlass")` (N = K = 4096) for M = 1, 16, 128 inside `with autotune(True)`. It counts the calls to
`delay_kernel` and their failures and the FlashInfer log records per level.

```
python repro.py            # broken CUDA_HOME
python repro.py --as-is    # unchanged CUDA_HOME, for comparison
```

Observed with main 5209e883 (broken CUDA_HOME):

```
"tune_seconds": 87.63,
"successful_configs": {},
"total_configs": {"mxfp8_gemm": 8},
"failed_tactics": {"mxfp8_gemm::CutlassMxfp8GemmRunner": 32},
"profiling_cache_entries": 0,
"delay_kernel_calls": 448,
"delay_kernel_failures": 448,
"delay_kernel_seconds": 37.3,
"first_error": "Ninja build failed. Ninja output:",
"flashinfer_log_records_by_level": {"INFO": 18}
```

i.e. 448 build attempts (14 profiles x 32 tactics), all failing, no WARNING, and the GEMM silently runs the fallback tactic
(results are finite). The same script on the same GPU type:

| flashinfer | CUDA_HOME | tune s | delay_kernel calls / failures | delay_kernel s | successful configs | records |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.6.18 | broken | 94.3 | 448 / 448 | 39.9 | 0 | INFO 16 |
| 0.7.1 | broken | 89.9 | 448 / 448 | 36.8 | 0 | INFO 18 |
| 0.7.2 | broken | 84.5 | 448 / 448 | 36.5 | 0 | INFO 18 |
| main 5209e883 | broken | 87.6 | 448 / 448 | 37.3 | 0 | INFO 18 |
| main 5209e883 | with headers | 53.4 | 256 / 0 | 3.6 | 8 | INFO 4 |

With a `CUDA_HOME` whose `include/` has the headers, `trtllm_utils` builds once and the same sweep succeeds (8 profiles
tuned, no failed tactic; most of the 53 s is the first build of the `mxfp8_gemm_cutlass` module). (The working row was measured
with `--as-is` and `CPATH=<toolkit>/targets/sbsa-linux/include`.) For this GEMM the fallback is ~3x slower than the tuned tactic
(about 100 us vs. <= 36 us per call at M <= 16, N = 25600, K = 6144, eager timing, 0.6.18), so a silent fallback can also cost
throughput.

Expected: one build attempt, then a clear WARNING (or an error) that profiling is unavailable, instead of N x 32 build attempts
and "unsupported tactic" at INFO level.

## Suggestions

1. Remember the failure of the `trtllm_utils` build (e.g. cache the exception, or build it once when entering
   `autotune(True)`), so a broken build costs one attempt instead of one per tactic.
2. Treat infrastructure errors (JIT build / import failures of the profiling helpers) differently from a tactic that fails on
   a given shape: log them once at WARNING with the first error line, and either abort the sweep for that op or fall back to
   timing without the delay kernel.
3. Optionally, include the number of failed vs. successful profiles in the "Autotuning process ends" message, so a sweep that
   produced nothing is visible at INFO level.

<details><summary>repro.py</summary>

```python
"""Repro: flashinfer.autotune retries a failed JIT build for every tactic and reports it only at debug level.

Usage (any GPU with the CUTLASS mm_mxfp8 backend, e.g. SM100/103/107/110):

    python repro.py                # breaks the JIT build on purpose: CUDA_HOME copy whose include/ has no CUDA headers
    python repro.py --as-is        # keep the current CUDA_HOME (shows the healthy behaviour on a normal toolkit)

The script runs in a fresh FLASHINFER_WORKSPACE_BASE, so nothing is reused from an existing JIT cache.  It tunes
mm_mxfp8(b
