items.title: DGX Spark (SM121) Current Support Audit
items.author: kahyunnam
items.body_excerpt:
# FlashInfer — DGX Spark (SM121) Current Support Audit

**Date:** 2026-04-24
**Scope:** Audit of SM121 (compute capability 12.1, DGX Spark) support across FlashInfer ops, APIs, backends, and testing.
**Goal:** Improve Spark usability on FlashInfer by identifying existing gaps.

**Note: skip to "15. Consolidated Action Items" for TLDR.**

---

## Architecture Context

| Gencode | Target | CUDA Requirement |
|---------|--------|------------------|
| `compute_120a` / `sm_120a` | RTX 5090 (SM120) | CUDA 12.8 |
| `compute_120f` / `sm_120f` | SM12x family (120 + 121) | CUDA 12.9 |
| `compute_121a` / `sm_121a` | DGX Spark (SM121) | CUDA 12.9 |

### SM120 vs SM121: Implications for FlashInfer

Per the [CUDA 13.2 Programming Guide — Compute Capabilities](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/archive/13.2.0/cuda-programming-guide/05-appendices/compute-capabilities.html) (Tables 29–33), SM120 and SM121 share a single "12.x" spec column: identical shared memory (99 KB/block, 100 KB/SM), warps (48/SM), registers (64K/SM), tensor core data types (TF32, BF16, FP16, FP8, FP6, FP4, INT8), TMA, and cluster support. [Table 28](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/archive/13.2.0/cuda-programming-guide/05-appendices/compute-capabilities.html#compute-capabilities-family-specific-compatibility) confirms `compute_120f` is compatible with **both** CC 12.0 and 12.1. The chip-level differences (SM121 = aarch64 host, unified LPDDR5x, 84 SMs vs SM120's x86_64, discrete GDDR7, up to 170 SMs) do not affect kernel correctness — only SM-count-based heuristics and host toolchain.

### `f` vs `a` compilation targets: performance implications

Per the [PTX ISA 9.3](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/parallel-thread-execution/index.html) (§9.7.15.5.14 for dense `mma`, §9.7.15.6.3 for sparse `mma.sp`), `120f` (family) is a subset of `120a`/`121a` (arch-specific). Most SM12x features — including **dense** NVFP4/MXFP4 block-scaled MMA — are family-specific and available via `120f` from PTX ISA 8.8. The arch-specific restriction (requiring `sm_120a`/`sm_121a`) applies **only to sparse MMA** (`mma.sp`) with `.kind::mxf4nvf4`/`.kind::mxf4`:

| PTX Feature | `compute_120` (baseline) | `compute_120f` (family) | `compute_120a` / `compute_121a` (arch) |
|-------------|--------------------------|------------------------|----------------------------------------|
| FP4/FP6/FP8 conversions (`cvt`) | No | Yes | Yes |
| FP4/FP6 MMA, block-scaled MMA (`.kind::mxf8f6f4`) | No | Yes | Yes |
| **Dense** NVFP4 MMA (`.kind::mxf4nvf4`) | No | **Yes** (PTX ISA ≥ 8.8) | **Yes** |
| **Dense** MXFP4 MMA (`.kind::mxf4`) | No | **Yes** (PTX ISA ≥ 8.8) | **Yes** |
| **Sparse** NVFP4 MMA (`mma.sp` `.kind::mxf4nvf4`) | No | **No** | **Yes** |
| **Sparse** MXFP4 MMA (`mma.sp` `.kind::mxf4`) | No | **No** | **Yes** |

FlashInfer's b12x GEMM kernel (`dense_blockscaled_gemm_sm120_b12x.py`) uses `cute.nvgpu.warp.MmaMXF4NVF4Op` — a **dense** block-scaled MMA atom. This means `sm_120f` wheels already emit native NVFP4/MXFP4 dense MMA instructions. Only **sparse** NVFP4/MXFP4 MMA (not currently used in FlashInfer) requires `sm_120a`/`sm_121a`.

> **Correction (2026-06-12):** An earlier version of this table stated that ALL `.kind::mxf4nvf4`/`.kind::mxf4` MMA was arch-specific-only. Per [Harry-Chen's feedback](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/issues/3170#issuecomment-4677810517) and PTX ISA §9.7.15.5.14 vs §9.7.15.6.3, the restriction is limited to the sparse (`mma.sp`) variant.

### Wheel build arch targets

The release wheel CI (`.github/workflows/release.yml`) builds the following SM12x targets:

| CUDA Version | SM12x target in `FLASHINFER_CUDA_ARCH_LIST` |
|---|---|
| < 12.9 | `12.0a` (SM120 arch-specific; no SM121 support) |
| >= 12.9, < 13.0 | `12.0f` (family; covers SM120 + SM121; includes dense NVFP4/MXFP4 MMA) |
| >= 13.0 | `12.0f` (same) |

**No `121a` target is included in any wheel build.** However, since FlashInfer's FP4 kernels use **dense** block-scaled MMA (`MmaMXF4NVF4Op`, not sparse), the `120f` wheels already emit native NVFP4/MXFP4 MMA instructions. The `121a` target would only be needed for future sparse MMA kernels. JIT compilation on SM121 still produces `121a` cubins for forward-compatibility.

### What this means for FlashInfer

- **Any kernel that runs on SM120 is architecturally compatible with SM121.** Hardcoded `sm_version == "sm_120"` or `minor == 0` checks in backend dispatch are over-restricting without justification.
- **Separate cubins matter for JIT but not for wheels.** `CompilationContext` correctly emits `sm_121a` for JIT on SM121. Since FlashInfer uses only dense block-scaled MMA (available on `120f`), the wheels do not lose FP4 GEMM performance. The `121a` JIT path provides forward-compatibility for future sparse MMA use.
- **SMEM capacity maps, tile configs, and MMA atoms are identical.** Code using `get_smem_capacity_in_bytes("sm_120")` returns the correct value for SM121 too — the only risk is `KeyError` if a map expects an `"sm_121"` key and doesn't have one.

### Key utility functions

| Function (`utils.py`) | Behavior for SM121 |
|------------------------|--------------------|
| `is_sm12x_supported` | True (CUDA ≥ 12.9) |
| `is_sm121a_supported` | True (CUDA ≥ 12.9) |
| `is_sm120a_supported` | **False** (12.0 only) |
| `device_support_pdl` | True (`major >= 9`) |
| `determine_attention_backend` | Returns `fa2` (fa3 is SM90-only) |
| `determine_gemm_backend` | Returns `sm80` (no SM12x branch) |

---

## 1. Attention

### 1.1 Decode (batch paged KV)

| Backend | CC Gate | SM121 Status | Notes |
|---------|---------|--------------|-------|
| **fa2** | Generic | **Supported** | Default via `determine_attention_backend` for non-FP8 tensor-core decode |
| **fa3** | SM90 only | **Not available** | `determine_attention_backend` returns fa3 only on SM90 |
| **xqa** | `major in {9, 10, 12}` | **Supported** | `trtllm_batch_decode` auto → xqa when `major != 10` |
| **trtllm-gen** | `major == 10` only | **Not available** | Auto selects this

items.title: [cake deslop] cake_sage_block_sparse_attention (2): drop 5 degenerate SM120 modules and dead code, regenerate as one SM120 kernel
items.author: yyihuang
items.body_excerpt:
**Background.** `csrc/cake_sage_block_sparse_attention` holds the Cake-generated Sage FP8 block-sparse attention kernels. The SM120 backend (#4951, specializations added in #5083/#5127) serves the public `bsa_attn_sm120_blk64_sage_fwd`, where `backend="cake"` is the default. The SM100/SM103 kernels and the fused quantizer (#5442) are opt-in through `bsa_attn_sm100_blk64_fwd(backend="cake")`. The first round (#5795, closed by #5907, merged 2026-10-03, +285/−19,944) did four things: added one shared SM120 launcher, merged the SM100/SM103 sources under `sm_100a/` (3 intentional `#if __CUDA_ARCH__ == 1000` blocks), replaced the JSON manifests with Python tables, and removed unused `#define`s. That took the unit from 64 files / 85,905 lines to 32 `.cu` files / 66,653 lines. sm_120a has 25 kernels (61,885 lines) and one 485-line binding; sm_100a has 3 kernels (3,403) and 3 bindings (880). There are also 1,558 Python lines. All 32 sources are JIT-compiled (25 SM120 modules, plus 3 stages × 2 arches). #5907 left the kernel-level items as follow-ups: one SM120 kernel, by-value TMA maps on SM100, and stride-aware TMA. No commit has touched the unit since. Counts are at main 3184bbea.

**Findings**
- **Degenerate SM120 modules.** 5 modules keyed `(UNIFORM_NONEMPTY=0, CONTIGUOUS=1)` (`0f9c7da2…`, `33204ab7…`, `4379d118…`, `59d2437f…`, `184ad196…`; 12,383 lines) are selected only when `uniform_block_count=True`, `contiguous_block_indices=True` and `block_sparse_num == 0` (`_bsa_attn_sm120_blk64_sage_fwd_cake`, `bsa_attn_sm120.py:401/492/518/524`). In that state `selected_count = block_sparse_num = 0` (kernel :397). The kernel skips the first K/V load (:424) and the only KV loop (:487), and writes zeros. Each file differs from its `(…,0,0)` sibling by one +4/−1 hunk inside `if (preload_count < selected_count)`, which never runs. The hash stems appear only in their own file and their `SM120_MODULES` row.
- **SM120 clones.** The 25 SM120 kernels (61,885 lines, 93% of the unit) are one ~2,474-line body. Against base `c214204e` (0,0,0,0,0) they differ by 0–6 hunks, at most +20/−23 lines. Examples: `386f` (1,0,0,0,0) adds `selected_count = q2k_block_nums[metadata_row]`; `ac8c` (0,0,1,0,0) drops the `valid_tokens` clamp. The first 336 lines are md5-identical in all 25 files (8,064 redundant lines). The SM100 attention kernel already takes `has_block_nums`/`block_sizes_mode` as runtime ints. Kernels with `has_block_nums=0` or mode 0 keep `q2k_block_nums`/`block_sizes` parameters they never read, and Python passes `q2k_block_index` as a dummy for both (`bsa_attn_sm120.py:491, :508`).
- **Never-compiled branches.** Every SM120 file has 8 `#if __CUDA_ARCH__ >= 1000` blocks with scalar `#else` fallbacks for `mul.rn.ftz.f32x2` (88 lines each, 2,200 total; plus 6 in the SM100 attention kernel at :1919-1927). Each module is built for a single target: `sm120a_nvcc_flags` is one `-gencode` (`flashinfer/jit/core.py:169`), and the SM100 sources build only for sm_100a/sm_103a. So the `#else` text never reaches device code. All 28 kernel files also keep two `#if defined(__CUDACC_RTC__)` blocks (280 lines), but nvcc is the only build path. Total: 2,486 lines.
- **Dead device helpers.** These counts include helpers that are only called from other dead helpers. 20 of 28 `__forceinline__` helpers per SM120 file are unused (182 lines each, 4,550 total). The SM100 attention kernel has 69 of 90 unused (640 lines) and `quantize_qk_vamax` 53 of 56 (478). Total: 5,668 lines. The bindings do not include the kernel `.cu`, so there are no hidden uses.
- **SM100 launch path.** `Run` in `sm_100a/cake_sage_block_sparse_attention_attention_binding.cu` launches a 1-warp `UploadCallerTmaDescriptors` kernel before every attention launch (:491, :498). Each call locks a `static std::mutex` and a heap `unordered_map` (:460-477), only to memoise `cudaFuncSetAttribute`. It also calls `cuTensorMapEncodeTiled` 3 times and `cudaGetDevice` twice. The SM120 kernels already take `const __grid_constant__ CUtensorMap` by value, so the replacement has an in-tree precedent.
- **Binding boilerplate.** All 4 bindings re-implement a 63–71-line `ScopedCudaDevice`/`Check*` block (276 lines), although they already include `tvm_ffi_utils.h`. Each SM120 call checks the device three times (Python `current_device()` plus two `cudaGetDevice`) and builds and loops over an 8-entry tensor dict (`bsa_attn_sm120.py:403-423`).
- **Strides and shapes.** All inputs must be contiguous (`bsa_attn_sm120.py:421-423`, `bsa_sage_sm100_cake.py:105`). The bindings compute TMA strides from sizes (sm_120a binding :143, :151-155; SM100 attention binding :157-202), so views are rejected and callers must copy. Geometry is fixed (head_dim 128, MHA-only on SM120), but there are no exact-shape routes: every legal shape maps to exactly one kernel.
- **Product-surface questions.** `sage_fp8_quantize_sm100` (`quantize_qk_vamax` + `quantize_v`: 1,419 lines, 4 JIT modules) has no in-repo caller besides its test and benchmark, and no package `__init__` re-exports it. `VariableBlockSparseAttentionWrapper` (`vsa_sm100_blk64`) never selects `backend="cake"`. The SM120 entry still accepts `tma_descriptor_workspace` ("accepted and ignored", `bsa_attn_sm120.py:375`). Its test fills a 0xA5 workspace only to assert that nothing touched it (`test_cake_sage_block_sparse_attention.py:712-769`).
- **Tests.** `test_cake_sage_block_sparse_attention.py` (73 cases) reaches all 25 SM120 modules. Only the 8 `topk_empty_contiguous_sizes{0..3}_k{320,257}` cases hit the 5 degenerate modules, and they assert zero output (:775). 16 `topk_empty_{omitted,uniform}_*` cases already drive the remap targets with `block_sparse_num=0`. No test asserts the `SM120_MODULES` size or module names. `test_cake_sage_block_sparse_attention_sm100.py` (11 tests) is the only coverage of the quantizer. Neither file has a CUDA-graph test. `benchmarks/bench_vsa_sage_sm120.py` runs `backend="cute_dsl"` only, so the Cake SM120 path has no ben

items.title: [Bug]: Qwen3-VL: rewriting video_metadata.total_num_frames without rescaling fps makes default HF frame sampling keep only min_frames and produces wrong `<t seconds>` timestamps
items.author: john-liu-dev
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

- TensorRT-LLM 1.3.0rc25 (`785c948`); transformers 5.5.4 (the version pinned in `requirements.txt`, also on `main`).
- Re-checked on `main` at `760a584` (2026-10-12): `_decide_do_sample_frames` and `Qwen3VLInputProcessorBase._preprocess` are identical to rc25 (main L169-221 and L349-425).
- Model: `Qwen/Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct` (the 8B model goes through the same code path).
- Seen end-to-end through the NVIDIA Dynamo TensorRT-LLM backend (`7e8b9fc2`) in aggregated multimodal mode; the reproduction below is CPU-only and needs only the HF processor.

### Who can help?

_No response_

### Information

- [ ] The official example scripts
- [x] My own modified scripts

### Tasks

- [ ] An officially supported task in the `examples` folder (such as GLUE/SQuAD, ...)
- [x] My own task or dataset (give details below)

### Reproduction

`Qwen3VLInputProcessorBase._preprocess` (`tensorrt_llm/_torch/models/modeling_qwen3vl.py`, L400-412 in rc25, L402-414 on `main`) forwards `VideoData.metadata` to the HF processor with `total_num_frames` rewritten to `len(vd.frames)`, so that HF's `sample_frames` (`np.linspace(0, total_num_frames - 1, num_frames)`) stays in range. The metadata `fps` (source video fps) and `frames_indices` are left untouched. When the IO layer has already subsampled the clip (e.g. 40 frames out of a 10 s / 24 fps / 240-frame video), HF's `Qwen3VLVideoProcessor` therefore believes the video is 40/24 = 1.67 s long and, with its class defaults (`fps=2`, `min_frames=4`), samples `int(40/24*2) = 3 -> 4` frames. This is the default path: when the caller passes no `do_sample_frames` / `num_frames` / `fps`, `_decide_do_sample_frames` (L167-219 in rc25, L169-221 on `main`) turns sampling on to match HF's class default. Two consequences:

1. Only 4 of the 40 decoded frames reach the ViT (1760 visual tokens instead of 11880). Any caller that does not pass `mm_processor_kwargs={"do_sample_frames": False}` (or an exact `num_frames`) silently gets a 4-frame summary of the video, regardless of clip length (a 30 s clip decoded to 40 frames gives the identical 4-frame result).
2. The `<t seconds>` timestamp tokens inserted by the processor are computed from the resampled indices over the rewritten `total_num_frames` divided by the *source* fps, so they are compressed by (decoded frames / source frames): for the 10 s clip the model sees `<0.3 seconds>` and `<1.4 seconds>` for frames that are actually at about 0 s, 3.3 s, 6.7 s and 10 s.

With `do_sample_frames=False` the processor uses `frames_indices / fps`, and both the frame count and the timestamps are correct, which shows the frame list itself is fine; only the sampling-path metadata is inconsistent. For comparison, HF sampling the 240-frame source itself at the default fps=2 would keep `int(240/24*2) = 20` frames with timestamps in source seconds, so the rewrite also makes the default path diverge from stock HF, which `_decide_do_sample_frames` intends to match.

Reproduction (CPU only, HF processor only):

- Decode a 10 s, 24 fps, 1280x720 H.264 clip into 40 uniformly spaced RGB float32 `(C, H, W)` tensors in [0, 1], metadata = `{"fps": 24.0, "total_num_frames": 240, "duration": 10.0, "frames_indices": linspace(0, 239, 40)}`.
- Apply the same rewrite as `_preprocess` (`total_num_frames := 40`) and call `AutoProcessor.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct")(text=[chat_template_text], videos=[frames], video_metadata=[meta], do_sample_frames=True, do_rescale=False, padding=True, return_tensors="pt")`.
- Observe `video_grid_thw == [2, 44, 80]`, 1760 `<|video_pad|>` tokens, timestamps `<0.3 seconds>`, `<1.4 seconds>`.
- Same call with `do_sample_frames=False`: `video_grid_thw == [20, 36, 66]`, 11880 tokens, timestamps `<0.1 seconds>`, `<0.6 seconds>`, `<1.1 seconds>`, `<1.6 seconds>`, ... (one per 0.5 s across the clip).
- Without the rewrite (original `total_num_frames=240`) HF raises `IndexError: index 50 is out of bounds for axis 0 with size 40`, which confirms why the rewrite exists.
- End-to-end: the Dynamo TensorRT-LLM worker's `/metrics` reports `trtllm_prompt_tokens_total = 1789` (= 1760 visual + 4 vision markers + 12 timestamp tokens + 13 text) for this request.

### Expected behavior

Either (a) when rewriting `total_num_frames` to the decoded count, also rescale `fps` to `len(frames) / duration` and reset `frames_indices` to `range(len(frames))`, so HF's duration and timestamps stay consistent with the frames it receives, or (b) default `do_sample_frames` to False whenever the caller passes an already-subsampled frame list with `frames_indices` (the IO layer has done the sampling), and only sample when the caller explicitly asks for `num_frames` / `fps`.

### actual behavior

With default `mm_processor_kwargs`, 4 of 40 decoded frames reach the ViT and the timestamps are compressed by 40/240 (details under Reproduction).

### additional notes

**Impact.** Silent quality loss for every video request that relies on defaults (temporal reasoning over a ~2 s window of a longer clip, wrong timestamps), plus misleading throughput numbers (the prompt is ~7x shorter than intended).

**Workaround.** Pass `mm_processor_kwargs={"do_sample_frames": False}` per request (the frame count is then whatever the IO layer decoded, e.g. `DYN_MM_VIDEO_NUM_FRAMES` in Dynamo).

The metadata rewrite and `_decide_do_sample_frames` were introduced in #15598.

**Related:** #20138 (Qwen3-VL video over the E/PD handoff; its reproduction passes `do_sample_frames=False` to get all decoded frames into the ViT, i.e. the workaround above).

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and checked the [documentation](https://nvidia.github.io/TensorRT-LLM/) and [examples](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/tree/main/examples) for answers to frequently asked questions.

items.title: [BUG] 02_dump_reg_shmem faults on sm_120: Fragment is 2-byte aligned but accessed through a 16-byte-aligned pointer
items.author: random25160765-collab
items.body_excerpt:
> **Correction (2026-09-13).** My original report framed this as an `nvcc` codegen bug specific to
> `sm_120`. That framing was wrong, and I have rewritten this issue. Further testing showed the
> codegen is identical on `sm_80`/`sm_90`/`sm_100`/`sm_120`, and that the underlying defect is on the
> CUTLASS side: the iterators access `Fragment` through a type that requires 16-byte alignment, while
> `Fragment` itself is only 2-byte aligned. Details and a verified fix below.

## Summary

`examples/02_dump_reg_shmem` aborts on `sm_120` with `cudaErrorMisalignedAddress` (error 716); the
example prints `Failed` and exits `255`. Reproduced on `main` @ `147295a3` with the stock example.

Root cause: `PredicatedTileIterator` reinterprets its `Fragment` (a plain `cutlass::Array`, 2-byte
aligned for `half_t`) as a 16-byte-aligned `AlignedArray` and accesses it 128 bits at a time. When the
compiler homes that fragment in local memory, it allocates the frame slot using the *declared*
alignment (2 → offset `+0xc`) but emits the stores using the *cast-implied* alignment (16 →
`STL.128`). The slot ends up at `12 (mod 16)`, so the 16-byte store is misaligned and the kernel
faults. Aligning the fragment moves the slot to `+0x10` and the example completes.

## Environment

| | |
|---|---|
| GPU | NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060, compute capability 12.0 (`sm_120`), driver 591.86 |
| Toolkit | CUDA 13.3 — nvcc V13.3.73 (`cuda_13.3.r13.3/compiler.38244171_0`) |
| OS | Linux (Ubuntu 26.04 LTS under WSL2), x86_64 |
| CUTLASS | `main` @ `147295a3`, unmodified (`git status` clean) |

## Where the alignment requirement comes from

The example itself is not at fault — `examples/02_dump_reg_shmem/dump_reg_shmem.cu:85` only declares

```cpp
typename GmemIterator::Fragment frag;
```

The requirement is imposed by the iterator
(`include/cutlass/transform/threadblock/predicated_tile_iterator.h`):

| Line | Code | Alignment |
|---|---|---|
| [181](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/main/include/cutlass/transform/threadblock/predicated_tile_iterator.h#L181) | `using AccessType = AlignedArray<Element, AccessSize, (AccessSize * sizeof_bits<Element>::value / 8)>;` | **16 bytes** (for `half_t`, `AccessSize == 8`) |
| [191](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/main/include/cutlass/transform/threadblock/predicated_tile_iterator.h#L191) | `using Fragment = cutlass::Array<Element, ThreadMap::Iterations::kCount * ThreadMap::kElementsPerAccess>;` | **2 bytes** — `cutlass::Array` has no `alignas` (`include/cutlass/array.h:101`; only `AlignedArray` at `array.h:2867` declares one) |
| [327](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/main/include/cutlass/transform/threadblock/predicated_tile_iterator.h#L327) | `AccessType *frag_ptr = reinterpret_cast<AccessType *>(&frag);` | casts the 2-byte-aligned object to the 16-byte-aligned type |

So the library relies on an alignment its own `Fragment` type does not declare. That dependency is
invisible to a caller who simply declares `typename GmemIterator::Fragment frag;`, which is the
documented idiom — and it is the reason the example breaks without any misuse on the caller's side.

## Evidence

**SASS of `kernel_dump` (`cuobjdump -sass`), stock example — the local slot is at `+0xc`:**

```sass
STL.128 [R1+0xc], R52 ;
STL.128 [R1+0x1c], R48 ;
STL.128 [R1+0x2c], R44 ;
STL.128 [R1+0x3c], R40 ;
STL.128 [R1+0x4c], R36 ;
STL.128 [R1+0x5c], R32 ;
STL.128 [R1+0x6c], R28 ;
STL.128 [R1+0x7c], R24 ;
```

Every offset is `≡ 12 (mod 16)`; `STL.128` requires a 16-byte-aligned address, and the kernel faults
at the first one.

**With the fragment aligned, the slot moves and the fault disappears:**

| | fragment slot | `STL.128` offsets | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| stock | `+0xc` | `0xc, 0x1c, … 0x7c` (all `≡12 mod 16`) | fault, exit 255 |
| `alignas(16)` | `+0x10` | `0x10, 0x20, … 0x80` (all 16-byte aligned) | **completes, exit 0** |

**Not architecture-specific.** Compiling the reproducer below for `sm_80`, `sm_90`, `sm_100` and
`sm_120` produces the identical 8 × `STL.128` at `[R1+0xc … R1+0x7c]`. The codegen is
architecture-independent; whether it faults depends on the runtime frame base, and on `sm_120` it
does. (I could only *execute* on `sm_120` — other architectures were compile-only.)

## Proposed fix

Minimal, verified on `sm_120`:

```cpp
// examples/02_dump_reg_shmem/dump_reg_shmem.cu:85
alignas(16) typename GmemIterator::Fragment frag;
```

However this only protects the example. Since `AccessType` is 16-byte aligned for every user of
`PredicatedTileIterator` (and the other iterators with the same pattern), the more principled fix
would be to declare the alignment on the `Fragment` typedef itself — e.g. make it an `AlignedArray`,
or add `alignas` — so that any caller declaring `Fragment frag;` is safe. That is a wider change, so
I'd rather leave the choice to the maintainers.

## Exposure (why this is not caught elsewhere)

A fragment that never has its address taken stays in registers and never touches local memory. Real
GEMM kernels therefore don't hit this. The fault needs the fragment's address to escape to a
non-inlined function — which is exactly what the dump/debug path does (`cutlass::debug::dump_fragment`,
`printf`). That is consistent with it showing up in this example and seemingly nowhere else.

## Note on the compiler side

I filed this with NVIDIA's compiler team as well. Their assessment was that the
`reinterpret_cast` to a 16-byte-aligned type is a source-level alignment promise that the object does
not satisfy, and therefore source-level UB rather than a codegen defect. I accept that reading — it
is why I have rewritten this issue rather than insisting on a compiler bug. The remaining point for
CUTLASS is narrower: the library should not depend on an alignment guarantee its own type does not
make.

<details>
<summary>Minimal reproducer (no CUTLASS)</summary>

The program below reproduces the same codegen and fault on `sm_120`. Note that the `Frame` layout is
deliberately constructe

items.title: JIT `topk` module ignores `FLASHINFER_CUDA_ARCH_LIST`: hardcoded `sm89_nvcc_flags` produce an sm_89-only binary
items.author: jhcdlg
items.body_excerpt:
> Filing against flashinfer (this is where the root cause is). We hit it through SGLang,
> which is why the reproduction below mentions SGLang  -  but the mechanism is entirely in
> `flashinfer/jit/`.

## Environment

- `flashinfer` **0.6.18** (installed via SGLang `main`, HEAD `5e9342d`, 2026-09-18)
- Two GPUs in one host, TP=2: **RTX 3080 (sm_86)** + RTX 4080 SUPER (sm_89)
- CUDA 13.0, torch 2.13.0+cu130, Python 3.11.16
- flashinfer JIT nvcc: **13.4 (V13.4.59, from the pip `nvidia/cu13` package)**  -  i.e. *not*
  the 13.0 that `torch.version.cuda` reports. The build metadata baked into the artifacts
  scanned below reads `Cuda compilation tools, 13.4, V13.4.59`.
- `FLASHINFER_CUDA_ARCH_LIST="8.6 8.9"` was **set** in the environment
- `FLASHINFER_EXTRA_CUDAFLAGS` was also tried, with `-gencode` for both 86 and 89  -  **no effect** on this issue

## Summary

The JIT-compiled `topk` module ships the hardcoded flag list `sm89_nvcc_flags`
(`flashinfer/jit/core.py`  -  line 123 in 0.6.18, which is the version we hit this on; the same
list is at line 156 on current `main`), which contains an explicit
`-gencode=arch=compute_89,code=sm_89`. `flashinfer/jit/cpp_ext.py:216` (same line in 0.6.18 and
on `main`) then decides that
**a module which already carries its own `-gencode` should not get the architecture list
appended**  -  so `FLASHINFER_CUDA_ARCH_LIST` is silently ignored for that module only.

Result: `topk.so` is built for sm_89 alone. On any other architecture it fails at **run
time**, not build time  -  and the failure surfaces on the *first real inference request*,
while the server looks perfectly healthy.

## Symptom (this part is what makes it expensive to diagnose)

- The server **starts normally**: `Uvicorn running`, `/v1/models` returns 200, weights
  loaded, no warning anywhere in the log.
- **Every real inference request fails.** `num_running_reqs` and `kv_used_tokens` stay **0**
  the whole time  -  the request never reaches the scheduler, so the first thing anyone
  suspects is the frontend / networking, not a kernel.
- The log accumulates (18 occurrences in our run):

```
RuntimeError: Check failed: (status == cudaSuccess) is false:
TopK failed with error code no kernel image is available for execution on the device
```

- A handful of other ops (`BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCache`) fail the same way, which is what
  made us first chase the *general* `FLASHINFER_CUDA_ARCH_LIST` question instead of
  looking at a per-module override.

## Where the message comes from

```
flashinfer/data/csrc/topk.cu:84:
    TVM_FFI_ICHECK(status == cudaSuccess)
      << "TopK failed with error code " << cudaGetErrorString(status);
```

Not torch: `torch.topk` works fine on sm_86 here  -  we tested 6 variants (different dtypes
and k values) on that GPU, all OK. So it is specifically flashinfer's JIT `topk` module.

## Decisive evidence: scan the architectures actually compiled into each JIT artifact

Scanning every `.so` under `~/.cache/sglang/.cache/flashinfer/0.6.18/86_89/cached_ops/`:

| Artifact | Architectures present | sm_86 usable? |
|---|---|---|
| `sampling/sampling.so` | **86, 89** | yes |
| `batch_prefill_with_kv_cache.../*.so` | **86, 89** | yes |
| **`topk/topk.so`** | **89 only** | no |

Everything else in the same cache directory got both architectures. Only `topk` did not.

## Root cause

```python
# flashinfer/jit/core.py:123   -  a hardcoded per-architecture flag list
sm89_nvcc_flags = ["-gencode=arch=compute_89,code=sm_89", "-DFLASHINFER_ENABLE_FP8_E8M0"]
```

```python
# flashinfer/jit/cpp_ext.py:216   -  if the module brings its own -gencode, the arch list is not appended
module_has_gencode = any(flag.startswith("-gencode=") for flag in extra_cuda_cflags)
```

`topk` is one of the modules that carries `sm89_nvcc_flags`, so it hits both: the module
declares sm_89 explicitly, and the general mechanism declines to add anything else.
`FLASHINFER_CUDA_ARCH_LIST="8.6 8.9"` therefore has no effect on this module.

Because the user-facing env var is documented as *the* way to control target
architectures, this failure mode is very hard to reason about from the outside: the same env
var works for `sampling` and `batch_prefill` in the very same build.

## Suggested fix direction

- Generate these per-architecture flag lists **from** the effective arch list instead of
  hardcoding a single `-gencode`, or
- In `cpp_ext.py`, treat a module's own `-gencode` as **additive** (append the arch list
  rather than skipping it), or at minimum warn when the two disagree  -  right now the
  mismatch is completely silent.
- A warning when the compiled artifact's architecture set does not cover the GPUs actually
  present would have saved us a lot of time.

## Impact / who else hits this

Anyone running flashinfer **0.6.18** on a GPU that is not sm_89  -  e.g. sm_86 (RTX 30-series),
sm_80 (A100), sm_75  -  **for the `topk` op path**. We only verified sm_86, and only on one
host, so we do not want to overstate the breadth; but the mechanism is architecture-list
logic, not hardware-specific.

Note that on our machine **a single-GPU run using only the 4080 SUPER (sm_89) works fine**  - 
the failure needs a non-sm_89 device to be part of the run. So a mixed-architecture host
fails on every request, while the same software on a single sm_89 card is completely healthy.

## Caveats

- Verified on one host, two architectures (sm_86 + sm_89), one flashinfer version (0.6.18).
- We did not bisect which flashinfer release introduced `sm89_nvcc_flags` for `topk`.
- Our evidence for "the arch list is ignored" is the built artifact's architecture set plus
  the source lines above  -  we did not instrument the JIT build to print the final nvcc
  command line. If that would help, we are happy to re-run with more logging.

## Workaround we are using

Remove the non-sm_89 GPU from the run (i.e. use a single sm_89 card), which sidesteps the
`topk` module entirely. Not viable for us long-term since our workload needs TP a

items.title: [Inductor] max-autotune fails with "invalid storage offset" when a Triton GEMM input is an as_strided view rebased to a negative offset
items.author: jeffdaily
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

My agent came up with this analysis, but I've read and approved it.

> Since #184232 Inductor rebases a storage-relative `as_strided` offset on a graph input onto the input's data pointer, so a view that reaches back before the input pointer gets a negative layout offset. Codegen handles that, but max-autotune benchmarking does not: `AlgorithmSelectorCache.get_inputs` (torch/_inductor/select_algorithm.py, `torch.as_strided(base, sizes, strides, storage_offset)` around line 5419) materialises each benchmark input on a freshly allocated `base` with the rebased offset, and eager `as_strided` rejects a negative offset. Compilation fails before any choice is benchmarked.
>
> Ablation: eager works; `torch.compile` without max-autotune works; `max_autotune=True` with `max_autotune_gemm_backends="TRITON"` fails. With the default config the error surfaces from `scheduler.speedup_by_fusion` -> `choice_timings`; with `benchmark_epilogue_fusion=False` it surfaces directly from `tuned_mm` -> `autotune_select_algorithm`; `autotune_in_subproc=True` does not help. Every variant ends in `get_inputs`.
>
> The harness needs to allocate `base` large enough to cover the rebased view and shift the offset accordingly (or build the example input from the original storage offset) instead of passing the rebased negative offset to `torch.as_strided`.

Minimal reproducer:

```python
import torch
import torch._inductor.config as cfg

def f(y):
    return torch.mm(y.as_strided((64, 32), (32, 1), 0), torch.ones(32, 64, device="cuda"))

y = torch.arange(4096, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)[2048:]
with cfg.patch(max_autotune=True, max_autotune_gemm_backends="TRITON"):
    torch.compile(f, fullgraph=True)(y)
```

Reproduced on ROCm on gfx90a, gfx942, gfx950, gfx1100 and gfx1201. The failing code is backend independent, so I expect CUDA to behave the same but have not confirmed it. Found while validating #196115; that PR does not touch this path.

### Error logs

```
torch/_inductor/lowering.py:527 wrapped
torch/_inductor/kernel/mm.py:868 tuned_mm
torch/_inductor/select_algorithm.py:6489 autotune_select_algorithm

torch/_inductor/select_algorithm.py:4694 benchmark

torch/_inductor/select_algorithm.py:5419 get_inputs
    example_inputs_extern.append(torch.as_strided(base, sizes, strides, storage_offset))
torch._inductor.exc.InductorError: RuntimeError: Tensor: invalid storage offset -2048
```

(frame chain with `benchmark_epilogue_fusion=False`; with the default config the same `get_inputs` frame is reached through `scheduler.speedup_by_fusion` -> `ir.choice_timings` -> `get_timings` -> `do_autotuning`)

items.title: [CI] AIBrix CI takes a large share of vllm-project's shared GitHub-hosted runners
items.author: Jeffwan
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

AIBrix's GitHub Actions workflows take a large share of the GitHub-hosted runners that every vllm-project repo shares. The org is on GitHub's Free plan, so all repos draw from one pool of about 20 concurrent jobs. AIBrix starts up to ~32 jobs on every merge to main and up to ~23 on every PR push, so a single AIBrix event can fill the whole pool, and jobs from other vllm-project repos wait for a runner.

This issue records the numbers and tracks changes to cut AIBrix's footprint.

## How the pool is shared

- GitHub-hosted runner concurrency is set per organization, not per repo. On the Free plan, all vllm-project repos share about 20 concurrent jobs. We observed a ceiling of 20–22.
- vllm's main CI runs on other infrastructure, but vllm and several other vllm-project repos still run some jobs on GitHub-hosted runners. Those jobs wait whenever the pool is full.

## Measurements

### Org-wide, two 2-hour samples

All GitHub-hosted jobs across vllm-project, counting only jobs that got a runner.

| Window (UTC) | Org concurrency (median / max) | AIBrix share | AIBrix jobs running (avg / max) | Median queue, vllm | Median queue, AIBrix |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Oct 16 19:00–21:00 | 17 / 20 | 51% (largest) | 7.8 / 20 | 25 min | 42 min |
| Oct 17 01:00–03:00 | 14 / 22 | 25% (second largest) | 3.6 / 11 | 2 min | 12 min |

In the first window, there were minutes when all 20 runners were running AIBrix jobs.

### AIBrix, 24 hours (Oct 16 04:00Z – Oct 17 04:00Z)

361 workflow runs, 20 merges to main, about 8,160 GitHub-hosted job-minutes. That keeps about 5.7 of the org's ~20 runners busy on average, around the clock.

| Workflow | Jobs per run | Job-minutes | Share | Triggered by |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Docker Push Images | 12 | 3,571 | 44% | every merge |
| Installation Tests | 8 | 1,834 | 22% | PRs and every merge |
| Linter and Unit Tests | 6 | 1,285 | 16% | PRs and every merge |
| Installation Smoke | 7 | 948 | 12% | PRs |
| Code Quality (CodeQL) | 3 | 159 | 2% | every merge |
| Docker Push kvcached-runtime | 1 | 151 | 2% | every merge |
| Others (Python tests, StormService E2E, Helm chart, docs, bot) | – | ~215 | 3% | – |

**62% of these minutes (5,083) come from merges to main, not from PRs.**

## Problems in AIBrix's workflows

1. **Every merge rebuilds and pushes every image.** Docker Push Images builds 6 images twice, once for Docker Hub and once for GHCR. Each build covers amd64 and arm64 through QEMU and takes 15–25 minutes. That is 12 long jobs per merge, about 20 times a day. These jobs themselves waited a median of 114 minutes for a runner.
2. **Every merge re-runs tests that already passed on the PR.** Installation Tests and Linter and Unit Tests run again on every push to main: about 1,150 job-minutes a day.
3. **Many small jobs per run.** Before its one e2e job, Installation Tests runs 5 image-build jobs (1–4 minutes each), a mock-app auth test (under 1 minute) and an artifact cleanup job. Installation Smoke builds 5 images again in its own jobs. Each small job takes its own runner and its own wait in the queue.
4. **Linter and Unit Tests uses 6 jobs**, including a coverage check that runs for about 20 seconds.

## Proposed changes

| Change | Jobs per merge | Jobs per PR push |
|---|---|---|
| Build and push images nightly, plus a manual trigger (release builds unchanged); one build pushes to both registries | −13 | – |
| Stop re-running Installation Tests and Linter and Unit Tests on push to main; keep them on `release-*`; add one nightly full run on main | −14 | – |
| Fold the image builds, mock-app auth test and artifact cleanup into the Installation Tests e2e job | – | 8 → 1 |
| Fold the image builds into the two Installation Smoke jobs | – | 7 → 2 |
| Merge lint and verify into one job; fold coverage into unit tests | – | 6 → 4 |
| **Total** | **~32 → ~3** | **~23 → ~9** |

Expected result: the number of jobs each AIBrix event starts drops by more than half, and AIBrix's job-minutes drop by about 55–60%.

Trade-offs:

- Docker Hub and GHCR no longer get a `:<commit-sha>` image for every merge, and `nightly` updates once a day. The manual trigger builds images on demand.
- If two PRs each pass but break main when combined, the nightly run catches it, up to a day later.
- The Installation Tests e2e job takes a few minutes longer, but it waits in the queue only once instead of after every build job.

## Alternatives considered

Moving the heavy e2e jobs to self-hosted or third-party runners. We deferred this: AIBrix's CI load is bursty (heavy around PRs and merges, idle most of the day), and billing for a runner service is hard to separate from vllm-project. The changes above cost nothing, don't add infrastructure to maintain, and are easy to revert.

## Method

Data from the GitHub Actions REST API (`/actions/runs` and `/actions/runs/{id}/jobs`), counting only jobs that ran on GitHub-hosted runners (`runner_group_name == "GitHub Actions"`). For each sample window, runs created in the hour before the window are included, so jobs already running when the window starts are counted. The script is available on request.

items.title: Experimental tracking: QSA sparse paged attention over an NVFP4 KV cache (SM80-SM90)
items.author: lesj0610
items.body_excerpt:
Owner: @lesj0610

This tracks the experimental `flashinfer.sparse.qsa_sparse_paged_attention` API, with its backend in `flashinfer/experimental/qsa_nvfp4/`: the main attention of the Qwen4Exp QSA layer, a gated sparse paged GQA attention over a per-row token selection, reading an NVFP4 KV cache on SM80 through SM90. vLLM runs this step with a Triton kernel that takes BF16 and FP8 caches. NVFP4 cuts one token's K or V head from 256 to 144 bytes, and vLLM already allocates and writes NVFP4 caches through `nvfp4_quantize_append_paged_kv_cache_with_slot_mapping`, so the attention step is the missing piece. The b12x QSA backend targets SM120/SM121 with BF16 and FP8 caches and does not cover this case.

It fits the experimental path as a new operation from a recent model: the arguments follow vLLM's kernel (`logical_indices` with a trailing count column, `block_table`, `token_to_req`, a sigmoid output gate), and the API should settle once the vLLM integration is in use. It is explicit-only, with no `backend="auto"` routing and no AOT packaging.

Execution contract: compute capability 8.x and 9.x, head_dim 256, 1 to 16 query heads per KV head, BF16 query, gate and output, packed E2M1 K/V with E4M3 block scales in FlashInfer's paged NVFP4 layout (NHD, or HND through its transposed view), int32 indices.

Graduation target: the first release on or after 2026-11-16, subject to maintainer review. Before graduation:

- Run the tests on SM90 through the experimental CI lane.
- Land the vLLM integration and confirm the API needs no change for it.
- Settle the stable name and module.
- Remove the backend instead if vLLM does not adopt it.

items.title: [Tracking] Frozen-KV MTP (Gemma 4) performance on non-Blackwell GPUs (Triton path)
items.author: riversky0014
items.body_excerpt:
# Context

Gemma-4 uses `trtllm_mha` on SM100 and uses Triton backend on other GPUs. #26596 tracked Gemma-4 bring-up and several optimizations, including `trtllm_mha` on Blackwell and prefill/MoE tuning on H200. Now it is closed, there is no open issue for speculative decoding performance on Triton path.

This issue continues that tracking for Gemma 4 Frozen-KV MTP performance on the Triton path.



# Current bottlenecks

All numbers blow were measured on Gemma-4-12B BF16 with its assistant model, on a single H20 with TP1 and Triton backend, uses steps 2 / topk 1 / 3 draft tokens.



**Table 1: Verify attention cost per round at bs128**

| Mode                  | Query tokens per request | Kernel                            | Attention time @ bs128 | Attention time @ bs8 |
| --------------------- | -----------------------: | --------------------------------- | --------------------: | ------------------- |
| Plain decode          |                        1 | `decode_attention_fwd` (split-KV) |               5.707ms | 0.758ms             |
| Verify (fixed 2-step) |                        3 | `extend_attention_fwd`            |              67.524ms | 5.45ms              |

- Verify adds two extra query token per request but takes 11.8x the attention time of plain decode, which indicates verify kernel is inefficient.



**Table 2: Fixed 2-step vs Plain decode by batch size**

| Batch | Plain decode | Fixed 2-step | Difference |
| ----: | -----------: | -----------: | ---------: |
|     1 |        106.2 |        137.1 |     +29.1% |
|     8 |        651.5 |        703.1 |      +7.9% |
|    16 |       1040.9 |        894.9 |     −14.0% |
|    24 |       1272.7 |        966.9 |     −24.0% |
|    32 |       1422.4 |       1000.5 |     −29.7% |
|   128 |       1699.7 |       1088.6 |     −35.9% |

- Fixed 2-step only impoves throughput at small batch; from bs16 to bs128, speculation is slower than plain decode.



**Table 3: Fixed 2-step vs plain decode under changing load**

| Concurrency | Plain decode tok/s | Fixed 2-step tok/s | Difference | Plain decode TPOT | Fixed 2-step TPOT |
| ----------: | -----------------: | -----------------: | ---------: | ----------------: | ----------------: |
|           4 |              366.9 |              484.1 |     +31.9% |          10.12 ms |           7.86 ms |
|          64 |             3008.9 |             1321.2 |     −56.1% |          19.75 ms |          45.52 ms |
|           8 |              871.3 |              853.6 |      −2.0% |          10.23 ms |           9.67 ms |

- At high concurrency, fixed 2-step is much slower than plain decode: -56% throughput and 2.3x TPOT at concurrency 64.



# Optimizations



### 1. Split-KV Verify Attention  (Tables 1 and 2)

PR: #44830

**Why.** `extend_attention_fwd` is built for prefill, it is split-Q, but verify has only 3 query tokens per request. Short queries need the work split-KV instead, as decode does.

**Fix.** This PR routes verify to the existing split-KV verify kernels `verify_shared_kv_fwd` and `verify_splitkv_fwd` (until now only enabled on AMD gfx95), and adds sliding-window support to `verify_splitkv_fwd`. It is opt-in, and unsupported shapes fall back to `extend_attention_fwd`.

**Results.** Gemma-4-12B, 256 input tokens:

| Metric                           |       Before |        After |      Change |
| -------------------------------- | -----------: | -----------: | ----------: |
| Verify attention per round, bs 8 |      5.45 ms |      1.75 ms | 3.1× faster |
| Throughput, bs 1                 |  137.1 tok/s |  177.4 tok/s |        +29% |
| Throughput, bs 8                 |  698.3 tok/s |  874.8 tok/s |        +25% |
| Throughput, bs 128               | 1078.9 tok/s | 1481.7 tok/s |        +37% |
| GSM8K (400 questions)            |          383 |          384 |           — |



### 2. Adaptive Speculative Decoding (Tables 2 and 3)

PR: #44914

**Why.** At high concurrency, decode is already compute-bound, so verifying extra draft tokens costs more than it saves and speculation becomes a net loss. Adaptive speculative decoding avoids this by changing the step count with load.

**Fix.** This PR connects Frozen-KV MTP to the existing `AdaptiveController`, so it can switch step counts at runtime. At zero steps, it runs plain decode. The example policy uses 2 steps below padded batch 16 and 0 steps above it.

**Results.** Throughput by batch size (tok/s):

| Batch | Plain decode | Fixed 2-step | Adaptive | Adaptive vs decode |
| ----: | -----------: | -----------: | -------: | -----------------: |
|     1 |        106.2 |        137.1 |    137.0 |             +29.0% |
|     8 |        651.5 |        703.1 |    703.0 |              +7.9% |
|    16 |       1040.9 |        894.9 |   1033.7 |              −0.7% |
|    24 |       1272.7 |        966.9 |   1262.0 |              −0.8% |
|    32 |       1422.4 |       1000.5 |   1407.6 |              −1.0% |
|   128 |       1699.7 |       1088.6 |   1674.9 |              −1.5% |

Throughput under changing load (tok/s):

| Concurrency | Plain decode | Fixed 2-step | Adaptive |
| ----------: | -----------: | -----------: | -------: |
|           4 |        366.9 |        484.1 |    483.4 |
|          64 |       3008.9 |       1321.2 |   3103.3 |
|           8 |        871.3 |        853.6 |    867.0 |
|  Whole 90 s |       1415.7 |        886.3 |   1484.6 |

Adaptive keeps the speedup at low-concurrency and stays within 1.5% of plain decode at high concurrency. Over the whole changing-load run, it is 4.9% faster than plain decode and 67.5% faster than fixed 2-step.



### Related works

- #39316 enables the per-head split-KV verify path for GQA full-attention layers on CUDA. It is complementary to #44830, which covers single-KV-head full attention and sliding-window layers.
- #42019 adds opt-in FA4 for Gemma 4 on Hopper. It has not been compared with split-KV verify.
- #23705 tracks adaptive speculative decoding; #44914 adds Frozen-KV MTP to it.

items.title: [Performance]: MLA chunked prefill builds context K with a cat per loop and a fixed buffer batch size
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### Proposal to improve performance

MLA context attention with chunked prefill (`MLA.forward_context_with_chunked_prefill` and `forward_context_with_cached_kv` in `tensorrt_llm/_torch/attention/mla.py`) builds the FMHA K for every cached-KV loop and for the current chunk as `maybe_compiled_cat((k_nope, k_pe.expand(-1, H, -1)), -1)` after a `split` and two `view`s. For a long prompt this runs once per loop per MLA layer, and the cached KV is expanded in loops of `chunk_size * chunked_prefill_buffer_batch_size` tokens, where the batch size is fixed at the dataclass default 4 (no config entry).

Measured on Rubin single GPU, Kimi K3 MLA layer (12 heads per rank, 2K-token chunks), the deepest chunk of a 128K prompt (129024 cached tokens), one layer forward:

| | kernels / layer | host enqueue µs | GPU µs |
|---|---|---|---|
| cat, buffer batch 4 (16 loops) | 112 | 3175 | 3659 |
| one Triton pack kernel, buffer batch 4 | 112 | 2781 | 2765 |
| pack kernel, buffer batch 16 (4 loops) | 40 | 1217 | 2132 |

Over 24 MLA layers that is about 1730 fewer launches, 47 ms less host time and 37 ms less GPU time for the deepest chunk, about half of that on average over a 128K prompt. Separately, when the K packing is a Triton kernel specialized on the token count, the first chunk whose token count is not a multiple of 16 (typically a prompt's last chunk) compiles a second variant mid-request, about 0.1 s once per process.

Proposal: pack K with one Triton kernel (a pure copy, bitwise the cat; the cat stays as fallback for layouts the kernel does not take), without specializing on the token count, and make `chunked_prefill_buffer_batch_size` settable (`TLLM_MLA_CHUNKED_PREFILL_BUFFER_BATCH_SIZE`, default 4). The KV cache profiling run already sizes its cached prefix from that value. PR to follow.

items.author: Crinton
items.body_excerpt:
I am trying to implement a fused Conv3d (NDHWC) + Bias operator using CUTLASS on an Ampere (SM80) GPU with Tensor Cores.

The goal is to achieve: Output = alpha * Conv3d(Input, Weight) + Bias.

When I don't use bias, the results are exactly the same as with `torch.conv3d`. However, when I use bias, a calculation error occurs, and this is not due to accumulated error.

**The Problem**

**Request**
Could the maintainers provide a clear example or confirm the correct Arguments structure for Conv3d + Bias on SM80 Tensor Cores? Specifically:

Is LinearCombination fully supported for OpClassTensorOp in 3D convolutions?

What is the correct way to pass the Bias vector?

items.title: [BUG] CuTe DSL `CopyUniversalOp` ignores `l1c_evict_priority` again (regression of #3199 since 4.6.0, loads and stores)
items.author: gau-nernst
items.body_excerpt:
### Which component has the problem?

CuTe DSL

### Bug Report

**Describe the bug**
A clear and concise description of what the bug is.

A gmem <-> rmem `cute.copy` through a `CopyUniversalOp` atom built with `l1c_evict_priority=...` emits plain `ld.global` / `st.global` without the `.L1::` qualifier, for both loads and stores and for every priority I tried (`NO_ALLOCATE`, `EVICT_FIRST`, `EVICT_LAST`).

This is the same symptom as #3199 (loads), which was resolved in 4.5.0. It works in 4.5.3 and regressed in 4.6.0. Releases checked: 4.5.3 (good), 4.6.0, 4.6.3, 4.7.0, 4.7.1, 4.8.0 (bad). The PTX operand type also changes from `.u64` to `.b64` at 4.6.0, which suggests the copy now goes through a different lowering path that drops the attribute.

`cute.arch.load` / `cute.arch.store` with `level1_eviction_priority=` still emit the qualifier on 4.8.0, so the problem looks limited to the copy-atom path.

**Steps/Code to reproduce bug**
Follow this guide http://matthewrocklin.com/blog/work/2018/02/28/minimal-bug-reports to craft a minimal bug report. This helps us reproduce the issue you're having and resolve the issue more quickly.

Compile-only (no GPU run needed). It prints the global loads / stores in the generated PTX:

```python
# CuTeDSL MRE: CopyUniversalOp drops l1c_evict_priority (regressed in 4.6.0).
#
# A gmem <-> rmem cute.copy through
#   make_copy_atom(CopyUniversalOp(), ..., l1c_evict_priority=NO_ALLOCATE)
# should emit ld/st.global.L1::no_allocate. 4.5.x does; 4.6.0 - 4.8.0 emit a
# plain ld/st.global for both loads and stores (EVICT_FIRST / EVICT_LAST are
# dropped the same way). cute.arch.load / cute.arch.store with
# level1_eviction_priority still emit the qualifier.
#
# Compile-only; prints the global loads / stores in the generated PTX.
#   python atom_evict_hint.py [NO_ALLOCATE|EVICT_FIRST|EVICT_LAST]
import glob
import importlib.metadata
import os
import re
import sys
import tempfile

DUMP = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="evict_hint_")
os.environ["CUTE_DSL_KEEP_PTX"] = "1"
os.environ["CUTE_DSL_DUMP_DIR"] = DUMP
os.environ["CUTE_DSL_DISABLE_FILE_CACHING"] = "1"

import cutlass.cute as cute  # noqa: E402
from cutlass import Int32  # noqa: E402

PRIO = getattr(
    cute.nvgpu.CacheEvictionPriority, sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "NO_ALLOCATE"
)


def make(hinted):
    @cute.kernel
    def kernel(src: cute.Tensor, dst: cute.Tensor):
        regs = cute.make_rmem_tensor(8, Int32)
        atom = cute.make_copy_atom(
            cute.nvgpu.CopyUniversalOp(), Int32, num_bits_per_copy=256,
            l1c_evict_priority=PRIO,
        )
        plain = cute.make_copy_atom(
            cute.nvgpu.CopyUniversalOp(), Int32, num_bits_per_copy=256
        )
        cute.copy(atom if hinted == "load" else plain, src, regs)
        cute.copy(atom if hinted == "store" else plain, regs, dst)

    @cute.jit
    def run(src: cute.Tensor, dst: cute.Tensor):
        kernel(src, dst).launch(grid=(1, 1, 1), block=(1, 1, 1))

    return run


t = cute.runtime.make_fake_tensor(Int32, (8,), stride=(1,), assumed_align=32)
print("nvidia-cutlass-dsl", importlib.metadata.version("nvidia-cutlass-dsl"), PRIO)
for hinted in ("load", "store"):
    cute.compile(make(hinted), t, t)
    ptx = max(glob.glob(f"{DUMP}/**/*.ptx", recursive=True), key=os.path.getmtime)
    ops = sorted(set(re.findall(r"(?:ld|st)\.global[\w.:]*", open(ptx).read())))
    print(f"  hinted {hinted:5s}: {ops}")
```

Output on 4.8.0 (same on 4.6.0 - 4.7.1):

```
nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.8.0 CacheEvictionPriority.NO_ALLOCATE
  hinted load : ['ld.global.v4.b64', 'st.global.v4.b64']
  hinted store: ['ld.global.v4.b64', 'st.global.v4.b64']
nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.8.0 CacheEvictionPriority.EVICT_FIRST
  hinted load : ['ld.global.v4.b64', 'st.global.v4.b64']
  hinted store: ['ld.global.v4.b64', 'st.global.v4.b64']
```

Output on 4.5.3:

```
nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.5.3 CacheEvictionPriority.NO_ALLOCATE
  hinted load : ['ld.global.L1::no_allocate.v4.u64', 'st.global.v4.u64']
  hinted store: ['ld.global.v4.u64', 'st.global.L1::no_allocate.v4.u64']
nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.5.3 CacheEvictionPriority.EVICT_FIRST
  hinted load : ['ld.global.L1::evict_first.v4.u64', 'st.global.v4.u64']
  hinted store: ['ld.global.v4.u64', 'st.global.L1::evict_first.v4.u64']
```

**Expected behavior**
A clear and concise description of what you expected to happen.

The hinted direction carries the requested qualifier, as in 4.5.3: `ld.global.L1::no_allocate...` / `st.global.L1::no_allocate...` (SASS `LDG.E.NA` / `STG.E.NA`). If the attribute is no longer supported on this atom, `make_copy_atom` should reject it instead of silently dropping it.

**Environment details (please complete the following information):**
 - Environment location: Bare-metal
 - GPU: NVIDIA GB300 (sm_103a), driver 610.43.02
 - OS: Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS (aarch64), Python 3.12.13
 - nvidia-cutlass-dsl: 4.8.0 (also checked 4.5.3, 4.6.0, 4.6.3, 4.7.0, 4.7.1 from PyPI)

**Environment details (please complete the following information):**
 - Environment location: [Bare-metal, Docker, Cloud(specify cloud provider)] 

**Additional context**
Add any other context about the problem here.

comments.author: yunweili3
comments.body:
Reproduced on B200 (sm_100a) with 4.8.0 vs 4.5.3, same output as above.

**Root cause:** the 4.6 update removed the memory attributes from the universal copy atom type itself. `CopyAtomSIMTSyncCopyType.get` now only takes `(value type, bits per copy)` (4.5.3 took `mem order, mem scope, l1 cache eviction priority, invariant` as well), but `CopyUniversalOp._make_trait` kept `**kwargs` and never looks at it, so the attribute is swallowed with no warning. The IR has no slot for it any more, so it cannot be restored on this atom. The specialized ops do carry it: the same MRE with `CopyG2ROp` for the load and `CopyR2GOp` for the store emits `ld.global.L1::no_allocate.v4.b64` / `st.global.L1::no_allocate.v4.b64` on 4.8.0, so that is the supported path.

Side effect of the same regression: the deprecated `cutlass.utils.distributed.ld_bypass` asked `CopyUniversalOp` for a `VOLATILE`/`SYS` load and has been emitting a plain `ld.global` since 4.6.

**PR #3713** makes `CopyUniversalOp` reject these attributes with a `TypeError` that points at the specialized ops (the second behaviour you asked for), and switches `ld_bypass` to `CopyG2ROp`.

comments.author: brandon-yujie-sun
comments.body: @gau-nernst thanks for reporting the issue. It's now fixed in 4.8.1.

items.title: [Performance]: Kimi K3 KDA prefill persistent kernels (fused K123, K4) hard-code a 148-block grid
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### Proposal to improve performance

The Kimi K3 KDA prefill path launches two persistent CuTe DSL kernels whose grid is fixed at 148 blocks, the SM count of B200:

- fused K1+K2+K3 (`cute_dsl_kernels/blackwell/kimi_k3_kda/fused_k123.py`: `NUM_SMS = 148`, used for the grid and as the `for_generate` stride);
- persistent K4 (`custom_ops/cute_dsl_kimi_k3_custom_ops.py`: `_launch_k4_persistent(..., num_sm=148)`, the grid ceiling and the size of its workspace).

On a GPU with more SMs, the extra SMs stay idle during these kernels, and K4 needs an extra persistent round as soon as the work units (sequences x heads) exceed 148. `is_kda_optimized_supported()` admits SM100, SM103 and SM107, which do not all have 148 SMs.

Measured on Rubin single GPU (200-SM engineering sample), Kimi K3 KDA shapes (96 heads, head dim 128), comparing the 148-block grid with a grid of the device's SM count:

- fused K123, one 8192-token prefill chunk: 124.9 us -> 110.2 us; summed over the model's KDA layers about 1.0 ms per 8K chunk (about 10-15 ms of TTFT at 128K context);
- K4 with 13 or more context sequences per step: 41-46% faster (two persistent rounds become one).

Outputs and the state pool are bitwise identical to the 148-block grid in all tested shapes (14-15 shapes, eager and CUDA graph replay), since each work unit is computed by exactly one block wherever it lands.

Proposal: size both grids by the launch device's SM count (queried once per device), and key the compiled-function caches on it. PR to follow.

items.title: [QST] SM120 FP8 MMA with FP32 accumulate, plain form against block-scaled form with unit scales
items.author: emre570
items.body_excerpt:
**What is your question?**

On an RTX 5080, the plain FP8 MMA with FP32 accumulate runs at half the rate of the block-scaled FP8 MMA with FP32 accumulate. When all scale bytes are `0x7F` (UE8M0 1.0), the two forms give equal bits.

My FP8 attention kernel in CuTe DSL used `MmaFP8Op`. I changed it to `MmaMXF8Op` with constant unit scales and no other change. The kernel time went from 123.6 ms to 83.6 ms and the output is byte-equal (sgl-project/sglang#43390). So a user can do this today. My question is about the default.

1. Is there a reason to keep the plain form for E4M3 x E4M3 with FP32 accumulate on SM120?
2. If there is no reason, do you want `MmaFP8Op` and `rr_op_selector_sm120` to emit the block-scaled form with unit scales for this case? I can send a PR.

### Related report

The same behavior is reported in flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#5963 for the FlashInfer SM120 FP8 attention kernel, with RTX 5090 numbers and a bit-identity check. That issue also points to the MXFP8 attention work in flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#3628 and flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#4149. The numbers below add an RTX 5080 and a CUTLASS GEMM measurement to that report.

### Scope

E4M3 x E4M3, FP32 accumulate, one RTX 5080 (driver 595.99.02, CUDA 13.3, CUTLASS `ffa119a12`). I did not measure other types or other cards.

### Raw MMA rate

Independent MMA chains, no memory access, 84 SMs. The rate is the same from 4 to 32 warps per SM.

| instruction | TFLOP/s |
|---|---:|
| `kind::f8f6f4.m16n8k32 ... f32.e4m3.e4m3.f32` | 246 |
| `kind::mxf8f6f4.block_scale.scale_vec::1X.m16n8k32 ... f32.e4m3.e4m3.f32.ue8m0` | 489 |

### Bit equality

- Random finite inputs. 0 of 704,643,072 accumulator registers differ.
- Negative control with scale 2.0. 704,643,071 registers differ.
- Edge cases (subnormal, ±448, NaN bytes, accumulator start at zero, FLT_MAX, subnormal, infinity, NaN). 30 classes, 176,160,768 registers each, 0 bits differ.

### CUTLASS GEMM

I used the SM120 `CollectiveBuilder` with `OpClassTensorOp`, pingpong schedule, tile 128x128x128, FP32 output. Then I changed only the instruction in `SM120_16x8x32_TN<float_e4m3_t, float_e4m3_t, float>` to the block-scaled form. The scale `0x7F7F7F7F` stays in a register. There is no scale factor tensor and no additional load. The patch is 34 lines.

I measured 30 shapes from real models. All 30 give 0 different output words. Five examples:

| shape source | M x N x K | plain | patched | speedup |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Wan 2.2 14B, `to_q` | 32760 x 5120 x 5120 | 236.1 | 398.6 | 1.69x |
| Llama 3.3 70B, MLP up | 4096 x 28672 x 8192 | 234.7 | 398.1 | 1.70x |
| FLUX.1-dev, FFN up | 4608 x 12288 x 3072 | 231.8 | 393.3 | 1.70x |
| MiniMax-H3, FFN up | 30272 x 14336 x 5376 | 234.6 | 363.5 | 1.55x |
| Gemma 3 27B, MLP up | 128 x 21504 x 5376 | 195.8 | 203.4 | 1.04x |

TFLOP/s. The speedup is 1.55x to 1.72x for the 22 shapes with M of 4096 or more. It is 1.04x to 1.82x for the 8 shapes with M = 128, where the low end is DRAM-bound.

Nsight Compute on the stock plain kernel shows the tensor pipe 96% busy. The MMA instruction rate is 47.9% of the peak.

One caution. These numbers use `max_swizzle_size = 8`. With the default of 1, three large shapes become DRAM-bound and the patched kernel is slower than the plain kernel (0.88x). I can open a different issue for that with the data.

### Where the plain form is used

- CuTe DSL `MmaFP8Op`
- `rr_op_selector_sm120` in `sm120_mma_builder.inl`, `sm120_array_mma_builder.inl` and `sm120_blockwise_mma_builder.inl`

cuBLASLt on the same card uses `QMMA.SF.16832.F32.E4M3.E4M3.E8` in its FP8 GEMM kernel and no plain `QMMA`.

I can share the benchmark source, the patch and the raw results if they are useful.

items.title: Expert Parallelism (EP) roadmap for SM12x b12x MoE kernel (b12x_fused_moe / B12xMoEWrapper)
items.author: ItamarTerem
items.body_excerpt:
Hi flashinfer team,
We're deploying a large MoE model (384 experts, top_k=8) on 8x RTX PRO 6000 (SM120/Blackwell workstation) using the b12x_fused_moe CuteDSL kernel via TensorRT-LLM's pytorch backend, and have hit the Expert Parallelism restriction:

b12x_fused_moe does not yet support Expert Parallelism
(num_local_experts={X} != num_experts={Y}).
Use a different MoE backend for EP configurations.

This comes from the explicit guard in flashinfer/fused_moe/cute_dsl/b12x_moe.py (both in the free function b12x_fused_moe and in B12xMoEWrapper.__init__), confirmed in flashinfer version 0.6.12.
Context on why this matters for us specifically: without EP, every GPU must retain workspace/routing capacity sized for the full state_E (all 384 experts), even though tensor parallelism already shards each expert's weights across GPUs. This is a meaningful, measured memory cost — in our case, the dynamic workspace's packed_input buffer alone accounts for roughly 7–11GB/GPU across a 60-MoE-layer model, purely from having to size for the worst-case "all experts active" scenario rather than a num_experts/ep_size subset.

What we're asking:

1. Is EP support for the SM12x b12x kernel family (static/dynamic/micro backends) on the roadmap, even at a preliminary stage?
2. Is there a rough timeline or tracking issue we could follow?
3. Are there known architectural blockers specific to SM120 (vs. SM100/SM103, where other kernels like MegaMoE already support EP) that make this a harder problem here?

We also note that vLLM's FlashInferB12xExperts (_supports_parallel_config) explicitly declines to use this backend when EP is requested, for the same underlying reason — so this appears to be a shared, cross-framework limitation rather than something specific to our integration.
Happy to provide more detail on our exact shapes/config if useful. Thanks for your work on this — the b12x kernel has otherwise been the only correctness-verified MoE path we've found for SM120 (CUTLASS produces silently incorrect output on this architecture in our testing).

items.title: [Umbrella][serve] Advanced Observability for Serve Autoscaler
items.author: nadongjun
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

This issue tracks the implementation of advanced observability for the Serve Autoscaler,
as proposed in https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues/41135#issuecomment-3162329187 and specified in detail in [this design document](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1KtMUDz1O3koihG6eh-QcUqudZjNAX3NsqqOMYh3BoWA/edit?usp=sharing).

The goal is to make it easier to debug scaling behavior by exposing structured logs, metrics, and detailed CLI outputs (`serve status -v`).

This work depends on the ongoing implementation of the Serve custom autoscaler (deployment-level, application-level, and external scaler).

Each observability feature builds on top of the corresponding autoscaler logic, so the sub-issues should be tackled in order: Skeleton -> Deployment -> Application -> External -> Docs.

### Sub-issues

- [ ] 1. [WIP] #55834
  - [x] Backend API PR: #55919
  - [ ] Cli
- [x] 2. Integrate Deployment-level autoscaling metrics and decision history PR: #56225
- [ ] 3. [WIP] Support Application-level custom policy observability PR: #59995
- [ ] 4. Add External scaler observability
- [ ] 5. Update docs with examples of serve status -v outputs, error cases, and troubleshooting

### Use case

The current `serve status` command only shows basic information such as replica counts and health.
As custom autoscaling (deployment-level, application-level, external scalers) becomes available, users need more detailed visibility to understand why scaling decisions are made.

`serve status -v` will let users:
- See scaling decisions and the policies/metrics that triggered them.
- Check metrics freshness (normal vs. delayed).
- Understand errors or abnormal events during autoscaler operation.
- Track application-level scaling when multiple deployments scale together.
- Debug external scaler behavior, e.g. webhook response codes and delivery history.

This extended visibility is essential for debugging complex autoscaling behavior and building confidence in custom scaling logic.


### Example Output (from RFC)
```bash
$ serve status -v

======== Serve Autoscaler status: 2025-08-19T15:05:30Z ========

    Target replicas: 5
    Replicas allowed: min=1, max=10
    Scaling status: scaling up
    Scaling decisions:
        2025-08-19T14:00:00Z - scaled down from 5 -> 3 (low traffic)
        2025-08-19T15:05:00Z - scaled up from 3 -> 5 (12 requests queued)
    Policy: Default (queue-length based)
    Metrics (look_back_period_s=30):
        queued_requests: 12
    Metric collection: delayed (last update 30s ago)
    Errors: (none)


Example 2: Deployment using a Custom Autoscaling Policy (latency-based)

======== Serve Autoscaler status: 2025-08-19T12:10:00Z ========
Deployment status
---------------------------------------------------------------
deployment_custom_latency_policy:
    Current replicas: 8
    Target replicas: 8
    Replicas allowed: min=1, max=20
    Scaling status: stable
    Scaling decisions:
        2025-08-19T11:30:00Z - scaled up from 2 -> 4 (cpu_usage_percent 85% > 80%)
        2025-08-19T11:50:00Z - scaled up from 4 -> 8 (latency_p95_ms 450ms > 300ms)
    Policy: Custom (my_custom_policy)
    Metrics (look_back_period_s=60):
        latency_p95_ms: 450.0
        cpu_usage_percent: 62.5
    Metric collection: healthy (last update 5s ago)

        2025-08-19T12:05:00Z - PolicyError: Exception in user policy (ZeroDivisionError) – scaling skipped


Example 3: Deployment using an External Webhook Scaler

Deployments:
```

items.title: [Bug] Batch templates emit arguments rejected by SGLang 0.5.22 and vLLM 0.32.0
items.author: Jackmeson1
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

Accepted optional batch settings produce incompatible arguments:

- **SGLang 0.5.22 translation:** `parallelism.pp=2` emits ambiguous `--pp 2`; `engine_args.block_size=16` emits unrecognized `--block-size 16`.
- **vLLM 0.32.0 compatibility:** `engine_args.swap_space=4` emits unrecognized `--swap-space 4`. `quantization.weight=bf16` emits `--quantization bf16`: argparse accepts it, but quantization validation rejects it as an unknown method.

Both baseline argument lists parse. SGLang forwards unmapped typed fields; vLLM emits flags independently of engine.version (`python/aibrix/aibrix/batch/manifest/engine_adapter.py:128,156,228,241`).

Report only; we are not working on a fix.

### Steps to Reproduce

At the AIBrix commit below, with its Python dependencies installed, save as `repro.py` at repository root:

```python
import argparse
import contextlib
import io
import json
import sys
from types import SimpleNamespace as NS

mode = sys.argv[1]
if mode == "render":
    from aibrix.batch.manifest.engine_adapter import build_engine_args
    from aibrix.batch.template import ModelDeploymentTemplateSpec as Spec

    rows = []
    for engine, version, changes in [
        ("sglang", "0.5.22", [{}, {"parallelism": {"pp": 2}},
                            {"engine_args": {"block_size": 16}}]),
        ("vllm", "0.32.0", [{}, {"engine_args": {"swap_space": 4}},
                          {"quantization": {"weight": "bf16"}}]),
    ]:
        for change in changes:
            spec = Spec.model_validate(dict(
                engine=dict(type=engine, version=version, image=engine),
                model_source=dict(type="huggingface", uri="Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B"),
                accelerator=dict(type="H100", count=change.get("parallelism", {}).get("pp", 1)),
                supported_endpoints=["/v1/chat/completions"], **change))
            rows.append([engine, build_engine_args(spec)])
    print(json.dumps(rows))
else:
    if mode == "sglang":
        from sglang.srt.server_args import ServerArgs
        parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog=mode)
        ServerArgs.add_cli_args(parser)
    else:
        from vllm.entrypoints.launchers.cli_args import make_arg_parser
        from vllm.utils.argparse_utils import FlexibleArgumentParser
        from vllm.config.model import ModelConfig
        parser = make_arg_parser(FlexibleArgumentParser(prog=mode))
    for engine, argv in json.load(open("cases.json")):
        if engine != mode:
            continue
        print("argv:", *argv)
        errors = io.StringIO()
        try:
            with contextlib.redirect_stderr(errors):
                parsed = parser.parse_args(argv)
        except SystemExit:
            print(errors.getvalue().splitlines()[-1])
            continue
        print("argparse: ACCEPT")
        if mode == "vllm":
            try:
                ModelConfig._verify_quantization(NS(
                    quantization=parsed.quantization,
                    model_arch_config=NS(quantization_config=None),
                    allow_deprecated_quantization=False))
            except ValueError as error:
                print("later validation:", error)
```

Render:

```sh
PYTHONPATH=python/aibrix python repro.py render > cases.json
```

Replay from the same directory in separate Python 3.12 environments:

```sh
# SGLang environment
pip install sglang==0.5.22
python repro.py sglang
# vLLM environment
pip install vllm==0.32.0
VLLM_TARGET_DEVICE=cpu python repro.py vllm
```

### Expected behavior

Accepted template settings produce arguments compatible with the selected engine/version.

### Environment

AIBrix `b389a59a58ea`; Linux CPU; Python 3.10 rendering/3.12 parsers; engine sources verified against tags v0.5.22/v0.32.0. Validation calls the real quantization validator without model initialization. No server launched. The sample pins vLLM 0.6.3; its launch behavior was not tested.

### Area

Batch

items.title: [Performance]: Kimi K3 decode runs the MoE-tail additions as separate kernels before the next attention-residual
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### Proposal to improve performance

In Kimi K3 decode, every MoE layer ends with `prefix_sum + (routed_out + shared_out)` (`KimiK3MoERuntime.forward` returns `routed_out + shared_out`, then `KimiLinearDecoderLayer.forward` adds it to the prefix sum). These are two small elementwise kernels per MoE layer. Their result is read first by the next layer's pre-attention attention-residual + RMSNorm, or by the model's output attention-residual + norm. In the decode window, that consumer is already `trtllm::attn_res_add_rmsnorm_fwd`'s kernel family, which loads the prefix sum as its last candidate and can already fold one addend into it.

Proposal: give `trtllm::attn_res_add_rmsnorm_fwd` an optional second addend (`layer_residual_add2`) that computes `bf16(prefix + bf16(routed + shared))`, rounding exactly like the two BF16 tensor additions. Then add an opt-in path in which a MoE layer hands `(prefix, routed, shared)` to that consumer instead of adding them itself. Wherever the consumer would not take the fused per-token kernel (a hidden-state capture layer for speculative decoding, no snapshots yet, the persistent kernel, shapes outside the fused window), the addition is done first and the existing code runs unchanged.

Measured on Rubin, TP8 across 2 nodes (MNNVL), Kimi K3 with speculative decoding, CUDA graphs, single request, decode step time, same change on our integration branch: -0.106 / -0.117 / -0.121 / -0.126 / -0.107 / -0.107 ms at 2K / 32K / 64K / 96K / 128K / 393K context. Accuracy and needle checks unchanged; the materialized prefix sums are bitwise identical.

PR to follow (draft, opt-in via an environment variable).

items.title: AIBRIX_PREFIX_CACHE_REMOTE_TOKENIZER_ENDPOINT is never consumed; remote tokenize calls all land on one pod
items.author: chiiydd
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Two related problems in the gateway's remote tokenizer path (observed on **v0.8.0**, line numbers below refer to the `v0.8.0` tag; the same logic exists on `main` after the `prefixcache` package refactor in #3064):

**1. `AIBRIX_PREFIX_CACHE_REMOTE_TOKENIZER_ENDPOINT` is validated but never consumed.**

The variable is defined in `pkg/constants/kv_event_sync.go:56-58`. Its only read site is a startup non-emptiness check in `pkg/cache/kv_event_manager_zmq.go:63-66` (inside `validateKVEventConfiguration`):

```go
// Check remote tokenizer endpoint
endpoint := utils.LoadEnv(constants.EnvPrefixCacheRemoteTokenizerEndpoint, "")
if endpoint == "" {
    return fmt.Errorf("KV event sync requires %s to be set", constants.EnvPrefixCacheRemoteTokenizerEndpoint)
}
```

The value is then discarded. The component that actually creates remote tokenizers — the prefix cache router's tokenizer pool — never reads it: `loadTokenizerPoolConfigFromEnv` (`pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms/prefix_cache.go:237-248`) builds `TokenizerPoolConfig` without any field for it, and `findVLLMEndpointForModel` (`pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms/tokenizer_pool.go:376-405`) only knows "1. Service endpoint (ModelServiceMap), 2. Direct pod endpoint". Setting the variable (e.g. to a Service that load-balances tokenize calls) silently has no effect.

**2. Without it, pod discovery pins all tokenize traffic of a model to one pod.**

`findVLLMEndpointForModel` returns the **first** ready, model-matching vLLM pod (`tokenizer_pool.go:384-401`), and the resulting tokenizer is cached per model in `createOrUpdateTokenizer` (`tokenizer_pool.go:262`) and reused while it stays healthy — `lastUsed` is refreshed on every request, so TTL cleanup never evicts an active entry. Every remote tokenize call of a model therefore goes to whichever pod was listed first, for that pod's whole lifetime, while other replicas receive none. We confirmed this in production logs: with a multi-replica vLLM deployment, all `remote_tokenize` requests landed on a single pod IP.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Deploy a multi-replica vLLM deployment behind the AIBrix gateway with prefix cache routing and remote tokenizer enabled.
2. Set `AIBRIX_PREFIX_CACHE_REMOTE_TOKENIZER_ENDPOINT` to a tokenizer Service endpoint.
3. Send requests and observe where `/tokenize` calls go.

**Observed:** the configured endpoint is ignored; all tokenize calls go directly to one pod IP.

### Expected behavior

- When `AIBRIX_PREFIX_CACHE_REMOTE_TOKENIZER_ENDPOINT` is set, the tokenizer pool uses it as the endpoint for all models, taking precedence over `ModelServiceMap` and pod discovery — pointing it at a Service actually load-balances tokenize calls across replicas.
- When it is unset, pod discovery spreads tokenize calls across the model's ready replicas instead of pinning the first match.

### Environment

- AIBrix version: v0.8.0

### Area

Gateway

items.title: [Performance]: copyBatchBlockOffsetsToDeviceKernel walks each long block-offset row with one CTA
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### Proposal to improve performance

`KVCacheManagerV2.copy_batch_block_offsets` launches `copyBatchBlockOffsetsToDeviceKernel` (`cpp/tensorrt_llm/batch_manager/kvCacheManagerV2Utils.cu`) once per manager per step. Its grid is `(num_pools, num_seqs)`: a single 128-thread CTA walks each whole row of block offsets, two `cp.async` loads deep, reading the pinned host table. For long-context pools the rows are long; at 32772 blocks per sequence, each CTA runs 64 sequential load iterations. The kernel is then latency bound, with a handful of CTAs on the whole GPU.

Measured on Rubin, Kimi K3 decode (target manager with 2 pools, draft manager with 1, 32772 blocks per sequence, 1 sequence): 28-33 µs per call, about 60 µs per decode step on the critical path between steps.

Proposal: add a third grid dimension that splits each row into tiles of 1024 offsets, one CTA each, keeping the per-element arithmetic and the read-at-execution-time semantics unchanged. A Triton prototype of exactly this tiling (same reads, same integer arithmetic, bitwise-equal output) took the call from 27.7 µs to 4.0 µs (2 pools) and from 27.0 µs to 3.6 µs (1 pool) in a microbenchmark. End to end on Rubin, TP8 across 2 nodes (MNNVL), single request, it reduced decode step time by 0.014-0.043 ms depending on context length, and 128K TTFT by 0.043 s.

PR to follow (draft; the C++ version still needs a GPU build and microbenchmark).

## Description

When TensorRT-LLM is built with `ENABLE_MULTI_DEVICE=OFF`, the default
single-GPU launch path fails with:

    NameError: name 'MPIPoolExecutor' is not defined

## Cause

In `tensorrt_llm/llmapi/mpi_session.py`, `MPIPoolExecutor` is imported only
inside `if ENABLE_MULTI_DEVICE:`, but
`GenerationExecutorProxy -> MpiPoolSession._start_mpi_pool` uses it on the
default startup path.

## Workaround

Set `TLLM_WORKER_USE_SINGLE_PROCESS=1`, which uses the single-process worker
path in `executor.py`.

## Environment

- TensorRT-LLM v1.3.0rc28
- Wheel built with
  `ENABLE_MULTI_DEVICE=OFF;BUILD_NCCL_EXTENSIONS=OFF;ENABLE_UCX=OFF;BUILD_DEEP_EP=OFF`
- CUDA 13.2, Python 3.10, PyTorch 2.13.0+cu130
- Single H200, PyTorch backend

## Notes

Follow-up requested in #20580, which fixes `mpi_allgather` for the same build
configuration. This issue is not addressed by that PR.
